The system has three kinds of participants: the **Scheduler**, which receives surgery‑booking requests; the **OR‑Manager**, which owns the coarse lock for an entire operating‑room block (e.g., “OR‑1‑Morning”); and the **Equipment‑Agent**, which holds fine‑grained locks for individual pieces of equipment such as a surgical robot or a C‑arm. The Scheduler maintains a variable indicating the current **requested surgery** (including its required equipment list) and a flag showing whether the **room capacity** (number of concurrent cases allowed) has been increased or decreased by the hospital admin. When a new request arrives, the Scheduler first acquires the OR‑Manager’s coarse lock for the target block; once granted it asks each relevant Equipment‑Agent to acquire its fine lock. If any fine lock is denied because the equipment is already in use, the Scheduler releases all previously taken locks, waits for a short back‑off, and retries. When the admin changes the room capacity at runtime, the OR‑Manager updates its capacity flag, and any Scheduler that is waiting at the coarse‑lock stage re‑evaluates whether the block can still admit the new surgery before proceeding. All participants release their locks immediately after the surgery start time is recorded, allowing the next request to use the room and equipment. 

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any moment, no two surgeries can hold the fine‑grained lock for the same piece of equipment in the same operating‑room block.
spec_text:
---- MODULE W4C0x8x0x4 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets, Sequences

CONSTANTS Rooms, Equipments

(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(*  Types and constants                                                *)
(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)

NullRoom == "None"               \* a value not belonging to Rooms

Request == [room : Rooms, eqSet : SUBSET Equipments]

NoReq == [room |-> NullRoom, eqSet |-> {}]   \* special value meaning “no pending request”

(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(*  Variables                                                          *)
(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)

VARIABLES curReq, coarseLock, ActiveSurgeries, capacity

(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(*  Initial state                                                      *)
(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)

Init ==
    /\ curReq = NoReq
    /\ coarseLock = [r \in Rooms |-> FALSE]
    /\ ActiveSurgeries = {}
    /\ capacity = 1                \* initial room‑capacity flag (value not used for safety)

(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(*  Actions                                                            *)
(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)

(* A new surgery‑booking request arrives *)
NewRequest ==
    /\ curReq = NoReq
    /\ \E r \in Request :
          /\ curReq' = r
    /\ UNCHANGED <<coarseLock, ActiveSurgeries, capacity>>

(* Scheduler acquires the coarse lock of the target OR block *)
AcquireCoarse ==
    /\ curReq # NoReq
    /\ coarseLock[curReq.room] = FALSE
    /\ coarseLock' = [coarseLock EXCEPT ![curReq.room] = TRUE]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<curReq, ActiveSurgeries, capacity>>

(* Scheduler successfully acquires all fine‑grained equipment locks *)
AcquireFine ==
    /\ curReq # NoReq
    /\ coarseLock[curReq.room] = TRUE
    /\ \A e \in curReq.eqSet :
          ~(\E s \in ActiveSurgeries :
                s.room = curReq.room /\ e \in s.eqSet)   \* equipment is free in this block
    /\ ActiveSurgeries' = ActiveSurgeries \cup {curReq}
    /\ coarseLock' = [coarseLock EXCEPT ![curReq.room] = FALSE]
    /\ curReq' = NoReq
    /\ UNCHANGED capacity

(* Scheduler fails to acquire at least one fine lock, releases coarse lock *)
FailAcquireFine ==
    /\ curReq # NoReq
    /\ coarseLock[curReq.room] = TRUE
    /\ \E e \in curReq.eqSet :
          (\E s \in ActiveSurgeries :
                s.room = curReq.room /\ e \in s.eqSet)   \* some equipment already held
    /\ coarseLock' = [coarseLock EXCEPT ![curReq.room] = FALSE]
    /\ curReq' = NoReq
    /\ UNCHANGED <<ActiveSurgeries, capacity>>

(* A surgery starts; all locks for that surgery are released *)
SurgeryStart ==
    /\ \E s \in ActiveSurgeries :
          /\ ActiveSurgeries' = ActiveSurgeries \ {s}
    /\ UNCHANGED <<coarseLock, curReq, capacity>>

(* Admin changes the room‑capacity flag (does not affect safety) *)
AdminChangeCapacity ==
    /\ capacity' = IF capacity = 1 THEN 2 ELSE 1
    /\ UNCHANGED <<curReq, coarseLock, ActiveSurgeries>>

(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(*  Next-state relation                                                *)
(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)

Next ==
    \/ NewRequest
    \/ AcquireCoarse
    \/ AcquireFine
    \/ FailAcquireFine
    \/ SurgeryStart
    \/ AdminChangeCapacity

(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(*  Specification                                                      *)
(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<curReq, coarseLock, ActiveSurgeries, capacity>>

(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(*  Safety invariant: no two surgeries hold the same equipment lock  *)
(*  in the same operating‑room block.                                   *)
(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)

SafetyInvariant ==
    \A s1 \in ActiveSurgeries :
        \A s2 \in ActiveSurgeries :
            (s1 /= s2) => (s1.room /= s2.room) \/ (s1.eqSet \cap s2.eqSet = {})

(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(*  Theorem (for TLC)                                                  *)
(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)

THEOREM Spec => []SafetyInvariant

====

The swarm consists of a set of surveillance drones (called “agents”) and a central command node that holds the current mission plan. Each agent keeps a local copy of the mission phase (e.g., “survey”, “hold”, “return”) and a timestamp of the last received plan update. When a drone wants to change the mission phase—such as to start fire‑perimeter mapping—it broadcasts a proposal containing the desired phase and its timestamp to all other agents. Every receiving agent votes “yes” if its own timestamp is not newer than the proposal’s timestamp, otherwise it replies “no” and sends its newer timestamp back. The proposing drone waits until it has received affirmative votes from a majority (quorum) of the agents; slow agents that have not replied yet are simply ignored for this round. Once a quorum is reached, the proposer commits the new phase locally, updates its timestamp, and informs the whole swarm of the committed change. Agents that later receive the committed change compare the included timestamp with their own; if the incoming timestamp is older they discard the message, otherwise they adopt the new phase.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No drone can cause the swarm to switch to a new mission phase unless a majority of currently up‑to‑date agents have voted for it, preventing actions by stale or unauthorized participants.

The system consists of three roles: the Loader, which places incoming cars into the queue; the Washer, which removes a car from the queue, washes it, and signals completion; and the Unloader, which takes washed cars off the conveyor and sends them to the exit lane.  
The shared bounded work queue holds at most N cars (for example, five) and provides two counters: the number of cars waiting to be washed and the number of cars already washed but not yet unloaded.  
The Loader may add a car only when the queue’s waiting count is below the bound, otherwise it pauses and applies backpressure by slowing the upstream feeder belt.  
The Washer repeatedly checks the waiting count; if it is positive, it atomically decrements the waiting count, processes the car, increments the washed‑but‑unloaded count, and then signals the Unloader.  
The Unloader removes a car only when the washed‑but‑unloaded count is positive, decrementing that count and signaling the Loader that space has opened in the queue.  
If the Washer becomes slow, the counts cause the Loader to stop adding new cars while the Unloader continues to drain the queue, preventing overflow without treating the Washer as failed.  
All three participants read and update the counters using atomic compare‑and‑set operations so that no two actors can claim the same slot and stale updates are discarded.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No car is ever removed from the queue for washing or unloading by a participant that has not observed the most recent queue counters, preventing any stale or unauthorized action.

The batch involves two banks, the Initiator and the Counterparty, and a shared compare‑and‑swap register that stores the current batch identifier together with a status flag (open, committed, or aborted). Each bank keeps a local copy of the last batch id it successfully processed and a flag indicating whether it has already submitted its settlement entries for the current batch. To start a new settlement the Initiator writes a new batch id and the status “open” to the register using a compare‑and‑swap that succeeds only if the register still contains the previous batch id and status “committed”. After preparing its debit and credit entries, each bank attempts a compare‑and‑swap that changes the status from “open” to “committed” only when the register still shows its own batch id and the “open” flag, thereby guaranteeing that both banks have recorded their entries before the batch can be closed. If a bank crashes after writing its entries but before performing the final compare‑and‑swap, the surviving bank may detect the stale status and retry the compare‑and‑swap until it succeeds or, after a timeout, write “aborted” to the register. The compare‑and‑swap register thus serialises the transition from “open” to either “committed” or “aborted”, ensuring that at most one of those final states can be recorded even if one participant disappears silently.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No bank can cause a settlement batch to be committed using an outdated batch identifier or without both participants having successfully recorded their entries.

The RouterController initiates a routing transaction whenever a new bag arrives at an input conveyor. It first sends a *prepare* request to the downstream BeltSegment and the Sorter, asking them to reserve space for the bag based on the current capacity reported by the CapacityManager. Each participant records the received transaction identifier and replies with a *ready* vote if it can accommodate the bag, or a *reject* vote if its local buffer is full. If all votes are *ready*, the RouterController broadcasts a *commit* message, and the BeltSegment and Sorter move the bag into their queues and update their local “last committed transaction” marker; otherwise the RouterController sends an *abort* and all participants discard the reservation. While a transaction is in the *prepare* phase, the CapacityManager may receive a sensor update that changes the overall capacity, and it immediately broadcasts the new level to the RouterController, which records the new capacity before any further prepare requests are issued. The protocol allows only one active transaction identifier at a time, so the state of each participant can be captured by the variables: currentPhase (idle, prepare, commit), capacityLevel, pendingBagId, and lastCommitId. All messages are exchanged reliably over the airport’s internal network, and participants ignore any vote or commit message that carries a stale transaction identifier.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No bag is moved into a belt segment or sorter unless that participant votes *ready* for the current transaction and the capacity information is up‑to‑date.

The system consists of a set of participating banks, a central settlement ledger, and a privileged administrator.  
Each bank holds a local copy of the batch state, which records the total amount of money pending settlement and a list of pending transfer instructions.  
To add a new transfer to the batch, a bank proposes the instruction to the group and all banks cast a vote; the transfer is recorded only when a quorum of banks approves it.  
When a quorum approves, each bank updates its local copy by increasing the pending amount by the transfer value and appending the instruction to the list.  
The administrator may invoke an override that forces a specific transfer to be accepted or rejected, bypassing the quorum, but the override must be logged in the ledger.  
After a batch is closed, all banks synchronise their copies, and the ledger finalises the net settlement by moving the pending amount from each sender to the corresponding receiver.  
Any bank detecting a mismatch between its local copy and the ledger can raise a dispute, which halts further actions until the discrepancy is resolved.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total sum of money recorded as pending in the batch never changes except by the exact amount of a transfer that has been accepted, ensuring no money is created or destroyed.

The system involves three roles: a Patron who submits reservation requests, a ReservationManager that queues and schedules those requests, and a NotificationWorker that finalizes reservations and sends confirmation emails. The ReservationManager keeps a bounded work queue whose size is limited to a fixed capacity. When a Patron adds a request, the manager tries to place it in the queue; if the queue is already full, the manager returns a back‑pressure signal and asks the patron to retry later. The NotificationWorker repeatedly removes the oldest request from the queue, marks the requested book as reserved, and dispatches a confirmation; after each successful step it deletes the request from the queue. Because the worker may be slow but never fails, the queue can temporarily fill, causing back‑pressure to flow back to patrons, but no request is ever lost. The manager never drops a request; it simply retains it in the queue until the worker has processed it. The whole system’s state can be represented with two variables: the current number of items in the queue and the reservation status of each book.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The number of reservation requests stored in the queue never exceeds its configured maximum capacity.
spec_text:
---------------------------- MODULE W4C19x4x4x3 ----------------------------
EXTENDS Naturals, Sequences, FiniteSets

CONSTANTS  Books, MaxCap

VARIABLES queue, reserved

(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* Helper definitions *)
QueueLen == Len(queue)

(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* Initial state *)
Init ==
    /\ queue   = << >>
    /\ reserved = {}

(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* Actions *)

(* A patron adds a reservation request for book b.
   The manager accepts it only if there is spare capacity. *)
AddRequest(b) ==
    /\ b \in Books
    /\ QueueLen < MaxCap
    /\ queue'   = Append(queue, b)
    /\ UNCHANGED reserved

(* The notification worker processes the oldest request.
   It removes the head of the queue and marks the corresponding book reserved. *)
Process ==
    /\ QueueLen > 0
    /\ LET b == Head(queue) IN
          /\ queue'    = Tail(queue)
          /\ reserved' = reserved \cup {b}

(* The overall next-state relation *)
Next ==
    \/ \E b \in Books : AddRequest(b)
    \/ Process

(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* Safety invariant: the queue never exceeds its configured capacity *)
QueueCapInv == QueueLen <= MaxCap

(* (Optional) type-correctness invariant – not used for the required safety check *)
TypeOK ==
    /\ queue \in Seq(Books)
    /\ reserved \subseteq Books
    /\ QueueLen <= MaxCap

=============================================================================

CONSTANT
    Books = {b1, b2, b3}
    MaxCap = 2

INIT Init
NEXT Next
INVARIANT QueueCapInv

The system consists of a Central Coordinator (CC) and a set of Load Controllers (LCs) that each manage a 5 MW load slot at a substation. Each LC keeps two pieces of state: the last advertised capacity of its own slot and a boolean flag indicating whether it has already voted for a shed action on that slot. When a capacity drop is detected, the CC broadcasts a Shed‑Request identifying the target slot and the amount of reduction needed; every LC that controls the requested slot records the request, updates its capacity estimate if it has received a runtime capacity‑change message, and then casts a vote (yes if the updated capacity still covers the requested reduction, no otherwise). The CC waits until a quorum of yes‑votes is collected for that request; once the quorum is reached it sends a Commit message to the participating LCs, which then mark the slot as “shed” and adjust their local capacity state accordingly. If a capacity‑change notification arrives while a request is pending, the affected LC re‑evaluates its vote and can send a revote before the quorum is closed. All messages are asynchronous, but the protocol guarantees that only one Commit can be issued for a given slot at any time, and any new capacity change resets pending requests for that slot.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two Load Controllers can be assigned to shed the same load slot simultaneously.

The system consists of a central BloodBankServer that stores the current inventory of blood units, a set of HospitalRequestor processes that ask for specific units, and an InventoryManager that may adjust the total storage capacity at any time. The server keeps three pieces of state: a version counter that is incremented on every change, a map from slot identifiers to the unit stored (or empty), and the current maximum capacity. When a HospitalRequestor wants a unit, it first reads the version and the current map, selects a free slot, and then writes a new map entry together with the version it read; the server accepts the write only if the version has not changed, otherwise the requestor retries with the latest version. The InventoryManager changes capacity by first reading the version, then writing a new capacity value together with the same version; the write is accepted only if the version matches, otherwise the manager retries. All writes are performed using an optimistic‑lock compare‑and‑swap operation that automatically retries until the version matches, guaranteeing that concurrent updates are serialized. When a capacity increase occurs, new slots become available in the map; when a decrease occurs, the server marks any slots beyond the new limit as unavailable but does not delete existing allocations. The protocol therefore coordinates concurrent allocations and capacity adjustments with only the version counter, the slot map, and the capacity value as state variables.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two HospitalRequestor processes can ever be assigned the same inventory slot at the same time.

The system has three participants: each elevator car (Elevator i), a central floor scheduler (Scheduler), and a load manager (CapacityController) that tracks the building’s current occupancy limit.  
Each elevator maintains a local variable “NextFloor” indicating the floor it intends to stop at and a flag “Prepared” that is set when it has checked that the floor is reachable within the current capacity.  
The Scheduler keeps a request queue and a Boolean “CommitPending” that signals whether a two‑phase commit for a batch of floor assignments is in progress.  
The CapacityController holds the current maximum passenger count “MaxLoad” and can change it at any time in response to fire‑alarm or event‑driven policies.  
In the first phase, the Scheduler sends a “Prepare” message with a set of floor assignments to each elevator; each elevator replies “Ready” only if its “Prepared” flag is true under the present “MaxLoad”.  
If all elevators respond “Ready”, the Scheduler issues a “Commit” message; otherwise it sends an “Abort” and the elevators keep their previous “NextFloor”.  
When a “Commit” is received, each elevator updates its “NextFloor” to the new assignment and clears “Prepared”, while the CapacityController may concurrently adjust “MaxLoad” but any change takes effect only after the current commit finishes.  
SAFETY PROPERTY: No floor assignment is overwritten without all elevators having first agreed that the assignment respects the current load limit.

The subway line is divided into track blocks, each of which can be claimed by a signal controller that wants to authorize a train to occupy it. Two independent controller instances, Controller‑A and Controller‑B, each keep a local copy of three state variables: the identifier of the current lease holder for a block, the time at which that lease expires, and a flag indicating whether the block is currently occupied by a train. When a controller needs to set a route, it first sends a lease request for every block on the route; if the shared lease pool shows no active lease or an expired lease, the controller records itself as the lease holder and sets a future expiry time. While the lease is valid, the controller may issue a proceed command to a train and set the occupancy flag; a lease automatically becomes invalid when its expiry time passes, forcing the controller to relinquish the block. If a controller receives a lease request for a block that already has a valid lease held by the other controller, it rejects the request and the requester must wait for the lease to expire or be released. Both controllers periodically refresh their leases before expiry as long as they continue to need the block, extending the expiry time in the shared pool. The coordination therefore guarantees that at any moment only one controller’s lease is active for a given block, and only that controller may claim the block as occupied.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two controllers may hold a valid lease for the same track block at the same time, ensuring that a block is never simultaneously occupied by more than one train.

The system consists of three agents: a RunwayController that manages the whole runway, several TaxiControllers that manage individual landing‑or‑take‑off slots, and a privileged Admin that can intervene at any time. The RunwayController holds a coarse lock called runwayLock which, when held, guarantees exclusive access to the runway’s overall capacity. A TaxiController must first acquire runwayLock, then a fine‑grained lock called slotLock that corresponds to a specific time slot before it can assign an aircraft to that slot. After the aircraft has landed or taken off, the TaxiController releases its slotLock while keeping runwayLock until all of its pending updates are finished, then it releases runwayLock. The Admin can pre‑empt any holder of runwayLock or slotLock by issuing an override command; when this occurs the locks are instantly transferred to the Admin, who may reset the allocation or clear a slot. All agents periodically read the shared state variable currentAllocation, which records the number of occupied slots, to decide whether a new request can be accepted. If an override is in effect, normal agents must wait until the Admin clears the override before attempting to reacquire any lock.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: At no time will the number of aircraft assigned to runway slots exceed the runway’s maximum capacity.
spec_text:
---- MODULE W4C1x8x4x5 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, TLC

(*--------------------------------------------------------------------
  Constants
  --------------------------------------------------------------------*)
CONSTANTS TaxiIds, Slots, Capacity

(*--------------------------------------------------------------------
  Simple identifiers for special owners
  --------------------------------------------------------------------*)
None  == "None"
Admin == "Admin"

(*--------------------------------------------------------------------
  Variables
  --------------------------------------------------------------------*)
VARIABLES runwayLock, slotLocks, currentAllocation, override

(*--------------------------------------------------------------------
  State predicates
  --------------------------------------------------------------------*)
Init ==
    /\ runwayLock = None
    /\ slotLocks = [s \in Slots |-> None]
    /\ currentAllocation = 0
    /\ override = FALSE

(*--------------------------------------------------------------------
  TaxiController actions
  --------------------------------------------------------------------*)
AcquireRunway(t) ==
    /\ t \in TaxiIds
    /\ runwayLock = None
    /\ ~override
    /\ runwayLock' = t
    /\ UNCHANGED <<slotLocks, currentAllocation, override>>

AcquireSlot(t, s) ==
    /\ t \in TaxiIds
    /\ s \in Slots
    /\ runwayLock = t
    /\ slotLocks[s] = None
    /\ ~override
    /\ slotLocks' = [slotLocks EXCEPT ![s] = t]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<runwayLock, currentAllocation, override>>

AssignAircraft(t, s) ==
    /\ t \in TaxiIds
    /\ s \in Slots
    /\ slotLocks[s] = t
    /\ currentAllocation < Capacity
    /\ currentAllocation' = currentAllocation + 1
    /\ UNCHANGED <<runwayLock, slotLocks, override>>

ReleaseSlot(t, s) ==
    /\ t \in TaxiIds
    /\ s \in Slots
    /\ slotLocks[s] = t
    /\ currentAllocation > 0
    /\ slotLocks' = [slotLocks EXCEPT ![s] = None]
    /\ currentAllocation' = currentAllocation - 1
    /\ UNCHANGED <<runwayLock, override>>

ReleaseRunway(t) ==
    /\ t \in TaxiIds
    /\ runwayLock = t
    /\ \A s \in Slots: slotLocks[s] = None
    /\ runwayLock' = None
    /\ UNCHANGED <<slotLocks, currentAllocation, override>>

(*--------------------------------------------------------------------
  Admin actions
  --------------------------------------------------------------------*)
AdminOverride ==
    /\ ~override
    /\ override' = TRUE
    /\ runwayLock' = Admin
    /\ slotLocks' = [s \in Slots |-> IF slotLocks[s] # None THEN Admin ELSE None]
    /\ UNCHANGED currentAllocation

AdminClearOverride ==
    /\ override
    /\ override' = FALSE
    /\ runwayLock' = None
    /\ slotLocks' = [s \in Slots |-> None]
    /\ UNCHANGED currentAllocation

(*--------------------------------------------------------------------
  Next-state relation
  --------------------------------------------------------------------*)
Next ==
    \/ \E t \in TaxiIds: AcquireRunway(t)
    \/ \E t \in TaxiIds, s \in Slots: AcquireSlot(t, s)
    \/ \E t \in TaxiIds, s \in Slots: AssignAircraft(t, s)
    \/ \E t \in TaxiIds, s \in Slots: ReleaseSlot(t, s)
    \/ \E t \in TaxiIds: ReleaseRunway(t)
    \/ AdminOverride
    \/ AdminClearOverride

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<runwayLock, slotLocks, currentAllocation, override>>

(*--------------------------------------------------------------------
  Safety invariant
  --------------------------------------------------------------------*)
CapacityInvariant == currentAllocation <= Capacity

=============================================================================

\* Model checking configuration for W4C1x8x4x5
CONSTANTS
    TaxiIds = {t1, t2}
    Slots   = {s1, s2, s3}
    Capacity = 2

INIT Init
NEXT Next
INVARIANT CapacityInvariant

The system contains two independent scheduling instances – the ElectiveScheduler, which plans routine procedures, and the EmergencyScheduler, which handles urgent cases – both of which draw from a single pool of operating‑room time slots. Each instance keeps a local record of the last slot it successfully booked and reads a shared compare‑and‑swap (CAS) register that stores the identifier of the next free slot together with a version counter. When a scheduler wishes to assign a new operation, it reads the current value of the register, decides whether the slot is suitable for its type of surgery, and then attempts a CAS update that writes its chosen slot identifier and increments the version counter. The CAS succeeds only if the register still contains the value that was read, thereby guaranteeing that the two instances cannot book the same slot concurrently. If the CAS fails, the scheduler discards the stale information, refreshes its view of the register, and retries with the new free slot indicated. The protocol therefore coordinates the two schedulers using a single atomic operation while allowing each to act independently, and it can be captured with variables for the local last‑booked slot, the shared register value, and its version number.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No surgery is ever scheduled into a time slot that has already been allocated by another scheduler, even if a participant retries with outdated information.

The system consists of three participants: a **Surgeon** client that requests a surgery slot, a **Scheduler** service that allocates operating‑room resources, and an **Admin** who may intervene in emergencies. The Scheduler keeps three pieces of state: a coarse‑grained lock indicating which day’s schedule is being edited, a fine‑grained lock identifying the exact operating‑room and equipment set for a slot, and an override flag that is set only by the Admin. To schedule a surgery, the Surgeon first asks the Scheduler to acquire the coarse lock for the desired day; once granted, the Scheduler then attempts to acquire the fine lock for the specific room and equipment needed. If the fine lock is unavailable because another surgery holds it, the Scheduler retries later, unless the Admin has set the override flag, in which case the Scheduler releases the current fine lock and grants it to the requesting Surgeon. The Admin can at any time set the override flag, which instantly preempts any fine lock, forces the current holder to release it, and grants the lock to the Admin’s emergency surgery request. After a surgery completes, the Scheduler releases both the fine lock and, when all rooms for the day are free, releases the coarse lock for that day. All participants observe the hierarchy: no fine lock may be taken without first holding the corresponding coarse lock, and the Admin override bypasses only the fine‑level lock while still respecting the coarse lock’s exclusive ownership.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total number of surgeries scheduled at any moment never exceeds the number of operating rooms available.

The system is made of several VendingNode controllers that manage individual vending machines and a central CapacityManager that records the total number of items each machine may hold.  
Each VendingNode stores two local variables: the current number of items in its dispenser (slotCount) and a version tag (vTag) that reflects the last capacity update it has seen.  
When a customer selects a product, the VendingNode reads its vTag, decreases slotCount by one, and sends a “reserve” request containing the new slotCount and the vTag to the CapacityManager.  
The CapacityManager checks that the received vTag matches the current version it holds; if it does, it applies the change, increments its global version, and replies with an acknowledgment and the new version number.  
If the versions differ—because the CapacityManager has adjusted the machine’s maximum capacity at runtime—the VendingNode discards the stale response, reloads the latest vTag and slotCount from the manager, and retries the reservation.  
Each retry is limited to a small number of attempts to avoid endless loops, after which the VendingNode reports a temporary out‑of‑stock condition to the user.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No vending transaction can succeed using a stale version of inventory or capacity, preventing an unauthorized or outdated participant from dispensing an item.

The system has two active participants: a Central Blood Depot (the “depot”) that stores master records of all blood units, and a Regional Clinic (the “clinic”) that may temporarily take ownership of a batch of units in order to fulfill local requests. Both participants keep a small shared state consisting of (1) the identifier of the participant that currently holds the lease for a given blood‑unit batch, (2) the time at which that lease expires, and (3) the current count of units that are allocated to the holder. When the clinic needs a batch it sends a lease‑request to the depot; the depot records the clinic as the lease owner, sets the expiry to a short deadline, and replies with the current inventory count. While the lease is valid the clinic may decrement the count as it dispenses units, and it must send a lease‑renewal before expiry to keep ownership; the depot will extend the expiry only for a clinic that is still listed as the owner. If the lease expires without renewal, the depot automatically re‑claims ownership and resets the count to the last known value, allowing another request to be granted. A participant that crashes silently simply stops sending renewals; after the lease timeout the depot treats the crashed participant as no longer owning the batch and proceeds as if it had released the lease. All messages are asynchronous, but the lease timeout guarantees that at most one participant believes it can modify the same batch at any moment.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No stale or unauthorized participant can change the inventory count of a blood‑unit batch after its lease has expired.

The system consists of a Router Manager, the inbound conveyor controller (IC), and the outbound conveyor controller (OC), each of which keeps a single flag indicating whether it is prepared to forward a bag. When a bag with tag B arrives, the Router Manager initiates a two‑phase commit by sending a “prepare” request to IC and OC. Upon receiving the request each controller checks that its segment is free, sets its prepared flag, and replies with a “vote‑commit” or “vote‑abort” message. The Router Manager collects the two votes; if both are commit it records a “commit” decision and broadcasts a “commit” command, otherwise it records an “abort” decision and broadcasts an “abort”. Because network links may reorder messages, a controller discards any “commit” or “abort” that arrives before its corresponding “prepare” has been processed, and it ignores duplicate messages. After sending the final command each controller either moves the bag onto the next segment (on commit) or returns the bag to a holding area (on abort) and then resets its prepared flag. The protocol terminates when the Router Manager receives acknowledgments from both controllers that the final action has been completed.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No bag is routed onto an outbound conveyor segment unless both the inbound and outbound controllers have explicitly committed to the transfer in the current two‑phase commit.

The yard operates two independent crane controllers, each running its own instance of the loading protocol, and both draw from a common pool of ten portable gantry lifts.  
Each controller maintains a local list of “reserved” lift IDs it believes it has locked and reads a shared counter “poolVersion” that records how many times the pool list has been updated.  
When a controller wants to move a container, it reads the current poolVersion, selects a lift that appears free, writes its ID into the shared lock table, and then proceeds to lift the container.  
After completing the lift, the controller increments the shared poolVersion and removes its entry from the lock table, returning the lift to the free pool.  
If a controller finds that its chosen lift is already listed in the lock table by the other instance, it aborts, rolls back its local reservation, rereads the newest poolVersion, and retries with a different lift.  
The optimistic‑locking‑with‑retry scheme thus guarantees that, despite both instances accessing the same pool concurrently, at most one instance can hold a given lift at any moment.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total number of lifts recorded as in use plus the number recorded as free always equals the total number of lifts in the pool.

The interbank settlement system consists of a small ring of three bank processors, each called a Settlement Node, that are connected in a token‑ring topology.  
Each node stores two pieces of state: a Boolean indicating whether it currently holds the exclusive token, and a status flag that records whether its current batch of outgoing payments has been committed.  
When a node holds the token it may broadcast a Settlement Request containing its batch identifier and a monotonically increasing sequence number, then waits for acknowledgments from the other nodes.  
Upon receiving a request, a node records the highest sequence number it has seen and, regardless of the order in which messages arrive, ignores any request whose sequence number is older than one already processed.  
After all acknowledgments are collected, the token holder updates its batch status to committed, sends a Commit Notice to the ring, and then passes the token to the next node.  
The next node will not start its own settlement until it has received the token and any pending Commit Notice, guaranteeing that only one batch is ever being committed at a time.  
If a message is reordered and a node receives a later Commit Notice before the corresponding Request, the node discards the out‑of‑order notice because it has no token and its batch status is still pending.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No batch of payments is committed more than once.

The system consists of a Train Controller that requests a block, a Signal Block that records whether it is free, occupied or pending, and a small quorum of three Quorum Agents that exchange votes. Each participant stores a single variable: the Block’s status (free/occupied/pending) and a vote flag (yes/no) that the agents use when a request arrives. When a controller wants to enter a block, it broadcasts a *request* message to all quorum agents and sets the block’s status to pending. Each quorum agent, upon receiving the request, replies with a yes vote after confirming that the block’s status is still free; a slow agent may delay its reply but never crashes. When the controller collects a majority of yes votes, it sends a *commit* message, all agents update their vote flag to committed and the block’s status changes irrevocably to occupied. If the controller does not achieve a majority within a timeout, it aborts the request, resets the block’s status to free, and the quorum agents discard any pending votes. Once a block is marked occupied, no subsequent request can transition it to occupied again until a separate *release* action clears it back to free.

SAFETY PROPERTY: A block can be set to occupied at most once before it is cleared.
spec_text:
---- MODULE W4C10x5x5x3 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets

CONSTANTS Agents

VARIABLES status, vote, occCount

(* The possible values for the block status *)
StatusVals == {"free", "pending", "occupied"}

(* The possible values for a quorum agent's vote flag *)
VoteVals == {"none", "yes", "committed"}

(* Initial state *)
Init ==
    /\ status = "free"
    /\ vote = [a \in Agents |-> "none"]
    /\ occCount = 0

(* Controller issues a request: block becomes pending, votes cleared *)
Request ==
    /\ status = "free"
    /\ status' = "pending"
    /\ vote' = [a \in Agents |-> "none"]
    /\ occCount' = occCount

(* A single quorum agent a votes "yes" while the request is pending *)
AgentVote(a) ==
    /\ a \in Agents
    /\ status = "pending"
    /\ vote[a] = "none"
    /\ vote' = [vote EXCEPT ![a] = "yes"]
    /\ UNCHANGED << status, occCount >>

(* The set of agents that have voted yes *)
YesVotes == {a \in Agents : vote[a] = "yes"}

(* Controller commits when it has a majority of yes votes and no prior occupancy *)
Commit ==
    /\ status = "pending"
    /\ Cardinality(YesVotes) >= 2
    /\ occCount = 0
    /\ status' = "occupied"
    /\ occCount' = occCount + 1
    /\ vote' = [a \in Agents |-> "committed"]

(* Controller aborts if it cannot obtain a majority *)
Abort ==
    /\ status = "pending"
    /\ Cardinality(YesVotes) < 2
    /\ status' = "free"
    /\ vote' = [a \in Agents |-> "none"]
    /\ occCount' = occCount

(* Release clears the occupied block *)
Release ==
    /\ status = "occupied"
    /\ status' = "free"
    /\ vote' = [a \in Agents |-> "none"]
    /\ occCount' = 0

(* The overall step relation *)
Next ==
    \/ Request
    \/ \E a \in Agents: AgentVote(a)
    \/ Commit
    \/ Abort
    \/ Release

(* Safety invariant: at most one occupancy before a release *)
OccCountBound == occCount <= 1

====
cfg_text:
CONSTANTS Agents = {1, 2, 3}
INIT Init
NEXT Next
INVARIANT OccCountBound

nl:
The matchmaker runs a central lobby server that holds a coarse lock called **LobbyLock**. Each player client that wants to join a game first acquires **LobbyLock** to read the list of pending game slots. After seeing an open slot, the client releases **LobbyLock** and then tries to acquire a fine‑grained lock on that specific game slot, named **SlotLock_i**. If the client obtains **SlotLock_i**, it records its player ID in the slot’s player list and marks the slot as reserved. While holding **SlotLock_i**, a slow client must periodically send a heartbeat; the server will only reclaim the lock if the heartbeat stops for a timeout period. Other clients that see the same open slot must wait until **SlotLock_i** is released before attempting to reserve it. Once the required number of players have reserved a slot, the server releases all **SlotLock_i** for that game, starts the match, and then reacquires **LobbyLock** to remove the slot from the pending list.

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any moment, at most one player can hold the fine‑grained lock for a given game slot.

The system consists of Student agents that generate registration requests, a Registration Server that processes those requests, and a Course Catalog that records the remaining seats for each course.  
Each Student places a request containing its student ID and the desired course into a bounded work queue that can hold only a fixed maximum number of pending requests.  
The Registration Server repeatedly removes the oldest request from the queue, checks the Course Catalog for an available seat, and if one exists, decrements the seat count and records the assignment; otherwise it records a rejection.  
Because the queue is bounded, when it becomes full the Student agents receive back‑pressure and must pause submitting new requests until the server has processed enough entries to free space.  
A slow participant—typically the Course Catalog lookup or the external payment verification—may delay processing a request, but the protocol never discards a request; the back‑pressure only throttles new submissions.  
The only state variables needed to model the protocol are the current queue length, the seat count for each course, the identifier of the request at the head of the queue, and a flag indicating whether the server is currently busy with a slow sub‑task.  
When the server finishes a slow sub‑task it immediately resumes pulling the next request, ensuring progress while respecting the bounded queue capacity.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two students are ever granted registration for the same seat in the same course.

The yard consists of a Coordinator process, a Loading Crane (LC) and an Unloading Crane (UC); each crane keeps a local flag indicating whether it has voted “ready” for a move and a persistent log of the last two‑phase commit identifier it processed. The protocol begins when the Coordinator receives a request to transfer container C23 from the inbound ship to the storage stack, and it broadcasts a PREPARE message containing a unique transaction ID to both cranes. Upon receiving PREPARE, each crane checks that its local “in‑use” flag for C23 is false, records the transaction ID in its log, sets its vote flag to “ready”, and replies with an ACK if it can proceed or a NACK if it is already handling another container. The Coordinator waits for ACKs from both cranes; if both arrive, it sends a COMMIT message, otherwise it sends an ABORT message. When a crane receives COMMIT it flips its “in‑use” flag for C23 to true, moves the container, and finally clears the vote flag; when it receives ABORT it simply clears the vote flag and discards the log entry. If either crane crashes silently after sending an ACK, the Coordinator’s timeout triggers an ABORT and the surviving crane rolls back by resetting its flags, while the crashed crane will recover later by replaying its persistent log and seeing the ABORT entry. This two‑phase exchange guarantees that either both cranes move the container or none do, despite a possible silent failure.

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any time, no two cranes may have their “in‑use” flag set for the same container, ensuring exclusive access to that container.

The system consists of three nodes – the Central Repository, a Regional Hub, and a Mobile Unit – each of which keeps a local count of the blood‑type units it currently holds. Exactly one node possesses the token at any time, and only the token holder is allowed to modify any inventory count. When a node holds the token it may record an incoming donation, record a dispatch to a hospital, or issue a transfer request to move units to the next node in the ring, after which it updates its local count accordingly. Once the update is complete the node passes the token to the next node clockwise; a node that is slow simply delays the pass but never loses the token. If a node receives a transfer request while holding the token it first checks that it still has the requested units, reserves them, and then forwards the request to the downstream node. The downstream node, upon receiving the token, either fulfills the request by decrementing its own count and incrementing the upstream node’s count, or rejects it if insufficient stock, and then forwards the token onward. After the token makes a full round, every node’s view of the total blood inventory in the system is consistent.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: A blood unit that is dispatched to a hospital is recorded as dispatched at most once.

The yard consists of multiple crane controllers (the participants) that each keep a local record of the last known version number for every cargo bay and a flag indicating whether they currently hold a tentative lock on that bay. When a controller wants to move a container from Bay 7 to a truck, it reads the current version number of Bay 7, records it, and sends a **lock‑request** message containing that version to the central lock manager. The lock manager replies with a **grant** if the version it has stored still matches the one in the request; otherwise it sends a **reject** with the new version. Because network links can reorder messages, a controller may receive an older grant after a newer reject, so it must verify that the version in any grant it processes is still current before proceeding. If the grant is stale, the controller discards it and retries by reading the latest version and sending a new lock‑request. Once a controller successfully acquires a grant with a matching version, it marks the bay as locked, performs the move, and finally sends a **release** message that increments the bay’s version number in the lock manager.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two crane controllers can hold a lock on the same cargo bay at the same time.

The system contains a ring of three router controllers – NorthGate, CentralHub, and SouthGate – each of which keeps a Boolean variable *hasToken* and a small queue of pending baggage‑routing record updates. When a controller finishes loading a piece of baggage it appends a *record‑update* (containing the baggage ID, the new destination belt, and a monotonically increasing sequence number) to its queue. If a controller’s *hasToken* is true, it dequeues the first pending update, sends the update to the shared routing database, and then forwards the token to the next controller in the ring. The token message carries the sender’s current sequence number so that any out‑of‑order database acknowledgments can be ignored by the receiver. A controller that receives the token checks the sequence number of the most recent database write it has seen; if the database reports an older sequence it discards the stale acknowledgment and keeps the token. If a controller has no pending updates when it receives the token, it immediately passes the token onward. The ring continually circulates, guaranteeing that at most one controller can write to the routing database at any moment, even though network messages may arrive reordered.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No update to the shared routing database is ever overwritten by an earlier‑dated update, so every baggage record reflects the most recent routing decision.

The system consists of a central Scheduler process and a set of Operating‑Room controllers, one for each physical OR. All participants keep three pieces of information: the current configuration epoch, the list of surgeries assigned to each time slot, and a flag indicating whether they have successfully recorded the latest assignment. When the Scheduler decides to change the plan it increments the epoch, creates a new slot‑to‑surgery list, and broadcasts the new epoch together with the list to every OR controller. Each OR controller, upon receiving a broadcast with a higher epoch than its own, stores the new list, updates its epoch, and sends an acknowledgment back to the Scheduler. The Scheduler waits for acknowledgments from a majority of OR controllers; once it has enough, it marks the new configuration as committed and may delete the previous epoch’s data. If one OR controller crashes silently, its lack of acknowledgment simply prevents it from being counted in the majority, allowing the Scheduler to progress with the remaining controllers and later recover the crashed node when it restarts. All participants only ever read or write the single epoch number, the single slot‑to‑surgery map, and the acknowledgment flag, keeping the state model very small.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two surgeries are ever assigned to the same operating‑room time slot in any committed configuration.

The protocol involves three kinds of actors: the settlement clerk who creates a new batch record, the clearing engine that processes the batch, and a senior administrator who can intervene. All actors share a single compare‑and‑swap (CAS) register that holds the identifier of the current batch together with a version tag. When the clerk wants to add a new transaction to the batch they read the register, construct a new batch identifier with an incremented version, and attempt a CAS that succeeds only if the register still contains the version they observed. The clearing engine periodically reads the register and, if it sees a newer version, replaces the pending batch with the processed version using its own CAS step. If the senior administrator issues an override, they write a special “admin‑override” flag into the register and then perform a CAS that replaces any existing batch, guaranteeing that the override wins regardless of concurrent clerk or engine attempts. All other actors treat the presence of the admin‑override flag as a signal to abort their own CAS attempts and to acknowledge that the administrator’s decision is now authoritative.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No update to the shared batch record can be lost after a successful compare‑and‑swap, even when an administrator performs an override.

The system consists of two independent reservation instances, each running on a different branch server, and a central pool manager that tracks the total copies of each book. Each instance keeps a local variable `pending` that records a user’s request for a specific title, while the pool manager maintains a counter `availableCopies` for that title. When a user requests a reservation, the instance starts a two‑phase commit by sending a `prepare` message to the pool manager asking to lock one copy. The pool manager checks `availableCopies`; if at least one copy is free it decrements a provisional lock count and replies with `ready`, otherwise it replies `abort`. If the instance receives `ready` from both the pool manager and the other instance (which shares the same pool), it sends a `commit` to the pool manager, which then permanently decrements `availableCopies` and releases the lock; otherwise it sends an `abort` and the provisional lock is rolled back. After a commit the instance records the reservation in its local `granted` set and notifies the user, while an abort leaves the request in a `failed` state.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No book copy can be granted to a user unless the pool manager has permanently decreased the availableCopies counter for that copy.

The swarm consists of a set of surveillance drones, each identified by a unique ID, and a central map repository that stores the latest fire‑intensity reading for each grid cell of the forest. Each drone locally keeps a copy of the cell’s current version number and a tentative update record containing a new intensity value and the version it observed. When a drone wants to report a new reading it first reads the repository’s version for that cell, writes its tentative update together with the observed version into a shared “lock” entry, and then attempts to commit: if the repository’s version still matches the one in the lock, the repository accepts the update and increments the version; otherwise the commit fails and the drone retries with the fresh version. The lock entry is cleared after a successful commit or after a timeout; the timeout allows the system to recover when a drone that held the lock crashes silently and never releases it. Drones that detect a cleared lock after a timeout may overwrite the stale lock entry with a new attempt, ensuring progress despite crashes. The protocol therefore uses optimistic locking—checking the version at commit time—and a simple retry loop to coordinate concurrent updates. All state needed for the model can be captured by the repository version number for a cell, the lock holder’s ID (or “none”), and a timeout flag.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two drones can permanently write different fire‑intensity values to the same map cell without one of them first seeing and respecting the other’s update.

The fleet consists of a central Scheduler and several mobile Robots that move pallets between storage aisles and loading docks. Each Robot stores two pieces of local state: the current epoch number of the warehouse layout it believes is active, and the identifier of the aisle it is currently occupying. The Scheduler maintains a single global epoch number and a table that records, for every aisle, the maximum number of Robots allowed to be in that aisle at the same time. When the Scheduler decides to reconfigure the layout (for example, to open a new aisle or close an old one), it increments the global epoch, updates the capacity table, and broadcasts the new epoch together with the updated capacity table to all Robots. Upon receiving a broadcast, a Robot first checks that the epoch is higher than its own; if so it adopts the new epoch and the new capacity constraints, then it may move to a different aisle only if the capacity table still permits another Robot in that aisle. If a Robot crashes silently, the Scheduler will eventually notice the missing heartbeat, keep the epoch unchanged, and continue to enforce the last known capacity limits for the remaining Robots. The epoch numbers guarantee that any Robot that later recovers will only act on the most recent configuration and will not violate the capacity limits established during the crash.

SAFETY PROPERTY: At no time can more Robots be present in any aisle than the capacity recorded for that aisle in the current epoch.

The system has two settlement processors, Processor A and Processor B, each responsible for collecting a batch of inter‑bank transfers before committing them to the shared clearing pool. Both processors keep a local counter of how many transfers they have already placed in the pool, and they also read a single global compare‑and‑swap register that stores the current total number of entries in the pool. When a processor is ready to add a new transfer, it first reads the register; if the read value plus the local counter would stay below the pool’s maximum capacity, it attempts a compare‑and‑swap that atomically updates the register from the old total to the new total. If the compare‑and‑swap succeeds, the processor records the transfer locally and increments its counter; if it fails, the processor re‑reads the register and retries the check. Because the two processors share the same register, only one of them can succeed in updating the total for any given transfer, preventing over‑commit. The protocol repeats until each processor’s batch is either fully committed or rejected when the pool is full. 

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total number of transfers recorded in the shared clearing pool never exceeds its configured capacity.
spec_text:
---- MODULE W4C3x7x4x2 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, TLC

CONSTANT Capacity

VARIABLES reg, localA, localB

(* ---- Initialization ---- *)
Init ==
    /\ reg = 0
    /\ localA = 0
    /\ localB = 0

(* ---- Processor A tries to commit one transfer ---- *)
AAdd ==
    /\ reg < Capacity               \* there is room in the pool
    /\ reg' = reg + 1               \* successful CAS updates the total
    /\ localA' = localA + 1         \* record the transfer locally
    /\ UNCHANGED <<localB>>

(* ---- Processor B tries to commit one transfer ---- *)
BAdd ==
    /\ reg < Capacity
    /\ reg' = reg + 1
    /\ localB' = localB + 1
    /\ UNCHANGED <<localA>>

(* ---- Stuttering step – no processor makes progress ---- *)
Stutter ==
    /\ UNCHANGED <<reg, localA, localB>>

Next ==
    AAdd \/ BAdd \/ Stutter

Spec ==
    Init /\ [][Next]_<<reg, localA, localB>>

(* ---- Safety invariant: the pool never exceeds its capacity ---- *)
Safe ==
    reg <= Capacity

=============================================================================
cfg_text:
SPECIFICATION Spec
CONSTANTS Capacity = 3
INVARIANT Safe

nl:
The system consists of multiple Router Workers that pull bags from the inbound conveyor and assign each bag to a numbered slot on a storage carousel. A shared compare‑and‑swap register holds the current highest slot index that is free, and a separate register records the carousel’s current capacity, which can be increased or decreased by a Capacity Manager at runtime. When a worker wants to place a bag, it reads the free‑slot register, proposes the next index (current value plus one), and executes a compare‑and‑swap that succeeds only if the register still contains the value it read and the proposed index is less than the current capacity. If the compare‑and‑swap succeeds, the worker records the assigned slot in its local state and proceeds to load the bag; if it fails, the worker retries with the newly observed free‑slot value. When the Capacity Manager reduces capacity, it first lowers the capacity register and then repeatedly performs compare‑and‑swap on the free‑slot register to clamp it to the new maximum, ensuring no new assignments exceed the reduced size. Workers continuously monitor the capacity register so that a retry after a failed compare‑and‑swap automatically respects any capacity change that occurred while they were waiting.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two workers ever assign the same carousel slot to different bags.

The auction has three roles: the Exchange Server that holds the opening‑price register, a Broker A that wants to submit a price, and a Backup Broker B that can step in if either broker crashes. The server stores two variables: a current best price and a version number that is incremented each time a price is successfully recorded. When a broker wants to propose a new price, it reads both the current best price and the version number, decides whether its price improves the auction, and then attempts a compare‑and‑swap that will replace the best price only if the version number has not changed since it was read. If the compare‑and‑swap succeeds, the server updates the price and increments the version; if it fails, the broker re‑reads the state and may try again. Brokers may crash at any moment without warning; the server treats a missing response as a failed compare‑and‑swap and the crashed broker simply stops participating. The Backup Broker monitors the server’s version number; if it notices that the version stops advancing while a price proposal is pending, it can resend its last successful proposal on behalf of the crashed broker. All participants therefore coordinate through the single compare‑and‑swap register, ensuring that only one price update can be committed at a time even in the presence of a silent crash.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The best‑price record is never overwritten by a stale or lost update, so the final price always reflects the highest successfully submitted proposal.

The system consists of two settlement engines, Engine A and Engine B, each responsible for processing batches of interbank transfers for a particular epoch.  
Both engines keep a local copy of the current epoch number, a flag that shows whether the shared pool of funds is locked for that epoch, and a list of transfers that have been prepared but not yet applied.  
When a new epoch begins, each engine broadcasts a reconfigure message containing the new epoch number and waits until it sees a matching message from the other engine before advancing its local epoch.  
After the epoch numbers match, the engines independently attempt to lock the shared pool; the first engine that successfully sets the lock flag records the lock in its local state and notifies the other engine.  
Once the lock is acknowledged, each engine adds its prepared transfers to a combined batch and then writes a commit record that references the current epoch and the shared pool identifier.  
The commit operation triggers the actual debit and credit of the pooled funds, after which both engines clear the lock flag and move to the next epoch.  
If an engine detects a mismatch in epoch numbers or a missing lock acknowledgement, it aborts its local batch and retries the reconfiguration protocol, ensuring that only one consistent batch can ever be applied per epoch.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: A settlement batch for a given epoch is applied to the shared pool at most once.

The system consists of a Train Controller on each train and a Block Authority server that owns a single compare‑and‑swap register for every track block.  
The register stores a pair (version, occupied) where version is a monotonically increasing integer and occupied is true when a train holds the block.  
When a train wants to enter a block it reads the current pair, remembers the version, and sends a request to the Block Authority to set occupied to true with the same version number.  
The Block Authority performs a compare‑and‑swap: if the stored version still matches the one supplied, it atomically updates occupied to true and increments the version; otherwise it rejects the request.  
The train proceeds into the block only after receiving a successful swap acknowledgement; if it receives a rejection it must retry with the new version it reads.  
Because messages can be reordered, a train may see an old acknowledgment after a newer one, but it discards any reply whose version is not the latest it knows.  
When a train leaves the block it performs the same compare‑and‑swap with occupied set to false, again using the current version to ensure exclusive update.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The block’s occupied flag can never be set to true by more than one train at the same time, so no update of the occupancy record is lost or overwritten.

The swarm consists of a set of autonomous fire‑monitoring drones (called **Nodes**) and a ground control station that hosts the **Epoch Manager**. Each Node stores two pieces of state: the current **epoch number** and the identifier of the **active flight plan** assigned for that epoch. When the Epoch Manager decides to reconfigure the swarm—e.g., to add a new sensor payload or to redirect coverage—it increments the epoch number, publishes a signed **epoch update** containing the new flight plan, and broadcasts it to all Nodes. Upon receiving a signed update, a Node validates the signature, discards any older epoch, installs the new flight plan, and acknowledges the change back to the Epoch Manager. A privileged **Admin Console** can issue an **override command** that carries a higher‑level signature; this command replaces the pending epoch update and forces all Nodes to adopt the override flight plan immediately, regardless of their current epoch. Nodes only act on a flight plan after they have stored the matching epoch number or an admin override that they have verified. The epoch‑numbered reconfiguration thus provides a simple, monotonic coordination mechanism while still allowing the admin to pre‑empt it in emergencies.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No drone may execute a surveillance maneuver or accept a reconfiguration unless it holds the most recent epoch number or a valid admin‑override signature, preventing actions by unauthorized or stale participants.
spec_text:
---------------------------- MODULE W4C14x9x6x5 ----------------------------
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets

(* ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* CONSTANTS *)
CONSTANTS
    Nodes,      \* Finite set of drone identifiers
    Plans,      \* Finite set of possible flight‑plan identifiers
    MaxEpoch    \* Upper bound on epoch numbers (inclusive)

(* ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* VARIABLES *)
VARIABLES
    epoch,          \* current epoch number (0 .. MaxEpoch)
    globalPlan,    \* flight plan associated with the current epoch
    nodeEpoch,     \* [n \in Nodes |-> epoch stored at node n]
    nodePlan,      \* [n \in Nodes |-> flight plan stored at node n]
    overrideActive,\* TRUE iff an admin‑override is in effect
    overridePlan,  \* flight plan supplied by the admin‑override
    nodeOverride,  \* [n \in Nodes |-> TRUE iff node n follows admin‑override]
    exec           \* [n \in Nodes |-> TRUE iff node n is executing a maneuver]

(* ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* Helper definitions *)
IsLatestEpoch(n) == nodeEpoch[n] = epoch
IsOverridden(n)   == nodeOverride[n]

(* ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* Initial state *)
Init ==
    /\ epoch = 0
    /\ globalPlan \in Plans
    /\ nodeEpoch = [n \in Nodes |-> 0]
    /\ nodePlan = [n \in Nodes |-> globalPlan]
    /\ overrideActive = FALSE
    /\ overridePlan \in Plans
    /\ nodeOverride = [n \in Nodes |-> FALSE]
    /\ exec = [n \in Nodes |-> FALSE]

(* ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* Epoch manager issues a new epoch‑numbered reconfiguration *)
EpochTick ==
    /\ epoch < MaxEpoch
    /\ LET newEpoch == epoch + 1
           newPlan  == CHOOSE p \in Plans : TRUE
       IN
          /\ epoch' = newEpoch
          /\ globalPlan' = newPlan
          /\ overrideActive' = FALSE
          /\ overridePlan' = CHOOSE p \in Plans : TRUE
          /\ nodeEpoch' = [n \in Nodes |-> newEpoch]
          /\ nodePlan' = [n \in Nodes |-> newPlan]
          /\ nodeOverride' = [n \in Nodes |-> FALSE]
          /\ exec' = [n \in Nodes |-> FALSE]

(* ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* Admin console issues an override that pre‑empts the pending epoch *)
AdminOverride ==
    /\ LET newPlan == CHOOSE p \in Plans : TRUE
       IN
          /\ overrideActive' = TRUE
          /\ overridePlan' = newPlan
          /\ nodeOverride' = [n \in Nodes |-> TRUE]
          /\ nodePlan' = [n \in Nodes |-> newPlan]
          /\ exec' = [n \in Nodes |-> FALSE]
          /\ UNCHANGED <<epoch, globalPlan, nodeEpoch>>

(* ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* A node starts executing a surveillance maneuver *)
Execute(n) ==
    /\ n \in Nodes
    /\ exec[n] = FALSE
    /\ (IsOverridden(n) \/ IsLatestEpoch(n))    \* safety pre‑condition
    /\ exec' = [m \in Nodes |-> IF m = n THEN TRUE ELSE exec[m]]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<epoch, globalPlan, nodeEpoch, nodePlan,
                   overrideActive, overridePlan, nodeOverride>>

(* ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* The system's possible next steps *)
Next ==
    \/ EpochTick
    \/ AdminOverride
    \/ \E n \in Nodes : Execute(n)

(* ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* Specification *)
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<epoch, globalPlan, nodeEpoch, nodePlan,
                               overrideActive, overridePlan,
                               nodeOverride, exec>>

(* ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* Safety invariant: a node may execute only if it holds the latest
   epoch number or a valid admin‑override *)
SafetyInvariant ==
    \A n \in Nodes :
        exec[n] => (IsOverridden(n) \/ IsLatestEpoch(n))

(* ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
THEOREM Spec => []SafetyInvariant
=====================================================================
