The system consists of several Collection Sites that add donated blood units to a shared pool, Hospital Requesters that ask for units for patients, and a quorum of Inventory Managers who mediate every change to the pool. All participants keep a lightweight view of the pool: the total number of available units, a list of which units are currently reserved by Instance A, and a list of which units are reserved by Instance B. When a Hospital Requester needs a unit, it sends a reservation request to the quorum specifying which instance (A or B) will use the unit. The quorum members each check the shared pool and the two reservation lists; if the requested unit is still free they cast a “yes” vote, otherwise they cast a “no” vote. Once a majority of quorum members have voted “yes”, the quorum records the reservation in the appropriate instance’s list and decrements the pool’s free count, then notifies the requester that the unit is allocated. When a unit is transfused or expires, the owning instance releases it, the quorum restores the pool count and deletes the entry from that instance’s reservation list. All quorum votes are performed atomically for each request, guaranteeing that the two instances never make conflicting reservations for the same physical blood unit.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two instances ever allocate the same blood unit slot.

A nurse and a lab technician each run a client that can add or remove units of a specific blood type from the central inventory server. The server maintains a Boolean flag indicating whether the whole inventory is locked, a second Boolean flag for the lock on the particular blood type being accessed, and an integer count of units currently stored for that type. To record a donation, a client first acquires the coarse‑grained inventory lock, then acquires the fine‑grained lock for the required blood type, increments the count, and finally releases the fine lock followed by the coarse lock. To record a transfusion, the client follows the same lock sequence but decrements the count instead of incrementing it. An administrator with privileged credentials can invoke an override operation that instantly clears both lock flags and may directly set the count to a corrected value, bypassing the normal lock acquisition. All other participants must retry their operation if they encounter a lock that has been cleared by the admin override.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total number of stored units for any blood type never exceeds the maximum capacity allowed for that type.

The system consists of a central Settlement Manager and a set of participating Bank Nodes that each hold a batch of pending interbank transfers.  
Each Bank Node maintains two pieces of state: the highest epoch number it has acknowledged and a flag indicating whether it has already submitted its batch for the current epoch.  
The Settlement Manager periodically opens a new epoch, broadcasting an epoch‑start message that includes the epoch identifier and a list of banks expected to submit.  
Upon receiving an epoch‑start, a Bank Node records the epoch identifier, and if it has not yet submitted for that epoch, it sends a settlement request containing its transfer batch and the epoch number.  
The Settlement Manager collects settlement requests, and once it has received a request from every expected bank for the same epoch, it marks the epoch as closed and issues a commit message that makes the transfers permanent.  
Because network messages can be reordered, a Bank Node may receive a commit for a later epoch before the request for the current epoch is processed, and the node must ignore any commit that references an epoch lower than the one it has already acknowledged.  
After sending its commit acknowledgment, a Bank Node updates its acknowledged epoch and clears its submit flag, ready for the next epoch.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: A bank’s transfer batch is committed at most once for any given epoch.

The settlement system consists of a single **Settlement Coordinator** that owns a compare‑and‑swap register called **CurrentSlot**, initially set to zero, and several **Bank Nodes** that each submit a batch of interbank payments. Each Bank Node reads the value of CurrentSlot, proposes the next integer as its desired slot, and issues a compare‑and‑swap operation that succeeds only if the register still holds the value it read. On a successful compare‑and‑swap, the Bank Node atomically writes its identifier into a second register **SlotOwner**, thereby claiming that slot and then places its payment instructions into the corresponding slot of the shared batch buffer. If the compare‑and‑swap fails, the Bank Node repeats the read‑propose‑swap loop until it secures a slot. Because messages carrying the read result, the compare‑and‑swap request, and the subsequent acknowledgment can arrive out of order, each node always validates the compare‑and‑swap outcome before committing its payment data, guaranteeing that only the node that actually changed CurrentSlot may write to the slot. The Coordinator periodically scans SlotOwner to confirm progress and to release slots that have been fully processed.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two banks can ever be recorded as the owner of the same settlement batch slot.

The system consists of a Block Manager that owns a bounded queue of release requests, a Signal Controller for each track segment, and the Trains that request entry to a block.  
The Block Manager keeps two state variables: the current number of pending release requests (queue depth) and the identifier of the block that is currently granted.  
When a Train approaches a block it sends a Request message to the Block Manager, which is enqueued if the queue is not full; if the queue is full the Train must wait (back‑pressure).  
The Signal Controller periodically checks the head of the queue; if the queued request matches the block it controls, it changes the signal to green and informs the Block Manager that the block is now occupied.  
The Block Manager then records the block as granted and removes the request from the queue, decreasing the queue depth.  
When the Train leaves the block it sends a Release message; the Block Manager clears the granted identifier, allowing the next request to be processed, but a slow Train may delay the Release without causing a failure.  
All participants operate concurrently, relying on the bounded queue to provide back‑pressure that prevents the system from granting more trains than the physical block can safely hold.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: A block is granted to at most one train at any time, so the signal can be set to green for a given block no more than once before the block is released.

The central Scheduler keeps a map that assigns each operating‑room (OR1, OR2, …) to a surgery and stores the current epoch number that identifies the latest configuration. Each OR Manager maintains locally the epoch it has most recently accepted and a flag indicating whether the room is currently reserved for a confirmed surgery. When a surgeon requests a new slot, the Scheduler creates a new configuration, increments the epoch, and sends the updated map together with the new epoch to every OR Manager. OR Managers may receive these messages out of order, but they only install a configuration whose epoch is larger than the epoch they have already stored, discarding older or duplicate messages. After installing a configuration, an OR Manager replies with an acknowledgment that includes the epoch it just applied, allowing the Scheduler to know when the whole system has converged on the new schedule. The epoch numbering thus provides a total order of reconfigurations that survives message reordering, guaranteeing that all participants eventually agree on a single, monotonic schedule.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total number of confirmed surgery reservations across all operating rooms is never increased by the protocol except when the Scheduler explicitly adds a new reservation.

The network is built from several smart‑door lock units, each running two independent lock‑control instances (a primary and a backup) that draw from a single pool of unique lock‑tokens. Each instance maintains only three local variables: whether it currently holds the token (TokenOwner), the identifier it believes to be the leader (LeaderId), and a heartbeat counter for detecting leader liveness. When the token pool is empty, any instance may broadcast a “Claim” message; the first claim observed by the other instances becomes the leader, and that claimant records itself as both TokenOwner and LeaderId. All other instances periodically exchange heartbeat messages with the leader; if a heartbeat is missed beyond a timeout, they broadcast a “Vacate” message and trigger a new election by sending their own Claim. If a leader fails while holding a token, the backup instance on the same door lock notices the missing heartbeat, issues Vacate, and the next Claim received from any instance in the pool becomes the new leader, ensuring failover without duplicate token ownership. The protocol guarantees that at any moment at most one instance in the whole pool is marked as TokenOwner, and any transition from “no owner” to “owner” is recorded exactly once.

SAFETY PROPERTY: A lock‑token is granted to at most one instance, and after a token is granted the same token cannot be granted again until the previous holder explicitly releases it.

The Exchange Coordinator initiates the opening‑auction two‑phase commit by broadcasting a *prepare* request that asks each participating broker to lock the orders it has submitted for the auction. Each broker records locally whether it has successfully locked its order book and then replies with a *ready* vote if the lock succeeded or an *abort* vote if it cannot lock. After collecting all replies, the Coordinator decides: if every broker voted ready it sends a *commit* message, otherwise it sends an *abort* message. Upon receiving a *commit*, a broker marks its locked orders as “matched” and releases the lock; upon receiving an *abort*, it discards the lock and keeps its orders unchanged. Because network links may deliver messages out of order, every message carries a phase identifier and each participant processes a *commit* or *abort* only if it has already recorded the corresponding *prepare* and vote, ignoring any stale messages that arrive later. Each participant therefore only needs to maintain two boolean flags (whether it has locked its orders and whether the transaction has been finalized) plus a small phase counter. The protocol guarantees that all brokers reach the same final decision despite possible reordering of the messages.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total number of shares that become matched in the auction is exactly the number of shares that were locked by the brokers, never more and never less.

The network consists of a central hub, several smart‑door locks, and an administrator console. Each lock keeps two pieces of state: the epoch number of the configuration it is currently using and a flag indicating whether it is in privileged‑override mode; the hub stores the globally agreed epoch and a boolean that shows whether an admin override is active. When the hub wants to change the lock settings it increments the global epoch, clears the override flag, and broadcasts the new epoch together with the new configuration to all locks. Upon receiving the broadcast, a lock updates its configuration only if the epoch it receives is exactly one greater than the epoch it currently holds, thereby moving all locks forward in lockstep. If an administrator issues an override, the console authenticates the admin, sets the hub’s override flag, and forces the hub to increment the epoch to a fresh value that supersedes any pending normal reconfiguration; every lock that sees the override flag will accept the new epoch even if it is not the expected next number. Locks that are not in privileged‑override mode will ignore any message that carries an epoch number older than the one they already store, preventing them from rolling back to stale configurations.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No door lock will apply a configuration change that was issued by a participant that is not the current admin or that carries an epoch number older than the lock’s current epoch.

The system consists of a block controller that manages a single signalling block, a train that wants to occupy the block, and a privileged administrator who can issue an emergency lock on the block. The controller keeps two pieces of state: the current status of the block (free, occupied or locked) and a compare‑and‑swap register that stores a ticket number representing the last successful reservation. When a train approaches, it reads the register, proposes the next ticket number and asks the controller to compare the stored ticket with the one it read; if they match and the block is free, the controller atomically writes the new ticket and changes the block status to occupied, thereby granting the train permission to enter. The controller may later receive a clear command from the train, which uses another compare‑and‑swap to set the register back to a cleared value and change the block status to free. At any time the administrator can issue an override that forces the block status to locked, bypassing the compare‑and‑swap logic and preventing any further train reservations until the lock is lifted. The compare‑and‑swap register therefore guarantees that only one train can succeed in changing the block from free to occupied, while the admin override provides a higher‑priority path to lock the block for safety or maintenance.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: A train may be granted entry to a block at most once before that block is cleared or locked.

The system consists of a Prescription Manager that owns pending prescriptions, a Dispenser that fills a physical slot with medication, and a Reconfigurator that maintains a global epoch number used to order reconfiguration actions. Each component stores the current epoch and, for the Manager and Dispenser, a single variable indicating which slot (if any) they have claimed for the active prescription. When a new prescription arrives, the Manager writes the desired slot number together with the next epoch value and sends this proposal to the Dispenser; the Dispenser replies with an acknowledgment that includes the same epoch, after which both parties permanently record the assignment for that epoch. The Reconfigurator periodically broadcasts the latest epoch to all participants; any participant that receives a higher epoch discards its old slot claim and adopts the new assignment, ensuring that stale information is never acted upon. If the Manager crashes silently, the Dispenser can still complete the current assignment because it already holds the epoch‑stamped slot number, and the Reconfigurator’s epoch broadcast guarantees that no new Manager proposal will be accepted for an older epoch. All messages are idempotent, so retransmission after a crash does not create duplicate assignments. The protocol therefore uses at most three state variables—epoch, slot claim, and a crash flag—to coordinate safe allocation of a single physical slot per epoch.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any time, no two prescriptions are assigned to the same dispenser slot.

The system consists of three worker nodes – a **Collector** that enqueues newly drawn blood bags, a **Lab Technician** that dequeues bags to perform testing, and an **Inventory Service** that records the final volume of each blood type. A bounded work queue holds at most N pending bags; the queue length and a simple “admin‑override‑active” flag are the only shared state variables. When the Collector receives a bag, it checks the queue length; if the queue is not full it adds the bag and increments the length, otherwise it blocks until space becomes available (backpressure). The Lab Technician repeatedly reads the head of the queue, removes the bag, runs tests, and then updates the Inventory Service, which decrements the queue length and increments the stored count for the bag’s blood type. An **Admin** may at any time set the override flag, which immediately clears the queue of any bags that have remained unprocessed for longer than a configurable timeout, effectively resetting the length to zero. While the override flag is set, the Collector is temporarily rejected from enqueuing new bags until the flag is cleared by the Admin, after which normal back‑pressure operation resumes. All participants respect the current values of the queue length and the override flag before taking any action, ensuring a deterministic flow of bags through the system.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No unauthenticated user or stale bag can be added to or removed from the inventory while the admin override flag is active.

The swarm consists of a collection of surveillance drones and a ground station called the Command Hub.  
Each drone maintains a local copy of the fire‑map quadrant it monitors together with a version counter for that quadrant.  
When a drone spots a new hot spot it creates a proposal containing the updated map segment and its version, then broadcasts this proposal to all other drones and to the Command Hub.  
The Command Hub waits until a majority of drones have echoed the same proposal; once a quorum is reached it sends a Commit message that carries the new version number.  
Every drone, upon receiving a Commit, replaces its local fire‑map segment with the committed version and discards any earlier proposals that have a lower version number.  
Because messages can be reordered, each drone only applies incoming messages whose version number exceeds the version it currently stores, ignoring any stale messages.  
The quorum‑based commit guarantees that all drones eventually converge on the same fire‑map state despite out‑of‑order deliveries.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No drone ever overwrites a fire‑map segment with an older version, so no update to the shared map is lost.

The system consists of a small set of blood‑bank nodes that each store a local copy of the inventory for the same set of blood types and a single logical leader that coordinates updates. Each node maintains three simple variables: the identifier of the current leader, the total capacity of the bank (the maximum number of units it can hold), and the current inventory count for each blood type. Periodically every node sends a “heartbeat” to the leader; if a node stops receiving heartbeats for a configurable timeout it initiates a leader‑election round by broadcasting its own identifier, and the node with the highest identifier that is still alive becomes the new leader. The leader processes two kinds of client requests: (1) donation or transfusion operations that adjust the inventory count, and (2) capacity‑change requests that modify the capacity variable at runtime. After applying a request the leader increments a monotonically increasing version number and multicasts the updated version, capacity, and inventory to all nodes, which accept the update only if the version is newer than the one they currently hold. Upon receiving a new leader announcement, all nodes discard any pending actions that were originated by the previous leader and will only forward future client requests to the newly elected leader. If the new leader later fails, the election process repeats, ensuring that the system always has a single active coordinator that reflects the latest capacity and inventory state.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No node ever applies a donation, transfusion, or capacity change that was proposed by a leader that is no longer the current elected leader.

The system consists of a set of regional Load Controllers (LCs) that each manage a cluster of substations, and a single Vote Pool that holds a fixed number of voting tokens. Each LC keeps two pieces of state: a flag indicating whether it is currently participating in a load‑shed proposal, and a boolean that records whether it has a token borrowed from the Vote Pool. When a LC detects an overload it starts a shed proposal, requests one token from the pool, and broadcasts the desired reduction amount to the other LCs. The other LCs, upon receiving the proposal, may cast a “yes” vote by attaching their own token; a proposal is executed once a quorum (more than half of the tokens in the pool) have voted “yes”. After the load is actually shed, every participating LC returns its token to the Vote Pool and clears its participation flag. Because two independent shedding instances share the same pool, a token that is still held for one instance cannot be borrowed by the other, preventing more than one quorum from forming simultaneously. The protocol repeats for subsequent overload events, always respecting the token bookkeeping rules.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total number of voting tokens in the shared pool plus the tokens currently held by all Load Controllers is invariant and never changes.
spec_text:
---- MODULE W4C9x5x2x2 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, Sequences, FiniteSets

CONSTANTS LCs, TokenCount

(*--------------------------------------------------------------------
  Variables
--------------------------------------------------------------------*)
VARIABLES pool, participating, heldTokens

(*--------------------------------------------------------------------
  Definitions
--------------------------------------------------------------------*)
(* Tokens currently free in the vote pool *)
Pool == pool

(* Set of load controllers that are currently participating in a proposal *)
Participating == participating

(* Set of load controllers that currently hold a token from the pool *)
HeldTokens == heldTokens

(* Quorum is more than half of the total tokens *)
Quorum == TokenCount \div 2 + 1

(*--------------------------------------------------------------------
  Initial state
--------------------------------------------------------------------*)
Init ==
    /\ pool = TokenCount
    /\ participating = {}
    /\ heldTokens = {}

(*--------------------------------------------------------------------
  Actions
--------------------------------------------------------------------*)
(* A load controller detects overload and starts a new proposal,
   borrowing a token from the pool. *)
Start(lc) ==
    /\ lc \in LCs
    /\ lc \notin participating
    /\ pool > 0
    /\ pool' = pool - 1
    /\ participating' = participating \cup {lc}
    /\ heldTokens' = heldTokens \cup {lc}
    /\ UNCHANGED << >>   \* no other variables

(* Another load controller votes “yes” on an already‑started proposal,
   also borrowing a token. *)
Vote(lc) ==
    /\ lc \in LCs
    /\ lc \notin participating
    /\ pool > 0
    /\ pool' = pool - 1
    /\ participating' = participating \cup {lc}
    /\ heldTokens' = heldTokens \cup {lc}
    /\ UNCHANGED << >>   \* no other variables

(* When a quorum of tokens has been gathered, the proposal is executed.
   All participating controllers return their tokens and clear their flags. *)
Execute ==
    /\ Cardinality(heldTokens) >= Quorum
    /\ pool' = pool + Cardinality(heldTokens)
    /\ participating' = {}
    /\ heldTokens' = {}
    /\ UNCHANGED << >>   \* no other variables

(*--------------------------------------------------------------------
  Next-state relation
--------------------------------------------------------------------*)
Next ==
    \/ \E lc \in LCs : Start(lc)
    \/ \E lc \in LCs : Vote(lc)
    \/ Execute

(*--------------------------------------------------------------------
  Specification
--------------------------------------------------------------------*)
Spec ==
    Init /\ [][Next]_<<pool, participating, heldTokens>>

(*--------------------------------------------------------------------
  Safety invariant: total number of tokens is constant
--------------------------------------------------------------------*)
TokenInvariant ==
    pool + Cardinality(heldTokens) = TokenCount

=============================================================================
cfg_text:
CONSTANTS
    LCs = {lc1, lc2, lc3, lc4}
    TokenCount = 3

INIT Init
NEXT Next
INVARIANT TokenInvariant

The print shop has a set of spooler nodes, each managing a queue of pending print jobs, and a single logical token that circulates on a ring connecting the nodes. Each node holds a Boolean flag `hasToken` and a counter `lastSeq` that records the sequence number of the last job it successfully wrote to the shared job‑log file stored on a networked disk. When a node receives the token, it may if it has a pending job, write that job to the log together with `lastSeq+1`, update its `lastSeq`, and then clear the token flag before passing the token to its successor on the ring. If the node has no pending job, it simply forwards the token without modifying the log. The token is forwarded by sending a short “token‑here” message to the next node; the receiver sets its `hasToken` flag upon receipt. If a node crashes while holding the token, the token is considered lost, and the next node detects the silence after a timeout and re‑generates a fresh token with `hasToken` set to true, but only if its `lastSeq` matches the highest sequence number seen in the log, thereby preventing duplicate writes. All other nodes continue to operate normally, using the token to gain exclusive write access and never overwriting entries they have not observed.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two distinct print jobs are ever written to the same position in the shared job‑log, so updates to the log are never lost or overwritten.

The swarm consists of many aerial drones, each running either the primary mission controller or the backup controller, and each drone maintains a local record of the current leader’s ID, its own health flag, and the surveillance slot it is currently covering. Every drone periodically broadcasts a heartbeat containing its ID and controller‑instance number; if a drone stops receiving a heartbeat from the current leader for two intervals, it initiates a leader election by sending an Election request to all drones of the same controller instance. The election proceeds by the drones of that instance comparing IDs and the highest‑ID drone replying with a Victory message, after which all drones update their leader ID to that victor’s ID. When a drone becomes leader it claims an unassigned surveillance slot from the shared pool, records the slot locally, and announces a SlotClaim message that includes both the controller instance and the slot number. All drones, regardless of instance, keep a small table of the latest SlotClaim for each slot; if they receive two different claims for the same slot, they discard the later claim and request a new slot from the pool. If the leader’s health flag flips to unhealthy, the leader sends a Relinquish message, releases its slot back into the pool, and the remaining drones trigger a new election in that instance. The backup instance runs the same protocol in parallel, but because both instances read and write the same shared pool, the SlotClaim coordination ensures that no slot is ever granted to two drones at once.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any time, a given surveillance slot in the shared pool is assigned to at most one drone across both controller instances.

The scheduler runs on a set of nodes that each represent a participant: a surgeon, an anesthesiologist, a nursing coordinator, and a central OR manager. Each participant keeps a tiny local record of two flags – whether it currently holds the coarse lock for an operating‑room block (e.g., “OR‑A‑Block”) and whether it holds the fine lock for a specific resource such as the laparoscopic tower. To start a surgery the surgeon first requests the coarse lock for the chosen block; once granted the central manager records the block as “reserved”. After the coarse lock is obtained, the nurse requests the fine lock for the needed equipment; the manager only grants it while the block lock is still held, preventing two surgeries from sharing the same equipment. If any participant takes longer than expected (for example, the anesthesiologist is delayed), it simply holds its locks longer; the protocol does not abort the whole operation but allows other participants to continue once they have released their own locks. When the procedure finishes, each participant releases its fine lock, then the surgeon releases the coarse block lock, and the manager clears the reservation. The hierarchical lock ordering guarantees that a slow participant cannot cause a dead‑end where a later surgery proceeds with resources that have not been safely reserved. 

SAFETY PROPERTY: No surgery can start using an operating‑room or equipment unless the participant that holds the coarse block lock has also granted the fine lock, preventing any unauthorized or stale access.
spec_text:
---- MODULE W4C0x8x6x3 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, Sequences, TLC

CONSTANTS Participants

VARIABLES coarseLock, fineLock, reserved

(* type constraints *)
TypeOK ==
    /\ coarseLock \in [Participants -> BOOLEAN]
    /\ fineLock   \in [Participants -> BOOLEAN]
    /\ reserved   \in BOOLEAN

(* initial state *)
Init ==
    /\ coarseLock = [p \in Participants |-> FALSE]
    /\ fineLock   = [p \in Participants |-> FALSE]
    /\ reserved   = FALSE

(* actions *)

SurgeonRequestsCoarse ==
    /\ ~coarseLock["Surgeon"]
    /\ coarseLock' = [coarseLock EXCEPT !["Surgeon"] = TRUE]
    /\ reserved'   = TRUE
    /\ UNCHANGED fineLock

NurseRequestsFine ==
    /\ coarseLock["Surgeon"]
    /\ ~fineLock["Nurse"]
    /\ fineLock' = [fineLock EXCEPT !["Nurse"] = TRUE]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<coarseLock, reserved>>

AnesthesiologistRequestsFine ==
    /\ coarseLock["Surgeon"]
    /\ ~fineLock["Anesthesiologist"]
    /\ fineLock' = [fineLock EXCEPT !["Anesthesiologist"] = TRUE]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<coarseLock, reserved>>

ReleaseFine(p) ==
    /\ p \in Participants
    /\ fineLock[p]
    /\ fineLock' = [fineLock EXCEPT ![p] = FALSE]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<coarseLock, reserved>>

SurgeonReleasesCoarse ==
    /\ coarseLock["Surgeon"]
    /\ \A p \in Participants : ~fineLock[p]   \* all fine locks released
    /\ coarseLock' = [coarseLock EXCEPT !["Surgeon"] = FALSE]
    /\ reserved'   = FALSE
    /\ UNCHANGED fineLock

Next ==
    \/ SurgeonRequestsCoarse
    \/ NurseRequestsFine
    \/ AnesthesiologistRequestsFine
    \/ \E p \in Participants : ReleaseFine(p)
    \/ SurgeonReleasesCoarse

(* safety invariant: a fine lock may be held only while the coarse block lock is held
   and the manager’s reservation is active *)
SafeFineUse ==
    \A p \in Participants :
        fineLock[p] => (coarseLock["Surgeon"] /\ reserved)

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<coarseLock, fineLock, reserved>>
====
cfg_text:
CONSTANTS Participants = {"Surgeon","Nurse","Anesthesiologist","Coordinator"}
INIT Init
NEXT Next
INVARIANT SafeFineUse

The system consists of three kinds of participants: a crane operator who wants to move a specific container, a yard controller that manages the lease for each container‑slot pair, and a privileged supervisor who can override any lease. The shared state for each container‑slot comprises (1) the identifier of the current lease holder (or “none”), (2) the lease expiration timestamp, and (3) a monotonically increasing version counter for the container’s location record. When an operator wishes to relocate a container, it sends a lease‑request to the yard controller; the controller grants the lease only if the slot is currently unowned or the existing lease has expired, and it records the operator’s ID, sets the expiry to a fixed time window, and increments the version counter. The operator may either perform the move before the expiry and then send a lease‑release (clearing the holder field) or request a lease‑extension, which the controller honors only if the request arrives before the current expiry. At any moment the supervisor may issue an override command that immediately clears the current holder, sets the version counter to a new value, and installs the supervisor as the holder with a fresh expiry, effectively pre‑empting any ongoing lease. All participants continuously read the shared state before acting, ensuring they see the most recent holder, expiry, and version. The protocol thus coordinates concurrent moves by allowing only one holder at a time, limiting the duration of ownership, and providing a single trusted escape hatch.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two operators can successfully update the location record of the same container‑slot without the version counter being incremented exactly once between them.

The lobby consists of a **Coordinator** process and a set of **Player** processes that have joined the same game room. Each player maintains a local flag `ready` and a chosen map identifier, while the coordinator keeps three state variables: the current lobby phase (`open` or `starting`), a counter of received votes for the map, and the map that achieved a quorum. When a player presses “Ready”, it sends its map vote to the coordinator; the coordinator increments its vote counter and records the map that reaches the required quorum (e.g., a majority). If some players are slow, the coordinator starts a timeout; when the timeout expires it proceeds with the votes it has, treating missing votes as abstentions, and moves the lobby phase to `starting`. The coordinator then broadcasts the selected map and the start signal to all players, who transition to the match once they receive it, even if they were delayed. A player that later receives the start signal simply joins the already‑started match; no new match can be started until the current one finishes. All participants agree on the same selected map and start time because the quorum decision is made only once per lobby phase.

SAFETY PROPERTY: At no time can two different matches be started in the same lobby simultaneously.

The system consists of three participants: the PharmacyServer that stores prescriptions, the DispenserUnit that holds medication bottles, and the PatientApp running on a patient’s phone. The DispenserUnit maintains a lease record that stores the identifier of the current holder (either a prescription id or “none”) and an expiry time, while the PharmacyServer keeps a pending‑prescription queue and a count of medication units available for each drug. When a patient scans a prescription, the PatientApp sends a *request* message to the PharmacyServer; the server creates a lease for that prescription, sets an expiry a few seconds in the future, and sends a *grant* message containing the lease id and expiry to both the PatientApp and the DispenserUnit. The DispenserUnit, upon receiving a *grant*, first checks that the lease id matches the one it currently holds (or that it holds none) and that the expiry is later than any previously stored expiry; if the check passes it records the new lease and prepares to dispense. The PatientApp can issue a *dispense* command before the lease expires; the DispenserUnit will only actually release a medication pill if the lease it holds is still valid at the moment of the command. If the lease expires before dispensing, the DispenserUnit discards the lease and returns an error, allowing the patient to retry a fresh request. All messages may arrive out of order, so each participant validates the lease’s timestamp and identifier before acting, ensuring that stale *grant* or *dispense* messages are ignored.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total number of medication pills in the system never increases or decreases except when a patient successfully receives a pill from the DispenserUnit.

The system consists of a Central Controller, several Vending Nodes (each controlling a physical dispenser), a Payment Processor, and a Monitoring Service.  
The Controller holds a coarse lock that guarantees at most one node can initiate a transaction at any time, while each node holds a fine lock on its own dispenser while the product is being delivered.  
When a customer selects a product, the node first asks the Controller for the coarse lock; once granted it acquires its fine lock, reads its local inventory counter, and sends a payment request to the Processor.  
After the Processor replies with a payment confirmation, the node decrements the inventory counter, releases the fine lock, and finally releases the coarse lock, allowing the next node to start.  
If the Processor crashes silently during a pending request, the node detects a timeout, aborts the transaction, releases any locks it holds, and reports the failure to the Monitoring Service without changing the inventory.  
The Monitoring Service can later restart the Processor, but no node ever proceeds to dispense an item without a confirmed payment.  
All state can be captured with four variables: the Controller’s coarse‑lock flag, each node’s fine‑lock flag, the node’s inventory count, and a pending‑payment boolean.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No product is dispensed unless a corresponding payment has been successfully recorded.

The system consists of three roles: a LoadController that decides how much load to shed, a GridMonitor that watches real‑time demand, and an AdminConsole used by a privileged operator. All nodes share three pieces of state: the measured currentLoad on the grid, a lockVersion integer that acts as an optimistic lock, and a boolean overrideFlag indicating an admin override. When the GridMonitor detects that demand exceeds a safety threshold, it reads the current lockVersion and requests the LoadController to compute a reduction amount. The LoadController writes the new currentLoad together with the same lockVersion it read; if the stored lockVersion has changed in the meantime, the write is rejected and the controller retries with the fresh version. If the AdminConsole sets overrideFlag to true, the next LoadController write is allowed to proceed even if the lockVersion differs, but only after the admin’s digital signature is verified. After a successful write, the winning participant updates lockVersion to the next integer and clears overrideFlag unless another admin override is pending. Any node that finds its write rejected must back off, read the latest state, and start its proposal cycle again.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No stale or unauthorized participant can cause a load‑shedding action that is not based on the latest lockVersion and a valid admin override.

The system consists of a small set of library server nodes, each holding a copy of the reservation state and a variable indicating who the current leader is.  
The leader node is responsible for accepting reservation requests for a given book, decreasing the available copy count, and broadcasting the updated count to the other nodes.  
Every node monitors heart‑beats from the leader; if a heartbeat is missed for a configurable timeout, the remaining nodes start a simple election by each announcing its identifier and the node with the highest identifier declares itself the new leader.  
When the election finishes, the new leader adopts the most recent reservation count that any node reports and resumes handling requests.  
An administrator may change the total capacity of the book at any time; the node that receives the capacity‑change command forwards the new total to the leader, which recomputes the available count and propagates the new value to all replicas.  
Clients send reservation requests to any server; if the server is not the leader it forwards the request to the current leader, which only grants a reservation when the available count is positive.  
All nodes keep only three pieces of state – the identifier of the leader, the total capacity of the book, and the current number of available copies – making the protocol modelable with three variables.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No reservation is granted by any node that is not the current leader or that uses an out‑of‑date available‑copy count.

The system consists of three participants: a Block Server that tracks each track segment, a Train Controller that issues movement commands, and individual Trains that occupy a block. The Block Server maintains three variables for each block: the current lease owner (the Train that may occupy it), the lease expiry timestamp, and a flag indicating whether the block is physically occupied. When a Train wishes to enter a block it sends a Lease‑Request to the Block Server; the server replies with a Lease‑Grant that records the Train as the lease owner and sets the expiry to the current time plus a safety margin. The Train must periodically send a Lease‑Renewal before expiry; if the server receives a Renewal it extends the expiry, otherwise the lease automatically lapses and the server clears the owner field. Because messages can arrive out of order, the server discards any Lease‑Grant or Lease‑Renewal whose timestamp is older than the most recent expiry it has recorded, ensuring that stale grants cannot resurrect an expired lease. Finally, when a Train leaves the block it sends a Release message; the server clears the occupied flag only if the releasing Train is still the recorded lease owner.

SAFETY PROPERTY: At no time can more than one Train be authorized to occupy the same track block.

The system consists of three router nodes (North, South, and Central) that each control a segment of the baggage conveyor and a central controller that decides which bag moves next.  
Each router node stores a flag indicating whether it currently holds a bag and a counter of votes it has received for the next routing action.  
When a bag reaches a router node, the node proposes to forward the bag to the next segment and sends a proposal message to the other two nodes.  
The nodes respond with a vote as soon as they are ready, and the proposing node proceeds with the move once it has collected votes from a quorum of two nodes, even if the third node is slow.  
If a node is slow, its lack of vote does not block progress; the quorum requirement ensures that the protocol tolerates delays without assuming node failure.  
After the move, the proposing node updates its flag to free the segment and notifies the recipient node, which then sets its flag to occupied.  
The central controller monitors the flags to ensure that no two nodes claim the same exclusive diverter at the same time.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two router nodes may occupy the exclusive diverter segment simultaneously, ensuring that only one bag can be routed through the diverter at any moment.

The system consists of two dispenser instances, each running a local controller, and a single shared medication reservoir that belongs to a central pool. Each controller keeps a coarse lock flag that indicates whether the whole pool is currently reserved, and a fine lock flag that indicates whether its own dispensing mechanism is in use. When a prescription arrives, the controller first asks the lock manager for the coarse lock; if granted, it checks that the pool still contains the required drug. After confirming availability, the controller then acquires its fine lock, withdraws the exact dose from the reservoir, and records that the dose has been dispensed. Once the dose is taken, the controller releases the fine lock, then releases the coarse lock so that the other instance may access the pool. The hierarchical ordering (coarse before fine) guarantees that the two dispensers never hold each other’s fine lock while competing for the shared pool. If the coarse lock is denied, the controller simply retries later without ever obtaining a fine lock.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two dispensers can hold a fine lock on the shared medication reservoir at the same time.

The system has three participants: the Runway Manager, each Aircraft that wants to land, and a Capacity Monitor that can increase or decrease the number of simultaneous landings allowed on the runway.  
The Runway Manager maintains a single lease record consisting of the identifier of the aircraft that currently holds the lease and a timestamp indicating when that lease expires.  
An aircraft may request a lease; if the lease is free and the current number of active leases is below the capacity reported by the Capacity Monitor, the Runway Manager grants a lease with a fixed duration.  
While holding a lease, an aircraft is allowed to occupy the runway and must either land before the lease expires or voluntarily release it early, upon which the manager clears the lease record.  
When the Capacity Monitor reports a lower capacity, the Runway Manager does not grant new leases until the number of active leases falls to the new limit, but it never forces an aircraft to relinquish a lease that is already in progress.  
If the capacity is increased, the manager resumes granting leases up to the new limit, using the same lease‑expiry mechanism to ensure that only a bounded number of aircraft can be on the runway at any time.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The expiration of a given runway lease occurs at most once.

The line has three active participants: the **Entry Sensor** that detects an approaching car, the **Gate Controller** that opens the entry gate, and the **Wash Unit** that starts the washing cycle. All three share a single compare‑and‑swap (CAS) register that holds a two‑field value – a *slot token* (either FREE, REQUESTED, or BUSY) and a monotonic *epoch* number. When the sensor sees a car it increments the epoch, writes (REQUESTED, new‑epoch) into the register using CAS, and sends a “car‑arrived” message to the controller; the controller, upon receiving any message, reads the register and succeeds with a CAS only if the register still contains (REQUESTED, same‑epoch), at which point it changes the token to BUSY and opens the gate. The Wash Unit periodically reads the register; if it sees (BUSY, epoch) it knows a car is in the wash and, after completing the wash, performs a CAS to set the token back to FREE while keeping the epoch unchanged. Because messages can be reordered, every message carries the epoch it was generated with, and each participant ignores any message whose epoch does not match the current epoch stored in the register. This ensures that only the most recent request can ever acquire the BUSY token, preventing an old “car‑arrived” notice from reopening the gate after the wash has already finished.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No stale or unauthorized participant can set the gate to open when the CAS register does not currently hold a matching REQUESTED entry for that participant’s epoch.

The line controller first obtains a coarse lock on the entire conveyor segment that a car is about to enter, preventing any other controller from assigning a new car to that segment. While holding the coarse lock, the controller then requests a fine lock on the specific wash‑bay slot (e.g., “Bay 3”) that it plans to use for the car. Each wash‑bay sensor acknowledges the fine‑lock request and records the car’s identifier, but because messages may be reordered, the controller re‑checks the sensor’s acknowledgment before proceeding to the next step. After both locks are confirmed, the controller sends a “move‑forward” command to the conveyor motor; the motor only acts if it still sees the coarse lock active. Once the car reaches the bay, the bay’s water‑spray module acquires its own internal lock, performs the wash cycle, and then releases the fine lock. Finally, the controller releases the coarse conveyor lock, allowing the next car to be scheduled. All participants periodically broadcast their lock state so that any out‑of‑order messages can be ignored if they refer to a lock that has already been released.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No wash‑bay slot is ever assigned to more than one car at the same time.
spec_text:
---- MODULE W4C4x8x3x1 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets, TLC

CONSTANTS Cars, Bays, Controllers

VARIABLES coarseLock, fineLock, sensorAck, bayAssignments

(* A distinguished value meaning “no lock / no car”. *)
Null == "null"

(* ---------- Initialization ---------- *)
Init ==
    /\ coarseLock = Null
    /\ fineLock = [b \in Bays |-> Null]
    /\ sensorAck = [b \in Bays |-> Null]
    /\ bayAssignments = {}

(* ---------- Actions ---------- *)

(* A controller grabs the coarse lock for the whole segment. *)
ObtainCoarseLock(c) ==
    /\ c \in Controllers
    /\ coarseLock = Null
    /\ coarseLock' = c
    /\ UNCHANGED << fineLock, sensorAck, bayAssignments >>

(* While holding the coarse lock, the controller asks a specific bay for a fine lock.
   The bay’s sensor records the car identifier. *)
RequestFineLock(c, b, car) ==
    /\ c \in Controllers
    /\ b \in Bays
    /\ car \in Cars
    /\ coarseLock = c
    /\ fineLock[b] = Null
    /\ fineLock' = [fineLock EXCEPT ![b] = c]
    /\ sensorAck' = [sensorAck EXCEPT ![b] = car]
    /\ UNCHANGED << coarseLock, bayAssignments >>

(* The controller re‑checks the sensor acknowledgment (messages may be reordered). *)
SensorAckCheck(c, b, car) ==
    /\ c \in Controllers
    /\ b \in Bays
    /\ car \in Cars
    /\ coarseLock = c
    /\ fineLock[b] = c
    /\ sensorAck[b] = car
    /\ UNCHANGED << coarseLock, fineLock, sensorAck, bayAssignments >>

(* After both locks are confirmed the controller tells the motor to move the car forward. *)
MoveForward(c, b, car) ==
    /\ c \in Controllers
    /\ b \in Bays
    /\ car \in Cars
    /\ coarseLock = c
    /\ fineLock[b] = c
    /\ sensorAck[b] = car
    /\ <<b, car>> \notin bayAssignments
    /\ bayAssignments' = bayAssignments \cup {<<b, car>>}
    /\ UNCHANGED << coarseLock, fineLock, sensorAck >>

(* The wash‑bay’s water‑spray module performs the wash (abstracted). *)
WashCycle(b, car) ==
    /\ b \in Bays
    /\ car \in Cars
    /\ <<b, car>> \in bayAssignments
    /\ UNCHANGED << coarseLock, fineLock, sensorAck, bayAssignments >>

(* The bay releases its fine lock after the wash is done. *)
ReleaseFineLock(c, b, car) ==
    /\ c \in Controllers
    /\ b \in Bays
    /\ car \in Cars
    /\ fineLock[b] = c
    /\ <<b, car>> \in bayAssignments
    /\ fineLock' = [fineLock EXCEPT ![b] = Null]
    /\ sensorAck' = [sensorAck EXCEPT ![b] = Null]
    /\ bayAssignments' = bayAssignments \ {<<b, car>>}
    /\ UNCHANGED coarseLock

(* Finally the controller releases the coarse lock, allowing the next car to be scheduled. *)
ReleaseCoarseLock(c) ==
    /\ c \in Controllers
    /\ coarseLock = c
    /\ \A b \in Bays : fineLock[b] = Null
    /\ coarseLock' = Null
    /\ UNCHANGED << fineLock, sensorAck, bayAssignments >>

(* ---------- Next-state relation ---------- *)
Next ==
    \/ \E c \in Controllers : ObtainCoarseLock(c)
    \/ \E c \in Controllers, b \in Bays, car \in Cars : RequestFineLock(c, b, car)
    \/ \E c \in Controllers, b \in Bays, car \in Cars : SensorAckCheck(c, b, car)
    \/ \E c \in Controllers, b \in Bays, car \in Cars : MoveForward(c, b, car)
    \/ \E b \in Bays, car \in Cars : WashCycle(b, car)          \* optional, does not change state
    \/ \E c \in Controllers, b \in Bays, car \in Cars : ReleaseFineLock(c, b, car)
    \/ \E c \in Controllers : ReleaseCoarseLock(c)

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<coarseLock, fineLock, sensorAck, bayAssignments>>

(* ---------- Safety invariant ----------
   No wash‑bay slot is ever assigned to more than one car at the same time. *)
NoDoubleAssign ==
    \A b \in Bays :
        \A c1, c2 \in Cars :
            (<<b, c1>> \in bayAssignments /\ <<b, c2>> \in bayAssignments) => c1 = c2

=============================================================================

The spooler consists of a set of printer nodes, each running a local spool manager that holds a queue of print jobs and a token ring that passes a single token around the nodes. Each node maintains two variables: the current capacity of its output buffer (the number of slots it can accept) and a flag indicating whether it currently holds the token. When a node receives the token, it may allocate one free buffer slot to the next waiting job in its queue, then optionally update its capacity if a technician has added or removed paper trays. After allocating, the node records the index of the allocated slot in a local log and forwards the token to the next node in the ring. If the node’s capacity changes while it does not hold the token, it records the new capacity but does not allocate any jobs until it regains the token. The token ensures that only one node can allocate a slot at a time, so competing nodes cannot assign the same slot simultaneously. The ring continues indefinitely, allowing each node to periodically re‑evaluate its capacity and allocate jobs as long as it holds the token.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two printer nodes ever allocate the same output‑buffer slot to different jobs.

The network consists of a set of vending machines grouped into two logical instances, the SnackCluster and the DrinkCluster, each running its own leader‑election algorithm. Every machine stores three local variables: its current role (leader or follower), a monotonically increasing term number, and a copy of the last known CentralCredit balance that all machines share. Machines periodically broadcast heart‑beat messages; if a follower does not receive a heart‑beat within a timeout it increments its term, announces a candidacy, and the machine with the highest identifier in that term becomes the new leader for its cluster. The elected leader acquires an exclusive lock on the CentralCredit record, applies any pending sales updates from its cluster, writes the new balance atomically, and then releases the lock. Should the leader crash, the lock is considered free and the next election proceeds, guaranteeing that exactly one machine holds the lock at any time. Both clusters obey the same lock protocol, so even though they run independent elections, only one leader—whether from SnackCluster or DrinkCluster—can modify CentralCredit at a time. The protocol also includes a fallback where a follower that observes an outdated term automatically steps down, preventing split‑brain scenarios.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No update to the CentralCredit balance is lost or overwritten by concurrent leaders.

The system consists of three smart‑home door locks – Front, Back and Garage – each running a lightweight controller that participates in a logical token ring. Each controller keeps two pieces of state: a Boolean flag “hasToken” that tells whether it currently owns the exclusive‑access token, and a queue of incoming unlock requests that arrived while it did not have the token. When a lock receives an unlock request from a resident’s smartphone, it appends the request to its queue; if it already has the token it immediately processes the request by unlocking the door, otherwise it simply records the request for later. A lock that holds the token checks its queue, serves the oldest request, and then passes the token to the next lock in the ring by sending a “token‑forward” message. Because network messages can be reordered, each token‑forward message carries a monotonically increasing sequence number and the receiver only accepts the token if the sequence number is higher than any it has already seen, discarding out‑of‑order duplicates. After receiving a valid token, the lock updates its “hasToken” flag, processes any queued requests, and repeats the forwarding step. The ring therefore guarantees that at most one lock can be in the unlocked state at any moment, even if messages arrive out of order.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No more than one door lock can hold the exclusive‑access token (and thus be unlocked) at any time.

The system consists of two wash‑controller instances, each responsible for a segment of the conveyor, and a shared pool of numbered wash slots that can hold a car while it is being cleaned. Each controller keeps a local copy of the pool’s version number and a flag indicating whether it currently holds a lock on a particular slot. When a car arrives, a controller reads the current version, selects an unused slot, writes a tentative “reserved” marker together with the version it read, and proceeds to the next step only if the write succeeds without detecting a newer version. If the write finds that another controller has already updated the version, the reservation is aborted, the controller backs off, refreshes the version, and retries the selection process. Once a reservation is confirmed, the controller marks the slot as “occupied,” performs the wash, and finally clears the slot and increments the shared version to signal completion. The optimistic‑locking protocol ensures that only one controller can successfully commit a reservation for any given slot, while the retry loop guarantees progress when conflicts occur. The two controllers therefore cooperate through the shared version counter and the slot status fields, never needing a centralized lock manager.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No wash slot is ever assigned to more than one car at the same time.

The system consists of a Load‑Shed Dispatcher that controls a bounded work queue of shed‑slot requests and a set of Load Devices (e.g., transformer units) that actually curtail load when instructed. The Dispatcher keeps two pieces of state: the current number of pending slots in the queue (which never exceeds a fixed capacity) and a map that records which slot, if any, is currently allocated to each device. Each Load Device maintains a single flag indicating whether it presently holds an allocated slot and a timestamp of the last acknowledgement it sent back to the Dispatcher. When the Dispatcher receives a new load‑shedding request, it inserts a slot into the queue only if the queue is not full; then it picks the next idle device, marks that slot as allocated to that device, and sends the allocation message. Upon receiving the allocation, a Device begins shedding, and once it has completed the action it sends an acknowledgment; the Dispatcher clears the allocation entry and removes the slot from the queue, freeing capacity for new requests. If a Device is slow, the Dispatcher observes the missing acknowledgment and, because the slot remains marked as allocated, it does not reuse that slot for any other Device, thereby applying backpressure by refusing to enqueue further requests once the queue is full. This coordination guarantees that each shed slot is owned by at most one Device at any moment, even when some Devices respond slowly but do not fail.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two devices are ever assigned the same shed slot at the same time.

Traders submit buy or sell orders together with the current auction epoch number to a central coordinator. The coordinator keeps a single epoch counter, a list of pending orders for that epoch, and a map that records which price‑time slot has been allocated to which order. When the coordinator decides to start a new auction it increments the epoch, clears the pending‑order list, and broadcasts the new epoch number to all participants. Each participant only accepts an order or an allocation message whose epoch matches the epoch it has most recently recorded, discarding any older or out‑of‑order messages. After the order‑collection phase ends, the matching engine processes the pending orders for the active epoch, creates a set of non‑conflicting slot allocations, and sends each allocation together with the epoch identifier back to the traders. Traders apply an allocation only if its epoch equals the one they stored, ensuring that a later reconfiguration cannot retroactively apply an earlier allocation.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No price‑time slot is ever allocated to more than one order within the same auction epoch.

The system consists of three kinds of participants: **Patients** who submit prescription requests, **Dispenser Slots** that hold a single medication package, and a **Capacity Manager** that can raise or lower the total number of active slots while the dispenser is running. All participants share a single compare‑and‑swap register called **SlotMap**, which stores a compact encoding of which slots are currently occupied and the current capacity limit. When a patient arrives, it reads the register, picks a free slot index, and attempts a compare‑and‑swap that changes the slot’s bit from 0 (empty) to 1 (filled) while also verifying that the total number of 1‑bits does not exceed the capacity field stored in the same word. The Capacity Manager periodically reads the register, computes a new capacity value based on inventory or staffing, and then performs a compare‑and‑swap that updates only the capacity field, leaving the slot occupancy bits unchanged. If a compare‑and‑swap fails because another participant modified the register first, the actor rereads the register and retries its operation. Dispenser Slots themselves never act; they are only represented by the bits in the register that indicate whether a package is present. This protocol can be modeled with three state variables: `slots` (a bit‑vector of occupied slots), `capacity` (the current limit), and `version` (used implicitly by the compare‑and‑swap to detect interference).

SAFETY PROPERTY: At no time does the number of occupied dispenser slots ever exceed the current capacity value.

The system consists of three signal controllers – North, Central and South – each responsible for one block of the line, and a central administrative console that can issue an override.  
Each controller keeps a local copy of the block’s “clearance level” (closed, approach, or cleared) and a flag indicating whether it has voted on the most recent requested change.  
When a train approaches a block, the controller that detects the train proposes a new clearance level and broadcasts the proposal to the other two controllers.  
The three controllers then exchange votes; the proposal is committed only when at least two controllers have voted “accept”, at which point each updates its local clearance level to the new value.  
If an admin issues an override through the console, the override carries a special “override” flag; the console’s message is automatically counted as two votes, so a single controller’s dissent is insufficient to block the change.  
When an override is accepted, all controllers replace their clearance level with the admin‑specified value, regardless of their previous votes, and reset their vote flags.  
If the quorum is not reached within a timeout, the proposal is aborted and the controllers retain their previous clearance level.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two controllers ever record different clearance levels for the same block at the same logical time.
spec_text:
---- MODULE W4C10x5x1x5 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, Sequences, FiniteSets

CONSTANTS Controllers

VARIABLES clearance, hasProp, propBlock, propLevel, propVotes

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Domain definitions
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Levels == {"closed", "approach", "cleared"}

Blocks == Controllers          \* each controller maintains a copy for each block

NoBlock == ""                 \* placeholder used when there is no active proposal

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Initial state
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Init ==
    /\ clearance = [c \in Controllers |-> [b \in Blocks |-> "closed"]]
    /\ hasProp   = FALSE
    /\ propBlock = NoBlock
    /\ propLevel = NoBlock
    /\ propVotes = {}

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Actions
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Propose(c, b, l) ==
    /\ c \in Controllers
    /\ b \in Blocks
    /\ l \in Levels
    /\ hasProp = FALSE                     \* no outstanding proposal
    /\ hasProp'   = TRUE
    /\ propBlock' = b
    /\ propLevel' = l
    /\ propVotes' = {c}                    \* proposer implicitly votes accept
    /\ UNCHANGED <<clearance>>

Vote(c) ==
    /\ c \in Controllers
    /\ hasProp = TRUE
    /\ c \notin propVotes
    /\ hasProp'   = TRUE
    /\ propVotes' = propVotes \cup {c}
    /\ UNCHANGED <<clearance, propBlock, propLevel>>

Commit ==
    /\ hasProp = TRUE
    /\ Cardinality(propVotes) >= 2        \* quorum reached
    /\ hasProp'   = FALSE
    /\ propBlock' = NoBlock
    /\ propLevel' = NoBlock
    /\ propVotes' = {}
    /\ clearance' = [c \in Controllers |-> 
          [b \in Blocks |-> IF b = propBlock THEN propLevel ELSE clearance[c][b]]]

Override(c, b, l) ==
    /\ c \in Controllers
    /\ b \in Blocks
    /\ l \in Levels
    /\ hasProp'   = FALSE                  \* any pending proposal is discarded
    /\ propBlock' = NoBlock
    /\ propLevel' = NoBlock
    /\ propVotes' = {}
    /\ clearance' = [c2 \in Controllers |-> 
          [b2 \in Blocks |-> IF b2 = b THEN l ELSE clearance[c2][b2]]]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<>>

Abort ==
    /\ hasProp = TRUE
    /\ hasProp'   = FALSE
    /\ propBlock' = NoBlock
    /\ propLevel' = NoBlock
    /\ propVotes' = {}
    /\ UNCHANGED clearance

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Next-state relation
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Next ==
    \/ \E c \in Controllers, b \in Blocks, l \in Levels: Propose(c, b, l)
    \/ \E c \in Controllers: Vote(c)
    \/ Commit
    \/ \E c \in Controllers, b \in Blocks, l \in Levels: Override(c, b, l)
    \/ Abort

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Specification
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<clearance, hasProp, propBlock, propLevel, propVotes>>

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Safety invariant (the property from the natural‑language description)
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Consistent ==
    \A b \in Blocks: \A c1, c2 \in Controllers: clearance[c1][b] = clearance[c2][b]

====

CONSTANT Controllers = {"North", "Central", "South"}

INIT Init
NEXT Next
INVARIANT Consistent
