The system consists of a central Inventory Service that holds the current count of each blood type and a version number, and many Hospital nodes that request to reserve or donate units. Each Hospital first reads the current count and version for the needed blood type from the Inventory Service, then locally computes the new count after adding or subtracting the requested units. The Hospital sends an Update message containing the proposed new count together with the version it observed; the Inventory Service checks whether its stored version still matches the one in the message. If the versions match, the Inventory Service records the new count, increments its version, and replies with an Acknowledge; otherwise it rejects the update, forcing the Hospital to retry the whole read‑compute‑write cycle. Because network messages may arrive out of order, a Hospital may receive an older Acknowledge after it has already issued a later request, so the Hospital discards any Acknowledge that does not reference the version it most recently submitted. This optimistic‑locking‑with‑retry loop guarantees that only one Hospital’s change is applied at a time, despite reordering, and that each change respects the current inventory state.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total number of stored blood units for any type never exceeds the maximum capacity defined for the inventory.

The router consists of two conveyor controllers, the Loader and the Unloader, and a shared compare‑and‑swap register that holds the identifier of the belt currently authorized to move a bag.  
Each controller maintains a local flag indicating whether it believes it owns the register and a counter of how many bags it has placed on or removed from the belt.  
When the Loader wants to forward a bag, it reads the register; if the register already contains Loader’s identifier it proceeds, otherwise it attempts a compare‑and‑swap from the current value to Loader’s identifier.  
The Unloader performs the symmetric operation: it reads the register and, if it does not already own it, tries a compare‑and‑swap to claim the register before taking a bag off the belt.  
If a compare‑and‑swap succeeds, the controller updates its local flag to true and increments its counter; if it fails, it leaves its flag false and retries later.  
A silently crashing controller may stop responding at any point, leaving the register unchanged, but the other controller can still read the unchanged value and eventually reclaim the register with a successful compare‑and‑swap.  
The protocol therefore ensures that at any moment at most one controller believes it owns the register and may move a bag, while the other either waits or retries.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total number of bags that have entered the router is always equal to the sum of bags currently on the belt plus the bags that have been unloaded, so no bag is created or destroyed.

The system consists of two blood‑bank instances, each running its own inventory service, but both draw units from a single shared pool of refrigerated slots. Each instance has a coordinator that first acquires a coarse lock on the whole pool to guarantee exclusive access while it decides which slot to allocate, then releases the coarse lock and acquires a fine‑grained lock on the chosen slot before actually recording the allocation. The shared state kept by each coordinator is: (1) the identifier of the slot currently locked at fine granularity, and (2) a flag indicating whether the coarse lock on the pool is held. When a hospital request arrives, the coordinator obtains the coarse lock, searches the pool for a suitable free slot, releases the coarse lock, takes the fine lock on that slot, and finally marks the slot as occupied with the blood type and expiration date. If the fine lock cannot be obtained because another instance already holds it, the coordinator aborts the allocation, releases any locks it holds, and retries later. A reclamation process that removes expired units also follows the same coarse‑then‑fine lock pattern, ensuring it never interferes with an active allocation. All communication between the two instances is limited to lock acquisition messages; no other shared data is exchanged.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two instances can ever mark the same refrigerated slot as occupied at the same time.

The network consists of a set of vending machines, a central inventory manager, and customers who send purchase requests. Each vending machine keeps two local variables: the identifier of the product slot it currently “owns” (leaseOwner) and the time at which that lease expires (leaseExpiry); the manager maintains a global stock count for each slot. When a customer selects a product, the machine sends a lease‑request to the manager indicating the desired slot; the manager replies with a lease‑grant that includes a fresh lease identifier and an expiry timestamp. The machine may dispense the item only while it holds a lease that has not expired, after which it decrements the manager’s stock count and sends a lease‑release; the manager updates the stock and may re‑grant the lease to another machine. If messages arrive out of order, each message carries the lease identifier and expiry; a machine discards a lease‑grant that does not match a pending request or that is already stale, and the manager ignores a release for a lease it has already re‑issued. Periodically the manager scans for leases whose expiry has passed and automatically revokes them, allowing other machines to obtain fresh leases. This lease‑based coordination guarantees that at any moment at most one machine can dispense from a given slot, despite reordered communication.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The number of items dispensed from any product slot never exceeds the physical stock count for that slot.

The fleet consists of autonomous robots (Pickers) and a central Lease Server that governs exclusive access to each pallet. Each robot keeps a local variable recording which pallet it currently believes it owns and the expiry time of that lease; the server maintains a single table entry for every pallet indicating the current holder and the lease deadline. When a robot wants to move a pallet, it sends a lease‑request to the server; the server grants the lease only if the pallet’s current lease has expired, updates the table, and returns the new deadline to the requester. While holding a lease, a robot may periodically send a lease‑renewal message; the server extends the deadline if the renewal arrives before expiry. If a robot crashes silently, it stops sending renewals, so the lease deadline eventually passes and the server marks the pallet as free, allowing another robot to request it. Any robot that receives a grant must first verify that its local expiry matches the server’s deadline before acting on the pallet. No robot ever moves a pallet unless it has a currently valid lease, and the server never assigns a pallet to two robots at the same time.

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any moment a pallet is assigned to at most one robot, so no pallet is created or destroyed by the leasing protocol.

The system consists of a LoadController that decides when to shed load, a RegionalLockManager that holds a coarse lock for the whole grid segment, and a set of SubstationLock agents that hold fine‑grained locks for individual substations. Each participant keeps only three pieces of state: the coarse‑lock flag (free or held), the list of fine‑lock identifiers currently owned, and the current aggregate load measured at the controller. When the controller detects that the total load exceeds the safe threshold, it first requests the coarse lock from the RegionalLockManager; once granted, it proceeds to request fine locks from the relevant SubstationLock agents for the substations it intends to curtail. After it has obtained all needed fine locks, the controller reduces the load on those substations, updates the load level, and then releases the fine locks followed by the coarse lock. A privileged admin may at any time issue an override command that instantly forces the release of the coarse lock and all fine locks, allowing an emergency shutdown to proceed regardless of the normal lock acquisition order. All participants obey the rule that no new fine‑lock request is accepted while an admin override is active, ensuring that the override can preempt the normal hierarchical locking sequence.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total load on any grid segment never exceeds its configured maximum capacity.

The network consists of a handful of smart‑door locks, each of which can act as a coordinator, and a privileged admin console that can issue an emergency override. Every lock stores three pieces of information: the identifier of the lock it currently believes to be the leader, a flag indicating whether the lock is in normal or override mode, and the current lock/unlock state of its own door. When a lock detects that the leader has stopped responding, it broadcasts an election request and the first lock that receives a majority of affirmative replies declares itself the new leader and updates its leader identifier. The new leader then sends a “heartbeat” message containing the current door state to all other locks; any lock that receives a newer heartbeat overwrites its stored leader identifier and synchronises its door state. If the admin console issues an override, it sets its override flag and forces the designated lock into the override mode, temporarily suppressing the normal election process until the admin clears the flag. Once the override flag is cleared, the affected lock resumes participating in elections, and the network reconverges on a leader using the same heartbeat mechanism.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No update to the shared record of the elected leader is ever lost, ensuring that at any moment only one lock is recorded as the leader.

The system consists of a set of library clients, a primary Reservation Manager, and a Backup Manager that can take over if the primary crashes. Each participant stores two pieces of state: the current epoch number and a table mapping book identifiers to the client that holds the reservation for that epoch. When a client wants to reserve a book it sends a Reserve request together with the epoch it believes is current to the Reservation Manager. The Reservation Manager first checks that the request’s epoch matches its own epoch, then records the reservation in its table and replies with an Acknowledge that includes the same epoch. If the primary Reservation Manager crashes silently, the Backup detects the missing heartbeat, increments the epoch, copies the latest reservation table it has, and assumes the role of primary. All future clients must include the new epoch in their requests, and any request bearing an older epoch is rejected as stale. The epoch number therefore guarantees that only the most recent manager can modify reservations and that stale or unauthorized requests are ignored.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No client can successfully reserve a book that has already been reserved by another client in a later epoch.

The Track Controller (TC) manages a single signalling block and initiates a reservation when a train requests entry.  
Each Train (the requester) holds a local flag indicating whether it has received a *prepare* request, a vote (“ready” or “abort”), and later a *commit* command from the TC.  
In the first phase the TC sends a prepare message to the train; the train checks that the block ahead is free in its local view and replies “ready” if it can enter, otherwise it replies “abort”.  
If the TC receives a ready vote from all participants before a timeout, it enters the second phase and sends a commit message that tells the train to occupy the block and updates the block’s state to “occupied”.  
If any vote is abort or a timeout expires (which could be caused by a silent crash of the train), the TC sends an abort message to all participants and resets the block state to “free”.  
A crashed train that never replies is treated as having voted abort, so the TC never commits a reservation that cannot be confirmed.  
All messages are reliable but may be delayed, and the TC ensures that at most one commit is ever issued for a given block.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No signalling block is ever occupied by more than one train at the same time.

The system consists of a Block Controller (BC) for each track block and the Train‑Control Unit (TCU) of every train that wants to enter that block. Each BC keeps a two‑bit state: `idle` or `prepared`, and each TCU records whether it has sent a `prepare` request and whether it has received a `commit` acknowledgment for a given block. When a train wishes to occupy a block, its TCU sends a `prepare` message to the BC; the BC records `prepared` and replies with a `ready` message that includes a monotonically increasing sequence number. After receiving `ready` from all BCs covering the block, the TCU broadcasts a `commit` message containing the same sequence number, and each BC, upon seeing the matching `commit`, atomically switches the block to `occupied` and sends back a `commit‑ok`. If a BC receives a stale or out‑of‑order message (detectable by the sequence number), it ignores it, ensuring that reordering cannot cause an inconsistent state. Should any BC fail to reply with `ready` within a timeout, the TCU issues an `abort` with the original sequence number, and every BC that is still in `prepared` reverts to `idle`. All participants rely on the two‑phase commit messages and sequence numbers to coordinate safely despite possible message reordering.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two trains can be granted the `occupied` state for the same track block at the same time.

The system consists of a Grid Operator (the coordinator) and a set of Substation Controllers that each manage a local load‑shedding actuator. Each Substation Controller maintains a binary flag “prepared” that indicates it has verified that its local loads can be shed, and a vote (“ready” or “abort”) it will send back to the Grid Operator. The Grid Operator runs a two‑phase commit: in the first phase it broadcasts a shed request, collects votes, and if all are “ready” it moves to a pre‑commit stage where it atomically reserves the required megawatts from the Shared Load Pool. In the second phase the Grid Operator issues a commit message, the Substation Controllers then execute the actual disconnection of their assigned loads, and finally the reserved megawatts are deducted from the pool. Two independent load‑shed instances (for example “day‑time” and “emergency”) share the same pool, so each instance must first check that the pool has enough free megawatts before entering the pre‑commit stage, preventing double‑reservation across instances. If any controller votes “abort”, the Grid Operator aborts the transaction, releases any provisional reservations, and the pool state is left unchanged. All messages are asynchronous but the two‑phase commit guarantees that either all controllers shed their loads or none do, even when both instances are active concurrently.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: A megawatt of load is physically disconnected by a substation at most once for any given load‑shed instance.
spec_text:
---- MODULE W4C9x2x5x2 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets

CONSTANTS Substations, Instances, TotalPool

VARIABLES pool, reserved, committed, state, vote, prepared, disconnectCount

(* -------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* Helper definitions *)

Needed == Cardinality(Substations) \* each substation sheds 1 MW

(* -------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* Initialization *)

Init ==
    /\ pool = TotalPool
    /\ reserved = [i \in Instances |-> 0]
    /\ committed = [i \in Instances |-> 0]
    /\ state = [i \in Instances |-> "idle"]
    /\ vote = [i \in Instances |-> [s \in Substations |-> "ready"]]
    /\ prepared = [i \in Instances |-> [s \in Substations |-> FALSE]]
    /\ disconnectCount = [i \in Instances |-> [s \in Substations |-> 0]]

(* -------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* Actions *)

Request(i) ==
    /\ i \in Instances
    /\ state[i] = "idle"
    /\ state' = [state EXCEPT ![i] = "collect"]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<pool, reserved, committed, vote, prepared, disconnectCount>>

Prepare(s,i) ==
    /\ s \in Substations /\ i \in Instances
    /\ state[i] = "collect"
    /\ prepared' = [prepared EXCEPT ![i][s] = TRUE]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<pool, reserved, committed, state, vote, disconnectCount>>

Vote(s,i,v) ==
    /\ s \in Substations /\ i \in Instances /\ v \in {"ready","abort"}
    /\ state[i] = "collect"
    /\ prepared[i][s] = TRUE
    /\ vote' = [vote EXCEPT ![i][s] = v]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<pool, reserved, committed, state, prepared, disconnectCount>>

Collect(i) ==
    /\ i \in Instances
    /\ state[i] = "collect"
    /\ \A s \in Substations: vote[i][s] # "abort"      \* all votes are “ready”
    /\ pool >= Needed                                 \* enough free MW
    /\ state' = [state EXCEPT ![i] = "precommit"]
    /\ pool' = pool - Needed
    /\ reserved' = [reserved EXCEPT ![i] = Needed]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<committed, vote, prepared, disconnectCount>>

AbortCollect(i) ==
    /\ i \in Instances
    /\ state[i] = "collect"
    /\ \E s \in Substations: vote[i][s] = "abort"
    /\ state' = [state EXCEPT ![i] = "idle"]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<pool, reserved, committed, vote, prepared, disconnectCount>>

Commit(i) ==
    /\ i \in Instances
    /\ state[i] = "precommit"
    /\ state' = [state EXCEPT ![i] = "commit"]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<pool, reserved, committed, vote, prepared, disconnectCount>>

Disconnect(s,i) ==
    /\ s \in Substations /\ i \in Instances
    /\ state[i] = "commit"
    /\ disconnectCount[i][s] = 0
    /\ disconnectCount' = [disconnectCount EXCEPT ![i][s] = @ + 1]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<pool, reserved, committed, state, vote, prepared>>

Finish(i) ==
    /\ i \in Instances
    /\ state[i] = "commit"
    /\ \A s \in Substations: disconnectCount[i][s] = 1
    /\ state' = [state EXCEPT ![i] = "idle"]
    /\ committed' = [committed EXCEPT ![i] = committed[i] + reserved[i]]
    /\ reserved' = [reserved EXCEPT ![i] = 0]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<pool, vote, prepared, disconnectCount>>

AbortPre(i) ==
    /\ i \in Instances
    /\ state[i] = "precommit"
    /\ state' = [state EXCEPT ![i] = "idle"]
    /\ pool' = pool + reserved[i]
    /\ reserved' = [reserved EXCEPT ![i] = 0]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<committed, vote, prepared, disconnectCount>>

(* -------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* Next-state relation *)

Next ==
    \/ \E i \in Instances: Request(i)
    \/ \E i \in Instances, s \in Substations: Prepare(s,i)
    \/ \E i \in Instances, s \in Substations, v \in {"ready","abort"}: Vote(s,i,v)
    \/ \E i \in Instances: Collect(i)
    \/ \E i \in Instances: AbortCollect(i)
    \/ \E i \in Instances: Commit(i)
    \/ \E i \in Instances, s \in Substations: Disconnect(s,i)
    \/ \E i \in Instances: Finish(i)
    \/ \E i \in Instances: AbortPre(i)

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<pool, reserved, committed, state, vote, prepared, disconnectCount>>

(* -------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* Safety invariant: a megawatt is disconnected at most once per instance *)

NoDoubleDisconnect ==
    \A i \in Instances: \A s \in Substations: disconnectCount[i][s] <= 1

=============================================================================

    Substations = {s1, s2, s3}
    Instances   = {"Day", "Emergency"}
    TotalPool   = 5

INIT Init
NEXT Next
INVARIANT NoDoubleDisconnect

The swarm consists of two independent surveillance instances, Instance A and Instance B, each driving a set of drones that collect fire‑hotspot images. Both instances submit image‑processing jobs to a single bounded work queue that holds at most N jobs; the queue is shared with a pool of M edge‑computing nodes that execute the jobs. Each instance maintains three simple state variables: the number of jobs it has queued, a flag indicating whether it is currently blocked by back‑pressure, and a local counter of jobs it has completed. When an instance wishes to add a new image‑processing job, it first checks whether the queue is full; if the queue is full, it sets its back‑pressure flag and pauses until a slot frees, otherwise it enqueues the job and increments its queued counter. Edge‑computing nodes repeatedly dequeue the oldest job, execute it, then return the result to the originating instance, which decrements its queued counter and increments its completed counter. After each job finishes, the node signals both instances that a queue slot is available, allowing any blocked instance to clear its back‑pressure flag and resume enqueuing. The two instances never directly compete for the same edge node; the queue’s bounded capacity and explicit back‑pressure ensure that jobs are handed out in FIFO order and that no node is assigned more than one job at a time.

**SAFETY PROPERTY:** No two instances may have a job executing on the same edge‑computing node simultaneously.

The system consists of three participants: the client’s reservation app, the central catalog service that holds the inventory of copies, and the notification service that sends confirmation emails. Each participant keeps a single Boolean flag indicating whether it has voted “ready” for a given reservation request, plus a shared record that stores the current reservation state (unreserved, pending, or confirmed). When a user requests a book, the client sends a *prepare* message to the catalog and notification services; both reply with “ready” only if the requested copy is still available and they can send a confirmation. If both replies are received, the client issues a *commit* message, causing the catalog to mark the copy as reserved and the notification service to dispatch an email, and finally records the reservation as confirmed. If either participant replies “abort” (e.g., because another reservation succeeded first) the client sends an *abort* message, and both participants discard any provisional change, leaving the shared record in the unreserved state. A privileged admin may send an *override* command at any time; upon receipt the catalog immediately forces the copy into the reserved state and marks the shared record as “admin‑reserved”, bypassing the normal two‑phase voting but still broadcasting a commit to the notification service for consistency. The two‑phase commit protocol therefore guarantees that, except for an admin override, all participants either all commit the reservation or all abort it, keeping the shared state consistent.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No reservation record is ever overwritten or removed without first being recorded as either aborted or committed.

The system consists of a set of printer nodes (Printer‑A, Printer‑B, …) that share a single token which grants the right to start a print job. Each node maintains two variables: a boolean `hasToken` indicating whether it currently holds the token, and an integer `queueCount` recording how many jobs are waiting for that printer. When a node receives the token it checks its `queueCount`; if the count is greater than zero it dequeues one job, sends a “job‑started” announcement to all nodes, and then passes the token to the next node in the ring. If the count is zero the node simply forwards the token without starting any job. Because messages may be reordered, every token‑pass and job‑started announcement carries a monotonically increasing sequence number, and a node only acts on a token or announcement whose sequence number is larger than any it has already processed. Nodes update their `queueCount` when they receive a new job request from the front‑desk and when they observe a “job‑started” announcement for their own printer. The token ring guarantees that at most one printer can be printing at any moment, even though the acknowledgments may arrive out of order. The protocol therefore requires only the two state variables per node and the global monotonic sequence number to be modelled.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total number of jobs in all printer queues plus the number of jobs currently printing never changes except when a new job is submitted or a finished job is removed.

The system consists of a set of settlement nodes, each run by a participating bank, that jointly process a daily inter‑bank settlement batch identified by a batch number. Every node stores three local variables: the current batch number it believes is active, a Boolean “leader” flag indicating whether it thinks it is the elected leader for that batch, and a Boolean “override” flag that is true only when the privileged administrator has issued an override command. At the start of each batch the nodes run a simple leader election by broadcasting their node ID; the node that receives the highest ID claim becomes leader and sets its leader flag true while all others set it false. The leader is responsible for writing the batch record to the shared settlement ledger and then propagating a “commit” message that causes every node to mark the batch as processed. If a node detects that the leader has failed to send a commit within a timeout, it clears its leader flag and restarts the election, allowing a new leader to take over the same batch number. At any moment the privileged admin can issue an override command that sets the override flag on a designated node; that node immediately assumes the leader role, writes a special “admin‑override” entry to the ledger, and forces all other nodes to abandon their current election and follow the overridden leader. Once the override flag is cleared, the normal election mechanism resumes for the next batch.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No update to the shared settlement ledger for a batch can be lost because every committed entry is written either by the elected leader or by the admin‑override leader and acknowledged by all nodes before the batch is considered complete.

The lobby consists of a set of player clients, each of which can be in one of three local states: **Idle**, **Waiting**, or **Leader**. Every client stores the identifier of the current lobby leader (the *leaderId* variable) and a Boolean *heartbeatSeen* that is set to true whenever it receives a heartbeat message from the leader within the last timeout interval. When a client joins the lobby it starts in the Idle state, sends a “join‑request” to the current leader, and transitions to Waiting; the leader replies with a “ready‑to‑match” message and records the client’s identifier in its *matchQueue*. The leader periodically broadcasts a heartbeat; any client that does not set *heartbeatSeen* to true before its timeout assumes the leader has crashed, clears its *leaderId*, and initiates a new election by broadcasting an “elect‑me” claim containing its own identifier, after which the client with the highest identifier that receives acknowledgements declares itself Leader. If a client receives an “elect‑me” claim with a higher identifier than its own, it aborts any pending election, records the higher identifier as *leaderId*, and returns to the Waiting state. When a new leader is elected, it recomposes the *matchQueue* from the Waiting clients and resumes sending ready‑to‑match messages. All clients continuously update *heartbeatSeen* on each heartbeat and reset it to false when a timeout occurs, ensuring that only the current, alive leader can assign players to matches.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No player client can start a match or be assigned to a match unless its *leaderId* refers to the most recently elected, non‑crashed leader.

The system includes RouterAgents that move bags along individual ConveyorSegments and a central SorterUnit that directs each bag to the proper flight belt. Each RouterAgent first acquires a coarse lock on the whole ConveyorSegment before it may obtain the fine lock on a specific belt lane. After taking the coarse lock the agent records the segment identifier and a busy flag; once the fine lock is held it records the lane identifier and a routing flag. A MaintenanceCrew can request the coarse lock for inspection, but it must first set a maintenance‑mode flag that temporarily blocks new fine‑lock requests. An AdminConsole holds an override key that can pre‑empt any coarse or fine lock, instantly setting an override flag and forcing all agents to release their locks. The protocol requires a RouterAgent to release the fine lock before releasing the coarse lock, unless an admin override is active, in which case the release order is ignored. All participants continuously broadcast their lock state so that conflicting requests are detected and resolved by the hierarchical lock manager.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No bag is loaded onto an outbound aircraft more than once.

The system consists of many game clients, two independent lobby manager processes (Instance A and Instance B), and a single shared pool of match slots identified by numeric IDs. Each lobby manager keeps three pieces of state: a Boolean flag `isLeader` indicating whether it currently holds the leadership role, a list `freeSlots` of slot IDs that are still unassigned, and a dictionary `assignments` that maps player IDs to the slot they have been placed in. A heartbeat exchange lets the managers detect when the current leader stops responding; the surviving manager then sets its `isLeader` flag to true, adopts the other’s `assignments` dictionary, and recomputes `freeSlots` accordingly. When a client requests a match, the leader removes the first ID from `freeSlots`, records the mapping in `assignments`, and sends a confirmation to the client; the follower simply forwards the request to the leader. If the leader crashes after updating `assignments` but before the client acknowledges, the new leader merges the two `assignments` dictionaries, discarding any duplicate entries and restoring `freeSlots` to contain only truly unused IDs. All state changes are atomic with respect to the shared memory that both instances read and write, ensuring that every slot is either free or assigned to exactly one player at any moment.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No match slot is ever allocated to more than one player at the same time.

There are three controllers in the system: a North controller, a South controller, and a Token manager that circulates a single permission token around a logical ring.  
Each controller keeps a boolean flag that records whether it currently holds the token and a status flag that records whether its track block is free or occupied.  
When a controller wants to set its signal to green for a train to enter its block, it first checks that it holds the token; if it does not, it waits for the token to arrive.  
The token is passed to the next controller by sending a token‑grant message, and because messages may be reordered the controller only accepts a token‑grant if its local token flag is false.  
Upon receiving a valid token‑grant, the controller sets its token flag to true, marks its block as occupied, and later broadcasts a token‑release message after the train has cleared the block.  
The token‑release message may arrive out of order, so a controller discards any release that arrives while it still holds the token, preventing duplication of the token.  
After sending the release, the controller clears its token flag and forwards a new token‑grant to the next controller, completing the cycle.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: A block can be set to green for a train at most once before it is set back to red.

The system has three kinds of participants: individual Players who want to join a game, a Lobby Manager that maintains the lobby state, and a Matchmaker that starts games once enough players are gathered. The Lobby Manager keeps three variables: the current lobby capacity, the number of players currently assigned to slots, and a lock status that can be either “coarse‑locked” (the whole lobby) or “fine‑locked” on a specific slot. When a Player requests to join, the Lobby Manager first acquires the coarse lock, checks that the capacity is not already full, and then acquires a fine lock on a free slot before incrementing the player count and granting the slot. If the capacity is changed at runtime (e.g., an admin raises the limit), the Lobby Manager performs the update while still holding the coarse lock, ensuring no new fine‑locks are granted until the new capacity is visible. After a Player has been placed, the fine lock on that slot is released while the coarse lock remains until the entire join operation completes. When the Matchmaker starts a game, it takes the coarse lock, records the set of players to be removed, decrements the player count accordingly, and then releases the coarse lock so new joins can resume.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any moment the number of players assigned to lobby slots never exceeds the lobby’s current capacity.

The HomeController maintains the network‑wide capacity limit (the maximum number of doors that may be unlocked simultaneously) and a version counter that is incremented whenever the limit changes. Each DoorLock device keeps a local flag indicating whether it is currently “unlocked‑pending” and stores the version number it most recently observed. When a resident’s MobileApp wants to open a door, it first sends a **coarse request** to the HomeController; the controller checks the current count of doors with the “unlocked‑pending” flag and, if the count is below the capacity, returns the current version token and grants permission. Upon receiving the token, the MobileApp forwards a **fine request** to the specific DoorLock, which compares the token with its stored version, sets its flag to “unlocked‑pending”, and then physically unlocks the bolt. If the HomeController later changes the capacity, it broadcasts the new version and capacity; DoorLocks that notice a higher version recompute whether their “unlocked‑pending” flag still satisfies the new limit and, if not, relock themselves and clear the flag. All participants periodically synchronize their view of the version so that stale or unauthorized unlocks are never kept after a capacity reduction.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No door remains unlocked as a result of a request made by a participant that does not hold a current capacity‑grant token.

A car arrives at the entry sensor and reads the current conveyor capacity and the number of slots already occupied, which are the two pieces of state kept by the controller. The car then writes a reservation request that includes the version number it observed; if the controller’s version has not changed, the request succeeds and the car is assigned a slot, otherwise the car must retry after rereading the state. The conveyor controller updates the version each time it accepts a reservation or releases a slot, ensuring that concurrent cars detect stale reads. A separate capacity manager may increase or decrease the maximum number of slots at any moment, and it does so by incrementing the version before changing the capacity value. When a car completes the wash it releases its slot, again incrementing the version so that pending cars know a new attempt may succeed. All participants use the same version‑based optimistic lock, so a car only proceeds when its reservation matches the latest version and the occupied‑slot count stays below the current capacity. If a retry is needed, the car simply loops back to read the latest capacity and version and attempts the reservation again.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two cars can be assigned to the same conveyor slot at the same time.

The fleet consists of autonomous picking robots and a lightweight coordinator that stores a version number for each storage bin. Each robot locally records the last version it observed for the bin it intends to access and a flag indicating whether it currently holds the optimistic lock for that bin. When a robot wants to place or retrieve an item, it reads the current version from the coordinator, writes a tentative lock request together with the next version number, and proceeds only if the coordinator’s version has not changed in the meantime. If the coordinator reports a newer version, the robot aborts its operation, updates its local version, and retries after a short back‑off. A robot that is slow to respond may still hold a pending lock, but the coordinator will not block other robots because the lock is optimistic: it only rejects conflicting updates based on version mismatches. Each retry clears any stale lock held by the slow robot, ensuring progress despite temporary slowness without treating the robot as failed. The protocol therefore uses only the bin’s version number and the lock flag as state variables to coordinate concurrent accesses.

SAFETY PROPERTY: At no time can a storage bin contain more items than its defined capacity.

The system has three kinds‑of participants: a Baggage Sorter that creates tagged bags, a set of Router Nodes that decide which conveyor a bag should follow, and the Conveyor Belts that finally carry the bags to their planes. All Router Nodes share a single compare‑and‑swap register that can hold either “empty” or the identifier of a bag that is waiting to be routed. When the Sorter has a new bag, it attempts to write the bag’s identifier into the register only if it currently contains “empty”. Each Router Node repeatedly reads the register; if it sees a bag identifier, it tries to claim the bag by atomically replacing the identifier with its own node name using the compare‑and‑swap operation. Once a Router Node succeeds in the claim, it moves the bag onto the correct conveyor based on the bag’s tag and then clears the register back to “empty”. If a Router Node is slow, it simply holds the claim longer, but because the compare‑and‑swap operation guarantees exclusive ownership, no other node will interfere and the bag will eventually be routed.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: A bag is placed onto a conveyor belt at most once.

The system consists of three load‑shed agents – a Generator Controller, a Substation Controller, and a Demand‑Response Controller – each running on its own node and connected in a logical token ring. Each agent keeps a Boolean flag `hasToken` and a counter `shedUnits` that records how many megawatts it has already reduced. When an agent receives the token it may either request to shed load, increasing its `shedUnits` by a fixed step size, or pass the token without acting if it is currently slow processing a previous request. After performing (or skipping) its action the agent forwards the token to the next agent in the ring, resetting its own `hasToken` flag. If an agent holds the token longer than a configurable timeout, the following agent treats the token as stale, re‑issues the token to itself, and the slow agent continues in a “recover” mode until it can safely hand over the token again. This design guarantees that at any moment only one controller can issue a new shed command, so the total load‑shed never exceeds the pre‑calculated safe bound.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total megawatts shed by all agents never exceeds the maximum allowable load reduction for the grid.

The LobbyManager owns a single coarse‑grained lock that protects the whole lobby list, while each pending match has its own fine‑grained lock protecting the match record. A player who wishes to join first requests the coarse lock; once granted, the player adds its identifier to the lobby list and then releases the coarse lock. When the LobbyManager decides that enough players are ready, it reacquires the coarse lock, selects a group, and then each player in that group acquires the fine lock for the new match before writing their chosen character and skin into the shared match record. A player may pause for a long time after acquiring a lock (e.g., waiting for a network round‑trip), but it never crashes, so the lock remains held until the player explicitly releases it. If a player is slow, other players attempting to join the lobby must wait on the coarse lock, and players waiting to finalize a match must wait on the fine lock, preserving the hierarchical ordering. Once all fine‑grained updates are applied, the match record is marked “ready” and the fine lock is released, after which the LobbyManager releases the coarse lock and opens the lobby for new arrivals. The protocol therefore uses a two‑level lock hierarchy to serialize lobby‑wide changes first and then match‑specific changes, tolerating slow participants without losing consistency.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No update to the shared match record can be overwritten or lost due to concurrent modifications.

The system consists of a fixed set of lobby servers, each hosting a queue of waiting players and linked together in a logical ring.  
Each server maintains two state variables: a boolean `hasToken` that tells whether it currently holds the match‑making token, and an integer `queueSize` that records how many players are waiting at that server.  
When a server holds the token it may create a new match by taking up to the maximum match size (e.g., four) from its queue and broadcasting the match invitation to the selected players.  
After it finishes, the server passes the token to its clockwise neighbour, setting its own `hasToken` to false and the neighbour’s `hasToken` to true.  
If a server receives the token but its `queueSize` is zero, it immediately forwards the token without creating a match.  
A slow server may retain the token longer than usual while it contacts slow players, but it never relinquishes the token until it has either formed a match or decided the queue is empty.  
Because the token circulates continuously, every server eventually gets a chance to form matches despite occasional delays.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total number of players assigned to any match never exceeds the configured maximum match size.

The system has three participants: aircraft controllers that request runway time, a runway manager that keeps the lock state for each runway, and a privileged admin that can pre‑empt any lock.  
The runway manager maintains a coarse lock indicating whether a runway is globally free or reserved, and a fine lock that records which specific aircraft currently holds the runway.  
When a controller wants to land, it first acquires the coarse lock for the desired runway; if successful it then acquires the fine lock for its own aircraft identifier.  
If the coarse lock is already held, the controller must wait, and it examines the fine lock only after the coarse lock has been obtained, preserving the hierarchical ordering.  
At any moment the admin may issue an override that instantly clears both the coarse and fine locks for a runway, forcing all pending controllers to restart their acquisition sequence.  
After a controller has obtained both locks it signals “runway allocated” and later releases the fine lock when the aircraft vacates, after which the coarse lock is released when no other fine locks remain.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: A runway is assigned to a specific aircraft at most once before that aircraft releases the runway.
spec_text:
---- MODULE W4C1x8x5x5 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, TLC

CONSTANTS Runways, Aircraft

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\*   Constants, auxiliary definitions
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
NONE == "None" \* special value meaning “no aircraft”

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\*   Variables
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
VARIABLES coarseLock, fineLock, history

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\*   Type invariant (helps TLC, not the safety property we are checking)
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
TypeOK ==
    /\ coarseLock \in [Runways -> {"Free","Reserved"}]
    /\ fineLock   \in [Runways -> Aircraft \cup {NONE}]
    /\ history    \in [Runways -> Aircraft \cup {NONE}]

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\*   Initial state
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Init ==
    /\ coarseLock = [r \in Runways |-> "Free"]
    /\ fineLock   = [r \in Runways |-> NONE]
    /\ history    = [r \in Runways |-> NONE]

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\*   Controller actions
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
AcquireCoarse(a, r) ==
    /\ a \in Aircraft
    /\ r \in Runways
    /\ coarseLock[r] = "Free"
    /\ fineLock[r] = NONE
    /\ coarseLock' = [coarseLock EXCEPT ![r] = "Reserved"]
    /\ UNCHANGED << fineLock, history >>

AcquireFine(a, r) ==
    /\ a \in Aircraft
    /\ r \in Runways
    /\ coarseLock[r] = "Reserved"
    /\ fineLock[r] = NONE
    /\ history[r] # a          \* hierarchical ordering – cannot reacquire same aircraft consecutively
    /\ fineLock' = [fineLock EXCEPT ![r] = a]
    /\ UNCHANGED << coarseLock, history >>

ReleaseFine(a, r) ==
    /\ a \in Aircraft
    /\ r \in Runways
    /\ fineLock[r] = a
    /\ fineLock' = [fineLock EXCEPT ![r] = NONE]
    /\ history'  = [history EXCEPT ![r] = a]
    /\ UNCHANGED coarseLock

ReleaseCoarse(r) ==
    /\ r \in Runways
    /\ coarseLock[r] = "Reserved"
    /\ fineLock[r] = NONE
    /\ coarseLock' = [coarseLock EXCEPT ![r] = "Free"]
    /\ history' = [history EXCEPT ![r] = NONE]
    /\ UNCHANGED fineLock

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\*   Admin action
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
AdminOverride(r) ==
    /\ r \in Runways
    /\ coarseLock' = [coarseLock EXCEPT ![r] = "Free"]
    /\ fineLock'   = [fineLock   EXCEPT ![r] = NONE]
    /\ history'    = [history    EXCEPT ![r] = NONE]
    /\ UNCHANGED << >>

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\*   Next-state relation
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Next ==
    \/ \E a \in Aircraft, r \in Runways : AcquireCoarse(a, r)
    \/ \E a \in Aircraft, r \in Runways : AcquireFine(a, r)
    \/ \E a \in Aircraft, r \in Runways : ReleaseFine(a, r)
    \/ \E r \in Runways               : ReleaseCoarse(r)
    \/ \E r \in Runways               : AdminOverride(r)

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\*   Safety invariant (the property we must check)
\*   “A runway is assigned to a specific aircraft at most once before that
\*    aircraft releases the runway.”
\*   Expressed as: if a runway currently holds a fine lock for aircraft a,
\*   then the most‑recently released aircraft for that runway is different
\*   from a (i.e., a cannot reacquire without a prior release).
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Inv ==
    \A r \in Runways :
        IF fineLock[r] # NONE
        THEN history[r] # fineLock[r]
        ELSE TRUE

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\*   Specification
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<coarseLock, fineLock, history>>

THEOREM Spec => []Inv

====

nl:
The spooler consists of a set of printer nodes, each called a “spooler agent”, that maintain a local copy of the current leader ID and a flag indicating whether they are currently processing a print job.  
When an agent starts up it reads its local leader ID; if the ID refers to a node that has not sent a heartbeat in the last timeout, the agent initiates a leader election by broadcasting an “election” message with its own ID.  
All agents that receive an election message compare the candidate ID with their own ID and reply with a “higher” message only if their own ID is larger, otherwise they forward the election message unchanged.  
The candidate that finally receives no “higher” reply declares itself leader, updates its local leader ID, and starts sending periodic heartbeats to all agents.  
When a non‑leader receives a heartbeat it resets its timeout; if the timeout expires it assumes the leader is failed and restarts the election, but a slow agent that simply delays heartbeats will still be recognized as alive because the timeout is longer than its worst‑case delay.  
The leader is the only agent allowed to write the shared job‑queue record, and before each write it acquires a local lock and broadcasts a “commit” notice so that other agents can update their copy of the queue state.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The job‑queue record is never updated by the leader without all agents eventually seeing the same update, ensuring no print‑job entry is lost.

The system consists of three cooperating nodes – the Hospital‑A server, the Regional‑B server, and the Backup‑C server – each of which keeps a local copy of the blood‑type inventory count and a monotonically increasing version number for the whole database. When a donation of a specific blood type arrives, the node that receives it creates a proposal that includes the blood type, the quantity to add, and the next version number, then sends this proposal to the other two nodes. Every node that receives the proposal checks that the version number it carries is exactly one greater than its own current version; if the check passes it replies with a “yes” vote, otherwise it replies “no”. The proposing node waits until it has received votes from at least two of the three nodes (a quorum) and, if all received votes are “yes”, it updates its own inventory and version and broadcasts a commit message so the other nodes also apply the update; if any vote is “no” or a timeout occurs, it aborts the proposal and reverts any local tentative change. A removal (e.g., a transfusion request) follows the same voting and commit steps, using a negative quantity in the proposal. If any node crashes silently, the remaining nodes eventually notice the lack of a response, treat the missing vote as a “no”, and only commit when the required quorum of two affirmative votes can still be obtained, guaranteeing progress despite a single crash.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No blood‑type inventory change is ever committed unless a quorum of non‑crashed nodes has voted affirmatively, preventing actions by unauthorized or stale participants.

The lobby server keeps a single lease that names the current match‑maker (a player who is allowed to assemble a game) and an expiration time for that lease. Each player stores the lease’s owner identifier and the expiry timestamp it learned from the server, and also a local copy of the lobby’s player list. When a player wishes to become match‑maker it sends a **request‑lease** message; the server grants the lease by recording the requester’s id and a new expiry time that is several seconds in the future. The current match‑maker must periodically send **renew‑lease** messages before the expiry; if the server does not receive a renewal, the lease automatically expires and any other player may acquire it with a new request. While holding a valid lease a player may update the shared lobby record (e.g., add a ready‑status entry) and then broadcast the updated record; other players accept the update only if the lease owner they see matches the one recorded in the message. A slow player that fails to renew in time simply loses the lease but remains in the lobby, and can later request a new lease without causing inconsistency.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The lobby record is never overwritten by an update from a player who does not hold the current valid lease.

The system consists of a central Scheduler, several OR Managers each responsible for a group of operating rooms, and individual Surgery Teams (surgeon and nurse) that request room time.  
Each OR Manager keeps a coarse‑lock flag indicating whether any room in its group is currently being allocated, and a fine‑lock table that records which specific room and time slot is assigned to which Surgery Team.  
A Surgery Team first sends a “coarse‑request” to the Scheduler, which forwards it to the appropriate OR Manager; if the manager’s coarse lock is free it sets the flag and replies with a coarse‑grant message containing a request token.  
Using the token, the team then sends a “fine‑request” naming the exact OR and time slot; the OR Manager checks the fine‑lock table, reserves the slot if it is still free, and sends a fine‑grant that also carries the token and a monotonically increasing version number.  
Because network messages may arrive out of order, each participant discards any grant or release whose version number is older than the latest one it has recorded for that token, guaranteeing that stale information never overwrites a newer state.  
After the surgery is completed, the team sends a release message with the same token; the OR Manager clears the fine‑lock entry, and if no other fine locks are active it also clears the coarse lock flag.  
All participants therefore progress by acquiring the coarse lock before any fine lock, and by using versioned tokens to ignore reordered messages, ensuring that only one active surgery occupies a given operating room at any time.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No surgery may start in an operating room unless the OR Manager currently holds both the coarse lock for that room group and the fine lock for that specific room‑time slot, and any stale or unauthorized request is ignored.

The system has three kinds of participants: surgeons who request operating‑room time slots, a set of scheduler nodes that keep the current lease information, and a privileged administrator who can intervene at any moment. Each scheduler node stores a small amount of state: the identifier of the surgeon that currently holds the lease for a given OR‑slot, the lease’s expiration timestamp, and a flag indicating whether an admin override is active. When a surgeon needs a slot, it sends a lease‑request to any scheduler; the scheduler grants the lease by recording the surgeon’s ID, setting the expiration to “now + maximum‑lease‑duration”, and broadcasting the update to the other nodes. The surgeon must periodically send a lease‑renewal before the expiration; each renewal updates the expiration timestamp on all nodes. If the expiration passes without renewal, all nodes automatically clear the lease, making the slot free again. At any time the administrator may issue an override command; the scheduler nodes immediately set the override flag, replace the lease holder with the admin’s ID, and ignore any later renewals from the previous holder until the admin releases the override. All participants respect the most recent lease record they have received before performing any scheduling or starting a surgery.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No surgeon or scheduler node may schedule or start a surgery in an operating‑room slot unless it holds a currently valid, non‑expired lease or the admin override is active.

The system is composed of several Runway Controllers (RCs) that manage landing requests and a single Capacity Manager (CM) that broadcasts the current runway capacity. Each RC stores a short list of pending landing slots (its *slotQueue*) and a flag indicating whether it has already voted in the current decision round. When an aircraft requests a landing, the RC that receives the request sends a **PROPOSE** message containing the desired slot to all other RCs; at the same time the CM may issue a **CAPACITY_UPDATE** that changes how many concurrent landings the runway can support. Upon receiving a proposal, every RC records the proposal, clears its vote flag, and participates in a quorum vote: the proposal is accepted only after a majority of RCs reply with **ACK**. If a capacity update arrives that would make the proposed slot exceed the new limit, the RCs collectively reject the proposal and ask the requester to submit a different slot. When a majority of ACKs is reached, the proposing RC adds the slot to its *slotQueue*, informs the CM, and the CM records the allocation in its global *activeSlots* variable. Any RC that later learns of a capacity reduction must invalidate any pending proposals that no longer satisfy the limit and restart the vote with a fresh proposal.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No landing slot is granted by a controller that has not participated in the most recent quorum or that is acting on an outdated runway‑capacity value.

The protocol involves three roles: the Settlement Coordinator (SC) and two participating banks, Bank A and Bank B. Each bank keeps a local “batch state” that records whether it has received the current batch identifier and whether it has sent a **prepare‑ok** vote for that batch. The SC maintains a single variable indicating the identifier of the batch it is trying to commit and a flag showing whether it has collected votes from all participants for that identifier. In phase 1 the SC broadcasts a *prepare* message containing the batch identifier; each bank, upon receiving the identifier (even if messages arrive out of order), updates its batch state and replies with *prepare‑ok* for the latest identifier it knows. In phase 2 the SC waits until it has a *prepare‑ok* from both banks for the same identifier; once both votes are present it broadcasts a *commit* message with that identifier. Each bank, upon receiving a *commit* whose identifier matches its current batch state, marks the batch as settled and sends an acknowledgment back to the SC. The SC considers the batch fully committed only after it has received acknowledgments from both banks, and it then clears the flags for that identifier before moving to the next batch. Any out‑of‑order messages that carry an older identifier are ignored by both the banks and the SC, ensuring that stale information never influences the current decision.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No bank can cause a settlement batch to be committed unless it has previously voted to commit for the same, current batch identifier and the coordinator has recorded a matching commit decision.

The system involves three participants: a Baggage Scanner that attaches a tag to each piece of luggage, a Router Controller that decides which conveyor segment will carry the bag, and a pair of Transfer Slots that serve as the critical hand‑off points between conveyor belts. Each Transfer Slot maintains a tiny state that is either “free” or “occupied”, and a shared compare‑and‑swap (CAS) register stores the identifier of the slot currently being claimed. When a bag is ready, the Scanner sends a claim request to the Controller; the Controller attempts a CAS on the register, swapping the value “none” with the identifier of a free slot only if the register still contains “none”. If the CAS succeeds, the Controller marks that slot as occupied and instructs the conveyor to move the bag there; if it fails, the Controller retries with another slot. Because network messages can be reordered, a stale claim message that arrives later will see the register already holding a different identifier and therefore will not overwrite the current owner. The protocol also attaches a monotonically increasing version number to each claim so that out‑of‑order messages can be recognized as outdated and ignored. Consequently, at any moment only one controller can hold the CAS register for a given slot, guaranteeing a single active assignment.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two bags are ever assigned to the same Transfer Slot at the same time.

A student reads the current seat count and version number for a course from the registration server.  
The server stores, for each course, a small record containing the number of free seats, a version counter, and an admin‑override flag.  
When the student submits a registration request, the server checks that the version it still holds matches the one the student saw; if they match and at least one seat is free, the server decrements the seat count, increments the version, and confirms the enrollment.  
If the version has changed, the request is rejected and the student must read the new values and retry the whole process.  
An administrator may set the override flag on a course, which tells the server to ignore the version check and any seat‑availability constraint, allowing the enrollment to succeed immediately.  
After an overridden enrollment, the server still increments the version so that subsequent student retries will see the updated state.  
All participants – students, the registration server, and privileged admins – operate concurrently, each following these read‑check‑write steps, with retries automatically triggered on version mismatches.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No student can enroll in a course using an outdated version or without proper admin override, preventing unauthorized or stale registrations.

The opening auction involves three roles: the Exchange Scheduler, a set of Trading Terminals, and a Capacity Manager.  
Each Trading Terminal holds a lease on a slice of the order‑book capacity, recording the lease holder and an expiry time.  
The Exchange Scheduler periodically checks the leases and announces the start of the auction only when a terminal’s lease is still valid.  
A Trading Terminal may request a new lease or extend an existing one, and the Capacity Manager grants it if the total allocated capacity does not exceed the current market limit.  
When the Capacity Manager detects a runtime change in the market limit, it updates the global capacity variable and forces any lease that now exceeds the limit to expire immediately.  
Expired leases are removed from the order‑book, preventing the corresponding terminal from submitting orders until it acquires a fresh lease.  
All participants respect the lease expiry: no terminal may submit an order after its lease has expired, and the scheduler will not match those orders.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The opening of the auction can occur at most once during a trading day.

The system has three kinds of participants: (1) two independent print‑job submitters, each running in its own instance, (2) a shared pool of printer workers, and (3) a bounded work queue that holds at most N pending jobs.  
Each submitter keeps a local counter of how many of its own jobs are currently in the queue, while the queue maintains a single integer “size” representing the total number of enqueued jobs.  
When a submitter wants to add a new job, it first checks that its local counter is below a per‑client limit and that the queue’s size is less than N; if both checks succeed it increments its counter and the queue size and places the job into the queue.  
If the queue is full, the submitter must wait (backpressure) until a worker removes a job, at which point the queue size is decremented and the worker notifies the originating submitter to decrement its local counter.  
Workers repeatedly dequeue the oldest job, print it, and then signal the submitter that created the job so that the submitter can update its counter.  
Because both submitters share the same queue, the backpressure mechanism guarantees that neither instance can overflow the queue or exceed its own per‑client limit.  
All state updates are atomic: the queue size, the per‑client counters, and the dequeue operation are performed together so that the system never observes an intermediate inconsistent state.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No job is ever printed that was submitted by a client that has not successfully reserved a slot in the shared bounded queue.

  N = 3
  ClientLimit = 2
  CLIENTS = {0, 1}

INIT Init
NEXT Next
INVARIANT SafetyInvariant

nl:
The warehouse contains a set of storage bins, each identified by a bin ID, and a fleet of mobile robots that can pick items from inbound pallets and place them into bins. Each robot keeps a local copy of the bin’s version number and the list of items it has assigned to that bin, while the central controller maintains the authoritative version number and the current inventory for every bin. When a robot wants to store items, it reads the current version number from the controller, adds the items to its local list, and then attempts an optimistic‑lock update by sending the new inventory together with the version it observed; the controller accepts the update only if the version still matches, otherwise it rejects it and the robot must retry with the latest version. A privileged admin console can issue an override request that forces the controller to set a bin’s inventory to a new state and also reset its version, bypassing the normal reject‑on‑conflict rule. While the override is in progress, the controller temporarily blocks normal robot update attempts for that bin, ensuring the admin change is applied before any robot retries are processed. After the override completes, normal optimistic‑locking updates resume, and robots continue their retry loops with the refreshed version number.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No robot’s update to a bin’s inventory can be lost or silently overwritten, even when an admin override occurs.

The warehouse runs two identical fleet‑manager instances, each controlling a set of Picker robots that fetch items from shelves and a set of Loader robots that place the items onto delivery pallets. All robots share a single TaskPool that contains a list of pending pick‑tasks, each task entry storing the ID of the robot currently assigned (or “none”) and a version counter. When a robot wants to start a task it reads the task entry and its version, writes its own ID into the entry only if the version it saw is still current, and then increments the version; this is the optimistic‑lock “claim” step. If the write fails because another robot has updated the version in the meantime, the robot discards the stale data and retries the whole claim sequence with the latest version. After a robot successfully claims a task, it proceeds to the execution phase, and once the item is placed on a pallet the robot marks the task as “completed” and removes its assignment, again using a versioned write. The two manager instances coordinate solely through the shared version counters: they never exchange messages directly, and each instance retries until its write succeeds, guaranteeing that only one robot ever holds a claim on a given task at any moment. The protocol therefore requires only three shared state variables per task – the assigned robot ID, the version number, and a completion flag – making it easy to model and verify.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: A pick‑task is marked completed at most once.
spec_text:
---- MODULE W4C2x0x5x2 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, Sequences, TLC

CONSTANTS Robots, TaskIds

VARIABLES taskPool, completedTimes

(* --definition of the task record-- *)
TaskRecord == [assigned : Robots \cup {"none"},
               version  : Nat,
               completed: BOOLEAN]

(* Initial state *)
Init ==
    /\ taskPool = [t \in TaskIds |-> [assigned |-> "none",
                                      version  |-> 0,
                                      completed|-> FALSE]]
    /\ completedTimes = [t \in TaskIds |-> 0]

(* Claim a task: robot reads the entry, sees it unassigned, and writes its id, bumping the version *)
Claim(r, t) ==
    /\ r \in Robots
    /\ t \in TaskIds
    /\ taskPool[t].assigned = "none"
    /\ taskPool[t].completed = FALSE
    /\ taskPool' = [taskPool EXCEPT ![t] = [assigned  |-> r,
                                            version   |-> taskPool[t].version + 1,
                                            completed |-> FALSE]]
    /\ UNCHANGED completedTimes

(* Complete a task: robot that currently holds the claim marks it completed,
   clears the assignment, bumps the version, and records the completion *)
Complete(r, t) ==
    /\ r \in Robots
    /\ t \in TaskIds
    /\ taskPool[t].assigned = r
    /\ taskPool[t].completed = FALSE
    /\ taskPool' = [taskPool EXCEPT ![t] = [assigned  |-> "none",
                                            version   |-> taskPool[t].version + 1,
                                            completed |-> TRUE]]
    /\ completedTimes' = [completedTimes EXCEPT ![t] = completedTimes[t] + 1]

(* The next-state relation: any robot may claim or complete any task, or the system may stutter *)
Next ==
    \/ \E r \in Robots, t \in TaskIds: Claim(r, t)
    \/ \E r \in Robots, t \in TaskIds: Complete(r, t)
    \/ UNCHANGED <<taskPool, completedTimes>>

(* Specification *)
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<taskPool, completedTimes>>

(* Safety invariant: a task can be marked completed at most once *)
TaskCompletedAtMostOnce == \A t \in TaskIds : completedTimes[t] <= 1

=============================================================================

nl:
The system consists of two elevator controller instances, each managing a distinct bank of shafts, and a shared lock pool that provides both a coarse lock for a whole bank and fine locks for individual elevators. Each instance keeps a variable indicating whether it holds the bank‑wide coarse lock, and a per‑elevator flag indicating if it owns that elevator’s fine lock. To move an elevator, an instance first requests the coarse lock for its bank from the pool; if granted, it may then request the fine lock for the specific car it wants to command. Once both locks are held, the instance writes a new target floor into the elevator’s command register and then releases the fine lock followed by the coarse lock. If the coarse lock is already held by the other instance, the request is queued and the instance must wait before attempting any fine‑lock acquisition. The lock pool enforces that at any time only one instance can hold a coarse lock for a given bank, and that a fine lock can be granted only to the holder of the corresponding coarse lock, preventing interleaved updates to the same elevator command.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two instances can simultaneously update the same elevator’s command register, so every target‑floor record is written by at most one controller.

The system is a ring of dispenser nodes, each acting as either a Prescription Loader (PL) that loads new orders or a Medication Retriever (MR) that hands medication to the patient.  
Each node keeps two pieces of state: the identifier of the current token holder (TokenOwner) and the number of free slots it believes are available (Capacity).  
When a node holds the token it may request a new slot, increment its local Capacity, broadcast a CapacityUpdate to its successor, and then pass the token.  
If a node receives a CapacityUpdate while it does not hold the token, it adjusts its local Capacity to the received value and forwards the update around the ring.  
To dispense medication, a token‑holding node checks that Capacity > 0, decrements Capacity to allocate a slot, performs the dispense, and then passes the token.  
When the pharmacy manager changes the physical number of slots, a ResizeCommand is sent to any node; that node, on its next turn with the token, sets Capacity to the new size and propagates the change as a CapacityUpdate.  
Because only the token holder can modify Capacity or allocate a slot, the ring guarantees exclusive access even while the total capacity can be increased or decreased at runtime.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: At no moment can two different dispenser nodes allocate the same prescription slot.

The system has two participants: an Air‑Traffic Controller (ATC) process that issues landing requests and a Runway Manager process that assigns the single runway. Both processes keep a shared compare‑and‑swap register that stores a tuple (owner, token) where owner is either “none”, “ATC”, or “RM” and token is a monotonically increasing integer. When the ATC wants to schedule a plane, it reads the register; if owner is “none” it attempts a compare‑and‑swap, replacing “none” with “ATC” and incrementing the token. The Runway Manager periodically reads the same register; if it sees owner “ATC” it performs the landing, then uses compare‑and‑swap to change owner back to “none” while also bumping the token. Because network messages can be reordered, each process validates that the token it reads matches the token it expects before issuing its compare‑and‑swap, discarding stale replies if the token has changed. This way only one process can hold the “owner” field at a time, guaranteeing exclusive use of the runway despite out‑of‑order messages.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The runway is never assigned to more than one aircraft at the same time.

INIT Init
