INVARIANT AtMostOneOwner

nl:
The swarm consists of autonomous surveillance drones and a ground‑based control station that together manage access to a high‑resolution camera feed covering a wildfire‑hotspot sector. Each drone maintains a local copy of the sector’s lock version number and the identifier of the drone that currently holds the lock, while the control station stores the authoritative version and a flag indicating whether an administrator override is active. When a drone wants to capture the feed, it reads the current version, attempts to write its identifier as the new holder together with an incremented version, and then checks the control station to see if the write succeeded; if the version it observes later is unchanged, the drone proceeds, otherwise it retries with the updated version. If the write collides with another drone’s attempt, both drones detect the version mismatch and each backs off for a random short interval before retrying, implementing optimistic locking with retry. An administrator can at any moment set the override flag, which immediately forces the control station to clear any existing holder and grant exclusive access to a privileged “admin‑drone” that the admin designates. While the override flag is set, any normal drone’s lock attempts are rejected and the admin‑drone may acquire the lock without retry. When the admin clears the override flag, the lock returns to normal operation and the version number continues from its last value. All participants respect the same protocol steps, ensuring that at most one entity holds the camera feed at any time.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two drones, including the admin‑drone, can hold the wildfire camera feed simultaneously.

The system consists of a set of Block Controllers (BC) that each manage a signalling block, a Train Controller (TC) that requests block occupancy, and a privileged Admin Node (AN) that can intervene. Every BC stores a single token that circulates clockwise among the controllers; the token indicates which controller currently has the right to modify the shared block‑status record. When a BC holds the token, it may accept a request from the TC, update the block‑status record to “occupied” or “clear,” and then pass the token to the next BC in the ring. The AN holds a flag that, when set, preempts the ring: it captures the token from whichever BC currently holds it, performs an emergency‑override update to the block‑status record, clears the flag, and returns the token to the BC that was preempted. If the admin flag is not set, the token simply moves from one BC to the next after each successful update, guaranteeing that only one controller can write to the record at a time. All participants obey the rule that a BC may not modify the block‑status record unless it either holds the token or the admin flag is active, and the token is never duplicated.   

SAFETY PROPERTY: The block‑status record is never updated concurrently, so no update to the shared record can be lost.

The system has three participants: patrons who submit reservation requests, a reservation manager that enqueues those requests into a bounded work queue, and a queue worker that dequeues requests and assigns a free copy of a book to a patron. The manager keeps a single counter for the number of queued requests (never exceeding the queue capacity) and a map from book‑ISBN to the copy currently held for reservation. The worker repeatedly checks whether the queue is non‑empty, removes the oldest request, looks up a free copy of the requested book, and updates the map to record that copy as reserved for the patron. If the queue is full, the manager applies backpressure by rejecting new patron requests until the worker has freed at least one slot. The worker may crash silently at any time, after which it stops processing the queue but the manager continues to accept new requests up to the capacity, preserving the existing map entries. When the worker restarts, it resumes dequeuing from the head of the queue, using the unchanged map to avoid overwriting any reservation that was already recorded.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No book copy is ever assigned to more than one patron at the same time.

The system consists of a Dispatch Server that owns the lease for each elevator car, and a set of Floor Controllers that may obtain a lease to command a car to stop at their floor. Each car has a lease record containing the ID of the current owner and an expiry time after which the lease is considered invalid. When a Floor Controller wants to serve a pending call, it sends a lease‑request to the Dispatch Server; if the lease is free or has expired, the server updates the record with the controller’s ID and a fresh expiry timestamp. The Floor Controller then moves the car and must periodically send a lease‑renewal before the expiry, otherwise the lease automatically reverts to the server. If a controller is slow and fails to renew, the server may re‑grant the lease to another controller, ensuring progress despite the slowdown. All participants treat the lease as the single source of truth for who may issue commands to a car, and they ignore any command that arrives without a valid, unexpired lease.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any moment, each elevator car is leased to at most one controller, so no two controllers can command the same car simultaneously.

The conveyor line is built from three stations—Entry Scanner, Washing Booth, and Drying Booth—each running on its own controller.  
Each controller keeps two tiny pieces of state: a flag indicating whether it currently holds the token and a counter remembering the last car ID it processed.  
The token travels clockwise; a controller may only read from or write to the shared car‑record database while it holds the token.  
When a station finishes handling its car, it tries to forward the token to the next station; if that station is still busy, the token is retained for a short timeout before being retried.  
If a station is slow, it simply maintains the token until it completes its work, ensuring that no other station can access the shared record during that period.  
After receiving the token, the next station increments its local counter, updates the shared record with the new car ID, and then proceeds with its own processing.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two stations ever write different values to the same car record at the same time, so updates to the shared record are never lost.

The system consists of a set of branch servers that each hold a copy of the reservation table for every book.  
Each server keeps three pieces of state: the identifier of the current leader, a flag indicating whether the leader is suspected down, and a local queue of pending reservation requests.  
When a patron submits a reservation, the request is sent to the current leader, which appends it to the global reservation list and acknowledges the patron.  
If a server does not receive a heartbeat from the leader within a timeout, it marks the leader as suspected down and initiates an election by broadcasting its own identifier; the server with the highest identifier becomes the new leader.  
The new leader obtains the latest reservation list from a majority of servers before accepting new requests, ensuring continuity after failover.  
An administrator can issue an override command that immediately sets the leader to a designated admin node and clears any pending suspect flag, pre‑empting the normal election.  
All other servers accept the admin’s designation as authoritative, update their leader variable, and discard any in‑flight reservation that has not been committed.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No reservation request ever disappears or overwrites another request without being recorded in the shared reservation list.

The system consists of a central fleet controller, a set of autonomous robots, and a set of storage zones. Each robot stores two local variables: the epoch number it is currently following and the count of items it is carrying. The fleet controller keeps a single epoch‑wide capacity variable that records how many items may be present in the zone during that epoch. When a robot wants to pick up an item, it sends a request to the controller; if the controller’s current capacity minus the sum of all robots’ loads is positive, the controller replies with a grant and the robot increments its load count. After delivering an item, the robot decrements its load count and reports the completion to the controller. When the controller decides to reconfigure the warehouse (for example, to accommodate a new shipment), it increments the epoch number, broadcasts the new capacity, and robots that still hold the old epoch suspend further pickups until they receive the updated epoch. If the new capacity is lower than the current total load, robots that are still holding items are instructed to finish deliveries but are prohibited from taking additional items until the load drops below the new limit.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total number of items in the system (items on robots plus items stored in zones) never changes; items are neither created nor destroyed.

The system consists of three keepers: the Block Controller (BC) that owns a track block, the Train Detector (TD) that senses train presence, and the Interlocking Server (IS) that authorises train movements.  
Each keeper stores two state variables: a Boolean “BlockOccupied” indicating whether a train is currently on the block, and an integer “VoteCount” counting how many alive participants have voted to change the block’s status.  
When a train approaches, the BC initiates a “Release” action by broadcasting a proposal to set BlockOccupied to false, and each participant that currently sees the block clear replies with a vote “yes”.  
The IS collects votes and, once VoteCount reaches a quorum of two (out of three possible), it sends a commit message that all participants apply, updating BlockOccupied accordingly.  
If a participant crashes silently, its vote never arrives; after a bounded timeout the collector treats the missing vote as “no” and aborts the action, leaving the previous state unchanged.  
Any participant that receives a commit must first verify that its local BlockOccupied value matches the committed value before applying it, otherwise it discards the message as stale.  
After a commit, all alive participants reset VoteCount to zero, ready for the next proposal.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: A block may be released only if no alive participant currently observes the block as occupied, guaranteeing that a crashed or stale participant cannot cause an unauthorized release.

The yard system has three kinds of participants: a fleet of automated cranes, a central Yard Manager that tracks which loading slots are free, and the ship’s loading plan controller that proposes which crane should work on which slot. Each crane maintains a local variable “mySlot” that is either empty or holds the identifier of the slot it believes it has reserved. The Yard Manager holds a single compare‑and‑swap register whose value is the identifier of the currently unallocated slot; a crane can issue a reservation request that atomically swaps the register’s value with the crane’s own identifier only if the register still contains the expected free‑slot identifier. After a successful swap, the crane writes the received slot identifier into its “mySlot” variable and notifies the loading‑plan controller; if the swap fails, the crane retries with the new register value. Because network messages can be reordered, a crane may receive an old “slot now free” notification after it has already moved on, but the compare‑and‑swap operation guarantees that only one crane can ever replace the register’s value for that slot. The loading‑plan controller periodically queries the Yard Manager to confirm that each slot appears in exactly one crane’s “mySlot” before issuing a “lift container” command. If a crane detects that its “mySlot” no longer matches the register (because another crane succeeded later), it releases the slot and retries with the next free slot reported by the manager.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two cranes can ever be assigned the same loading slot at the same time.
spec_text:
---- MODULE W4C7x7x3x1 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets, Sequences

CONSTANTS Cranes, Slots      \* Finite sets of identifiers

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* State variables
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
VARIABLES mySlot, reg

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Helper definitions
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* A special value meaning “no slot reserved”
NoSlot == "None"

\* The set of cranes that currently hold a reservation for a concrete slot
CranesWithSlot(s) == { c \in Cranes : mySlot[c] = s }

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Initial state
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Init ==
    /\ mySlot = [c \in Cranes |-> NoSlot]
    /\ reg \in Slots          \* the register initially points to some free slot

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Actions
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* A crane attempts a compare‑and‑swap reservation.
\* The operation succeeds only if the register still contains the expected free‑slot identifier.
Reserve(c) ==
    /\ c \in Cranes
    /\ mySlot[c] = NoSlot                 \* crane is currently idle
    /\ LET expected == reg IN
       /\ expected \in Slots               \* the value we expect to be a free slot
       /\ reg' = c                         \* swap: register now holds the crane id
       /\ mySlot' = [mySlot EXCEPT ![c] = expected]  \* crane records the slot
    /\ UNCHANGED << >>                    \* no other variables change

\* A crane notices that its reservation is no longer reflected in the register
\* (e.g., because another crane later succeeded for the same slot) and releases it.
Release(c) ==
    /\ c \in Cranes
    /\ mySlot[c] # NoSlot                 \* crane believes it holds a slot
    /\ LET s == mySlot[c] IN
       /\ mySlot' = [mySlot EXCEPT ![c] = NoSlot]   \* forget the slot
       /\ reg' = s                                 \* make the slot free again
    /\ UNCHANGED << >>                    \* no other variables change

\* The manager may also freely set the register to any currently free slot.
ManagerAdvance ==
    /\ \E s \in Slots :
          (\A c \in Cranes : mySlot[c] # s)   \* no crane currently owns s
       /\ reg' = s
    /\ UNCHANGED mySlot

Next ==
    \/ \E c \in Cranes : Reserve(c)
    \/ \E c \in Cranes : Release(c)
    \/ ManagerAdvance

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Safety invariant: no two cranes can ever be assigned the same loading slot
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
NoDuplicateSlot ==
    \A s \in Slots :
        Cardinality(CranesWithSlot(s)) <= 1

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Specification
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<mySlot, reg>>

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* THEOREM (for TLC) – the invariant holds
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
THEOREM Spec => []NoDuplicateSlot

=============================================================================

The protocol involves three roles: the *Sender Bank*, the *Receiver Bank*, and a *Settlement Coordinator* that manages the inter‑bank batch. Each bank keeps a local copy of the batch ledger containing the total amount it intends to send or receive, a flag indicating whether it has voted, and a commit marker that is initially false. When a new settlement batch is ready, the Sender Bank proposes the batch to the Coordinator, which then broadcasts a vote request to both banks. Each bank replies with a “yes” vote only after locally verifying that its ledger entry balances (its outgoing amount equals the incoming amount of the other side). The Coordinator records votes; once it has received votes from a quorum of two participants, it sets the commit marker to true and tells both banks to finalize the batch. If a bank crashes silently, the Coordinator proceeds as long as it still has votes from the remaining two participants; the crashed bank’s lack of response is tolerated because the quorum size is chosen to accommodate one failure. After commit, each bank updates its ledger to reflect the settled amounts and clears its vote flag, ready for the next batch. 

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total amount of money recorded as settled across all banks never changes except by the addition of a new, balanced batch, so no money is created or destroyed.

The system consists of a **Dispenser Controller** that manages the drug‑tray, **Pharmacist Terminals** that submit refill requests, and **Inventory Sensors** that report the number of pills currently stored. The controller keeps two pieces of state: an *epoch number* that is incremented each time the tray’s capacity is re‑configured, and a *capacity* value that may be changed at runtime by a pharmacist. When a pharmacist submits a new prescription, the terminal sends the request together with the controller’s current epoch; the controller records the request only if the total pills to be dispensed plus the pills already present do not exceed the current capacity. If a pharmacist changes the capacity, the controller first increments the epoch, updates the capacity variable, and then rejects any pending requests that were recorded under the previous epoch because they might now exceed the new limit. Inventory sensors periodically send the current pill count together with the epoch they observed; the controller uses this to verify that the count is consistent with the capacity of that epoch before allowing any dispense operation. A dispense operation is performed only after the controller has confirmed (i) the request’s epoch matches the controller’s current epoch, (ii) the capacity constraint is satisfied, and (iii) the sensor’s latest count agrees with the controller’s view, after which the controller decrements the pill count and marks the request as completed.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: A pill is physically removed from the tray at most once for any given prescription request.

The system has three kinds of participants: the Scheduler service, the OR‑Room manager for each operating room, and the Capacity controller that can raise or lower the number of simultaneous surgeries allowed.  
The Scheduler keeps a coarse lock indicating whether the overall schedule is being modified, and each OR‑Room manager holds a fine‑grained lock that protects the assignment of a particular room.  
When a new surgery request arrives, the Scheduler first acquires the coarse lock, checks the current capacity, and then asks the appropriate OR‑Room manager to acquire its fine lock for the desired time slot.  
If the fine lock is granted, the OR‑Room manager records the surgery in its local schedule and releases the fine lock; the Scheduler then releases the coarse lock and returns a confirmation to the requester.  
If the Capacity controller changes the maximum concurrent surgeries while a coarse lock is held, it updates a shared capacity variable that the Scheduler will read after releasing the coarse lock, ensuring no new surgery is scheduled that would exceed the new limit.  
A surgery that has already been recorded in an OR‑Room manager’s schedule is never removed by capacity changes; the capacity variable only blocks further bookings.  
All participants periodically broadcast a “heartbeat” so that a failed manager can be detected and its fine lock considered free for reallocation.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: A surgery is assigned to an operating‑room time slot at most once, and once the assignment is confirmed it cannot be overwritten by any later scheduling action.

The swarm consists of several autonomous fire‑monitoring drones that each keep a small local record containing (1) its current role—either *leader* or *follower*—and (2) the most recent election term it has observed. When a drone detects that it has not received a leader heartbeat for a configurable interval, it increments its term, switches to *candidate* mode, and broadcasts an “I’m running” message containing the new term to all other drones. Upon receiving such a message, a follower compares the advertised term with its own; if the incoming term is newer, the follower records the term, votes for the sender, and sends back an acknowledgement, otherwise it discards the message as stale. The candidate that gathers acknowledgements from a majority of the swarm declares itself the new leader, starts sending periodic heartbeat messages that include its current term, and assumes responsibility for assigning the high‑resolution thermal camera to scan the most active fire hotspot. If a follower receives a heartbeat with a higher term than its stored term, it updates its term, records the sender as the current leader, and resumes normal operation; heartbeats with older terms are ignored, which protects the protocol from reordered messages. Should the leader fail or its heartbeats stop arriving, the election process restarts automatically, ensuring continuous coordination without manual intervention. All drones use the same term numbers to order events, so even if messages arrive out of order, only the most recent term influences state changes, keeping the system consistent with only two variables per drone.

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any time, at most one drone is authorized to operate the high‑resolution thermal camera on a given fire hotspot.

The system consists of a central Coordinator and two lock controllers, FrontDoorLock and BackDoorLock, each of which runs on a separate embedded processor. Each lock controller stores a boolean flag coarseGranted indicating whether the Coordinator has given it permission to start a fine‑grained unlock sequence, and a field fineHolder that records which user (if any) currently holds the fine lock for that door. When a user requests to unlock a door, the lock controller first sends a *coarse request* to the Coordinator; the Coordinator records the request in its own variable coarseOwner and replies with an acknowledgement, setting the controller’s coarseGranted to true. After receiving the coarse acknowledgement, the controller then sends a *fine request* specifying the user’s identity; the Coordinator checks that no other controller currently has a fine lock (its fineOwner is nil) and, if so, records the user as fineOwner and instructs the controller to complete the unlock, which it records by setting fineHolder to that user. If a lock controller crashes silently after receiving the coarse acknowledgement, it will stop responding to the fine request; the Coordinator detects the lack of a fine‑request reply within a timeout and clears its coarseOwner and fineOwner entries, allowing other doors to proceed. The protocol therefore proceeds through a two‑phase grant (coarse then fine) and uses timeout‑driven rollback to handle a silent crash. Throughout, only one controller may have its fineHolder set to a non‑nil user at any time, ensuring exclusive access to the physical unlocking mechanism.

SAFETY PROPERTY: At no time can two doors be physically unlocked simultaneously by different users.
spec_text:
---- MODULE W4C18x8x0x0 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Constants
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
CONSTANTS Users   \* the set of possible user identities

Door == {"FrontDoor", "BackDoor"}
NilUser == "nil"

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Variables
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
VARIABLES coarseGranted, fineHolder, coarseOwner, fineOwner

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Types
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
CoarseGrantedType == [Door -> BOOLEAN]
FineHolderType    == [Door -> (Users \cup {NilUser})]
CoarseOwnerType   == Door \cup {NilUser}
FineOwnerType     == Users \cup {NilUser}

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Initial state
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Init ==
    /\ coarseGranted = [d \in Door |-> FALSE]
    /\ fineHolder    = [d \in Door |-> NilUser]
    /\ coarseOwner   = NilUser
    /\ fineOwner     = NilUser

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Actions
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
CoarseGrant(d) ==
    /\ d \in Door
    /\ ~coarseGranted[d]
    /\ coarseOwner'   = d
    /\ coarseGranted' = [coarseGranted EXCEPT ![d] = TRUE]
    /\ UNCHANGED << fineHolder, fineOwner >>

FineGrant(d, u) ==
    /\ d \in Door
    /\ u \in Users
    /\ coarseGranted[d]           \* door has received the coarse ack
    /\ coarseOwner = d            \* request originates from the same door
    /\ fineOwner = NilUser        \* no other fine lock held
    /\ fineOwner'   = u
    /\ fineHolder'  = [fineHolder EXCEPT ![d] = u]
    /\ coarseGranted' = [coarseGranted EXCEPT ![d] = FALSE]
    /\ coarseOwner'   = NilUser
    /\ UNCHANGED << >>

Timeout(d) ==
    /\ d \in Door
    /\ coarseOwner = d
    /\ coarseGranted[d]           \* coarse grant was given
    /\ fineOwner = NilUser        \* fine request never arrived
    /\ coarseOwner'   = NilUser
    /\ coarseGranted' = [coarseGranted EXCEPT ![d] = FALSE]
    /\ UNCHANGED << fineHolder, fineOwner >>

Release(d) ==
    /\ d \in Door
    /\ fineHolder[d] # NilUser
    /\ fineHolder' = [fineHolder EXCEPT ![d] = NilUser]
    /\ fineOwner'  = NilUser
    /\ UNCHANGED << coarseGranted, coarseOwner >>

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Next-state relation
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Next ==
    \/ \E d \in Door : CoarseGrant(d)
    \/ \E d \in Door, u \in Users : FineGrant(d, u)
    \/ \E d \in Door : Timeout(d)
    \/ \E d \in Door : Release(d)

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Safety property (the required invariant)
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* At most one door may have a non‑nil fineHolder at any time.
NoSimultaneousUnlock ==
    Cardinality({ d \in Door : fineHolder[d] # NilUser }) <= 1

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Specification
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<coarseGranted, fineHolder, coarseOwner, fineOwner>>

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Theorem (for TLC checking)
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
THEOREM Spec => []NoSimultaneousUnlock

====
cfg_text:
CONSTANTS Users = {"Alice", "Bob"}

INIT Init
NEXT Next
INVARIANT NoSimultaneousUnlock

The system consists of two dispenser controller instances, each running on separate hardware but both drawing medication units from the same shared cartridge pool. Each instance keeps a local copy of the pool count and a version number that is read from the central database when it starts a transaction. When a pharmacist scans a prescription, the instance reads the current version, checks that enough units of the requested drug are available, and then attempts to write a new pool count decrementing the requested quantity while incrementing the version. The write succeeds only if the version in the database still matches the one the instance read; otherwise the write is rejected. If the write is rejected, the instance reloads the latest version and pool count, and retries the whole check‑and‑write sequence up to a limited number of times. While one instance is retrying, the other instance may successfully complete its own transaction, updating the version and pool count. Once a write succeeds, the instance commands its hardware to dispense the medication and marks the prescription as completed.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: A medication pack for any given prescription is dispensed at most once.

The system consists of two load‑shedder controllers, Instance A and Instance B, each responsible for a distinct sub‑grid but both drawing from a common pool of “shed‑slots”. Each instance maintains a Boolean flag “hasCoarseLock” indicating whether it currently holds the coarse lock on the shared pool, and an integer “fineLockCount” that records how many fine‑grained shed‑slot reservations it has acquired. To begin a shedding operation, an instance first attempts to acquire the coarse lock; if the flag is false for both instances it may set its own flag to true. Once the coarse lock is held, the instance can request individual shed‑slots one at a time, incrementing its fineLockCount only after the pool reports the slot is free. When the instance has finished using a slot, it decrements fineLockCount and releases the slot back to the pool; when fineLockCount reaches zero the instance releases the coarse lock, resetting its flag. If an instance finds the coarse lock already set by the other instance, it must wait and retry, guaranteeing that at any moment only one instance can hold the coarse lock and therefore control the allocation of the shared shed‑slots.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: At most one load‑shedder instance can hold a particular shed‑slot at any time, ensuring mutual exclusion of the shared shedding resource.
spec_text:
---- MODULE W4C9x8x0x2 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets

CONSTANTS Instances, Slots, MaxSlots, None

VARIABLES hasCoarseLock, fineLockCount, slotOwner

(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* Type definitions to keep the state space finite                       *)
(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
TypeOK ==
    /\ hasCoarseLock \in [Instances -> BOOLEAN]
    /\ fineLockCount \in [Instances -> 0..MaxSlots]
    /\ slotOwner \in [Slots -> Instances \cup {None}]

(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* Initial state                                                        *)
(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
Init ==
    /\ hasCoarseLock = [i \in Instances |-> FALSE]
    /\ fineLockCount = [i \in Instances |-> 0]
    /\ slotOwner    = [s \in Slots    |-> None]

(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* Actions                                                              *)
(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)

(* Acquire the coarse lock when nobody holds it *)
AcquireCoarse(i) ==
    /\ i \in Instances
    /\ ~hasCoarseLock[i]
    /\ \A j \in Instances : ~hasCoarseLock[j]
    /\ hasCoarseLock' = [hasCoarseLock EXCEPT ![i] = TRUE]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<fineLockCount, slotOwner>>

(* Release the coarse lock – only allowed when no fine slots are held *)
ReleaseCoarse(i) ==
    /\ i \in Instances
    /\ hasCoarseLock[i]
    /\ fineLockCount[i] = 0
    /\ hasCoarseLock' = [hasCoarseLock EXCEPT ![i] = FALSE]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<fineLockCount, slotOwner>>

(* Reserve a free shed‑slot while holding the coarse lock *)
AcquireSlot(i, s) ==
    /\ i \in Instances
    /\ s \in Slots
    /\ hasCoarseLock[i]
    /\ slotOwner[s] = None
    /\ slotOwner'    = [slotOwner EXCEPT ![s] = i]
    /\ fineLockCount' = [fineLockCount EXCEPT ![i] = @ + 1]
    /\ UNCHANGED hasCoarseLock

(* Release a previously‑acquired slot *)
ReleaseSlot(i, s) ==
    /\ i \in Instances
    /\ s \in Slots
    /\ slotOwner[s] = i
    /\ slotOwner'    = [slotOwner EXCEPT ![s] = None]
    /\ fineLockCount' = [fineLockCount EXCEPT ![i] = @ - 1]
    /\ UNCHANGED hasCoarseLock

(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* Next-state relation                                                   *)
(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
Next ==
    \/ \E i \in Instances: AcquireCoarse(i)
    \/ \E i \in Instances: ReleaseCoarse(i)
    \/ \E i \in Instances: \E s \in Slots: AcquireSlot(i, s)
    \/ \E i \in Instances: \E s \in Slots: ReleaseSlot(i, s)

(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* Specification                                                         *)
(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<hasCoarseLock, fineLockCount, slotOwner>>

(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* Safety invariant: at most one instance holds any given slot         *)
(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
SlotMutex ==
    \A s \in Slots :
        \A i1, i2 \in Instances :
            (slotOwner[s] = i1 /\ slotOwner[s] = i2) => i1 = i2

(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* Optional type invariant – also useful for TLC boundedness            *)
(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
TypeInvariant == TypeOK

====
cfg_text:
CONSTANTS
  Instances = {"A", "B"}
  Slots     = {1, 2}
  MaxSlots  = 2
  None      = "None"

INIT Init
NEXT Next
INVARIANT SlotMutex

The system consists of two independent allocator instances, A and B, each responsible for granting runway slots to incoming flight requests. Both instances keep a shared record that stores the current “runway‑version” number and the identifier of the runway that is presently allocated, and each instance also maintains a local copy of that record. When a request arrives, an instance reads the shared record, records the version it saw, and tentatively assigns the requested runway in its local copy. It then tries to write its updated record back using a compare‑and‑swap operation that succeeds only if the version in the shared record has not changed. If the compare‑and‑swap fails, the instance knows another allocator has intervened; it discards its tentative assignment, reads the new record, and retries the whole process. Successful compare‑and‑swap increments the version and makes the assignment visible to the other instance. Because each allocator repeats this optimistic‑lock‑and‑retry loop, the two instances eventually agree on a single allocation for each runway slot without explicit communication.

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any moment, a given runway is assigned to at most one flight.

The system consists of a DoorLock device, a HomeHub that forwards commands, and one or more MobileApp clients that request the lock to be opened or closed. Each DoorLock stores a simple version counter and a Boolean lockState (locked or unlocked); the MobileApp keeps a copy of the last version it observed. When a client wants to change the lock, it reads the current version from the DoorLock, sends an Unlock (or Lock) request together with that version to the HomeHub, and then proceeds without waiting for a response (optimistic step). The DoorLock, upon receiving a request, compares the attached version with its own counter; if they match, it updates lockState, increments the version, and sends an acknowledgment; if they differ, it discards the request and the client must retry with the new version. Because messages may arrive out of order, a late acknowledgment carrying an old version is ignored, ensuring only the most recent successful request takes effect. The HomeHub simply forwards messages and does not maintain any state, so the protocol can be modeled with the DoorLock’s version and lockState variables and the client’s last‑seen version. Retries continue until a client receives an acknowledgment that matches the version it sent, guaranteeing progress despite reordering. 

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any moment the DoorLock’s lockState reflects at most one successful unlock (or lock) command, so the lock is never simultaneously considered unlocked by more than one client.

The system consists of three participants: the **JobSpooler**, which receives print‑job submissions from users; the **PrinterNode**, which pulls jobs from the spooler and prints them; and the **CapacityManager**, which can raise or lower the maximum number of jobs the spooler may hold at any moment.  
The spooler keeps two state variables: the current **queue length** and a **version counter** that is bumped whenever the CapacityManager changes the maximum capacity.  
When a user submits a job, the JobSpooler reads the current version, checks whether the queue length is below the current capacity, increments the queue length, and writes back the same version; if the version has changed in the meantime the write fails and the submitter retries with the new version.  
The PrinterNode similarly reads the version and the queue length, decrements the queue length when it picks a job, and aborts the operation if the version changed, forcing a retry.  
Whenever the CapacityManager decides to adjust capacity (for example, because a new printer is added or a printer goes offline), it increments the version counter and updates the capacity limit; this version change causes any in‑flight optimistic updates to be rejected and retried, ensuring they see the new limit.  
All participants operate independently and only coordinate through the shared version and queue‑length variables, guaranteeing progress despite concurrent updates and runtime capacity changes.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total number of jobs submitted to the system is always equal to the sum of jobs waiting in the spooler queue plus jobs currently being printed, so no job is ever lost or created spontaneously.

The system consists of two runway‑allocation services, A and B, each responsible for a different airline but both drawing from a single pool of time‑slots on the shared runway. A lightweight token circulates around a logical ring formed by the three nodes: service A, service B, and a central token manager; only the node that currently holds the token may modify the pool. Each service maintains a single variable “nextSlot” that records the next free slot it intends to reserve, and the token manager keeps a Boolean “tokenIsFree” indicating whether the token is currently in the ring. When a service needs a slot, it waits until it receives the token, checks the pool for a free slot, records that slot in its nextSlot, marks the slot as taken, and then passes the token onward. The token manager, upon receiving the token, simply forwards it to the other service; it never changes the pool itself, ensuring that the token’s movement is the only coordination point. If a service finishes using a slot, it releases the slot back to the pool without needing the token, because releasing does not affect exclusivity of future allocations. 

SAFETY PROPERTY: No time‑slot on the runway is ever assigned to both services at the same time.

The system consists of a set of block controllers, one for each track segment, and a central reconfiguration manager. Each block controller stores the current epoch number, its allocated capacity (the maximum number of trains allowed in the block), and a flag indicating whether it is locked for reconfiguration. When the manager decides to change capacities, it increments a global epoch counter and broadcasts the new epoch together with the desired capacity map to all block controllers. Upon receiving the broadcast, a controller compares the new epoch to its stored value; if the new epoch is higher, it sets its lock flag, updates its capacity to the advertised value, records the new epoch, and sends an acknowledgment back to the manager. The manager waits until it has acknowledgments from every controller before clearing all lock flags, thereby allowing trains to be scheduled under the new capacities. While a block is locked, any train‑movement command for that block is rejected, ensuring no train enters or leaves during the reconfiguration. After all locks are cleared, normal dispatch resumes and the system can start a new epoch at any later time.

SAFETY PROPERTY: A block’s capacity is altered for a given epoch at most once.

The swarm consists of many surveillance drones and a central command node that holds the current **SectorCapacity** value indicating how many drones may simultaneously monitor a given wildfire sector. Each drone keeps a local **Lease** record that stores the identifier of the sector it owns and a **LeaseExpiry** timestamp after which the ownership is considered void. When a drone wishes to start monitoring a sector, it sends a **LeaseRequest** to command; command grants the lease only if the number of active leases for that sector is below the current **SectorCapacity**, and it returns an expiry time. While operating, a drone may **RenewLease** before the expiry, extending the **LeaseExpiry**; it may also **ReleaseLease** voluntarily when it finishes its sweep. If command later adjusts **SectorCapacity** (e.g., due to battery constraints or increased fire spread), it does not retroactively revoke existing leases but refuses new lease grants that would exceed the new limit. Drones whose leases expire without renewal automatically relinquish ownership, freeing capacity for others. The protocol therefore coordinates access to the limited surveillance slots while tolerating dynamic changes in how many drones can be assigned to each sector.

SAFETY PROPERTY: A drone can declare a hotspot extinguished at most once.

The system consists of three participants: a Runway Manager that owns the runway resource, an Aircraft Agent for each arriving or departing aircraft, and a Capacity Controller that can raise or lower the runway’s simultaneous‑use limit at any time. Each participant keeps a tiny local state: the Runway Manager stores the current capacity limit and a flag indicating whether a two‑phase commit is in the “prepare” or “commit” stage; each Aircraft Agent stores whether it is in the “requested”, “prepared”, or “committed” phase; the Capacity Controller stores the latest capacity value it has broadcast. An Aircraft Agent starts by sending a **request** message to the Runway Manager asking for a slot; the Runway Manager records the request, checks that the number of already prepared agents is below the current capacity, and then issues a **prepare** message to all agents that have pending requests. Each Aircraft Agent that receives the prepare message replies with a **vote‑yes** if it can still meet its timing constraints, otherwise it replies **vote‑no**; the Runway Manager collects all votes, and if every vote is positive it broadcasts a **commit** message, otherwise it aborts the transaction and informs the agents. The Capacity Controller may, at any moment, broadcast a new capacity value; upon receipt, the Runway Manager updates its capacity limit and may immediately abort any ongoing prepare phase that would now exceed the limit, forcing a new round of requests. Throughout the protocol the two‑phase commit guarantees that either all agents obtain a runway slot together or none do, even while the permissible number of simultaneous slots changes dynamically.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two aircraft are ever granted the right to occupy the same runway segment at the same time.

The yard contains a shared pool of eight container slots, each of which can be occupied by a container either for loading onto a ship or for unloading to the dock. Two crane controllers, called Loader and Unloader, each run an independent instance of the loading protocol but both draw from the same slot pool. Each controller keeps a local variable indicating the index of the slot it intends to claim, and a global compare‑and‑swap register that stores the index of the currently free slot together with a version counter. When a controller wants to move a container, it reads the register, compares the stored index with its desired slot, and if they match it attempts a compare‑and‑swap that writes its own index and increments the version. The compare‑and‑swap succeeds only if no other controller has updated the register since the read, thereby granting exclusive right to the chosen slot. Upon success the controller marks the slot as occupied in the pool, performs the lift or place operation, and finally writes a release value back to the register to make the slot free again. If the compare‑and‑swap fails, the controller discards its stale index, reads the new register value, and retries with a different free slot.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No crane controller can occupy or release a container slot based on a stale register value, ensuring that only the controller that successfully performed the compare‑and‑swap may act on that slot.

The elevator bank consists of a set of controller modules, one attached to each elevator shaft, that communicate over a shared network. Each controller maintains three local variables: (1) the identifier of the current leader, (2) the term number of the most recent election it has witnessed, and (3) the floor‑slot it is currently responsible for serving. Periodically every controller broadcasts a “heartbeat” containing its known leader and term; if a controller receives a heartbeat with a higher term it updates its leader variable, otherwise it ignores the message. When a controller detects that it has not received a heartbeat for two consecutive intervals, it initiates an election by incrementing its term and sending an “election‑request” to all other controllers, proposing itself as the new leader. Upon receiving an election‑request, a controller replies with an “ack” only if the request’s term is at least as large as its own term, and it then adopts the requester as leader. The elected leader, after collecting a majority of acks, broadcasts a “leader‑announce” message that includes the new term and a mapping of floor‑slots to elevators; all controllers adopt this mapping and reset their slot assignments accordingly. Because messages may be reordered, controllers always compare term numbers and ignore any message with a stale term, ensuring that only the most recent leader assignment is applied.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two elevators are ever assigned to serve the same floor‑slot at the same time.

A library patron sends a reservation request for a specific title, which is enqueued in the bounded reservation queue only if the queue is not full; otherwise the patron is asked to retry later (backpressure).  
The queue maintains a single integer counter representing the current number of pending requests, never exceeding its fixed capacity.  
A ReservationProcessor repeatedly dequeues the oldest request, checks the book’s availableCopies counter, and if a copy is free it decrements availableCopies and records the reservation as fulfilled.  
If no copies are free, the processor leaves the request in the queue and retries later, leaving the counters unchanged.  
An admin user may issue an override command that instantly decrements availableCopies (even to zero) and marks a reservation as fulfilled, bypassing the queue and ignoring backpressure.  
When the override is used, the admin flag is set for that operation and cleared once the reservation is recorded, preventing further overrides until the flag is reset.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The sum of a book’s available copies and the number of fulfilled reservations for that book never changes.

The line consists of a central Controller, a WashStation, and a Dryer, each of which runs on its own computer. The Controller keeps an epoch number and a configuration record that lists which stations are active and what parameters (soap level, temperature, speed) they should use. Each station stores a local copy of the latest epoch it has seen and a flag indicating whether it is currently processing a car. When the Controller wants to change the configuration—for example, to add a new wax module—it increments the epoch, updates the configuration record, and broadcasts the new epoch together with the new settings to both stations. Upon receiving a newer epoch, a station first checks its processing flag; if it is still washing a car it finishes that car before adopting the new settings, otherwise it switches immediately. Slow stations may lag behind the Controller, but they never drop the broadcast, and the Controller waits for an acknowledgment from each station before moving on to the next epoch. This coordination guarantees that every station that has accepted a given epoch is using exactly the configuration associated with that epoch.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No car ever receives wash settings that differ from the configuration recorded by the Controller for the epoch under which the car entered the line.

The BatchFeeder reads pending inter‑bank settlement instructions from the bank’s staging database and attempts to place each instruction batch into a bounded work queue called the SettlementQueue. The queue has a fixed capacity; when it is full the feeder receives backpressure and must wait before offering more batches. The SettleEngine continuously dequeues the oldest batch from the SettlementQueue, applies the net transfers to the central ledger, and records a confirmation entry in the AuditLog. Both the feeder and the engine maintain a simple state: the index of the next batch to enqueue, the index of the last batch successfully applied, and the current occupancy of the queue. If the SettleEngine crashes silently, its crash flag is set to true, the queue retains the unprocessed batches, and a watchdog process detects the flag, restarts a fresh SettleEngine, and resumes processing from the same queue contents. The watchdog never discards any batch that remains in the queue, ensuring that backpressure is re‑applied to the feeder until the restarted engine has caught up. All participants cooperate only through the bounded queue and atomic updates to the shared ledger and audit log, keeping the overall protocol describable with just three state variables.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No settlement batch that has been successfully placed in the SettlementQueue can be lost without being applied to the central ledger.

The YardScheduler maintains a global counter `yardCapacity` that records how many containers may be stored on the dock at any moment, and a version number `capacityVersion` that is incremented whenever the ship’s off‑load plan changes the allowed capacity. Each CraneController keeps a local copy of `capacityVersion` and a flag `busy` that tells whether it is currently handling a container. When a crane finishes unloading a container, it reads the current `yardCapacity` and `capacityVersion`, then writes a provisional reservation for the next container together with the version it observed; this write succeeds only if the stored `capacityVersion` has not changed in the meantime. If the write is rejected because another crane or a capacity update has altered the version, the crane retries: it rereads the latest `capacityVersion`, updates its local copy, and attempts the reservation again. When the ship’s navigation system decides to increase or decrease the yard’s allowed capacity, it atomically increments `capacityVersion` and updates `yardCapacity`, causing any in‑flight reservations with the old version to be discarded. Cranes that discover a rejected reservation backtrack any partially moved container and wait for a short back‑off period before retrying, guaranteeing progress despite the dynamic capacity. The protocol therefore coordinates the cranes’ reservations using optimistic locking on the shared `capacityVersion` while allowing the capacity limit to change at runtime.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two cranes may reserve the same storage slot in the yard at the same time.

The system has three active participants: the central Scheduler, each Surgeon who requests an operating‑room slot, and the Anesthesiologist who must confirm the slot before the surgery can start. The Scheduler keeps a single versioned schedule for each OR, indicating which time slot is currently assigned and the version number of that assignment. When a Surgeon wants to book a slot, it reads the current version, proposes the new slot together with the next version number, and sends the proposal to the Scheduler. The Scheduler atomically checks that the version it read is still the latest; if it is, it writes the new assignment and notifies the Anesthesiologist, otherwise it rejects the proposal and the Surgeon retries with the fresh version. The Anesthesiologist, upon receiving a confirmed assignment, records the slot in its own local list and sends an acknowledgment back to the Scheduler; if the acknowledgment is delayed the Scheduler simply retries the notification without aborting the assignment. All participants are allowed to be slow—messages may take extra time—but none are considered failed, so the Scheduler will keep retrying until the acknowledgment arrives. The protocol therefore coordinates access to the OR schedule using optimistic locking, where version numbers detect conflicts and retries resolve them without needing a central lock holder.

SAFETY PROPERTY: An operating‑room slot is permanently booked for a surgery at most once.

The system consists of a fixed ring of lobby servers, each holding a local queue of waiting players, and a single privileged admin client that can intervene at any time. Each server maintains two variables: a boolean “hasToken” indicating whether it currently holds the exclusive matchmaking token, and a flag “overrideRequested” that the admin can set remotely. When a server’s hasToken is true, it may dequeue up to four players, create a match, and then pass the token clockwise to the next server in the ring. If the admin sets overrideRequested on a server, that server immediately creates a match with the first four players in its queue, regardless of whether it holds the token, and then it injects a special “override token” that skips the normal ring order and is given to the admin‑controlled server, which then passes the regular token to its successor. All other servers, upon receiving the token, first check the overrideRequested flag; if it is set they reset the flag and wait for the admin‑controlled server to hand back the token before proceeding. The admin can only issue one override at a time, and the override flag is cleared as soon as the overridden match is launched. All token transfers and flag updates are performed atomically to avoid races between servers and the admin.

SAFETY PROPERTY: A specific group of players can be placed into a match at most once.
spec_text:
---- MODULE W4C5x1x5x5 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets

CONSTANTS NumServers, NumPlayers, AdminServer, SpecialGroup

Servers == 1..NumServers
Players == 1..NumPlayers
N == NumServers

VARIABLES TokenHolder, OverrideRequested, queues, Matches

vars == <<TokenHolder, OverrideRequested, queues, Matches>>

(* Ring successor *)
Next(s) == IF s = N THEN 1 ELSE s + 1

(* Initial state *)
Init ==
  /\ TokenHolder = 1
  /\ OverrideRequested = {}
  /\ queues = [s \in Servers |-> {}]
  /\ Matches = {}

(* Normal operation when the holder has no override flag *)
NormalStep_NoOverride ==
  \E s \in Servers :
    /\ TokenHolder = s
    /\ s \notin OverrideRequested
    /\ \E players \in SUBSET queues[s] :
         /\ Cardinality(players) <= 4
         /\ Matches' = IF players = {} THEN Matches ELSE Matches \cup {players}
         /\ queues' = [queues EXCEPT ![s] = queues[s] \ players]
    /\ TokenHolder' = Next(s)
    /\ OverrideRequested' = OverrideRequested

(* Normal operation when the holder's override flag is set: just clear it *)
NormalStep_ClearFlag ==
  \E s \in Servers :
    /\ TokenHolder = s
    /\ s \in OverrideRequested
    /\ OverrideRequested' = {}
    /\ TokenHolder' = Next(s)

(* Admin issues an override: creates a match on a chosen server and
   transfers the regular token to the successor of the admin server. *)
OverrideAction ==
  /\ OverrideRequested = {}
  /\ \E s \in Servers :
        /\ \E players \in SUBSET queues[s] :
               /\ Cardinality(players) <= 4
               /\ Matches' = IF players = {} THEN Matches ELSE Matches \cup {players}
               /\ queues' = [queues EXCEPT ![s] = queues[s] \ players]
        /\ TokenHolder' = Next(AdminServer)
        /\ OverrideRequested' = {}

NextAction == NormalStep_NoOverride \/ NormalStep_ClearFlag \/ OverrideAction

Spec == Init /\ [][NextAction]_vars

(* Safety property: each player in SpecialGroup appears in at most one match *)
SpecialGroupAtMostOnce ==
  \A p \in SpecialGroup :
    Cardinality({ m \in Matches : p \in m }) <= 1

====================
cfg_text:
CONSTANTS
  NumServers = 3
  NumPlayers = 5
  AdminServer = 1
  SpecialGroup = {1,2}
SPECIFICATION Spec
INVARIANT SpecialGroupAtMostOnce

nl:
The system has two independent tracker instances, each running at a different hospital but both accessing the same central blood‑bank pool. Each instance keeps a local copy of two pieces of state: a version counter for the pool and a table of slot identifiers that record which blood bag (type and expiration) is stored in each slot. When an instance wants to allocate a slot for a newly donated bag, it first reads the current version number and the slot table, picks an empty slot, and then attempts to write a new entry that includes the bag’s details together with the version number it observed. The write succeeds only if the pool’s version counter still matches the one the instance read; on success the instance increments the version counter and commits the new slot allocation. If the version check fails because the other instance has already updated the pool, the transaction is aborted and the instance retries the whole read‑choose‑write cycle with the latest state. Occasionally an instance may also release a slot when a bag is dispatched, following the same read‑verify‑write pattern to avoid stepping on another instance’s release. All operations are performed without holding a long‑lived lock, relying on optimistic locking and retry to resolve conflicts.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two instances can ever allocate the same blood‑bank slot to different bags.

A customer device sends a purchase request to the nearest vending‑machine node, which forwards the request to a shared work queue that holds at most N pending orders. Each vending‑machine continuously monitors the queue and, when it is idle, dequeues the oldest request and checks its local inventory before dispensing the selected item. If the queue is full, the customer device receives a back‑pressure signal and must retry later; the queue length is therefore a shared state variable. An admin console can issue a privileged “override” command that either forces a specific machine to dispense an item immediately or clears the entire queue, but the command is accepted only when the admin’s authentication token is valid. The override command sets a single‑bit “admin‑active” flag that temporarily supersedes the normal dequeue order, after which the flag is cleared and normal back‑pressure resumes. All participants keep only the minimal state needed: the current queue length, each machine’s inventory count for the requested product, and the admin‑active flag. The protocol guarantees that normal requests and admin overrides are serialized by the bounded queue, ensuring that no more than N requests are in flight at any time.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No unauthenticated or outdated participant can cause a vending machine to dispense an item that has not been freshly requested and is not presently in stock.

The network is made up of three vending machines that share a single limited‑stock item, such as a bottle of water.  
Each machine stores only two pieces of information: a local copy of the stock count and a flag that tells whether it has already voted on the current dispense request.  
When a customer inserts money at any machine, that machine broadcasts a *request‑dispense* message to the other two machines and marks itself as awaiting votes.  
Every receiver checks its local stock count; if the count is greater than zero it replies with a “yes” vote and sets its vote flag, otherwise it replies “no”.  
The initiating machine proceeds with the actual dispensing only after it has collected at least two “yes” votes, treating any missing reply as a “no” so that a single silent crash does not block progress.  
Once the dispense succeeds, each machine that participated decrements its local stock count and clears its vote flag, returning to the idle state.  

**SAFETY PROPERTY:** No two vending machines will dispense the same stocked item for the same customer request.

The line consists of three participants: a CarSensor that detects an incoming vehicle, a ConveyorMotor that moves cars through the wash, and a WashStation that applies soap and water. Each participant stores a single flag indicating whether it has “prepared” for the next car and a local copy of the car’s identifier. When the CarSensor sees a car, it broadcasts a PREPARE message containing the car ID; each participant records the ID, sets its prepared flag, and replies with a VOTE‑COMMIT. The CoordinationController gathers the votes; if all votes are COMMIT it sends a GLOBAL‑COMMIT message, otherwise it sends GLOBAL‑ABORT, and the participants either advance the car or roll back their preparation. Because network links can reorder messages, each participant ignores any PREPARE or VOTE that carries a car ID different from the one currently stored in its flag. After receiving a GLOBAL‑COMMIT the ConveyorMotor increments a shared counter of cars on the line, and after the car exits the WashStation the counter is decremented, ensuring the line’s capacity is tracked consistently.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The number of cars simultaneously on the conveyor never exceeds its maximum capacity.

The protocol involves a Settlement Manager that coordinates a single settlement batch, and two participating banks, Bank A and Bank B. Each participant keeps a local flag indicating whether it has prepared its portion of the batch, and the manager maintains a batch‑status variable that can be *open*, *coarse‑locked*, *fine‑locked*, or *committed*. To start, the manager acquires a coarse lock on the whole batch, which blocks any new batches from being opened while the current one is being processed. After the coarse lock is obtained, each bank independently requests a fine lock on its own ledger entries, prepares its debit and credit records, and sets its prepared flag. When both banks have signaled preparation, the manager upgrades the batch to the fine‑locked state, writes a commit record, and changes the batch‑status to *committed*. If either bank fails to respond within a timeout (modeling a silent crash), the manager aborts the batch, releases both coarse and fine locks, and resets the status to *open* so that the batch can be retried later. All lock acquisitions and releases are performed in a strict hierarchical order—coarse before fine and release in reverse—to avoid deadlock.

SAFETY PROPERTY: A settlement batch is committed at most once.
cfg_text:
INIT Init
NEXT Next
INVARIANT CommitAtMostOnce

CONSTANT Banks = {"A","B"}
