The system consists of a **BatchPool** that holds a fixed number of settlement slots for inter‑bank transfers, and two independent settlement processors, **Inst‑A** and **Inst‑B**, each running its own instance of the settlement software. Each processor keeps a local record of the slot it currently owns (if any) and the lease‑expiration time announced by the BatchPool; the BatchPool maintains a table mapping each slot to the processor that holds its valid lease and the lease’s expiry timestamp. When a processor needs to settle a batch it sends a *lease‑request* for a free slot; the BatchPool grants the lease only if the slot is unassigned or its previous lease has expired, records the new owner and sets a future expiry time, and returns the slot identifier to the requester. The owning processor then performs the settlement using the slot and must either *release* the slot back to the pool when finished or let the lease expire, after which the BatchPool may reassign the slot to the other processor. If a processor crashes or becomes unresponsive, its lease will eventually expire, allowing the other processor to request and obtain the same slot without interference. Processors may also send a *renew‑lease* message before expiry to extend ownership of a slot they are still using, and the BatchPool updates the expiry time accordingly.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No settlement slot is ever allocated to more than one processor at the same time.

The system consists of a set of Track Segment Managers (one for each block of track) and a set of Train Controllers that request exclusive access to a segment before a train enters it. Each manager keeps a small record with three variables: the identifier of the controller that currently holds the segment (or NONE), a version counter that is incremented on every successful allocation, and a timestamp of the last heartbeat from the holder. When a controller wants to enter a segment it reads the manager’s record, proposes to write its own identifier together with the version+1, and sends the write as an optimistic lock request. If the manager’s version has not changed since the read, the write succeeds and the controller proceeds; otherwise the controller retries after a short back‑off, reading the new version first. A silent crash of a controller is detected by the manager when the heartbeat timestamp exceeds a configurable timeout, at which point the manager automatically resets the holder field to NONE, allowing other controllers to acquire the segment. All controllers obey the same retry loop, so progress is eventually made as long as at least one participant remains alive.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two Train Controllers can ever hold the same track segment at the same time.

The system contains two independent spooler processes, called SpoolerA and SpoolerB, that both draw print jobs from a single shared job pool.  
Each spooler maintains a tiny local state: the epoch number it is currently operating under and a copy of the pool’s configuration record that lists the jobs it owns.  
When a spooler finishes a job, it deletes the job identifier from its local copy and writes a completion entry together with its current epoch into the shared configuration record.  
To reconfigure the pool, the initiating spooler first increments the global epoch counter, writes the new epoch value into the shared record, and then notifies the other spooler of the new epoch.  
The receiving spooler accepts the new epoch only if its own epoch matches the previous value, discarding any stale updates, and then refreshes its local configuration to match the shared record.  
All subsequent job assignments and completions must carry the current epoch, so that actions taken under an old epoch cannot interfere with actions performed after a reconfiguration.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No job that has been removed from the shared pool in one epoch can later be re‑added by another spooler in a subsequent epoch, preventing lost updates to the shared job list.

There are two load‑shed controllers, each running an independent instance that decides when to cut power to its own set of customer segments. Both controllers compete for a single token that grants the right to issue a shed command to the shared high‑voltage breaker pool. Each controller keeps a local variable indicating whether it currently holds the token and a counter of how many shed actions it has performed since the last token hand‑off. When a controller decides a shed is needed, it first checks that it holds the token; if it does, it sends a “shed request” message to the breaker pool, receives acknowledgment, and then increments its counter. After completing a shed, the controller passes the token to the next controller in the ring by sending a “token release” message that includes its counter value. The successor controller accepts the token only if the counter in the release message matches its own expected value, preventing stale or duplicated token use. If a controller does not hold the token, it simply waits and periodically polls its neighbor for a token release, ensuring that at most one controller can command the breaker pool at any time.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No controller can issue a shed command to the shared breaker pool unless it currently holds the valid token.
spec_text:
---- MODULE W4C9x1x6x2 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, Sequences, TLC

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* CONSTANTS
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
CONSTANTS Controllers, NoShed

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* DEFINITIONS
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* The two controllers
CONSTANT C1, C2

\* Set of controllers (must be defined in the .cfg)
\* Controllers == {C1, C2}

\* Successor function for the ring
Succ(i) == IF i = C1 THEN C2 ELSE C1

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* VARIABLES
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
VARIABLES holder,               \* which controller currently holds the token
          counter,              \* number of shed actions performed since last hand‑off
          lastShed              \* controller that performed the most recent shed (or NoShed)

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* INITIAL STATE
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Init ==
    /\ holder \in Controllers
    /\ counter = [c \in Controllers |-> 0]
    /\ lastShed = NoShed

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* ACTIONS
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Shed action for a controller i (must hold the token)
Shed(i) ==
    /\ holder = i
    /\ counter' = [counter EXCEPT ![i] = @ + 1]
    /\ UNCHANGED << holder, lastShed >>
    /\ lastShed' = i

\* Pass token from i to its successor
Pass(i) ==
    /\ holder = i
    /\ LET j == Succ(i) IN
       /\ holder' = j
       /\ counter' = [counter EXCEPT ![i] = 0]   \* reset i's counter after hand‑off
       /\ lastShed' = NoShed                     \* clear record of last shed
    /\ UNCHANGED << >>

\* A controller that does not hold the token can simply wait (no state change)
Idle ==
    /\ UNCHANGED << holder, counter, lastShed >>

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* NEXT STATE RELATION
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Next ==
    \/ \E i \in Controllers : Shed(i)
    \/ \E i \in Controllers : Pass(i)
    \/ Idle

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* SPECIFICATION
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<holder, counter, lastShed>>

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* SAFETY INVARIANT
\* No controller can issue a shed command unless it currently holds the token.
\* This is captured by asserting that whenever a shed has occurred and not yet
\* been “forgotten” by a token hand‑off, the holder must be the controller that
\* performed that shed.
TokenSafety == (lastShed = NoShed) \/ (holder = lastShed)

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* THEOREM (optional, for TLC)
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
THEOREM Spec => []TokenSafety

====
cfg_text:
INIT Init
NEXT Next
INVARIANT TokenSafety
CONSTANTS
  Controllers = {C1, C2}
  NoShed = "None"
  C1 = "C1"
  C2 = "C2"

nl:
The system consists of three kinds of participants: (1) aircraft controllers that submit landing‑slot requests, (2) the runway manager that dequeues requests and assigns the sole runway, and (3) a privileged admin who can pre‑empt the queue to grant an emergency landing.  
Each controller maintains a local flag “requestPending” that is true while its request is stored in the bounded work queue, which holds at most N pending requests.  
The runway manager keeps two state variables: the identifier of the aircraft currently occupying the runway (or “none”) and a Boolean “adminPreempt” indicating whether the admin has issued an override.  
When a controller’s request is accepted, it is placed at the tail of the queue; if the queue is full the controller must wait (backpressure) before sending another request.  
The runway manager repeatedly looks at the head of the queue: if “adminPreempt” is false it assigns the runway to that aircraft and removes the entry; if “adminPreempt” is true it discards the normal head and immediately assigns the runway to the admin‑designated emergency aircraft, resetting “adminPreempt” afterward.  
The privileged admin can set “adminPreempt” at any time, causing the next scheduling step to ignore the normal queue order and to clear any pending request at the head, thereby guaranteeing the emergency aircraft’s exclusive access.  
All participants observe that when the runway manager reports a non‑none occupant, no other controller may have a requestPending flag that corresponds to the same runway, and the admin’s override never results in two occupants simultaneously.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: At no time can more than one aircraft, including an emergency one, be assigned to the runway simultaneously.

A Train Controller process creates a request to reserve the next signalling block and pushes that request onto a bounded work queue that is shared with the Block Manager process.  
The Block Manager continuously pulls the oldest request from the queue, but only if the target block is currently free; when it grants the reservation it marks the block as occupied.  
If the queue reaches its maximum capacity, the Train Controller receives back‑pressure and must wait until the Block Manager has removed at least one entry before sending more requests.  
An Admin Console may at any moment issue a privileged override request that is placed at the front of the queue, bypassing normal ordering and allowing the Block Manager to pre‑empt the current head of the line.  
When an override is present, the Block Manager first checks whether the block is occupied; if it is, it forces the current occupant to release the block before granting the admin’s request.  
Both the Train Controller and the Admin Console keep a single flag indicating whether they have an outstanding request in the queue, while the Block Manager keeps a Boolean indicating whether the block is occupied.  
The system guarantees that once a request is granted, no other request—whether normal or privileged—can be granted for the same block until the occupancy flag is cleared.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any time no two trains are authorized to occupy the same track block simultaneously.

The Grid Controller maintains a global capacity counter and the identifier of the current lease‑holder, together with the lease’s expiration time. Each Substation Agent keeps a local list of its controllable loads and a flag indicating whether it has a valid lease. When a Substation Agent wants to initiate a load‑shed, it sends a lease‑request to the Grid Controller; the controller grants the lease to the first requester, records the requester’s ID, and sets an expiry based on the latest capacity forecast. The lease‑holder Substation Agent then selects loads to disconnect, marks each chosen load as “shed” and notifies the controller, which updates the global capacity counter accordingly. If the controller later receives a capacity‑increase signal (e.g., a new generation source coming online), it resets the expiration time of the existing lease so the holder may continue shedding without re‑requesting. When the lease expires, the Grid Controller clears the lease holder field, allowing another Substation Agent to acquire the lease and continue shedding if needed. All parties periodically resend heartbeat messages; a missed heartbeat automatically aborts the lease and forces the holder to stop any further shedding until a new lease is obtained.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No individual load can be disconnected more than once.

The line consists of three cooperating controllers: **Conveyor**, **Washer**, and **Dryer**. Each controller keeps a single Boolean flag, *prepared*, indicating whether it has finished its local initialization for the next car. The protocol begins with a **prepare phase** in which the conveyor signals the other two controllers to set *prepared* true; each controller replies with a **vote** (yes if *prepared* is true, no otherwise). If all votes are yes, a **commit phase** is launched and every controller advances its state to *active* for the car; if any vote is no, an **abort** is broadcast and all controllers reset *prepared* to false. A privileged **Admin** can at any moment send an **override** message that forces all controllers to either commit immediately (ignoring pending votes) or abort immediately (resetting *prepared*). The override is accepted only when the admin’s token flag is set, and it supersedes any ongoing two‑phase commit. All controllers must acknowledge the admin’s decision before proceeding to the next car.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total number of cars on the conveyor never increases or decreases without a corresponding commit or abort transition.

The YardController keeps the current queue capacity and the number of pending container moves. Each CraneWorker maintains whether it is idle or currently handling a container. When a CraneWorker finishes a lift it posts a “work request” to the bounded work queue; the queue accepts the request only if its length is below the controller’s capacity, otherwise the worker must wait (backpressure). The YardController can increase or decrease the capacity at any time when a new berth opens or a crane goes offline, and the queue instantly honors the new limit for subsequent requests. If the capacity is reduced below the current queue length, the controller blocks new requests until the queue drains to the new limit. A CraneWorker that is idle repeatedly checks the queue, dequeues the next container move when one is available, and marks itself as busy until it finishes the lift. When a lift is done, the worker marks itself idle again and may submit a new request, restarting the cycle. 

SAFETY PROPERTY: At no time can two CraneWorkers be assigned to lift the same container from the same vessel berth.

The system consists of a finite ring of BlockControllers, each responsible for one contiguous subway track block and for maintaining a local copy of the shared occupancy record (which records which train occupies which block). Each controller stores two variables: a Boolean **hasToken** indicating whether it currently holds the ring token, and an integer **recordVersion** that records the version number of the occupancy record it most recently wrote. When a controller detects a change in its block (a train entering or leaving), it first checks **hasToken**; if it already holds the token it immediately writes the new occupancy information, increments **recordVersion**, and then passes the token to its clockwise neighbour. If it does not hold the token, it places a “pending update” flag and waits until it receives the token, at which point it performs the pending write before forwarding the token. A controller that is slow to process its update simply retains the token longer, but the token is never discarded; after completing its write it must forward the token, guaranteeing progress for the rest of the ring. The ring order is static, so each controller knows exactly which neighbour to hand the token to, and the token itself carries no data other than the right to write. If a controller’s processing is delayed, subsequent controllers will still eventually receive the token once the slow controller finishes, ensuring exclusive access without requiring failure detection.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The shared occupancy record is never overwritten with an older version, so no train‑position update is lost.

The system consists of a central Prescription Manager and two participants: the Medication Stocker, which holds the pills, and the Label Printer, which prints patient labels. Each participant keeps a simple flag indicating whether it has “prepared” its resource for a given prescription request (e.g., “stock ready” or “label ready”). When a pharmacist submits a prescription, the Prescription Manager broadcasts a *prepare* request to both participants; each replies with an acknowledgment when its flag is set to ready. After the manager has received acknowledgments from both, it sends a *commit* command, prompting the Stocker to dispense the pills into the tray and the Printer to attach the printed label. If a participant is slow, the manager simply waits for its acknowledgment before issuing the commit, but it never aborts the transaction because no participant ever fails outright. Finally, once the commit is issued, the participants perform their irreversible actions and then reset their flags to idle for the next prescription.

SAFETY PROPERTY: A prescription’s medication is dispensed at most once.

The system consists of a set of aircraft controllers, each acting as a participant that requests a runway time slot for an incoming or departing plane. Each controller keeps a local copy of the next available slot number and a flag indicating whether it is currently holding the global compare‑and‑swap register. To allocate a slot, a controller reads the current value of the shared register, proposes the next slot number, and performs a compare‑and‑swap that succeeds only if the register still contains the value it read. If the compare‑and‑swap succeeds, the controller updates its local copy to the next slot and announces the allocation to the tower; if it fails, it rereads the register and retries later. A slow controller may take many retry attempts, but it never abandons its request, ensuring eventual progress as long as the register is accessed by at least one active participant. The tower monitors the announced allocations and feeds the latest confirmed slot number back into the shared register, allowing all controllers to converge on a consistent view. Because the compare‑and‑swap operation is atomic, at most one controller can succeed for any given slot, preventing overlapping assignments even when some controllers are delayed.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two aircraft are ever assigned the same runway time slot.

The network consists of a central DoorLockController, several SmartLock devices on each door, and a homeowner’s mobile app that issues lock or unlock commands. Each SmartLock stores a local version counter and a flag indicating whether it is currently processing a request; the controller keeps the latest global version for the whole house. When the app sends a command, the controller reads the current global version, increments it, and attaches that version to the command before broadcasting it to the targeted SmartLock. A SmartLock that receives the command checks its own version; if the attached version is higher than its current version, it atomically applies the lock or unlock action, updates its version, and replies with an acknowledgment containing the same version. Because messages may arrive out of order, a SmartLock discards any command whose version is not strictly greater than the version it already holds, and the controller retries the operation by resending the command with a fresh incremented version until an acknowledgment is received. This optimistic‑locking with retry ensures that only the most recent command can affect a lock, even when network reordering causes older messages to be delivered later.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No lock state change can be lost or overwritten by an older command, so the shared door‑state record always reflects the latest successful update.

The participants are the floor request panels (one on each floor), a central scheduler that runs in the building’s control room, and the elevators themselves that execute assignments.  
Each panel maintains a single Boolean flag indicating whether it has an outstanding request, while the scheduler keeps a shared compare‑and‑swap register that either holds the identifier of a pending floor request or the special value EMPTY.  
When a passenger presses the call button, the panel attempts a compare‑and‑swap on the register: it succeeds only if the register currently contains EMPTY, in which case it writes its floor number; otherwise it retries after a short delay.  
The scheduler repeatedly reads the register; if it finds a floor number it selects the nearest idle elevator, marks that elevator as busy, and then uses a compare‑and‑swap to replace the floor number with EMPTY, signalling that the request has been taken.  
If a panel crashes silently after having written its floor number, the scheduler’s periodic timeout will eventually detect that the request has not been serviced and will reset the register to EMPTY, allowing other panels to issue new requests.  
All state can be captured with three variables: the register, a panel’s request flag, and each elevator’s idle/busy flag, keeping the model small enough for formal analysis.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The set of pending floor requests stored in the register always equals the set of requests that have been issued by panels and not yet assigned to an elevator.

The system consists of three participants – a Blood Collector that picks up donations, a Central Warehouse that stores inventory, and a Transfusion Center that dispenses units to hospitals. Each participant stores a small table for each blood‑type batch containing (1) the identifier of the current lease holder, (2) the lease’s expiration timestamp, and (3) the version number of the last update. When a Transfusion Center needs a unit of O‑negative blood it sends a lease‑request message to the Warehouse; the Warehouse replies with a lease grant that includes a freshly generated lease ID, an expiration time (e.g., 5 minutes), and increments the version number. The Transfusion Center must acknowledge the grant before the lease expires; if the acknowledgment arrives after the expiry, the Warehouse discards the lease and may re‑grant it to another requester. Because network links can reorder messages, every lease message carries its version number and expiration; recipients ignore any message whose version is older than the one they already hold. Lease expiry is enforced locally: each participant periodically checks the stored expiration and, when it passes, automatically clears the lease holder field, allowing a new lease to be issued. The Collector updates the Warehouse’s inventory only when it sees a valid lease owned by the Warehouse, preventing it from overwriting a batch that is currently leased for transfusion. This lightweight protocol can be modeled with the three state variables described above.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any moment, at most one Transfusion Center holds a valid lease for a given unit of O‑negative blood, guaranteeing exclusive access to that unit.

The line has three participants: a central Controller, a BrushUnit that holds the water‑spray valve, and a Dryer that follows the BrushUnit on the conveyor. Each participant stores two pieces of state: the current epoch number it believes is active and a flag indicating whether it currently owns the water‑spray valve. When the Controller decides to change the wash configuration, it increments its epoch and broadcasts an “epoch X, new‑config” message to the BrushUnit and the Dryer. Upon receiving a message, a participant updates its epoch only if the received epoch is greater than its stored one, thereby discarding any older or reordered messages. After the BrushUnit and Dryer have both sent back an “epoch X‑ack” message, the Controller sends a “commit‑epoch X” that grants the BrushUnit exclusive ownership of the water‑spray valve for that epoch. The BrushUnit releases the valve only after it receives a “release‑epoch X” from the Controller, which happens after the Dryer signals that it has finished its downstream stage. Because every action is tied to a monotonically increasing epoch, out‑of‑order messages cannot cause two participants to think they hold the valve simultaneously.

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any time, at most one BrushUnit may have exclusive control of the water‑spray valve.

The system consists of a Central Scheduler, one controller for each elevator shaft, and a privileged Admin Console.  
The Scheduler and every controller each keep a single integer called the configuration epoch, and the controllers also store a mode flag that is either normal service or maintenance.  
When the Scheduler wants to reconfigure the bank, it increments its epoch, writes the new epoch and the desired mode into a broadcast message, and sets a pending flag.  
Each controller receives the broadcast, and if the epoch in the message is greater than its own epoch it updates its epoch, switches to the announced mode, and clears the pending flag; otherwise it ignores the message.  
The Admin Console holds a privileged override token; when an operator uses it, the console forces the Scheduler to increment the epoch, broadcast a maintenance‑mode command, and records that an admin override has been exercised.  
The override can be issued at any time, but because it also raises the epoch, all controllers will apply the maintenance mode exactly once for that epoch, even if other reconfiguration attempts are in flight.  
After a controller has entered maintenance mode for a given epoch, it will never revert to normal service until the Scheduler later announces a higher epoch with a new mode.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: At most one transition to maintenance mode may occur for any given configuration epoch.

The system consists of a central pharmacy server and several dispensing terminals that patients use to request medication. Each terminal keeps a local copy of the prescription record’s version number and a flag indicating whether it currently holds the optimistic lock for that record. When a patient initiates a dispense, the terminal reads the current version from the server, checks the lock flag, and, if unlocked, sends a lock‑request containing the version it observed. The server replies with either a grant (including the same version) or a denial; because messages may arrive out of order, terminals compare the returned version with their stored version before proceeding. If the terminal receives a grant and its stored version still matches, it decrements the medication stock, updates the prescription record, increments the version locally, and sends a commit message; otherwise it aborts, restores its lock flag, and retries the whole process. A commit from the terminal causes the server to advance the authoritative version and release the lock, after which the terminal can accept new requests. Any lock request that arrives with an older version than the server’s current version is ignored, forcing the requesting terminal to refresh its view and retry.

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any moment, at most one dispensing terminal can hold the lock for a given prescription, ensuring that only one terminal can update the medication stock for that prescription.

The system consists of a Block Controller that maintains a single compare‑and‑swap register for each track section, and a set of trains that act as participants. Each train keeps a local flag indicating whether it is requesting the block and a copy of the last value it read from the register. When a train wants to enter a section it reads the register; if the value shows the block is free, it issues a compare‑and‑swap that tries to replace “free” with its own identifier atomically. If the compare‑and‑swap succeeds, the train records that it now owns the block and proceeds; if it fails, the train waits and retries later. When the train has cleared the section it writes “free” back to the register using another compare‑and‑swap, ensuring that only the current owner can release it. The protocol tolerates a slow train because the register can only be changed by the train that currently holds the block, so a delayed release merely blocks other trains but does not cause inconsistent ownership.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two trains are ever authorized to occupy the same track block at the same time.

The system consists of a central Scheduler, a set of Elevator Cars, and floor Request Panels that generate ride requests. Each car maintains a single state variable `slot`, which records the time‑slot (a numbered window) it has been granted to stop at the next floor. The Scheduler holds a compare‑and‑swap (CAS) register that stores the highest slot number currently assigned; a car proposes a new slot by reading the register, incrementing the value, and issuing a CAS that succeeds only if the register still contains the old highest value. When a car’s CAS succeeds, it writes the new slot into its own `slot` variable and the Scheduler updates the register; if the CAS fails, the car retries with the current register value. Floor Request Panels send “pick‑up” messages to the Scheduler, but because the network can reorder messages, a request for a higher floor may arrive before a lower‑floor request. The Scheduler processes requests in the order they are received, each time performing a CAS to allocate the next free slot, which guarantees that even out‑of‑order messages cannot cause two cars to receive the same slot. Cars use the slot number to determine when to open their doors, and they release the slot after the stop is completed, allowing the Scheduler to reuse it for later requests.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two elevator cars are ever assigned the same time‑slot to serve a floor.

The yard contains a fixed set of crane operators, each responsible for moving containers in a specific berth, and each operator runs a local controller that holds a Boolean flag “hasToken”. The token circulates in a logical ring connecting the controllers; only the controller whose flag is true may command its crane to lift a container. When an operator finishes a lift, it clears its flag and forwards the token to the next controller in the ring by setting that controller’s flag to true. If a controller crashes without clearing its flag, the token is considered lost and a watchdog timer at the next controller expires, prompting that controller to issue a “recovery” message that resets the ring and grants the token to the first alive controller. Each controller also records the identifier of the last container it moved, allowing it to detect stale token messages that refer to an earlier operation. Upon receiving a token, a controller first checks that the recorded identifier matches the current operation sequence; if it does not, the token is discarded and the recovery procedure is triggered. The protocol therefore ensures that at any moment at most one crane is active and that a crashed controller cannot permanently block the ring.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No crane is ever commanded to lift a container by a controller that does not currently hold the valid token.

The swarm consists of multiple surveillance drones, a central ground‑station server that holds a bounded work queue of scan‑tasks, and an admin console that can issue privileged overrides. Each drone keeps a local flag indicating whether it is idle or executing a task, while the ground station maintains the queue length and a boolean “override‑active” flag. When a drone finishes a scan it sends a completion notice and asks the server for the next task; if the queue is not empty the server dequeues the oldest task and assigns it, otherwise the drone remains idle. If the queue reaches its capacity, the server signals backpressure to the task‑ingestion service so that no new routine scans are added until space opens. An admin may at any time activate an override, causing the server to prepend a high‑priority emergency scan to the front of the queue and temporarily suspend backpressure for that task. While an override is active, the “override‑active” flag stays true and the server allows the emergency task to be delivered even if the queue is full, after which the flag is cleared. All participants continuously update a shared surveillance log that records each task’s identifier, drone identifier, and timestamp.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No update to the shared surveillance log can be lost or overwritten by concurrent task assignments.

The system consists of two monitoring controllers, each running an autonomous instance of the surveillance algorithm, and a fleet of drones that can be assigned to high‑resolution imaging tasks.  
All drones share a common pool that records the number of available imaging slots and a version number that is incremented each time the pool is modified.  
When a controller wants to allocate a slot, it reads the current version and the number of free slots, decides to claim one if any are free, and then writes back the new count together with the version it observed incremented by one.  
If the write fails because the version in the pool no longer matches the one the controller read, the controller discards its tentative claim and retries the whole read‑modify‑write cycle.  
Once a controller successfully writes, the claimed slot is considered locked to that controller and a drone is dispatched to perform the high‑resolution scan.  
The other controller continues its own retries independently, but because the version check guarantees that only one write can succeed for any given version, the two instances never assign the same slot to different drones.  

**SAFETY PROPERTY:** At any moment no two controllers can assign the same high‑resolution imaging slot to different drones.

The system consists of a fleet of autonomous picking robots and a central warehouse manager that shares a single compare‑and‑swap (CAS) register called **CapacityReg**. Each robot locally keeps a Boolean flag **hasSlot** indicating whether it currently holds a reservation for a pallet slot in the loading zone. When a robot needs to place a pallet, it reads the current value of CapacityReg, which encodes the total number of free slots, and then attempts a CAS operation that decrements the count and atomically sets its own **hasSlot** to true. The manager may change the total capacity at runtime by writing a new value into CapacityReg; this write is only accepted if no robot is in the middle of a CAS, ensuring the register always reflects a consistent capacity. If a robot finishes loading its pallet, it resets **hasSlot** to false and performs a CAS that increments the free‑slot count in CapacityReg. Robots that fail their CAS retry after a short back‑off, guaranteeing progress without interfering with capacity updates. All state can be captured by the three variables: the integer stored in CapacityReg, each robot’s **hasSlot**, and the manager’s desired capacity value.

SAFETY PROPERTY: A pallet is loaded into a specific loading‑zone slot at most once.

The system has three participants: a Student client that initiates a registration request, a Registration Server that holds the authoritative course catalog, and a Course Record that stores the current enrollment count and a version number. Each Course Record maintains two state variables – the current enrollee list and an integer version that is incremented on every successful update. When a Student wants to register for a class, the client first reads the course’s version number, then sends an enrollment request together with that version to the Registration Server. The server checks whether the supplied version still matches the record’s current version; if it does, the server adds the student to the enrollee list, increments the version, and acknowledges the change, otherwise it rejects the request and the client retries with the latest version. If the server crashes silently after acknowledging but before persisting the update, the client treats the missing acknowledgment as a failure and repeats the whole read‑modify‑write cycle, which will succeed only when the server recovers and the version numbers are consistent. The optimistic‑locking protocol therefore guarantees that only one successful enrollment can be applied to a given version of a course, and any stale attempt is retried until it sees the newest version. This protocol can be modeled with the two state variables (enrollee list and version) plus a flag indicating whether the server is alive.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No student is enrolled in a course using a stale version of the course record, preventing any unauthorized or out‑of‑date enrollment.

The swarm consists of a set of autonomous drones, each responsible for scanning a specific fire‑line segment and maintaining a local view of the segment’s **lock version** and the **owner ID** of the high‑resolution thermal camera slot for that segment. When a drone wishes to capture a thermal image, it reads the current lock version, increments it locally, and broadcasts an *Acquire* message containing the new version and its own ID. Upon receiving an *Acquire* message, a drone compares the incoming version with its stored version; if the incoming version is newer it adopts the new owner ID and version, otherwise it ignores the message. After broadcasting its own *Acquire*, the initiator waits for an *Ack* that confirms no higher version has been observed; if the *Ack* arrives with a version equal to the one it sent, the drone proceeds to use the camera, otherwise it discards its claim and retries with a fresh version. Because messages may be reordered, a drone treats any later‑arriving *Acquire* with a higher version as authoritative, even if it arrives after an earlier *Ack*, thereby ensuring that the most recent claim takes precedence. The retry loop is bounded: a drone will repeat the acquire‑ack cycle until it receives an *Ack* that matches the version it broadcast, guaranteeing eventual progress despite reordering. All state updates (version and owner) are monotonic, so the protocol can be modeled with just the two variables “currentVersion” and “currentOwner”.

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any moment, at most one drone holds the high‑resolution thermal camera slot for a given fire‑line segment.

The Conveyor Controller acts as the transaction coordinator and initiates a wash cycle by writing a new *WashTicket* record with status “INIT” and a monotonically increasing version number. It then sends a **prepare** request to the Wash Station Controller, the Billing Server, and the Exit Gate Controller, each of which records the same version and replies “READY” if its local resources (water pressure, payment ledger, gate lock) are available, or “ABORT” otherwise. After receiving a “READY” from all three participants, the Conveyor Controller broadcasts a **commit** message, causing each participant to atomically apply its part of the wash (activate spray, debit the customer, unlock the gate) and finally update the *WashTicket* status to “COMMITTED”. If any participant replies “ABORT”, the Coordinator instead sends an **abort** message, and every participant rolls back its tentative changes, setting the status to “ABORTED”. A privileged Admin can at any time issue an **override** command that forces the Coordinator to ignore pending “ABORT” replies and either force a **commit‑override** or a **abort‑override**, which the participants must obey even if they have already prepared. The override is recorded in the *WashTicket* as a special flag, and once processed the ticket’s version is incremented again, guaranteeing that later normal cycles see the most recent decision.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No wash cycle can overwrite a *WashTicket* record that has already been committed or overridden, ensuring that every update to the shared record is preserved and never lost.

The protocol involves a Central Settlement Coordinator (CSC) and a fixed set of participating banks (Bank A, Bank B, …). Each bank maintains a local “ready” flag that reflects whether its current settlement capacity can accommodate the batch amount it is assigned. The CSC keeps a single batchStatus variable (INIT, PREPARED, COMMITTED) together with a pendingVotes counter that tracks how many READY responses are still expected. In phase 1 the CSC broadcasts a PREPARE request containing the total batch amount; each bank checks its capacity and replies READY if it can settle the share, or NOT_READY otherwise. If a bank’s capacity changes after the request arrives but before it replies, it includes the new capacity in the vote and the CSC only records a READY vote when the updated capacity still covers the required share. When the CSC has received READY from every bank, it sets batchStatus to PREPARED and sends a COMMIT message; any NOT_READY or a capacity reduction that invalidates a previous READY forces the CSC to change batchStatus to ABORT and broadcast a ROLLBACK. After a COMMIT, all banks atomically update their ledgers and permanently record the settlement, and the CSC finally marks batchStatus as COMMITTED.

SAFETY PROPERTY: A settlement batch can be committed at most once, and once it is committed it can never be aborted.

The system consists of a set of elevator controllers, one for each car in the bank, arranged in a logical ring. Each controller keeps two variables: a Boolean flag indicating whether it currently holds the exclusive token, and a counter of the number of passengers it is permitted to board in the current service cycle. When a controller holds the token it may open its doors, allow up to the counter‑specified passengers to board, close the doors, and then pass the token to the next controller in the ring. After passing the token the controller resets its counter to zero until it receives the token again. If a controller crashes silently while holding the token, the controller downstream detects the lack of a token arrival within a fixed timeout and injects a recovery token, thereby breaking the stale hold and continuing the ring. All controllers obey the rule that they never increase the passenger counter beyond the car’s maximum capacity, and they only load passengers while the token is in their possession. The token therefore guarantees that at most one elevator is loading passengers at any moment, preventing simultaneous overloads.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The number of passengers inside any elevator never exceeds its rated capacity.

The system consists of a single Runway Manager and several Aircraft agents that may request a landing slot.  
The manager maintains two pieces of state: the identifier of the aircraft that currently holds the runway and a counter of acknowledgments received for the pending assignment.  
When an aircraft wants to land it sends a Request to the manager; the manager records the request and broadcasts a Proposal naming that aircraft as the next holder.  
Every aircraft that receives the Proposal replies with an Ack, and when the manager has collected acknowledgments from a quorum of the known aircraft it broadcasts a Commit to finalize the assignment.  
To survive message reordering, each Proposal and Commit carries a monotonically increasing term number, and agents only act on messages whose term is newer than any term they have already processed.  
If a stale Proposal arrives after a Commit for a later term, the agent discards it, preventing an earlier proposal from overwriting the committed assignment.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: Once a runway assignment has been committed by a quorum, no subsequent message can cause that assignment to be lost or overwritten.

The conveyor line consists of three stations—Pre‑Wash, Rinse, and Dryer—each of which can hold a lease that gives it exclusive right to move a car through that stage.  
Every station maintains a small state: (i) whether it currently holds the lease, (ii) the expiry time of the lease, and (iii) whether a car is physically present in its section.  
When a station finishes processing its car it writes a new lease request to a shared lease register, sets its expiry to a short timeout, and then moves the car to the next station.  
If the lease expires before the station has renewed it, any other alive station may claim the lease and, if a car is still stuck, it will take control of the car and continue the wash.  
A station that crashes silently simply stops renewing its lease; other stations periodically read the lease register, detect the missed renewal, and reclaim the lease after the timeout.  
To prevent two stations from acting on the same car, a station will only start processing when it both holds a valid lease and sees that the downstream station does not already have a car.  
When a lease is reclaimed after a crash, the recovering station first checks for a leftover car and, if found, clears the stale car flag before resuming normal operation.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any moment the total number of cars on the conveyor line equals the number that entered minus the number that have exited, so cars are never created or destroyed by the protocol.

The swarm consists of a set of surveillance drones that each store a local role (“leader” or “follower”), a numeric capacity indicating how many fire‑hotspots it can monitor, and a term identifier for the current election round. Periodically each drone broadcasts a heartbeat containing its current term and capacity; followers record the highest‑capacity leader they hear from and update their view of the swarm’s total capacity. If a follower stops receiving a heartbeat for a configurable timeout, it increments the term, declares itself a candidate, and broadcasts a “candidacy” message that includes its capacity. All drones that receive a candidacy message compare the advertised capacity with any other candidates they have heard in the same term and vote for the highest‑capacity candidate; the candidate that collects a majority of votes becomes the new leader. When the leader’s capacity changes at runtime—e.g., because a battery pack is swapped—it immediately broadcasts an updated heartbeat so followers can recompute the swarm’s effective monitoring power. Any follower that learns of a higher‑capacity leader in the same term immediately drops its own candidacy and re‑aligns to the new leader. The protocol repeats this election and capacity‑update cycle continuously to guarantee that the swarm always has a single, up‑to‑date leader able to assign hotspot‑monitoring tasks.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No drone that is not the current elected leader or that holds a stale term may issue surveillance assignments or modify the shared capacity view.

The fleet consists of autonomous picker robots and a single central dispatcher that assigns picking tasks and tracks the total load capacity of the warehouse.  
Each robot stores locally the current configuration epoch and the list of tasks it is currently executing.  
The dispatcher maintains the global configuration epoch and the current maximum load capacity, which may be changed by an operator at any time.  
When the dispatcher decides to change the capacity, it increments the global epoch, records the new capacity, and broadcasts the new epoch to all robots.  
A robot that receives a higher epoch abandons any pending task updates that were based on the old epoch and requests a fresh assignment from the dispatcher.  
When a robot finishes a pick, it sends a completion record together with its current epoch to the dispatcher, which only writes the record if the epoch matches the dispatcher’s current epoch.  
If a robot’s request or completion arrives with an outdated epoch, the dispatcher replies with the latest epoch, forcing the robot to retry using the up‑to‑date configuration.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No robot’s completed pick record is overwritten or lost because updates are accepted only when they carry the current configuration epoch.

The system consists of a RunwayController process, a set of Aircraft processes that request landings, and a privileged Admin process.  
The controller maintains three state variables: the current epoch number, an allocation map that records which aircraft is authorized for each epoch, and a Boolean adminOverride flag.  
When an aircraft wishes to land it sends a request to the controller; the controller increments the epoch, records the aircraft’s identifier in the allocation map for that epoch, and broadcasts the new epoch number to all participants.  
Before an epoch begins, each controller permits only the aircraft listed for that epoch to enter the runway and rejects all others.  
If the admin issues an override, it sets the adminOverride flag and directly writes a new aircraft identifier into the allocation map for the current epoch, and every controller must obey this override regardless of the previous assignment.  
The override is cleared automatically when the overridden epoch ends, after which normal epoch‑numbered reconfiguration resumes.  
All participants treat the runway as free only when the allocation map for the current epoch contains no aircraft, and they must wait for the next epoch before attempting another landing.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any time, at most one aircraft is authorized to occupy the runway.

The system consists of a Central Controller (CC) and three Elevator Controllers (EC1, EC2, EC3), each responsible for one elevator shaft. Each EC keeps a single variable “slot” that records the floor it plans to stop at next, while the CC keeps a list of pending floor requests and a “prepare” flag for each EC. When a new floor request arrives, the CC starts a two‑phase commit by broadcasting a “prepare” message asking each EC to promise not to reserve that floor slot. An EC that can accommodate the request records the slot locally and replies “ready”; otherwise it replies “abort”. The CC gathers the replies, and if every EC replied “ready” it sends a “commit” message causing each EC to finalize its reservation, otherwise it sends “abort” and all ECs discard any tentative slot. If an EC crashes after replying “ready” but before receiving the final decision, it recovers with its tentative slot marked as uncertain and waits for a recovery message from the CC. The CC, after a timeout, treats a missing reply as an “abort” to avoid deadlock and later informs any recovered EC of the decision so it can roll back its tentative reservation.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any moment, no two elevators may be assigned the same floor slot for their next stop.

The swarm consists of many surveillance drones and a ground‑control station that together own a single shared register called **FireMap**, which records the current list of detected wildfire hotspots and a monotonically increasing version number.  
Each drone periodically reads the version number from FireMap, adds any newly observed hotspot to its local copy, and prepares a compare‑and‑swap request stating “if the version is still X, replace the hotspot list with Y and set the version to X+1”.  
The drone sends this request over the wireless mesh; because messages can be reordered, the acknowledgment from the ground station may arrive before the request itself.  
When the ground station receives a request, it atomically checks whether the stored version matches the expected value; if it does, it swaps the hotspot list and increments the version, otherwise it discards the request and returns a failure response.  
Drones that receive a failure response repeat the read‑modify‑write cycle using the latest version they just observed, ensuring progress despite out‑of‑order delivery.  
The only mutable state in the whole system is the FireMap’s version number and its hotspot list, so the protocol can be modelled with two variables.  
By using the compare‑and‑swap primitive, all drones coordinate on a single coherent record even when network packets are shuffled.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No drone’s hotspot update that succeeds in the compare‑and‑swap can be overwritten by another later update without that later update also succeeding on the same current version, guaranteeing that no updates to the shared FireMap are lost.

The fleet consists of three robots—R A, R B, and R C—arranged in a logical ring order A → B → C → A. Each robot stores a single state variable “hasToken” that is true only when the token resides with it, and a second variable “inAisle” that is true while it is occupying the narrow aisle, the sole critical resource. When a robot’s “hasToken” is true it may request access to the aisle; if the aisle is free it sets “inAisle” to true, moves through, and upon completion it clears “inAisle”. After leaving the aisle the robot passes the token to its successor by setting its own “hasToken” to false and sending a token‑forward message that causes the successor’s “hasToken” to become true. If a robot is slow, it simply retains the token longer; the other robots keep their “hasToken” false and continuously poll for the token, but they never assume the token has been lost. The token‑forward message is guaranteed to be delivered, so no robot ever crashes or permanently blocks the ring, only experiences delay. The protocol thus requires only the two Boolean variables per robot and the ring topology to coordinate exclusive aisle usage.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any moment, no more than one robot is inside the narrow aisle.
spec_text:
---- MODULE W4C2x1x0x3 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets

CONSTANT Robots

(* ---- Variables ---- *)
VARIABLES hasToken, inAisle

(* ---- Helper definitions ---- *)
vars == <<hasToken, inAisle>>

Succ == [r \in Robots |-> 
          IF r = "A" THEN "B"
          ELSE IF r = "B" THEN "C"
          ELSE "A"]

(* ---- Initial state ---- *)
Init ==
    /\ hasToken = [r \in Robots |-> IF r = "A" THEN TRUE ELSE FALSE]
    /\ inAisle = [r \in Robots |-> FALSE]

(* ---- Actions ---- *)

Enter(r) ==
    /\ r \in Robots
    /\ hasToken[r] = TRUE
    /\ inAisle[r] = FALSE
    /\ \A s \in Robots : inAisle[s] = FALSE   \* aisle is free
    /\ inAisle' = [inAisle EXCEPT ![r] = TRUE]
    /\ UNCHANGED hasToken

ExitAndPass(r) ==
    /\ r \in Robots
    /\ hasToken[r] = TRUE
    /\ inAisle[r] = TRUE
    /\ inAisle' = [inAisle EXCEPT ![r] = FALSE]
    /\ hasToken' = [hasToken EXCEPT ![r] = FALSE,
                                   ![Succ[r]] = TRUE]
    /\ UNCHANGED << >>

(* A robot may simply do nothing (e.g., delay) *)
Idle ==
    UNCHANGED <<hasToken, inAisle>>

Next ==
    \/ \E r \in Robots : Enter(r)
    \/ \E r \in Robots : ExitAndPass(r)
    \/ Idle

(* ---- Specification (optional, not used by the cfg) ---- *)
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

(* ---- Safety invariant ---- *)
NoTwoInAisle ==
    \A r1, r2 \in Robots :
        (inAisle[r1] /\ inAisle[r2]) => r1 = r2

======
cfg_text:
CONSTANTS
    Robots = {"A", "B", "C"}

INIT Init
NEXT Next
INVARIANT NoTwoInAisle

Traders submit a buy or sell offer by attempting a compare‑and‑swap on a shared register that holds the current best price and whether it is a bid or an ask.  
The auctioneer repeatedly reads that register; if the CAS succeeds it updates the stored price to the higher bid or lower ask, thereby moving the auction forward.  
The auctioneer also maintains a single status flag indicating whether the opening auction is “open” or “closed”.  
A privileged admin can at any moment write an override flag together with a price; when the flag is set the next CAS operation by any participant must replace the existing price with the admin’s price regardless of its value.  
After the override has been applied, the admin clears the flag so that normal CAS competition resumes.  
All participants interact only with the one register and the status flag, so no additional coordination state is required.  
The protocol ensures that only one effective price—either a trader’s best bid/ask or the admin’s override—is ever recorded at a time.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any moment exactly one effective price is stored, so no price is inadvertently created or lost.

The batch consists of a set of participating banks, each running a Settlement Agent that holds a local ledger of pending transfers and a counter called epoch. A central Coordinator maintains the global epoch number, the total settlement capacity for the current epoch, and a list of banks authorized to send or receive funds in that epoch. At the start of an epoch the Coordinator broadcasts the new epoch number together with the current capacity, and each Agent updates its epoch counter and rejects any new transfer request that would exceed the announced capacity. While the epoch is active, agents may submit a Transfer Request to the Coordinator, which atomically decrements the remaining capacity, records the request in a batch log, and acknowledges the sender. When a bank needs to change its own processing capacity (for example, because it has refreshed its liquidity), it sends a Capacity Adjustment message to the Coordinator; the Coordinator incorporates the adjustment into the remaining capacity for the ongoing epoch without changing the epoch number. Once the Coordinator observes that no pending requests remain and the capacity is fully consumed or the epoch timeout expires, it finalizes the batch, sends a Commit message to all agents, and increments the global epoch, starting a new configuration. All agents, upon receiving the Commit, apply the recorded transfers to their local ledgers, reset their pending request list, and wait for the next epoch broadcast.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total amount of money moved in each epoch is exactly equal to the capacity announced for that epoch, so no funds are created or destroyed during settlement.

The swarm consists of a set of surveillance drones, each identified by a unique ID, and a ground‑control node that oversees the ring.  
Every drone stores a local Boolean flag *hasToken* that indicates whether it currently holds the exclusive right to overfly the fire front, and a variable *next* that names the ID of the drone that should receive the token next.  
When a drone’s *hasToken* becomes true it activates its thermal camera, streams fire‑line data for its allotted time slice, then clears its flag and passes the token to the drone named in *next*.  
The ground‑control node can at any moment issue a *resize* command that changes the ring size; the command updates the *next* pointers of the affected drones so that the token will continue to circulate over the new set of participants.  
If the new size is smaller, the drones being removed are instructed to set *hasToken* to false and drop out of the ring, while if it is larger, newly added drones are inserted with *hasToken* initially false and appropriate *next* links.  
The protocol guarantees that a token is never duplicated because the sender clears its *hasToken* flag before the receiver sets it, and only the holder may perform surveillance actions.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No drone that does not currently hold the token may capture or transmit fire‑line imagery.

In the vending‑machine network there are three roles: the Central Inventory Manager (CIM), a set of local Vending Nodes (VN) and a client device that initiates a purchase.  
Each VN keeps a local count of how many units of each product it can dispense, while the CIM stores the global stock record that aggregates those counts.  
When a client requests a product, the VN that will vend starts a two‑phase commit by sending a prepare message to the CIM indicating the product and quantity.  
The CIM checks the global stock and replies with a vote to commit only if the aggregated count remains non‑negative after the tentative deduction.  
After receiving a commit vote, the VN records a tentative dispense, the CIM updates its global count, and both send an acknowledgment; if any participant aborts, both revert to their previous counts.  
Capacity changes, such as a restock or a removal of a product, are performed by a special Capacity Update operation that also runs through the two‑phase commit so that the new limits are visible to all participants only after the commit succeeds.  
The protocol therefore ensures that every update to the shared inventory either completes atomically across all machines or has no effect at all.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No update to the global inventory record is lost or partially applied, so the total count of any product always reflects either the state before a transaction or the state after it fully commits.

The system consists of three registration nodes (Node A, Node B, and Node C) that each keep a local copy of the number of seats left for a specific course and a flag indicating whether they currently hold the token. Only the node that holds the token may accept a student’s enrollment request; when it receives such a request it checks its local seats‑remaining count, decrements it if a seat is free, records the student ID, and then forwards the registration record to a central log. After processing any pending request, the token‑holder clears its own token flag and sets the token flag of its clockwise neighbour, thereby passing exclusive access around the ring. Each node also runs a watchdog timer; if a node does not see the token arrive within a preset interval, it assumes that the predecessor has crashed silently. The suspecting node then initiates a recovery phase in which it creates a new token, resets its own token flag, and notifies the remaining nodes so that the ring can continue without duplication of the token. Throughout the protocol the total number of seats for the course never changes; seats are only transferred from the “available” pool to the “registered” pool.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total number of seats, whether still available or already assigned to students, always remains equal to the original capacity of the course.
spec_text:
---- MODULE W4C8x1x2x0 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, Sequences, FiniteSets

CONSTANTS SeatsCap \* total capacity of the course
CONSTANTS Nodes \* {"A","B","C"}

\* Helper for clockwise neighbour
NextNode(n) == 
  CASE n = "A" -> "B"
  []  n = "B" -> "C"
  []  n = "C" -> "A"

VARIABLES seatsAvail,        \* seats still free (global truth)
          regCount,         \* number of students already registered
          tokenHolder,      \* which node currently holds the token
          seatsCopy         \* each node's local copy of seatsAvail

\*=================================================================
\* Initial state
\*=================================================================
Init ==
  /\ seatsAvail = SeatsCap
  /\ regCount   = 0
  /\ tokenHolder = "A"
  /\ seatsCopy = [n \in Nodes |-> SeatsCap]

\*=================================================================
\* Actions
\*=================================================================
\* A node that holds the token may accept a registration request
Request ==
  \E n \in Nodes :
    /\ tokenHolder = n
    /\ seatsAvail > 0               \* a seat is free
    /\ seatsAvail' = seatsAvail - 1
    /\ regCount'   = regCount + 1
    /\ tokenHolder' = NextNode(n)   \* pass the token clockwise
    /\ seatsCopy' = [seatsCopy EXCEPT 
                       ![n] = seatsCopy[n] - 1,
                       ![tokenHolder'] = seatsAvail']   \* new holder gets fresh copy
    /\ UNCHANGED << >>               \* no other variables change

\* The token can be passed without a registration (e.g., idle step)
PassToken ==
  \E n \in Nodes :
    /\ tokenHolder = n
    /\ tokenHolder' = NextNode(n)
    /\ seatsCopy' = [seatsCopy EXCEPT ![tokenHolder'] = seatsAvail]
    /\ UNCHANGED << seatsAvail, regCount >>

\* Watchdog‑triggered recovery: a node that has not seen the token creates a new one
Recovery ==
  \E n \in Nodes :
    /\ tokenHolder' = n                \* new (unique) token
    /\ seatsCopy' = [m \in Nodes |-> seatsAvail]   \* all nodes refresh their copy
    /\ UNCHANGED << seatsAvail, regCount >>

\*=================================================================
\* Next-state relation
\*=================================================================
Next == Request \/ PassToken \/ Recovery

\*=================================================================
\* Specification
\*=================================================================
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<seatsAvail, regCount, tokenHolder, seatsCopy>>

\*=================================================================
\* Safety invariant: total seats (available + already assigned) never changes
\*=================================================================
SeatsInvariant == seatsAvail + regCount = SeatsCap

\*=================================================================
\* Theorems (optional)
\*=================================================================
THEOREM Spec => []SeatsInvariant

====
cfg_text:
CONSTANTS SeatsCap = 3
CONSTANTS Nodes = {"A","B","C"}

INIT Init
NEXT Next
INVARIANT SeatsInvariant

The system has three regular participants: a **DonationScanner** that posts new blood‑unit records, an **RequestHandler** that removes units to satisfy hospital orders, and an **InventoryManager** that periodically reconciles the current stock. All three share a bounded work queue called **UpdateQueue** that holds at most N pending inventory operations; each participant inserts an operation only when the queue is not full, otherwise it backs off until space is available. The queue stores a tuple (type, unitID, quantity) and the shared state consists of the queue length, the current total stock count, and a flag indicating whether an admin override is active. When an operation is dequeued, the InventoryManager updates the total stock count accordingly and records the change in a persistent ledger. An **Admin** may at any time set the override flag, which instantly clears the queue, forces the InventoryManager to apply a special “adjust‑to‑desired” operation, and then resets the flag. While the override flag is true, the regular participants are blocked from inserting new updates, providing backpressure until the admin finishes. Once the admin reset occurs, normal queuing and back‑pressure resume.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No update to a blood‑unit record is ever lost; every operation placed in the queue is eventually reflected in the persistent ledger.

The line consists of a set of wash stations (Station 1, Station 2, Station 3) that share a distributed controller called the Coordinator.  
Each station keeps a local variable indicating whether it believes it is the current leader and a heartbeat counter that it increments on every cycle.  
Periodically every station broadcasts its heartbeat value; if a station receives a higher heartbeat than its own, it steps down and adopts the sender as leader.  
The leader is responsible for updating the shared CarQueue pointer, which records the ID of the next car to be sent onto the conveyor.  
When a station thinks the leader has become unresponsive because it has not heard a heartbeat for a timeout period, it starts a leader election by sending an Election message with its own heartbeat value.  
A slow station may delay its heartbeat but will still eventually send one, so other stations only declare it failed after the timeout and will revert to it if its heartbeat later arrives and outweighs their own.  
Once a new leader is accepted, it resumes incremental updates of the CarQueue pointer, and all stations apply the updates only after they have been acknowledged by the leader.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The shared CarQueue pointer is never overwritten by two different stations without one of the updates being recorded, ensuring no lost updates to the shared record.

The swarm consists of a set of surveillance drones, called **Scouts**, and a single command hub, the **Base**.  
Each Scout keeps a local flag that records whether it has committed to a coordinated fire‑hotspot scan.  
When a new hotspot is detected, the Base starts a two‑phase commit by sending a **PREPARE** request to all Scouts, asking them to reserve the necessary battery and the shared high‑resolution camera slot.  
A Scout replies **READY** only if it has sufficient battery and is not already executing a higher‑priority task; otherwise it replies **ABORT**.  
After the Base receives **READY** from every Scout, it broadcasts a **COMMIT**, causing each Scout to set its flag to *SCANNING* and to occupy the camera slot.  
At any time a privileged admin can send an **OVERRIDE** message that forces all Scouts to abort the current scan and release the camera slot, overriding any pending commit.  
If the Base receives an **OVERRIDE**, it immediately sends **ABORT** to every Scout, resetting their flags.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two Scouts may occupy the shared high‑resolution camera slot simultaneously.

The system involves three roles: the Settlement Manager that opens and closes a settlement batch, the Batch Processor nodes that insert individual interbank payment records, and the Capacity Controller that may raise or lower the batch size while the batch is open. All nodes share a single compare‑and‑swap register that holds the index of the next free slot in the batch together with the current capacity limit. When a Batch Processor wants to add a payment it reads the register, checks that the index is lower than the capacity, and then attempts a compare‑and‑swap that atomically increments the index if the value it read is still present. If the compare‑and‑swap succeeds, the processor writes the payment into the slot it reserved; if it fails, it rereads the register and retries. The Capacity Controller can change the capacity by performing a compare‑and‑swap that updates the capacity field only when the register’s index has not moved beyond the new limit, otherwise it first forces the batch to close. The Settlement Manager periodically closes the batch by setting a special “closed” flag in the register; after closure no further compare‑and‑swap updates are accepted. The protocol therefore requires only the register’s index, the capacity limit, and the closed flag as the shared state, which can be captured with three variables.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No payment record can be written by a processor that reads a stale register value or that is not authorized after the batch has been closed or its capacity has been reduced below the slot it tries to claim.

Patrons send a Reserve request for a specific book to the Reservation Manager, which records the request together with the current epoch number.  
The Reservation Manager maintains three variables: the current epoch, a list of pending reservations for each book up to its copy limit, and an admin‑override flag that is initially false.  
When the manager receives a Reserve request, it accepts the request only if the list for that book has fewer entries than the number of copies and the request’s epoch matches the manager’s current epoch.  
Periodically, the system performs a Reconfigure step that increments the epoch number, clears the override flag, and discards any reservations that were made in the previous epoch but not yet fulfilled.  
A privileged admin can issue an Override command at any time, which sets the override flag to true and forces the manager to accept a new reservation even if the copy limit for that book has already been reached, provided the command carries a higher epoch than the current one.  
When the Override flag is true, the manager records the overriding reservation with the new epoch and temporarily raises the effective copy limit for that book by one, ensuring the admin’s request is served while other patrons continue to operate under the normal limit.  
All participants observe the same epoch value through the manager, so any request bearing an older epoch is silently rejected, guaranteeing that concurrent updates are coordinated by the epoch number.  
If the admin later issues a CancelOverride command, the flag is cleared, the extra copy slot is removed, and any reservations that exceed the original copy limit are automatically cancelled in the next Reconfigure step.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: At no time does the number of active reservations for a given book exceed the total number of copies plus one extra slot granted only by an active admin override.

Robots in the warehouse act as agents that want to pick up a load of pallets and store them in a shared staging area. Each robot maintains a local copy of the staging area’s current load and the version number of the last capacity update it observed. When a robot wants to add pallets, it reads the current load and version, computes a new load, and then attempts to write the new load together with the same version number; this write succeeds only if the version has not changed, otherwise the robot discards the attempt and retries after rereading the state. A central Capacity Manager can change the maximum allowed load of the staging area at any time; when it does so it increments the version number and updates the max‑capacity value that robots will see on their next read. Robots that experience a failed write because the version changed must retry the whole read‑modify‑write sequence, thereby ensuring they only commit when their view of the capacity is up‑to‑date. The protocol therefore coordinates many robots concurrently without a global lock, while still allowing the capacity limit to be adjusted dynamically. All participants eventually succeed in their reservation attempts or give up after a bounded number of retries.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total number of pallets stored in the staging area never exceeds the current maximum capacity.

The lobby consists of a **Matchmaker** process that holds a single compare‑and‑swap (CAS) register containing the current game capacity and a list of waiting players. Each **Player** thread can read the register, decide whether it can join the pending match, and then attempt a CAS to increment the waiting‑list size if the capacity has not changed. The **Capacity Manager** may, at any moment, write a new capacity value into the register using a CAS that succeeds only when no player is currently performing a join operation. When a player’s CAS succeeds, it records its identifier in the waiting list and the lobby state records one more slot occupied. If a player’s CAS fails because the capacity was updated, the player re‑reads the register and either retries or aborts if the new capacity is already full. When the waiting list reaches the current capacity, the Matchmaker atomically swaps the register to a special “full” marker, preventing any further joins, and triggers the start of the game. After the game starts the lobby resets the register to the next capacity value supplied by the Capacity Manager, clearing the waiting list for the next round.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No player can be added to a full lobby more than once.

The network consists of a set of vending machines M₁…Mₙ, each of which holds a collection of product slots and participates in a shared coordination layer.  
Every machine locally stores a *leaderID* that records which machine it believes is the current leader, and a *slotOwner* table that maps each slot to the machine assigned to restock it.  
If a machine stops receiving heartbeats from the current leader for a timeout period, it broadcasts an election request; the first machine to obtain acknowledgments from a majority becomes the new leader and updates the *leaderID* on all machines.  
The elected leader periodically issues *slotGrant* messages that assign unfilled slots to specific machines, and the recipient updates its entry in *slotOwner* accordingly.  
A privileged administrator may at any moment invoke an *adminOverride* that forces a designated machine to become the owner of a chosen slot, setting an override flag that makes all machines ignore any conflicting grant for that slot.  
Should the overridden machine fail, the leader clears the override flag and re‑assigns the slot using the normal grant process.  
All other machines simply forward election and grant messages and never change *slotOwner* for a slot whose override flag is active.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two machines ever believe they are the owner of the same product slot at the same time.
spec_text:
---- MODULE W4C13x3x3x5 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, Sequences, TLC

CONSTANTS Machines, Slots

VARIABLES leaderID, slotOwner, slotOwnerView, overrideFlag, overrideOwner

(*--algorithm Dummy
variables dummy = 0
end algorithm*)

(* Initial state *)
Init ==
    /\ leaderID \in Machines
    /\ slotOwner \in [Slots -> Machines]
    /\ overrideFlag = [s \in Slots |-> FALSE]
    /\ overrideOwner = [s \in Slots |-> leaderID]   \* default owner when not overridden
    /\ slotOwnerView = [m \in Machines |-> slotOwner]

(* Election: any machine may become the leader *)
Election(m) ==
    /\ m \in Machines
    /\ leaderID' = m
    /\ UNCHANGED <<slotOwner, slotOwnerView, overrideFlag, overrideOwner>>

(* Leader grants a slot to a machine, only if no override flag is set *)
Grant(s, d) ==
    /\ s \in Slots
    /\ d \in Machines
    /\ ~overrideFlag[s]
    /\ slotOwner' = [slotOwner EXCEPT ![s] = d]
    /\ slotOwnerView' = [m \in Machines |-> [slotOwnerView[m] EXCEPT ![s] = d]]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<leaderID, overrideFlag, overrideOwner>>

(* Administrator forces an ownership override for a slot *)
AdminOverride(s, d) ==
    /\ s \in Slots
    /\ d \in Machines
    /\ overrideFlag' = [overrideFlag EXCEPT ![s] = TRUE]
    /\ overrideOwner' = [overrideOwner EXCEPT ![s] = d]
    /\ slotOwner' = [slotOwner EXCEPT ![s] = d]
    /\ slotOwnerView' = [m \in Machines |-> [slotOwnerView[m] EXCEPT ![s] = d]]
    /\ UNCHANGED leaderID

(* Leader clears an existing override flag (e.g., after failure) *)
ClearOverride(s) ==
    /\ s \in Slots
    /\ overrideFlag[s] = TRUE
    /\ overrideFlag' = [overrideFlag EXCEPT ![s] = FALSE]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<leaderID, slotOwner, overrideOwner, slotOwnerView>>

(* The next-state relation *)
Next ==
    \/ \E m \in Machines : Election(m)
    \/ \E s \in Slots, d \in Machines : Grant(s, d)
    \/ \E s \in Slots, d \in Machines : AdminOverride(s, d)
    \/ \E s \in Slots : ClearOverride(s)

(* Full specification *)
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<leaderID, slotOwner, slotOwnerView, overrideFlag, overrideOwner>>

(* Safety invariant: no two distinct machines both believe they own the same slot *)
NoDupOwner ==
    \A s \in Slots :
        ~\E m1, m2 \in Machines :
            /\ m1 # m2
            /\ slotOwnerView[m1][s] = m1
            /\ slotOwnerView[m2][s] = m2

=============================================================================
