The fleet consists of a central Dispatcher robot and several Picker robots that handle individual shelves. Each Picker maintains a two‑bit state: a “prepared” flag that is set when it has successfully reserved its target shelf, and a “commitAck” flag that is set after it has completed the move; the Dispatcher maintains a table recording which Pickers have replied to the current request. The protocol begins when the Dispatcher broadcasts a “prepare” request to all Pickers that are needed for a shipment. Upon receiving the request, a Picker verifies that its assigned shelf is still free, sets its prepared flag, and sends a “ready” reply to the Dispatcher. The Dispatcher waits until it has collected a “ready” from every Picker, tolerating arbitrarily long delays from slow Pickers but not treating them as failures. Once all replies are ready, the Dispatcher sends a “commit” message; each Picker that still has its prepared flag set proceeds to move the item and then sets its commitAck flag. After the Dispatcher receives a commit acknowledgment from every Picker that was prepared, it marks the shipment as completed, and any Picker that later receives the commit after a timeout will abort because its prepared flag will have been cleared.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No Picker that has not received a current commit message may move an item.

The system consists of a central Scheduler, several ORRoom nodes that control individual operating rooms, and Surgeon agents that submit surgery requests. Each participant holds two pieces of state: the current epoch number and the list of surgeries assigned to its room for that epoch. When a Surgeon submits a new request, the Scheduler increments the epoch, creates an updated schedule, and broadcasts the new epoch together with the schedule to all ORRoom nodes. Each ORRoom node replies with the epoch it has stored; the Scheduler proceeds once it has received acknowledgments from a quorum, allowing a slow node to respond later without blocking progress. After the quorum is reached, the Scheduler marks the schedule as committed and notifies every participant of the committed epoch. A slow ORRoom node that later receives the committed schedule updates its local epoch and schedule, discarding any older proposals it may have held. Because every update is tied to a unique, monotonically increasing epoch, two different schedules can never be applied for the same epoch, eliminating the chance of lost updates.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The shared surgery schedule record is never overwritten by an older or conflicting update; each committed schedule reflects the latest epoch.

The yard has a set of container slots and a small pool of mobile cranes, each identified by a controller process (e.g., Crane A, Crane B). A central Yard Manager keeps two pieces of state for each slot: the current lease holder (the crane that is allowed to operate on that slot) and the lease’s expiry timestamp. When a crane wants to load or unload a slot it first sends a lease‑request to the Yard Manager; the manager grants the lease to the first requester and records a timeout based on the crane’s expected operation time. The holding crane may perform a move, and before the timeout it must send a lease‑renewal to extend its ownership; if the renewal is not received before expiry, the manager automatically revokes the lease and may grant it to another waiting crane. A crane that is merely slow can still finish its move after the timeout, but once its lease has been revoked it must abort the operation and wait for a new lease before touching the slot again. All cranes continuously monitor the manager’s lease table so that they never act on a slot for which they do not hold a valid lease. This simple lease‑based coordination, together with explicit expiry handling, ensures that only one crane can manipulate a given slot at any moment even when some participants are delayed.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total number of containers in the yard never changes; containers are only moved between slots and cranes, never created or destroyed.

The system consists of a central pharmacy server, several dispensing modules, and a capacity manager that can add or remove dispensers at runtime. Each participant keeps a tiny local copy of the shared record containing two fields: the number of pending prescriptions in the queue and the current total dispensing capacity. When a pharmacist submits a new prescription, the server proposes an increment of the queue length; each dispensing module votes on the proposal and the change is committed only after a quorum of modules acknowledges it. After a dispenser finishes a prescription, it proposes to decrement the queue length and, if it frees capacity, to update the capacity field; again a quorum must accept before the update takes effect. When the capacity manager decides to add a new dispenser or retire an existing one, it broadcasts a capacity‑change proposal that must achieve quorum before the new capacity value replaces the old one. The quorum voting rule guarantees that every action—adding a prescription, completing a dispense, or changing capacity—is applied atomically across all nodes, keeping the two‑field record consistent. Because the record has only the queue length and capacity variables, the whole protocol can be modeled with just those two state variables.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No update to the shared (queue length, capacity) record can be lost or overwritten without a quorum‑approved commit, ensuring that every prescription addition or removal is reflected exactly once.
spec_text:
---- MODULE W4C16x5x1x4 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, Sequences, FiniteSets

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* State variables: the shared record consisting of a queue length and the
\* current total dispensing capacity.
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
VARIABLES queue, capacity

\* Upper bound on capacity for model‑checking (kept small enough for exhaustive
\* exploration).  The exact number is not important for the safety property.
CapBound == 5

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Initial state: empty queue, a non‑zero capacity.
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Init ==
    /\ queue = 0
    /\ capacity \in 1 .. CapBound

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Actions corresponding to the three kinds of operations described.
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
AddPrescription ==
    /\ queue < capacity            \* there is free capacity
    /\ queue' = queue + 1
    /\ UNCHANGED capacity

CompleteDispense ==
    /\ queue > 0
    /\ queue' = queue - 1
    /\ UNCHANGED capacity

IncreaseCapacity ==
    /\ capacity < CapBound
    /\ capacity' = capacity + 1
    /\ UNCHANGED queue

DecreaseCapacity ==
    /\ capacity > 1
    /\ queue <= capacity - 1      \* after removal the queue still fits
    /\ capacity' = capacity - 1
    /\ UNCHANGED queue

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* The system can perform any of the above actions.
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Next ==
    \/ AddPrescription
    \/ CompleteDispense
    \/ IncreaseCapacity
    \/ DecreaseCapacity

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Full specification (initial condition and always‑next).
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<queue, capacity>>

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Safety invariant: the (queue,capacity) record is always consistent.
\* No update is lost or overwritten: the queue length is never negative and
\* never exceeds the total capacity.
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
SafeRecord ==
    /\ queue >= 0
    /\ queue <= capacity

=============================================================================

INVARIANT SafeRecord

The router consists of four belt‑segment controllers (North, South, East, West) that share a single token circulating clockwise on a logical ring. Each controller stores a Boolean flag “hasToken” and an integer “pendingBags” that counts bags waiting to be forwarded from its inbound scanner. When a controller receives the token, it may move at most one bag from its buffer onto the outbound belt, decrement its pendingBags, and then passes the token to the next controller on the ring. If a controller’s pendingBags is zero when it gets the token, it immediately forwards the token without moving a bag. A controller that is slow simply holds the token longer before forwarding it, but it never discards or duplicates the token, and the ring protocol does not require any controller to restart or be replaced. All controllers periodically broadcast a “heartbeat” on a side channel so that others can detect that a controller is still present, even if it is taking extra time to forward the token. The token itself is the sole authority granting exclusive access to the belt segment, ensuring that at most one controller attempts to load a bag onto a shared junction at any moment. When a controller finishes forwarding the token, it resets its “hasToken” flag and sets the next controller’s flag to true, completing the hand‑off.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No baggage is moved onto a shared belt segment by a controller that does not currently hold the token.

The system consists of a set of VendingUnits, each controlling a single product slot, and a central InventoryManager that holds the authoritative stock count for every product. Each VendingUnit keeps a local lease timer and a copy of the last known stock level for its slot; the InventoryManager keeps the current stock record and the identifier of the unit that currently holds the lease for that slot. When a customer inserts money, the VendingUnit requests a lease from the InventoryManager; if the manager grants it, the unit records the lease identifier, decrements its local copy, and sends a stock‑update message to the manager before the lease expires. The manager, upon receiving a valid update from the lease holder, writes the new stock count and clears the lease; if the lease timer runs out without an update, the manager assumes the unit crashed and reclaims the lease so another unit may acquire it. A unit that crashes silently stops sending messages, but its lease will eventually expire, allowing the manager to restore coordination without losing any pending updates. All normal operations and crash‑recovery steps are expressed using only the lease holder ID, the lease expiry time, the local stock copy, and the manager’s authoritative stock record.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The shared stock record is never updated with an older value, so no vending transaction can be lost or overwritten.

The system consists of a set of Elevator Controllers (one per car) and a central Dispatcher that holds a bounded work queue of pending floor‑call requests.  
Each Controller keeps a local variable “nextStop” indicating the next floor it will serve, while the Dispatcher maintains two counters: “queueDepth” (the number of enqueued calls) and “headIndex” (the index of the next request to assign).  
When a passenger presses a call button, the Dispatcher enqueues a CallRecord (floor, direction) if queueDepth is below the maximum capacity; otherwise the button light stays on to apply backpressure.  
A Controller repeatedly pulls the request at headIndex, updates its nextStop to that floor, and acknowledges the assignment, causing the Dispatcher to increment headIndex and decrement queueDepth.  
If a Controller becomes slow in reaching its assigned floor, it still sends periodic “still‑processing” heartbeats so the Dispatcher knows the request is not lost and does not re‑queue it.  
The Dispatcher never removes a CallRecord until it receives the explicit acknowledgment from the assigned Controller, ensuring that a slow car does not cause the request to disappear.  
When the controller finally arrives at the floor, it clears nextStop, sends a completion message, and the Dispatcher marks the request as completed, allowing new calls to enter the queue.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No call request that has been placed in the Dispatcher’s queue can be lost or overwritten before a Controller acknowledges its completion.

The exchange runs an opening auction where a set of brokers (participants) submit their orders for a single security before the market opens. Each broker keeps a local variable `epoch` that records the current auction configuration number and a flag `submitted` indicating whether its order for that epoch has been sent to the auction server. The auction server maintains a global epoch counter and a list of received orders for the current epoch. At the start of a new epoch the server broadcasts the epoch number to all brokers; brokers that receive the broadcast reset their `submitted` flag and may send a new order tagged with that epoch. Once the server has collected orders from all non‑crashed brokers or a timeout expires, it declares the clearing price, records the price as immutable, increments the epoch, and informs every broker of the new epoch. If a broker crashes silently after receiving an epoch broadcast but before submitting, the server will not receive its order; after the timeout the server proceeds without that broker, and the crashed broker will later re‑join using the latest epoch number when it recovers. Brokers that recover compare the epoch they learned from the server with their own; if they are behind they discard any pending order for the old epoch and start a fresh submission for the current epoch.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The clearing price for any auction epoch is determined and recorded at most once.

The system consists of a Track Block Manager (the coordinator) and several Train Controllers that operate on the same line. Each participant stores three pieces of information: the current configuration epoch, a table that records which block slot is assigned to which Train Controller, and a flag indicating whether it has acknowledged the latest epoch change. When a Train Controller wants to occupy a new block, it sends a “request‑slot” message to the Block Manager containing its identifier and the desired slot. The Block Manager increments the epoch, records the new assignment in its table, and replies with a “grant‑slot” message that carries the new epoch number; the Train Controller updates its epoch and records the grant before moving onto the block. After the train has cleared the block, it sends a “release‑slot” notification, which the Block Manager records under the same epoch and then removes the entry from the table. If a Train Controller fails to respond after a grant, the Block Manager waits a timeout, then starts a new epoch and re‑issues the configuration to the remaining responsive controllers, thereby isolating the crashed participant while preserving consistency.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No block slot is ever assigned to more than one train at the same time.

The system consists of a central **Load Controller** that decides when a shedding slot is needed, a set of **Sheddable Loads** that can be turned off, and a **Bounded Work Queue** that holds pending shedding requests. Each Sheddable Load maintains a single flag *requested* indicating whether it has sent a request, and the Load Controller maintains the current index *nextSlot* of the next available shedding slot together with a counter *queueDepth* of how many requests are queued. When a load detects that the grid frequency is below the threshold, it sets its *requested* flag and sends a “shed‑request” message to the queue; the queue accepts the message only if *queueDepth* is below its capacity, otherwise it back‑pressures the load by refusing the send. The Load Controller repeatedly dequeues the oldest request, assigns the load the current *nextSlot*, increments *nextSlot*, and decrements *queueDepth*. Upon receiving its slot number, the load turns off, clears its *requested* flag, and sends an “ack” back to the controller so the slot can be marked as free after a configurable hold‑off time. Because messages may arrive out of order, the controller discards any stale ack that references a slot number lower than the one currently assigned to that load. The back‑pressure mechanism guarantees that the queue never exceeds its bounded size, preventing uncontrolled build‑up of pending shedding requests.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two loads are ever assigned the same shedding slot at the same time.

The opening auction involves three kinds of participants: many traders who wish to submit orders, a single Auctioneer process that controls the order‑book slots, and a privileged Admin who can intervene at any time.  
Each price‑level slot in the order book is represented by a variable `slotOwner` that is either empty or holds the ID of the trader that currently holds the lease, and a timestamp `leaseExpiration` indicating when that lease automatically becomes void.  
When a trader wants to submit a market‑on‑close order it sends a `RequestLease` message to the Auctioneer; if `slotOwner` is empty and the current time is before `leaseExpiration`, the Auctioneer records the trader’s ID in `slotOwner` and sets `leaseExpiration` to the current time plus a fixed lease duration.  
The trader may later send a `RenewLease` before the expiry, which the Auctioneer accepts by extending `leaseExpiration`; if the lease has already expired, the trader must request a new lease.  
At any moment the Admin can issue an `AdminOverride` that sets a Boolean `adminOverrideFlag` true and immediately writes its own ID into `slotOwner`, discarding any existing lease regardless of its remaining time.  
The Auctioneer always checks `adminOverrideFlag` first; when it is true the normal lease rules are ignored until the Admin clears the flag, after which the slot becomes free again and normal traders may acquire it.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No price‑level slot can be owned simultaneously by two different traders (or by a trader and the Admin) under any circumstance.
spec_text:
---- MODULE W4C15x6x3x5 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets

CONSTANTS Traders, SlotSet, LeaseDuration, MaxTime, AdminID

\* All possible participants (traders plus the privileged admin)
Participants == Traders \cup {AdminID}

\* Initial empty ownership for every slot
SlotOwnerInit == [s \in SlotSet |-> {}]

VARIABLES slotOwner, leaseExpiration, adminOverrideFlag, currentTime

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Init ==
  /\ slotOwner = SlotOwnerInit
  /\ leaseExpiration = [s \in SlotSet |-> 0]
  /\ adminOverrideFlag = FALSE
  /\ currentTime = 0

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
RequestLease(tr, s) ==
  /\ ~adminOverrideFlag
  /\ tr \in Traders
  /\ s \in SlotSet
  /\ slotOwner[s] = {}
  /\ currentTime < MaxTime
  /\ slotOwner' = [slotOwner EXCEPT ![s] = {tr}]
  /\ leaseExpiration' = [leaseExpiration EXCEPT ![s] =
        (currentTime + LeaseDuration) % (MaxTime + 1)]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<adminOverrideFlag, currentTime>>

RenewLease(tr, s) ==
  /\ ~adminOverrideFlag
  /\ tr \in Traders
  /\ s \in SlotSet
  /\ tr \in slotOwner[s]
  /\ currentTime < leaseExpiration[s]
  /\ leaseExpiration' = [leaseExpiration EXCEPT ![s] =
        (currentTime + LeaseDuration) % (MaxTime + 1)]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<slotOwner, adminOverrideFlag, currentTime>>

ExpireLease(s) ==
  /\ ~adminOverrideFlag
  /\ s \in SlotSet
  /\ slotOwner[s] # {}
  /\ currentTime >= leaseExpiration[s]
  /\ slotOwner' = [slotOwner EXCEPT ![s] = {}]
  /\ leaseExpiration' = [leaseExpiration EXCEPT ![s] = 0]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<adminOverrideFlag, currentTime>>

AdminOverride(s) ==
  /\ ~adminOverrideFlag
  /\ s \in SlotSet
  /\ adminOverrideFlag' = TRUE
  /\ slotOwner' = [slotOwner EXCEPT ![s] = {AdminID}]
  /\ leaseExpiration' = [leaseExpiration EXCEPT ![s] = 0]
  /\ UNCHANGED currentTime

ClearAdmin(s) ==
  /\ adminOverrideFlag
  /\ s \in SlotSet
  /\ adminOverrideFlag' = FALSE
  /\ slotOwner' = [slotOwner EXCEPT ![s] = {}]
  /\ leaseExpiration' = [leaseExpiration EXCEPT ![s] = 0]
  /\ UNCHANGED currentTime

Tick ==
  /\ currentTime < MaxTime
  /\ currentTime' = currentTime + 1
  /\ UNCHANGED <<slotOwner, leaseExpiration, adminOverrideFlag>>

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Next ==
  \/ \E s \in SlotSet, tr \in Traders: RequestLease(tr, s)
  \/ \E s \in SlotSet, tr \in Traders: RenewLease(tr, s)
  \/ \E s \in SlotSet: ExpireLease(s)
  \/ \E s \in SlotSet: AdminOverride(s)
  \/ \E s \in SlotSet: ClearAdmin(s)
  \/ Tick

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Safety invariant: a slot never has more than one owner (no two traders,
\* and never a trader together with the admin)
NoDoubleOwner ==
  \A s \in SlotSet: Cardinality(slotOwner[s]) <= 1

====

CONSTANTS
  Traders = {t1, t2}
  SlotSet = {s1, s2}
  LeaseDuration = 2
  MaxTime = 3
  AdminID = admin

INIT Init
NEXT Next
INVARIANT NoDoubleOwner

The RouterController receives a request to route a piece of baggage and initiates a two‑phase commit by sending a prepare message to Conveyor A and Conveyor B.  
Each conveyor keeps a local flag indicating whether it is in the “prepared” or “committed” stage, and the SharedPool maintains a list of free bag‑slot identifiers that both conveyors can draw from.  
When a conveyor gets a prepare, it checks the SharedPool for a free slot; if one exists it temporarily reserves that slot, records “prepared”, and replies affirmatively, otherwise it replies with abort.  
The RouterController waits for both replies; if both are affirmative it broadcasts a commit, and if either is abort it broadcasts abort.  
On receiving commit, each conveyor moves the bag into its reserved slot, marks its state “committed”, and the SharedPool marks the slot as occupied.  
If abort is received, any reservation a conveyor made is released back to the SharedPool and its local flag is cleared.  
Thus the two independent routing instances coordinate their use of the single pool without ever conflicting over the same physical slot.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two conveyors ever occupy the same shared‑pool slot simultaneously.

The system consists of a central BloodStation that stores the list of blood‑unit slots and a set of TransferAgents that move units between hospitals. The BloodStation keeps two pieces of state: the current total capacity (the number of slots that can be used) and a lease table that records, for each leased slot, which TransferAgent holds the lease and when that lease expires. When a TransferAgent needs a slot, it sends a lease‑request; the BloodStation grants the request only if the number of active leases is below the current capacity, records the lease with a timeout, and returns the slot identifier to the agent. A TransferAgent must explicitly release a slot when it finishes handling the blood unit, which removes the entry from the lease table, or else the lease expires automatically and the BloodStation may reuse the slot. If the capacity is increased or decreased at runtime, the BloodStation updates its capacity value and, when decreasing, it may refuse new lease requests until enough existing leases have naturally expired or been released. All participants act concurrently, relying on the lease expiry mechanism to eventually recover any slot whose owner crashes or forgets to release it.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two TransferAgents can ever hold a lease for the same blood‑unit slot at the same time.

The system has three participants: a JobSubmitter that enqueues print jobs, a Spooler that holds a bounded work queue, and a Printer that dequeues jobs to print. The Spooler maintains two integer counters—the number of jobs currently stored and the index of the next job to be processed—together with a Boolean flag indicating whether the Printer is alive. When the JobSubmitter wants to add a job, it first checks the queue length and, if the queue is not full, appends the job and increments the counter; otherwise it blocks until the Spooler reports space (backpressure). The Printer repeatedly reads the “next index” counter, fetches the corresponding job from the queue, prints it, and then increments the counter, signalling to the Spooler that one slot has been freed. If the Printer crashes silently, the alive flag remains true until the Spooler detects that the counter has not advanced for a timeout period, at which point it flips the flag to false and stops delivering new jobs. While the flag is false, the Spooler refuses to accept new submissions and signals the JobSubmitter to retry later, preserving the current queue contents. When a replacement Printer comes online, it resets the alive flag, reads the current next‑index counter, and resumes consuming jobs from the queue, ensuring that any jobs already in the queue are eventually printed.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No print job that has been accepted into the bounded work queue can be lost or overwritten before it is printed.

The central dispatcher assigns a picking task to a set of robots, each robot keeping a local flag “prepared” that indicates it has positioned itself at the item’s location and has secured the load. The dispatcher first sends a *prepare* request to all robots involved; each robot responds by setting its “prepared” flag and replying “ready” when the load is stable. After receiving “ready” from every robot, the dispatcher issues a *commit* command, and each robot then updates its state to “committed” and moves the item onto the destination shelf. If a robot is slow, it may delay its “ready” reply, but it never crashes; the dispatcher waits a bounded time before retrying the *prepare* request, ensuring progress without aborting the transaction. Robots that have already sent “ready” keep their load secured while waiting for the final commit, so no other robot can claim the same item. Once all robots have reported “committed”, the dispatcher marks the overall task as completed and releases the items from the robots’ hold.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total weight of items stored on any shelf never exceeds its rated capacity.

The matchmaker service, each game lobby, and each player client are the participants.  
The lobby maintains two state variables: the current lease holder (a player ID) and the lease expiration timestamp; the matchmaker also records the lobby’s current capacity.  
When a player wants to become the host, it requests a lease from the matchmaker; the matchmaker grants it only if the lobby has no current lease or the existing lease has expired.  
The granted lease includes an expiry time, after which the player must stop acting as host and the matchmaker may assign a new lease.  
If the matchmaker later changes the lobby capacity, it updates the capacity variable and broadcasts the new limit to all participants, but it does not affect the currently granted lease.  
Should the lease holder still be active when the capacity is reduced below the number of players it currently controls, the lease holder must voluntarily evict excess players before the next lease renewal request.  
Players periodically send heartbeat messages; the matchmaker revokes a lease early if it detects a missed heartbeat, allowing another player to acquire the host role.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any time, at most one player is recognized as the host of a given lobby.

The Load‑Controller continuously monitors the grid frequency and, when it detects an overload, writes a new target shedding amount into a shared record and enqueues a corresponding “shed‑X MW” work item on the bounded work queue.  
Each Shedder Worker repeatedly tries to dequeue a work item; if the queue is empty it stays idle, and if the queue is full the controller backs off and waits for space before posting more items.  
A worker that successfully dequeues an item marks its local “busy” flag, reduces its assigned load by the requested amount, updates the shared target record with the amount it actually shed, and then clears the flag.  
If a worker becomes slow, it simply holds its busy flag longer; the bounded queue’s backpressure prevents the controller from overwhelming it, so the slow worker’s progress is respected without being considered a failure.  
The queue size, the controller’s latest target value, and each worker’s busy flag together constitute the whole state that needs to be modelled.  
When the queue becomes empty and all workers are idle, the controller knows that the current shedding plan has been fully applied and can compute the next target if needed.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No update to the shared target shedding record is ever lost because every write is preceded by a read of the current value and the queue’s backpressure guarantees that only one worker can modify the record at a time.

The swarm consists of a set of autonomous surveillance drones that monitor a wildfire‑affected zone, and at any moment one drone holds the **Leader** role to coordinate flight paths and data aggregation. Each drone maintains two pieces of state: a **LeaderId** that records the identifier of the current leader, and a **CapacityLevel** that reflects how much additional sensor load it can accept (based on battery and processing resources). Periodically, every drone broadcasts its current CapacityLevel; if a drone detects that the leader’s CapacityLevel has fallen below a predefined threshold, it initiates a leader‑election round by sending a **Candidate** message containing its own identifier and capacity. All drones that receive a Candidate message compare the advertised capacity with any other candidates they have heard and forward the identifier of the highest‑capacity candidate; after a bounded timeout, the candidate with the greatest CapacityLevel becomes the new Leader and updates its LeaderId. If a drone’s own CapacityLevel rises above the threshold while it is not the leader, it may voluntarily announce a **Takeover** request, prompting the current leader to relinquish its role and the swarm to adopt the new leader. All state updates (LeaderId changes and capacity broadcasts) are performed atomically with respect to message handling to avoid ambiguous intermediate states. The protocol also includes a fail‑over step: if a leader stops sending any messages for a timeout period, the remaining drones assume the leader has failed and immediately start the election process using the latest CapacityLevel information. The mechanism therefore keeps the swarm coordinated despite drones joining, leaving, or changing capacity at runtime.

SAFETY PROPERTY: A drone can be appointed Leader at most once for any given election cycle.

The swarm consists of a central Dispatcher, a set of Surveillance Drones, and a shared Task Queue that holds geographic waypoints to be inspected. The Dispatcher maintains the current queue length and the current queue capacity, which may be raised or lowered at runtime based on bandwidth and weather constraints. Each Drone keeps a simple state of either *idle* or *busy* and periodically checks the queue; when it is idle and the queue is non‑empty, it removes the oldest waypoint and marks itself busy to fly the waypoint. The bounded queue provides backpressure: the Dispatcher will not insert a new waypoint when the queue length equals the current capacity, and it will pause new insertions if the capacity is reduced below the present length until enough Drones have taken tasks to bring the length down. When the capacity changes, the Dispatcher instantly updates the capacity variable and re‑evaluates the backpressure condition, allowing further insertions only when the length is strictly less than the new capacity. Drones report completion of a waypoint, return to idle, and the queue length is decremented accordingly, completing one cycle of the protocol.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The number of waypoints stored in the Task Queue is never greater than the queue’s current capacity.

The system consists of a central coordinator (the reservation service) and a set of branch libraries that each hold copies of a particular book.  
Each branch maintains a single state variable for that book: either “available” or “tentatively reserved”.  
When a patron requests a reservation, the coordinator sends a prepare request to all branches that have a copy of the book.  
Each branch that still has the book “available” records “tentatively reserved” and replies “agree”; if the book is already locked it replies “reject”.  
The coordinator waits for all replies, but if a branch is slow it continues to wait up to a configurable grace period; after the period, if no reject has been received, the coordinator sends a commit message, otherwise it sends an abort.  
Upon receiving commit, a branch changes its state to “reserved permanently”; upon abort it restores the state to “available”.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total number of reserved copies of the book never exceeds the total number of physical copies owned by all branches.
spec_text:
---- MODULE W4C19x2x2x3 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets

CONSTANTS Branch

VARIABLES branchState, pending, pendingTentative, rejectSeen

\* Number of physical copies owned by all branches
NumCopies == Cardinality(Branch)

\* Initial state: every branch has the book available, no transaction in progress
Init ==
    /\ branchState = [b \in Branch |-> "available"]
    /\ pending = FALSE
    /\ pendingTentative = {}
    /\ rejectSeen = FALSE

\* Coordinator initiates a reservation request
Request ==
    /\ ~pending
    /\ pending' = TRUE
    /\ pendingTentative' = {}
    /\ rejectSeen' = FALSE
    /\ UNCHANGED branchState

\* A single branch responds to the prepare request
BranchRespond(b) ==
    /\ pending
    /\ b \in Branch
    /\ b \notin pendingTentative
    /\ IF branchState[b] = "available"
          THEN /\ branchState' = [branchState EXCEPT ![b] = "tentative"]
               /\ pendingTentative' = pendingTentative \cup {b}
               /\ rejectSeen' = rejectSeen
          ELSE /\ branchState' = branchState
               /\ pendingTentative' = pendingTentative
               /\ rejectSeen' = TRUE
    /\ pending' = pending

\* Coordinator decides to commit (no reject was seen)
Commit ==
    /\ pending
    /\ ~rejectSeen
    /\ branchState' = [b \in Branch |-> IF b \in pendingTentative THEN "reserved" ELSE branchState[b]]
    /\ pending' = FALSE
    /\ pendingTentative' = {}
    /\ rejectSeen' = FALSE

\* Coordinator decides to abort (at least one reject was seen)
Abort ==
    /\ pending
    /\ rejectSeen
    /\ branchState' = [b \in Branch |-> IF b \in pendingTentative THEN "available" ELSE branchState[b]]
    /\ pending' = FALSE
    /\ pendingTentative' = {}
    /\ rejectSeen' = FALSE

Next ==
    \/ Request
    \/ \E b \in Branch : BranchRespond(b)
    \/ Commit
    \/ Abort

vars == <<branchState, pending, pendingTentative, rejectSeen>>

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

\* Safety invariant: the number of permanently reserved copies never exceeds the total number of copies
SafeReserved ==
    Cardinality({b \in Branch : branchState[b] = "reserved"}) <= NumCopies

====

The line consists of three participants: a **Car** that wants to enter the wash, a **ConveyorController** that assigns the next available slot, and a **CapacityManager** that may increase or decrease the line capacity at any moment. The shared state is kept in three variables: `capacity` (the current number of slots the line can hold), `nextSlot` (the index of the slot that will be offered to the next car), and `version` (a monotonically increasing number that changes whenever `capacity` is updated). When a car arrives it reads `capacity`, `nextSlot`, and `version`, then proposes to occupy `nextSlot` and increments `nextSlot` locally, sending this proposal together with the version it observed to the ConveyorController. The ConveyorController checks that the received version still matches the current `version`; if it does, it records the car’s assignment, otherwise it rejects the proposal and the car must retry the whole read‑modify‑write sequence. If the CapacityManager raises or lowers `capacity` it first increments `version` and then updates `capacity`; this forces any in‑flight proposals that were based on the old version to be retried, guaranteeing that no car is assigned to a slot that no longer exists. The retry loop continues until a car’s proposal is accepted, after which the car proceeds to the assigned slot and the wash cycle for that car begins. All participants operate independently and only communicate through the shared variables, making the protocol suitable for modeling with just the three state variables described.

SAFETY PROPERTY: A car’s wash cycle is started at most once.

The lobby consists of a set of player clients and a group of three matchmaker replicas that hold a shared view of the lobby’s waiting list. Each replica stores two variables: the current list of pending players and a proposal record that contains a proposed game‑start identifier together with a vote count. When a player clicks “ready”, its client sends a *join* message to all replicas; each replica appends the player to its local list and broadcasts an *ack* for that join. Once a replica sees that the waiting list contains the required quorum of players, it creates a start‑game proposal, increments the proposal identifier, and sends the proposal to the other replicas, who vote “yes” if their local list matches the proposal’s list. When a replica receives votes from a majority of the three replicas, it records the proposal as accepted and sends a *start* command to every player in the list; all replicas then clear the waiting list. If messages arrive out of order, a replica discards any proposal whose identifier is lower than the one it has already accepted, ensuring that only the most recent quorum decision is acted on.

SAFETY PROPERTY: A game‑start command is issued at most once for any given set of players.

The lobby consists of a set of Player nodes that connect to a Matchmaker service which holds the shared state `leaderId` (the current host), `epoch` (a monotonically increasing election round number), and a boolean `adminOverride`. When the lobby is created, all Players start with `leaderId = null` and the first Player to broadcast a “I‑am‑ready” message with `epoch = 0` becomes the provisional leader and writes its identifier into `leaderId`. Each leader periodically sends a heartbeat; if a Player does not receive a heartbeat for three intervals it increments `epoch`, clears `leaderId`, and the remaining Players race to claim leadership by writing their own identifier together with the new `epoch`. A privileged Admin client can at any time set `adminOverride = true` and write its identifier into `leaderId`, instantly pre‑empting any current leader regardless of the election round. When `adminOverride` is cleared, normal leader election resumes from the current `epoch`. All state changes are atomic writes to the Matchmaker’s shared register, ensuring that at most one identifier is stored in `leaderId` at any moment. The protocol guarantees that a new leader is always chosen either by the election process or by an admin override, and that the system never loses track of who is responsible for coordinating the match start.

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any time there exists exactly one leader identifier stored in `leaderId`, no more and no fewer.

The system consists of three active components – the **ConveyorController** that feeds incoming bags, the **Scanner** that reads tags, and the **Sorter** that dispatches bags to the proper carousel – together with a **QueueManager** that implements a bounded work queue. The QueueManager keeps two pieces of state: the current **queue length** (how many bags are waiting) and the **capacity** (the maximum number of bags the queue can hold). When the ConveyorController receives a new bag it first checks the queue length; if the length is below capacity it enqueues the bag, otherwise it asserts a back‑pressure signal that stalls the conveyor until space is freed. The Scanner repeatedly dequeues the oldest bag, annotates it with its destination, and re‑enqueues it for the Sorter, incrementing the queue length each time it adds a bag back. The Sorter removes a bag from the queue, moves it onto the appropriate sorting chute, and then notifies the QueueManager that one slot has become free, decrementing the queue length. If the airport operator adjusts the capacity at runtime (e.g., to accommodate a maintenance window), the QueueManager instantly adopts the new limit; if the new capacity is smaller than the current queue length, the back‑pressure signal remains asserted until the queue drains to the new limit.

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any moment, no two bags can occupy the same sorting chute simultaneously.

The system consists of two independent library servers, LibraryServerA and LibraryServerB, that both serve reservation requests from patrons and share a common pool of physical book copies. Each server keeps a lease record for every copy, indicating which server currently owns the lease and the time at which that lease expires. When a patron asks for a reservation, the contacted server first checks whether it already holds a valid lease for the requested copy. If it does not, the server sends a lease‑acquisition request to the other server, which replies affirmatively only if its own lease for that copy is empty or has already expired. After receiving the grant, the acquiring server records the lease, sets an expiration deadline, and creates a reservation entry linking the patron to that copy. If a lease reaches its expiration without being renewed, both servers treat the copy as free and may grant a new lease to the next request. Periodically, the two servers synchronize their lease tables so that each has a consistent view of which leases are active and which have timed out.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two servers ever consider the same book copy to be reserved for different patrons at the same time.

The system consists of several router controllers, each responsible for a conveyor segment, and a central admin console that can intervene in routing decisions.  
Every controller stores two pieces of state: the identifier of the current lease holder for the shared sorting belt and the time at which that lease expires.  
When a controller wants to move bags on the belt, it sends a lease‑request to a lease manager, receives a lease identifier together with a fresh expiration time, records them locally, and may operate the belt until the lease time runs out.  
If the expiration time passes without renewal, the controller must stop using the belt and clear its lease record, making the belt available for the next request.  
The admin console holds a privileged override that can instantly invalidate any existing lease and assign the belt to the admin, irrespective of the recorded expiration.  
When the admin issues an override, all controllers observe a revocation flag, immediately cease belt operation, and the admin becomes the sole owner until it explicitly releases the override.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any moment, at most one controller or the admin may have active control of the shared sorting belt.

The yard contains several autonomous cranes (C1 … Ck) that move containers from the ship onto a fixed set of storage slots (Slot 0 … Slot m).  
Each crane keeps a local copy of the yard’s total capacity, called `localCap`, together with a version number `capVer` that is updated whenever the capacity manager announces a change.  
To store a container, a crane first reads the global capacity `CAP` and `capVer`, then writes a tentative reservation entry (the container’s ID and the current `capVer`) into a shared reservation table, hoping that no other crane has written a conflicting entry.  
If the crane’s write observes the same `capVer` as when it started, the reservation is considered successful and the crane proceeds to place the container; otherwise the reservation is aborted, the crane refreshes `localCap` and `capVer` from the latest manager broadcast, and retries.  
The capacity manager may increase or decrease `CAP` at any moment, incrementing `capVer` and broadcasting the new values to all cranes.  
Whenever a crane detects a version mismatch during reservation, it must roll back any in‑flight reservation before retrying, guaranteeing that the number of active reservations never exceeds the current capacity even while it changes.  
The protocol completes when every container that obtained a reservation either occupies a slot or is retried until a consistent capacity view permits it.

SAFETY PROPERTY: At all times the number of containers stored in slots equals the number of containers successfully reserved and never exceeds the current capacity, so no container is created or destroyed.

The system consists of a central scheduler and several department heads who each request operating‑room time. The scheduler keeps a coarse lock that represents the entire block of operating‑room schedule and a fine lock for every individual operating‑room and time slot. A department head must first acquire the coarse lock before it can request the fine lock for the specific room and slot it needs. After the fine lock is granted, the department head records the reservation, releases the fine lock, and finally releases the coarse lock once it has confirmed the booking. If a department head crashes after holding the coarse lock but before releasing it, the scheduler detects the missing heartbeat and, after a timeout, automatically clears both the coarse lock and any fine lock that might still be held. The scheduler continuously updates its view of which rooms and slots are booked and advertises this availability to all department heads. Because every reservation passes through the coarse‑then‑fine locking sequence, no two department heads can ever hold a fine lock for the same room‑slot at the same time.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: At all times the number of confirmed operating‑room reservations never exceeds the number of operating rooms available.

The system consists of a fleet of autonomous robots and a set of stationary quorum controllers located at each aisle entrance.  
Each robot keeps a single Boolean variable “requestPending” that indicates whether it is currently asking to pick up the heavy pallet from the central dock.  
Each quorum controller maintains a small counter “votes” that records how many robots of its instance have granted a yes‑vote for the current request.  
When a robot wants the pallet it broadcasts a Request message, all quorum controllers for that robot’s instance receive it and each replies with a Vote (yes or no) based on whether the shared pallet pool still has an available token.  
The robot collects votes until it reaches a quorum (at least two out of three controllers) and then sends a Commit message, causing the pallet token to be decremented in the global pool and the robot to mark its request as satisfied.  
Because two independent instances (e.g., aisle A and aisle B) draw votes from the same global token pool, a controller that has already voted yes for an instance must refuse to vote yes for the other instance while the token is reserved.  
After the robot finishes handling the pallet it sends a Release message, the token is returned to the pool, and all quorum controllers reset their vote counters for the next round.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two robots can be granted the heavy pallet at the same time.

The yard contains a set of **cranes** that each request permission to lift a specific container, and a **queue manager** that holds a bounded work queue of pending lift requests. Each crane maintains a local flag indicating whether it is currently busy, while the queue manager maintains three shared state variables: the number of queued requests, a back‑pressure flag that is true when the queue is full, and an admin‑override flag that can be set by the **yard supervisor**. When a crane issues a lift request it is accepted into the queue only if the back‑pressure flag is false; otherwise the crane must wait until space opens. The queue manager dequeues the oldest request whenever the queue is non‑empty and the corresponding crane is idle, clearing the back‑pressure flag as soon as the queue size drops below the bound. The yard supervisor may at any time set the admin‑override flag, which immediately empties the back‑pressure flag and allows the supervisor’s chosen crane to bypass the queue and execute a lift, regardless of current load. After the privileged lift completes, the admin‑override flag is automatically cleared, restoring normal queue operation. All participants continually observe the shared state variables to decide whether to submit, wait, or execute a lift.

SAFETY PROPERTY: A container is lifted by an admin‑overridden crane at most once for any given lift request.

The system consists of two independent load‑shedder instances, Shedder‑A and Shedder‑B, that both draw from a single pool of controllable load‑shedding switches. Each instance keeps a local copy of the pool’s version number and a flag indicating whether it currently “owns” a switch for a given zone. When an instance detects that a zone is overloaded, it reads the current version, selects a free switch, writes a tentative claim together with the version it observed, and then attempts to commit the change. The commit succeeds only if the pool’s version has not changed since the read; otherwise the instance discards the tentative claim, increments its retry counter, and repeats the read‑claim‑commit cycle. If the commit succeeds, the instance updates its local flag to “owned” and increments the pool’s version, thereby making the switch unavailable to the other instance. While an instance holds the “owned” flag it may issue the actual circuit‑break command; after the command finishes it releases the flag and the switch returns to the free pool. The optimistic‑locking protocol guarantees that concurrent attempts to claim the same switch are resolved by retries rather than by blocking, keeping the overall state describable with just the version number, the free‑switch list, and each instance’s ownership flag.

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any moment, at most one load‑shedder instance holds the lock for a given shedding switch.

A Student Agent contacts the Registrar Server to request a lease on the record for a particular course section, specifying the desired semester. The server maintains two pieces of state for each section: the identifier of the current lease holder and the lease’s expiration time. If the record is free or the existing lease has expired, the server replies with a lease grant that includes a timestamp‑ed expiry and a version number for the section’s enrollment list. While holding the lease, the Student Agent may add or drop the course in its local copy and then send an “update” message containing the new version number before the lease expires. Upon receiving an update, the server checks that the lease is still valid and that the version number follows the one it last recorded; if both conditions hold, it commits the change, increments the version, and releases the lease. If the lease has timed out or the version number is out of order, the server discards the update and forces the student to request a fresh lease. Because messages can be reordered, each message carries the lease expiry timestamp, and the server always validates the current time against that timestamp before acting, ensuring that stale messages are ignored.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No student’s registration change can overwrite another student’s change to the same course record without both changes being ordered by increasing version numbers.

The system comprises two independent runway‑allocator instances, A and B, each of which receives take‑off‑slot requests from aircraft and tries to assign the single runway resource. Both instances share a common pool that holds one lease record describing which instance currently owns the runway and the time at which that ownership expires. Each instance keeps only two local variables: a flag that tells whether it believes it holds the lease, and the timestamp of the lease entry it most recently read from the shared pool. When an instance receives a request, it first reads the shared lease; if the lease is empty or its expiry time has passed, the instance writes its own identifier together with a fresh expiry time into the pool, thereby acquiring the lease. While it holds the lease, the instance records the assigned slot in its local schedule and refreshes the expiry time in the shared lease each time it grants another slot, extending its ownership. If the lease record shows the other instance’s identifier and the expiry is still in the future, the requesting instance must back off and retry after the lease expires. The lease automatically expires after a bounded interval, allowing the other instance to write a new lease and take control, which guarantees that only one instance ever records a slot for the runway at any moment.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The shared lease record is never overwritten by two instances simultaneously, so no runway‑slot assignment update can be lost.

The system consists of three participants: each smart‑door lock controller that generates lock or unlock requests, a central coordinator that runs a bounded work queue, and a mobile app that can submit user commands to the controller. The coordinator maintains only two pieces of state: the number of pending slots currently occupied in the queue (the load) and the index of the next free slot (the head). When a lock controller receives a command from the app it attempts to enqueue the request; if the load is already at the queue’s capacity the controller must back‑pressure the app and wait until a slot becomes free. The coordinator continuously dequeues the oldest pending slot, forwards the command to the appropriate door lock, and marks the slot as “in‑flight”. Upon receiving an acknowledgement the lock controller informs the coordinator, which then frees the slot and decrements the load; if no acknowledgement arrives within a timeout the coordinator assumes the lock has crashed silently, logs the failure, and also frees the slot so that new requests can be accepted. Back‑pressure from the full queue therefore prevents loss of commands and guarantees that the coordinator never exceeds its bounded capacity, while silent crashes are handled by reclaiming the stuck slot after the timeout.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two distinct lock or unlock commands are ever placed in the same queue slot at the same time.

The system consists of three Block Controllers (BC1, BC2, BC3), each responsible for a contiguous track segment. Each controller keeps two pieces of state: the identifier of the movement slot it currently owns for its segment (or “none”) and a local vote flag indicating whether it has voted for a pending slot request. When a train requests entry, the leading controller proposes a slot number and broadcasts a PROPOSE message to the other two controllers. Each receiving controller records the slot in its vote flag and replies with an ACK; once a controller has ACKs from a quorum (any two of the three), it records the slot as its owner and sends a GRANT to the train. If a controller does not receive a reply within a timeout, it assumes the missing participant has crashed silently and proceeds as long as a quorum of acknowledgments is still available. When the train exits, the owning controller broadcasts a RELEASE message that clears its slot and informs the other controllers, readying the segment for the next request.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: At no time do two different Block Controllers claim ownership of the same movement slot for the same track segment.

The system has three kinds of participants: players, a lobby server, and a matchmaker process. Each player maintains a local variable “desiredGameMode” and a boolean “joined”. The lobby server holds a single compare‑and‑swap register that stores the identifier of the current pending match (or empty). When a player wants to join, it sends a “join request” message to the lobby server; the server reads the register, and if it is empty it attempts a compare‑and‑swap from empty to the player’s identifier, thereby claiming the spot for a new match. If the compare‑and‑swap succeeds, the server records the player as the first member of the match and broadcasts a “match‑started” message; if it fails because another player already claimed the spot, the server adds the player to a waiting list and later includes them when the match fills. Because network messages may arrive out of order, the server tags each reply with a monotonically increasing version number and ignores any stale “join request” that carries a version lower than the current register value. Players only set their local “joined” flag when they receive a “match‑started” message that references the same version they sent, ensuring consistency despite reordering.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total number of players recorded by the lobby server as belonging to a match never exceeds the number of distinct join requests it has received, so no player is created or duplicated.
spec_text:
---- MODULE W4C5x7x2x1 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets, Sequences

CONSTANTS Player          \* Set of player identifiers

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Constants
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Empty == "empty"          \* value that denotes an empty CAS register

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Variables
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
VARIABLES
    reg,          \* compare‑and‑swap register (either Empty or a Player)
    regVer,       \* monotonically increasing version number of the register
    waiting,      \* set of players that have sent a join request but are waiting
    matchMembers, \* set of players that the lobby server records as belonging to the current match
    joinRequests, \* set of distinct join requests that have been received
    joined        \* [Player -> BOOLEAN] flag indicating whether each player has set its local “joined”

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Type correctness
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
TypeOK ==
    /\ reg \in Player \/ reg = Empty
    /\ regVer \in Nat
    /\ waiting \subseteq Player
    /\ matchMembers \subseteq Player
    /\ joinRequests \subseteq Player
    /\ joined \in [Player -> BOOLEAN]

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Initial state
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Init ==
    /\ reg = Empty
    /\ regVer = 0
    /\ waiting = {}
    /\ matchMembers = {}
    /\ joinRequests = {}
    /\ joined = [p \in Player |-> FALSE]

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Actions
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* A player p sends a join request; the server processes it immediately.
Join(p) ==
    /\ p \in Player
    /\ p \notin joinRequests
    /\ joinRequests' = joinRequests \cup {p}
    /\ IF reg = Empty THEN
          /\ reg' = p
          /\ regVer' = regVer + 1
          /\ matchMembers' = matchMembers \cup {p}
          /\ waiting' = waiting
       ELSE
          /\ reg' = reg
          /\ regVer' = regVer
          /\ waiting' = waiting \cup {p}
          /\ matchMembers' = matchMembers
    /\ UNCHANGED <<joined>>

\* When the match is considered “full” the server moves all waiting players
\* into the match record.
FillMatch ==
    /\ matchMembers' = matchMembers \cup waiting
    /\ waiting' = {}
    /\ UNCHANGED <<reg, regVer, joinRequests, joined>>

\* A player p sets its local joined flag after receiving a matching
\* “match‑started” message.
PlayerJoined(p) ==
    /\ p \in Player
    /\ p \in matchMembers
    /\ joined' = [joined EXCEPT ![p] = TRUE]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<reg, regVer, waiting, joinRequests, matchMembers>>

Next ==
    \/ \E p \in Player: Join(p)
    \/ FillMatch
    \/ \E p \in Player: PlayerJoined(p)

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Specification
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<reg, regVer, waiting, matchMembers, joinRequests, joined>>

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Safety property (non‑trivial invariant)
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
SafetyInv ==
    Cardinality(matchMembers) <= Cardinality(joinRequests)

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Theorems (optional)
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
THEOREM Spec => []SafetyInv

====

CONSTANTS Player = {p1, p2, p3, p4}
INIT Init
NEXT Next
INVARIANT SafetyInv

The system consists of three logical agents: a **Car** that arrives at the entrance, a **Washer** that owns the wash bay, and a **LineController** that tracks the number of cars on the conveyor. Each agent keeps a tiny amount of state: the LineController stores the current **capacity** (how many cars the line can hold) and the **load** (how many cars are presently on it); the Washer records the **leaseOwner** (the identifier of the car that currently holds the wash‑bay lease) and the **leaseExpiry** timestamp; the Car only knows whether it has a valid lease. When a Car reaches the entry point it sends a *request‑lease* message to the Washer; the Washer grants the lease only if the lease is free and the LineController’s load is below capacity, setting leaseOwner to that Car’s ID and leaseExpiry to the current time plus a fixed lease duration. The Car then proceeds onto the conveyor; the LineController increments its load, and the Car may start the wash only while the lease has not expired. After the wash finishes the Car notifies the Washer, which clears leaseOwner, and the LineController decrements its load; if the lease expires before the Car finishes, the Washer forcibly clears the lease so another Car can be granted access. Any time the operator changes the line capacity, the LineController updates its capacity variable, and the Washer will refuse new leases until the load is again ≤ capacity. 

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any moment, no more than one car can hold the wash‑bay lease, ensuring exclusive access to the critical wash resource.

The print shop has a **JobSubmitter** that places a new print request into a single shared **JobQueue**. Two independent **SpoolerInstance** processes (Instance A and Instance B) each keep a local flag indicating whether they have **prepared** the job and a copy of the job’s current status (Pending, Prepared, Committed, or Aborted). When a job appears in the queue, both instances receive a **prepare** message; each checks its printer availability and, if it can schedule the job, sets its local prepare flag to true and replies “ready”. A lightweight **Coordinator** (chosen as the first instance that received the prepare) collects the two replies; if both are ready it sends a **commit** command, causing each instance to advance the job’s status to Committed and write the final record into the shared queue. If either instance cannot prepare, the coordinator broadcasts an **abort** and both instances revert the job status to Aborted, removing any provisional entries. The two‑phase commit guarantees that only when both instances have agreed does the shared queue get updated, preventing simultaneous writes from interfering. Because the two instances share the same physical JobQueue, all write‑back operations are performed only after the commit phase, ensuring the queue’s single copy stays consistent.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No job entry in the shared spool queue can be lost or overwritten by concurrent updates; every job that reaches the Committed state remains present exactly once.

The system consists of a central scheduler and several robot agents that need to jointly reserve a high‑capacity pallet lift for moving a batch of crates. Each robot keeps a local flag “vote” that can be either “yes” (ready to use the lift) or “null” (not yet voted), and the scheduler maintains a counter of how many “yes” votes have been received. When a batch of crates is ready, the scheduler initiates a two‑phase commit by broadcasting a “prepare” request to all robots that could be involved. Upon receiving the prepare request, each robot checks its own task queue; if it can pause its current job, it sets its vote to “yes” and replies, otherwise it replies “no”. The scheduler waits until it has either collected a “yes” from every required robot or until a timeout expires; a slow robot may delay its reply but the scheduler does not consider it failed. If all required robots responded “yes” before the timeout, the scheduler sends a “commit” message telling them to move to the lift, and each robot changes its state to “using lift”. If any robot responded “no” or the timeout elapsed, the scheduler sends an “abort” message, all robots clear their vote flag, and the lift remains idle.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any moment, at most one robot may be positioned on the pallet lift.
spec_text:
---------------------------- MODULE W4C2x2x0x3 ----------------------------
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets

CONSTANTS Robots

VARIABLES vote, state, phase, counter, timeout

(* --algorithm placeholder for readability -- *)

Init ==
    /\ vote   = [r \in Robots |-> "null"]
    /\ state  = [r \in Robots |-> "idle"]
    /\ phase  = "idle"
    /\ counter = 0
    /\ timeout = FALSE

Prepare ==
    /\ phase = "idle"
    /\ phase' = "waiting"
    /\ UNCHANGED <<vote, state, counter, timeout>>

RobotVoteYes(r) ==
    /\ phase = "waiting"
    /\ vote[r] = "null"
    /\ vote'   = [vote EXCEPT ![r] = "yes"]
    /\ counter' = counter + 1
    /\ UNCHANGED <<state, phase, timeout>>

RobotVoteNo(r) ==
    /\ phase = "waiting"
    /\ vote[r] = "null"
    /\ vote'   = [vote EXCEPT ![r] = "no"]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<state, phase, counter, timeout>>

TimeoutOccur ==
    /\ phase = "waiting"
    /\ ~timeout
    /\ timeout' = TRUE
    /\ UNCHANGED <<vote, state, counter, phase>>

Commit ==
    /\ phase = "waiting"
    /\ \A r \in Robots : vote[r] # "no"
    /\ \A r \in Robots : vote[r] = "yes" \/ vote[r] = "null"
    /\ \E r \in Robots : vote[r] = "yes"
    /\ LET YesSet == { r \in Robots : vote[r] = "yes" } IN
         /\ counter = Cardinality(YesSet)
         /\ LET chosen == CHOOSE r \in YesSet : TRUE IN
                state' = [state EXCEPT ![chosen] = "usingLift"]
    /\ vote'   = [r \in Robots |-> "null"]
    /\ counter' = 0
    /\ phase'   = "committed"
    /\ timeout' = FALSE

Abort ==
    /\ phase = "waiting"
    /\ ( \E r \in Robots : vote[r] = "no" ) \/ timeout
    /\ vote'   = [r \in Robots |-> "null"]
    /\ counter' = 0
    /\ phase'   = "aborted"
    /\ timeout' = FALSE
    /\ state'   = [r \in Robots |-> "idle"]

Release ==
    /\ phase = "committed"
    /\ \E r \in Robots : state[r] = "usingLift"
    /\ LET r == CHOOSE r \in Robots : state[r] = "usingLift" IN
           state' = [state EXCEPT ![r] = "idle"]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<vote, phase, counter, timeout>>

Reset ==
    /\ phase \in {"aborted","committed"}
    /\ \A r \in Robots : state[r] = "idle"
    /\ phase' = "idle"
    /\ UNCHANGED <<vote, state, counter, timeout>>

Next ==
    \/ Prepare
    \/ \E r \in Robots : RobotVoteYes(r)
    \/ \E r \in Robots : RobotVoteNo(r)
    \/ TimeoutOccur
    \/ Commit
    \/ Abort
    \/ Release
    \/ Reset

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<vote, state, phase, counter, timeout>>

(* Safety invariant: at most one robot is on the pallet lift *)
LiftSafety == Cardinality({ r \in Robots : state[r] = "usingLift" }) <= 1

=============================================================================

CONSTANTS Robots = {r1, r2, r3}
INIT Init
NEXT Next
INVARIANT LiftSafety

The system consists of two independent wash lines, Line A and Line B, each controlled by a line controller that schedules cars onto its conveyor and requests the shared cleaning‑solution pump. Each line maintains a small local state: the number of cars currently on its conveyor (0 or 1) and a version number that records the last observed state of the pump. When a car reaches the wash bay, the line controller reads the pump’s current version; if the pump is free it writes a new version to claim it, otherwise it aborts and retries after a brief back‑off. If the write succeeds, the controller marks the pump as occupied and starts the wash cycle; when the cycle finishes the controller releases the pump by resetting its version. If the write fails because another line updated the version in the meantime, the controller retries the whole acquisition step, leaving its conveyor unchanged. Both controllers run concurrently but never block each other; they only communicate through the shared pump’s version field, which provides optimistic locking with automatic retries. The protocol therefore needs only three state variables in total: the pump version, the pump‑occupied flag, and the per‑line conveyor count.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The cleaning‑solution pump is never allocated to more than one car at the same time.
spec_text:
---------------------------- MODULE W4C4x0x4x2 ----------------------------
EXTENDS Naturals, TLC

CONSTANTS Lines

VARIABLES pumpVersion, pumpOccupied, conveyor, lineVersion

(* --algorithm definition omitted; using actions directly *)

Init ==
    /\ pumpVersion = 0
    /\ pumpOccupied = FALSE
    /\ conveyor   = [l \in Lines |-> 0]
    /\ lineVersion = [l \in Lines |-> 0]

CarArrives(l) ==
    /\ l \in Lines
    /\ conveyor[l] = 0
    /\ conveyor' = [conveyor EXCEPT ![l] = 1]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<pumpVersion, pumpOccupied, lineVersion>>

Acquire(l) ==
    /\ l \in Lines
    /\ conveyor[l] = 1
    /\ IF ~pumpOccupied
          THEN
              LET newV == pumpVersion + 1 IN
                  /\ pumpOccupied' = TRUE
                  /\ pumpVersion'   = newV
                  /\ lineVersion'   = [lineVersion EXCEPT ![l] = newV]
          ELSE
              /\ UNCHANGED <<pumpVersion, pumpOccupied, lineVersion, conveyor>>
    /\ UNCHANGED conveyor

WashComplete(l) ==
    /\ l \in Lines
    /\ pumpOccupied = TRUE
    /\ lineVersion[l] = pumpVersion
    /\ pumpOccupied' = FALSE
    /\ pumpVersion'   = 0
    /\ conveyor'     = [conveyor EXCEPT ![l] = 0]
    /\ lineVersion'  = [lineVersion EXCEPT ![l] = 0]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<>>

Next ==
    \/ \E l \in Lines: CarArrives(l)
    \/ \E l \in Lines: Acquire(l)
    \/ \E l \in Lines: WashComplete(l)

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<pumpVersion, pumpOccupied, conveyor, lineVersion>>

(* Safety invariant: the pump is never allocated to more than one car *)
PumpSafety ==
    ~(\E l1, l2 \in Lines :
          /\ l1 # l2
          /\ pumpOccupied
          /\ lineVersion[l1] = pumpVersion
          /\ lineVersion[l2] = pumpVersion)

=====================================================================

nl:
Two signalling controllers, Controller A and Controller B, each manage a set of track blocks but both draw block‑allocation tokens from a single shared pool called the TokenBank.  
Each controller keeps a local variable `currentToken` that records which token it believes it holds, while the TokenBank records the total number of free tokens.  
When a controller wants to grant a train permission to enter its next block, it first reads the TokenBank, selects a free token, writes the token identifier into its `currentToken`, and proceeds assuming the allocation is valid.  
If during the write the controller discovers that another controller has concurrently taken the same token (detected by a mismatch between the token it read and the token now recorded as taken), it aborts the operation, releases any provisional reservation, and retries from the start with a fresh read.  
After a train has cleared the block, the controller returns its token to the TokenBank, incrementing the count of free tokens.  
The optimistic‑locking protocol therefore allows both controllers to work independently while ensuring that at most one controller holds any particular token at a time, and retries guarantee eventual progress when conflicts occur.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total number of tokens in the TokenBank plus the tokens held in the controllers’ `currentToken` variables is constant, never creating or destroying a token.

The system consists of a Central Scheduler (CS) that owns a coarse lock for each floor‑range block (e.g., floors 1‑10, 11‑20), and a set of Elevator Controllers (EC1…ECn), each of which can acquire a fine lock on an individual cabin slot once the coarse lock is held. Each EC keeps a tiny state variable “mySlot” that records which cabin slot it currently controls, while the CS maintains “currentBlock” indicating which floor block it is coordinating at the moment. When a passenger request arrives for a floor inside a block, the CS first acquires the block’s coarse lock, then signals an EC; that EC attempts to grab the fine lock for a free cabin slot, records the assignment in its “mySlot”, and notifies the CS that the request is allocated. After the elevator departs, the EC releases its fine lock, clears “mySlot”, and the CS subsequently releases the block’s coarse lock so other blocks can be serviced. If an EC crashes silently while holding a fine lock, other ECs detect the missing heartbeat, the CS times‑out the coarse lock for that block, and a recovery routine forcibly clears the crashed EC’s fine lock before the block is re‑opened. All participants follow this two‑stage lock protocol, guaranteeing that only one EC ever holds the fine lock for a given cabin slot while the CS holds the corresponding coarse lock for the block. The protocol therefore uses only three state variables: currentBlock, mySlot, and a heartbeat flag.

SAFETY PROPERTY: At no time can two elevators be assigned to serve the same floor‑request slot simultaneously.

The fleet consists of autonomous robots, a centralized Lock Manager, and an Admin Console. Each robot keeps a small local record of its current lock level (none, aisle, or shelf), while the Lock Manager maintains a global table that records which robot holds a coarse aisle lock and which robot holds fine shelf locks. To begin moving, a robot first sends a request to the Lock Manager for a coarse lock on the target aisle; if the lock is granted, the robot may travel within that aisle. Once inside the aisle, the robot requests a fine lock on the specific shelf it needs to service; the lock is granted only if no other robot holds that shelf lock. After completing the shelf operation, the robot releases the fine lock and then releases its coarse aisle lock. An admin may issue an override command from the Admin Console that instantly clears all entries in the lock table and grants the admin‑designated robot exclusive access, bypassing normal lock acquisition. The Lock Manager enforces the override by ignoring any pending lock requests and rejecting actions from robots that lack the admin token while the override is active.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No robot may access a shelf or move through an aisle while another robot holds the corresponding lock unless an authorized admin override is in effect.

The system consists of three participants: a central coordinator, a local blood‑bank node, and a hospital that consumes blood units. The blood‑bank node keeps two pieces of state – a count of available units for each blood type and a flag indicating whether a two‑phase‑commit transaction is in the “prepare” stage. The central coordinator also tracks the current storage capacity for each blood type, which can be increased or decreased at any time by an administrator. When a hospital needs a unit, it sends a request to the blood‑bank; the bank records the request, moves the requested amount to a pending field, and sends a “prepare” message to the coordinator. The coordinator checks the pending amount against its current capacity, replies with a vote‑commit if the capacity still permits, or a vote‑abort if the new capacity would be exceeded, and then the bank either finalises the deduction (commit) or restores the pending amount (abort). All participants only modify the inventory count or the pending flag during the commit phases, ensuring that any capacity change does not retroactively create or destroy blood units.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total number of blood units recorded across all inventory counts plus any pending transaction amounts never increases nor decreases except by explicit donation or consumption actions.

The fleet consists of autonomous robots that move pallets and a shared compare‑and‑swap (CAS) register representing a loading bay. Each robot keeps a local copy of two variables: the identifier of the robot that currently owns the bay (or “none”) and the number of pallets already placed in the bay. To start loading, a robot reads the register; if the owner field is “none” it issues a CAS operation that tries to replace “none” with its own identifier, leaving the pallet count unchanged. If the CAS succeeds the robot becomes the exclusive owner, loads pallets one by one while incrementing the local count, and finally writes a release entry that sets the owner back to “none” and resets the count to zero. Because messages may be reordered, a robot may see an outdated owner value, but the atomic CAS guarantees that only the first robot whose CAS succeeds actually changes the register. Robots that lose the CAS simply retry later, preserving the invariant that at most one robot believes it owns the bay at any time. The protocol therefore requires only the two state variables (owner and count) to capture all relevant information.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The number of pallets in any loading bay never exceeds its maximum capacity.
