nl:
Patrons and branch servers form a logical ring, and a single token circulates around the ring to grant the right to modify the reservation table. Each node keeps two pieces of state: (1) whether it currently holds the token, and (2) a map that records for each BookCopyID which patron (if any) has reserved it. When a patron wishes to reserve a copy of *The Great Gatsby* (copy C42), it sends a reservation request to the next node in the ring; the request may arrive out of order but will be ignored until that node receives the token. Once a node obtains the token, it processes any pending requests in the order they were received, checks the map to see if C42 is free, and, if so, records the patron’s ID as the new owner of that slot. After updating the map, the node forwards the updated reservation map to the next node, releases the token, and the token continues its round‑robin journey. If a later, reordered request for the same copy arrives while the token is elsewhere, the node simply queues it, guaranteeing that only the node with the token can make a reservation decision.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two patrons can reserve the same copy of a book at the same time.

The system consists of a MasterController, a FrontDoorCoarseLock, several InsideDoorFineLocks (one per interior door), and a CapacityManager that can raise or lower the allowed number of occupants at any time. Each lock keeps a Boolean state (locked or unlocked) and the MasterController keeps a counter of how many fine‑locks are currently granted. When a user wants to enter, the FrontDoorCoarseLock receives an “enter‑request” and, if the fine‑lock counter is below the current capacity, it temporarily unlocks to let the user pass and notifies the InsideDoorFineLock that controls the next room. The InsideDoorFineLock then checks the same capacity counter; if it is still below limit it grants the fine‑lock, increments the counter, and locks again. The CapacityManager may asynchronously issue a “capacity‑change” command that updates the capacity value; the MasterController immediately adjusts the maximum allowed fine‑locks but does not alter the current counter. If the capacity is lowered below the current counter, no new fine‑locks are granted until enough occupants leave and the counter drops accordingly. All participants communicate only through these lock state changes and the shared capacity value, making the whole protocol describable with the three variables: coarse‑lock state, fine‑lock counter, and current capacity.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The number of fine‑locks granted at any moment never exceeds the current capacity value.

The system consists of three roles: Student clients that issue registration requests, a Registration Server that records accepted enrollments, and a Capacity Manager that can raise or lower the seat limit of a course while the term is in progress.   All three components maintain a shared epoch number; each time the Capacity Manager changes a course’s seat limit it increments the epoch and broadcasts the new value to the server and all students.   A student’s request carries the epoch it was generated in, and the server only processes a request if its epoch matches the server’s current epoch, thereby preventing stale requests from being applied after a capacity change.   When the server receives a request in the current epoch, it checks the recorded enrollment count for the course; if the count is below the current capacity it increments the count and records the student’s enrollment together with the epoch.   If the capacity manager reduces the seat limit, the new epoch causes the server to reject any pending requests from the previous epoch and to drop registrations that would exceed the new limit, forcing those students to re‑submit in the new epoch.   Students may retry in the new epoch after receiving a rejection, and the capacity manager may later increase capacity, which again triggers a new epoch broadcast.   The entire protocol therefore proceeds in discrete, numbered epochs that synchronize capacity updates with registration actions while keeping the state variables small: the epoch number, the current capacity, the enrollment count, and the set of enrolled students.

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any moment, the number of students enrolled in a course never exceeds the capacity that is active for the current epoch.

The system has three participants: the central OR‑Scheduler, a set of OR‑Workers (each representing a physical operating room), and a bounded request queue that holds pending surgery jobs. The Scheduler maintains the queue length (up to a fixed capacity) and a list of which OR‑Workers are currently idle; each OR‑Worker keeps a flag indicating whether it is busy with a surgery or free. When the queue is not full, the Scheduler may enqueue a new surgery request; otherwise it applies backpressure and waits until some worker finishes and frees a slot. An idle OR‑Worker repeatedly dequeues the oldest pending request, marks itself busy, and starts the surgery; when the surgery completes it marks itself idle again and informs the Scheduler. If an OR‑Worker crashes silently, it stops sending completion messages, so the Scheduler detects the missing heartbeat after a timeout, removes the worker from the idle list, and re‑queues the surgery that was in progress. The backpressure mechanism ensures that no new request is added while the queue is at capacity, preventing overload of the workers. All state changes (queue length, worker busy/idle flags, and timeout‑driven recovery) can be captured with four variables, keeping the model small enough for formal analysis.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two operating rooms may be assigned the same surgery at the same time.

The system consists of three roles: the Conveyor Controller, the Pre‑Soap Station, and the Rinse Station, each running on its own node.  
Each node stores a single integer “epoch” that records the most recent wash cycle it has agreed to start, and a boolean flag “ready” indicating whether it is prepared to perform its next action.  
When a car arrives, the Conveyor Controller increments its epoch, broadcasts the new epoch to the two stations, and then asks both stations to vote “ready” for that epoch.  
Each station, upon receiving the epoch message, updates its local epoch (ignoring any older value that may have arrived later because of reordering) and replies with a ready vote only after it has finished its current sub‑process.  
The Conveyor Controller proceeds to move the car onto the conveyor only after it has collected a quorum of two ready votes for the current epoch; it then resets its ready flag and notifies the stations of the completed step.  
The stations acknowledge the completion, reset their ready flags, and wait for the next epoch broadcast, thus ensuring that all actions are performed in the same logical cycle despite possible out‑of‑order messages.  
Any node that receives a message with an epoch lower than its current epoch discards it as stale and does not participate in the voting for that cycle.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No station or controller may perform a wash‑line action for a car using an epoch that is not the latest agreed‑upon epoch, preventing actions by stale or unauthorized participants.

The system consists of three branch servers – North, South, and East – each of which holds a local counter of pending reservations for a particular book and a flag indicating whether it believes itself to be the current leader. Periodically every server sends a heartbeat containing its own identifier and its reservation counter to the other two servers; if a server receives a higher‑valued leader identifier it adopts that server as the leader and updates its flag. When a server detects that the leader’s heartbeat has not arrived for two consecutive intervals, it initiates a simple election by broadcasting a “candidate” message that includes its own reservation counter; the candidate with the smallest counter wins and becomes the new leader. The elected leader is responsible for assigning the next available reservation slot to any incoming patron request and incrementing its own counter, then broadcasting the updated counter to the followers. A follower that is merely slow may miss a heartbeat once but will recover when it receives the next broadcast and will not trigger a new election unless the leader truly stops sending heartbeats. All servers keep only two state variables – the leader identifier and the local reservation counter – to make the protocol easy to model.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total number of reserved slots for the book never changes except when a patron request is processed, so reservations are never created or destroyed arbitrarily.

The system consists of three participants: a LoadController that decides when to reduce demand, a group of Substation agents that own individual feeder circuits, and a privileged Admin that can intervene in emergencies. Each Substation maintains a coarse‑grained “grid lock” flag indicating whether any load‑shedding operation is in progress, and a fine‑grained “feeder lock” flag for its own circuit. When the LoadController wants to shed load, it first sets the grid lock; only after the grid lock is observed as set do the Substations each try to acquire their feeder lock, and a Substation that succeeds will open its circuit breaker to drop load. After the breaker is opened, the Substation clears its feeder lock, and when all feeders have responded the LoadController releases the grid lock. The Admin override can be invoked at any time: the Admin acquires the grid lock (or waits until it is free), sets an “override” flag, and then forces a specific Substation to open its breaker without needing that Substation’s feeder lock. The protocol guarantees that once a breaker has been opened for a particular load‑shedding request, no other participant will attempt to open it again for the same request.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: A feeder’s circuit breaker is opened at most once for any single load‑shedding activation.
spec_text:
---- MODULE W4C9x8x5x5 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, Sequences, TLC

CONSTANTS Substations

VARIABLES gridLock, feederLocks, breakerOpen, openCount, overrideFlag

\*---------------------------------------------------------------------- 
\*  Initialization
\*---------------------------------------------------------------------- 
Init ==
  /\ gridLock = FALSE
  /\ feederLocks = [s \in Substations |-> FALSE]
  /\ breakerOpen = [s \in Substations |-> FALSE]
  /\ openCount   = [s \in Substations |-> 0]
  /\ overrideFlag = FALSE

\*---------------------------------------------------------------------- 
\*  LoadController actions
\*---------------------------------------------------------------------- 
StartLoadShedding ==
  /\ ~gridLock
  /\ gridLock' = TRUE
  /\ openCount' = [s \in Substations |-> 0]
  /\ breakerOpen' = [s \in Substations |-> FALSE]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<feederLocks, overrideFlag>>

ReleaseGridLock ==
  /\ gridLock
  /\ gridLock' = FALSE
  /\ overrideFlag' = FALSE
  /\ UNCHANGED <<feederLocks, breakerOpen, openCount>>

\*---------------------------------------------------------------------- 
\*  Substation actions
\*---------------------------------------------------------------------- 
AcquireFeederLock(s) ==
  /\ gridLock
  /\ s \in Substations
  /\ feederLocks[s] = FALSE
  /\ feederLocks' = [feederLocks EXCEPT ![s] = TRUE]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<gridLock, breakerOpen, openCount, overrideFlag>>

OpenBreaker(s) ==
  /\ gridLock
  /\ s \in Substations
  /\ feederLocks[s] = TRUE
  /\ openCount[s] = 0               \* not opened yet for this request
  /\ breakerOpen' = [breakerOpen EXCEPT ![s] = TRUE]
  /\ feederLocks' = [feederLocks EXCEPT ![s] = FALSE]
  /\ openCount'   = [openCount EXCEPT ![s] = 1]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<gridLock, overrideFlag>>

\*---------------------------------------------------------------------- 
\*  Admin actions (override)
\*---------------------------------------------------------------------- 
AdminForceOpen(s) ==
  /\ ~gridLock
  /\ s \in Substations
  /\ openCount[s] = 0               \* must not have opened yet for this request
  /\ gridLock'     = TRUE
  /\ overrideFlag' = TRUE
  /\ breakerOpen'  = [breakerOpen EXCEPT ![s] = TRUE]
  /\ openCount'    = [openCount EXCEPT ![s] = 1]
  /\ UNCHANGED feederLocks

\*---------------------------------------------------------------------- 
\*  Next-state relation
\*---------------------------------------------------------------------- 
Next ==
  \/ StartLoadShedding
  \/ ReleaseGridLock
  \/ \E s \in Substations: AcquireFeederLock(s)
  \/ \E s \in Substations: OpenBreaker(s)
  \/ \E s \in Substations: AdminForceOpen(s)

\*---------------------------------------------------------------------- 
\*  Safety invariant: a feeder’s breaker is opened at most once per request
\*---------------------------------------------------------------------- 
NoDoubleOpen == \A s \in Substations : openCount[s] <= 1

=============================================================================

CONSTANT Substations = {s1, s2, s3}
INIT Init

INVARIANT NoDoubleOpen

nl:
The system consists of two independent dispenser controllers, Instance A and Instance B, that both access the same prescription queue and the shared medication‑stock ledger. Each controller keeps a small amount of state: a role flag (“leader” or “follower”), the identifier of the last prescription it successfully processed, and a heartbeat timestamp received from the current leader. The controller that holds the leader role dequeues the next prescription, dispenses the medication, writes a debit entry to the stock ledger, updates its last‑processed identifier, and broadcasts a heartbeat to the other controller. The follower constantly monitors the heartbeat; if it does not receive an update within a timeout it initiates a simple leader‑election by sending an “elect‑me” message, and the first controller to obtain a quorum of acknowledgments assumes the leader flag. When a leader crashes after broadcasting a heartbeat but before updating the ledger, the survivor will detect the missing heartbeat, win the election, and re‑process the same prescription using the shared queue, ensuring only one controller ever writes the ledger entry for a given prescription. All other actions – reading the queue, checking stock levels, and displaying status – are performed locally and never modify the shared ledger.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The shared medication‑stock ledger never loses an update; every prescription that is dispensed results in exactly one corresponding debit entry in the ledger.

The batch processor consists of a fixed set of settlement nodes, each representing an inter‑bank participant, and one node that acts as the current leader, called the Coordinator. Every node stores the identifier of the current Coordinator, the number of the next settlement slot it is allowed to claim, and a heartbeat timer that is reset whenever a message is received from the Coordinator. The Coordinator periodically broadcasts a *next‑slot* proposal containing the slot number and waits for acknowledgments; each participant that receives the proposal records the slot as “reserved for me” and replies with an ack. If a participant’s ack is not received before the Coordinator’s timeout, the Coordinator treats the participant as slow, leaves the slot unassigned, and proceeds with the next slot; if the Coordinator itself does not receive any heartbeat from a majority of participants within its own timeout, the participants start a simple leader‑election using a round‑robin ordering of node IDs. Once a new Coordinator is elected, it adopts the highest slot number seen in the system, continues the batch sequence, and re‑issues the pending proposals, ensuring that only one node ever holds the right to write to a given slot.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No settlement slot is ever assigned to more than one participant in the same batch.

The system consists of a central Load Controller and several Distributed Substations that each can request a load‑shed lease.  
Each substation maintains two state variables: a lease timer indicating the remaining time on its current lease, and a flag showing whether it currently holds the “shed‑slot” for a particular feeder line.  
When a substation detects that the grid frequency falls below the threshold, it sends a LeaseRequest to the Load Controller for the shed‑slot of the overloaded feeder.  
The Load Controller grants the lease by replying with a LeaseGrant that includes a lease duration; the substation then sets its lease timer and its shed‑slot flag to true.  
While the lease is valid the substation may execute a load‑shed action, but it must periodically send a LeaseRenewal before the timer expires; if the renewal is delayed the lease automatically expires.  
Because a substation may be slow, the Load Controller does not wait for an acknowledgement before allowing another substation to acquire the lease once the previous lease’s timer reaches zero.  
If a substation’s lease expires without renewal, it clears its shed‑slot flag, stops shedding load, and the Load Controller may reassign the lease to another substation.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any time at most one substation holds a valid lease for a given feeder line, ensuring that only one entity can perform load shedding on that feeder concurrently.

The network consists of three participants: each DoorLock unit, a homeowner’s MobileApp, and a CentralHub that stores a single compare‑and‑swap (CAS) register called `ownerToken`. Every DoorLock keeps a Boolean `locked` flag and a copy of the most recent `ownerToken` it has seen. When the MobileApp wishes to unlock a door, it sends an “unlock request” containing a newly generated token to the CentralHub; the Hub attempts a CAS on `ownerToken`, replacing the old value only if it still matches the one recorded at the hub. If the CAS succeeds, the Hub broadcasts an “unlock grant” message with the new token; each DoorLock that receives this message checks that the token matches its stored copy and, if so, flips its `locked` flag to false. Because messages may arrive out of order, a DoorLock will ignore any grant whose token does not equal the one it currently holds, preventing a stale grant from unlocking the door. The MobileApp can also send a “master‑override” request that tries a CAS with a special token; once this token is installed, no further CAS operation can replace it, effectively making the door permanently unlocked until manual reset. All participants act only on the outcome of the CAS operation, ensuring that despite reordering, at most one token change can be accepted at a time.

SAFETY PROPERTY: A master‑override unlock can be installed at most once.

The car‑wash line consists of three roles: the **Controller** that tracks how many vehicles are currently on the conveyor, the **Sensor Nodes** (one at the entrance and one at the exit) that propose to add or remove a car, and an **Admin** who can issue an override command. Each Sensor Node maintains a local flag indicating whether it has a pending proposal (“add” at the entrance, “remove” at the exit). The Controller keeps a single counter for the total number of cars and a Boolean flag saying whether an admin override is active. When a Sensor Node wants to act, it broadcasts its proposal to the Controller; the Controller waits until it has received matching proposals from a quorum (both entrance and exit nodes must agree on the direction of change) before updating the counter. If the Admin issues an override, the Controller immediately sets the override flag, processes the requested change regardless of quorum, and then clears the flag after the action completes. Normal operation resumes only when the override flag is cleared, and the quorum mechanism is re‑enabled for subsequent proposals. All participants reset their local proposal flags after each action so that the system can accept new proposals.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The number of cars on the conveyor belt never exceeds its maximum capacity.

The system has three participants: a Student client, the CourseCatalog service that stores the current seat count for each section, and a RegistrationServer that mediates enrollment requests. Each course section maintains a version number and a remaining‑seat counter; the RegistrationServer also keeps a temporary “pendingStudent” identifier while a request is being processed. A Student begins by reading the section’s version and seat count, then sends an enrollment request together with the observed version to the RegistrationServer. The RegistrationServer re‑reads the current version; if it still matches the student’s value and seats are available, it decrements the seat counter, increments the version, records the student as enrolled, and clears the pendingStudent field. If the versions differ, the server discards the attempt, updates its view of the version, and asks the student to retry with the new version. Because a participant may be slow, the RegistrationServer waits a bounded time for the student’s retry; if the timeout expires it aborts the pending operation but leaves the course state unchanged, allowing the student to start a fresh attempt later. All retries are performed without holding any lock, so concurrent students can keep proposing enrollments while only the version check enforces consistency.

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any moment, the number of students enrolled in a course section never exceeds the section’s seat capacity.

The system consists of a set of Substation Controllers (SCs) that each monitor a local load segment, a Grid Coordinator (GC) that initiates load‑shedding actions, and a privileged Admin who can issue an override command.  
Each SC maintains a local variable `vote` (either “yes” or “no”) and a shared flag `pending` that indicates whether a load‑shedding request is currently being considered.  
When the GC detects that total demand exceeds the safe capacity, it broadcasts a “shed request” to all SCs and sets `pending` to true.  
Every SC, upon receiving the request, decides whether it can safely reduce its load and sends its `vote` back to the GC; the GC counts votes until it reaches a predefined quorum number.  
If the quorum of “yes” votes is reached and the Admin has not set the `override` flag, the GC orders all SCs to execute the shedding, and each SC updates its local load accordingly while clearing `pending`.  
The Admin can at any time set the `override` flag to true, which either forces immediate shedding regardless of votes or blocks shedding if the flag indicates a protection mode, and the GC must respect this flag before acting.  
After the action is completed or cancelled, the GC clears `pending` and the `override` flag, returning the system to the idle state.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total load on any transmission line never exceeds its rated capacity.

The network consists of two vending‑machine instances, VM‑A and VM‑B, that both draw stock from a single shared inventory pool maintained by the central stock server. Each machine keeps a local record of the current lease holder for the pool, the lease’s expiration time, and the quantity of the item it believes is available. When a machine needs to dispense an item, it first sends a lease‑request to the lease manager; if no valid lease exists, the manager grants a lease to that machine with a time‑limited lease‑token. While the lease is valid the holder may decrement the shared quantity and write the new count back to the stock server, after which it may either renew the lease before expiry or release it early. If the lease expires without renewal, any pending lease‑request from the other machine becomes eligible, ensuring that both machines eventually regain exclusive access. The lease manager tracks only the holder identifier and the expiry timestamp, which together are enough to enforce mutual exclusion despite the two independent instances sharing the same pool. All update operations are aborted if the requester does not hold the current, unexpired lease, preventing concurrent writes to the same inventory record.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The shared inventory count is never updated by two machines at the same time, so no update to the stock record is lost.

The system consists of a Central Registry that stores the global inventory of each blood type and a set of Blood‑Bank Nodes that hold the local stock for the same types. Each node keeps a local copy of the inventory count together with a version number that the Registry increments on every successful update. When a node wants to record a donation or a transfusion it reads the current version, computes the new count, and sends the proposed update together with the version it observed to the Registry. The Registry checks whether the version it received matches the current global version; if it does, the Registry applies the update, increments the version, and acknowledges the node, otherwise it rejects the request and the node retries with the latest version. Because a node may be slow to reply, the Registry never blocks waiting for an acknowledgement; it simply processes each incoming request independently and lets the slow node retry later. Each retry is a fresh optimistic‑locking attempt that uses the most recent version, guaranteeing forward progress even when some participants are delayed. The protocol therefore coordinates updates without locks that hold across network delays, while still preventing conflicting changes to the inventory.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total units stored for any blood type never exceed the predefined maximum capacity for that type.

The system consists of a set of DoorLock nodes, each controlling a physical lock, and a central CapacityManager that stores the current maximum number of simultaneous unlocked doors.  
Each DoorLock keeps a local flag “requested” and reads the shared compare‑and‑swap register which holds the pair (currentUnlocked, maxCapacity).  
When a user presents a credential, the DoorLock sets its requested flag and attempts a compare‑and‑swap: it succeeds only if currentUnlocked < maxCapacity, in which case it increments currentUnlocked and unlocks the door.  
If the compare‑and‑swap fails because the capacity is full, the DoorLock leaves the door locked and retries later.  
The CapacityManager may change maxCapacity at any time; it writes a new value to the register using a compare‑and‑swap that succeeds only when no DoorLock is in the middle of an update (the register’s version field matches).  
When a DoorLock closes the door, it performs a compare‑and‑swap that decrements currentUnlocked, guaranteeing the count reflects only fully closed doors.  
All participants base their decisions solely on the atomic outcome of the compare‑and‑swap, so no two DoorLocks can believe they have unlocked the door while exceeding the advertised capacity.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No door can remain unlocked due to an unauthorized user or a stale lock request that was based on an out‑of‑date capacity value.

The system consists of a set of smart door locks (Lock_i), a mobile app acting as a client, and a Lease Server that issues time‑limited leases for exclusive control of a lock.  
Each lock stores two variables – currentOwner (the identifier of the client that holds the lease, or none) and leaseExpiry (a timestamp after which the lease is considered invalid).  
When a user wants to open a door, the mobile app sends a LeaseRequest to the Lease Server; the server records the request, selects the lock, and replies with a LeaseGrant that contains the client’s ID and a deadline.  
The lock, upon receiving a LeaseGrant, updates currentOwner to the client ID and sets leaseExpiry to the deadline, but before acting on any Unlock command it checks that the current time is before leaseExpiry and that the command’s sender matches currentOwner, thereby tolerating out‑of‑order messages.  
If the leaseExpiry time passes without renewal, the lock automatically clears currentOwner to none, making the lock free for a new lease, and any late Unlock messages that arrive after expiry are ignored.  
A client may extend its lease by sending a LeaseRenewal before the current lease expires; the server replies with a new LeaseGrant that overwrites the lock’s leaseExpiry, and the lock accepts the renewal only if the renewal’s client ID matches currentOwner.  
All messages (LeaseGrant, LeaseRenewal, Unlock) are stateless and may be reordered in the network, so the lock’s decision logic always bases actions on the latest stored leaseExpiry and the identity of currentOwner.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any moment, at most one client can hold a valid lease for a given door lock, preventing two different clients from unlocking the same door simultaneously.

Air traffic controllers run a distributed allocator that manages the single runway “R1”. Each aircraft sends a request to the allocator, which records the request’s timestamp and reads the current version number of R1’s status. The controller then tries an optimistic lock: it writes a new allocation record for that aircraft only if the version number it read is still current, otherwise it retries with the updated version. If the write succeeds, the runway state is set to “occupied” together with the aircraft’s identifier and the version number is incremented. A privileged admin can issue an override command that atomically forces the runway state to “admin‑override” and records a special admin token, cancelling any pending or existing allocation before the override takes effect. All participants—aircraft, controller, and admin—continue to respect the version number, so after an override normal allocation attempts must again read the new version and succeed only on the next retry.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The runway is never allocated to more than one aircraft simultaneously.

The protocol involves three participants: the Origin Bank that creates settlement messages, the Clearing House that runs a bounded work queue, and the Destination Bank that receives and acknowledges settled amounts.  
The Origin Bank maintains a counter “outstandingAmount” representing the total value of all messages it has produced but not yet confirmed as settled.  
The Clearing House maintains two state variables: “queueDepth”, the current number of messages in the bounded queue, and “processedAmount”, the sum of values of messages it has successfully dequeued and forwarded.  
The Destination Bank holds “receivedAmount”, the total value of settlement messages it has accepted and recorded.  
When the Origin Bank has capacity (queueDepth < MAX), it enqueues a new settlement message containing its amount, increments “outstandingAmount”, and the queue depth grows; if the queue is full, the Origin Bank must wait (backpressure) until the Clearing House processes some entries.  
The Clearing House repeatedly dequeues messages in FIFO order, but because the network can reorder deliveries, it may forward them to the Destination Bank out of order, updating “processedAmount” and decrementing “queueDepth”.  
Upon receiving a settlement message, the Destination Bank adds its amount to “receivedAmount” and sends an acknowledgment back to the Origin Bank, which then subtracts the amount from “outstandingAmount”.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The sum of the Origin Bank’s outstandingAmount, the Clearing House’s processedAmount, and the Destination Bank’s receivedAmount remains constant throughout the protocol.

The system consists of three autonomous routing agents – the Sorter, the Diverter, and the Loader – each of which needs temporary exclusive control of a shared conveyor segment called the “routing slot”. All agents read and write a single compare‑and‑swap register that stores the identifier of the agent that currently owns the routing slot, or the special value FREE. When an agent wants to use the slot it reads the register; if the value is FREE it attempts a compare‑and‑swap from FREE to its own identifier, succeeding only if no other agent has changed the value in the meantime. The privileged administrator runs a separate Override process that can atomically replace any register value with the identifier ADMIN, thereby pre‑empting the current holder and taking control of the slot for emergency re‑routing. After the admin finishes, it writes the register back to FREE, allowing the normal agents to compete again. Any agent that loses a compare‑and‑swap attempt simply retries after a short back‑off, while the admin’s override operation never retries – it succeeds immediately. The protocol therefore requires only two state variables – the register’s current owner and a Boolean “override active” flag – to capture all possible configurations.

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any moment, at most one routing agent or the administrator can hold the routing slot.
spec_text:
---------------------------- MODULE W4C17x7x0x5 ----------------------------
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets, Sequences

CONSTANTS Agents, ADMIN, FREE

(*--------------------------------------------------------------------*)
(* State variables *)
VARIABLES reg, OverrideActive

(*--------------------------------------------------------------------*)
(* Helper definitions *)
IsAgent(a) == a \in Agents

(*--------------------------------------------------------------------*)
(* Initial state *)
Init ==
    /\ reg = FREE
    /\ OverrideActive = FALSE

(*--------------------------------------------------------------------*)
(* Agent actions: try to acquire the slot when it is FREE and no
   override is active. *)
AgentTry(a) ==
    /\ IsAgent(a)
    /\ ~OverrideActive
    /\ reg = FREE
    /\ reg' = a
    /\ UNCHANGED OverrideActive

(*--------------------------------------------------------------------*)
(* Administrator actions *)
AdminOverride ==
    /\ ~OverrideActive
    /\ reg' = ADMIN
    /\ OverrideActive' = TRUE

AdminRelease ==
    /\ OverrideActive
    /\ reg = ADMIN
    /\ reg' = FREE
    /\ OverrideActive' = FALSE

(*--------------------------------------------------------------------*)
(* Stuttering step to avoid deadlock *)
Stutter ==
    UNCHANGED <<reg, OverrideActive>>

(*--------------------------------------------------------------------*)
(* Next-state relation *)
Next ==
    \/ \E a \in Agents: AgentTry(a)
    \/ AdminOverride
    \/ AdminRelease
    \/ Stutter

(*--------------------------------------------------------------------*)
(* Specification *)
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<reg, OverrideActive>>

(*--------------------------------------------------------------------*)
(* Safety invariant: at most one holder of the routing slot *)
SlotExclusive ==
    /\ (reg = ADMIN)      => OverrideActive = TRUE
    /\ OverrideActive     => reg = ADMIN
    /\ (reg \in Agents)   => OverrideActive = FALSE
    /\ (reg = FREE)       => OverrideActive = FALSE

(*--------------------------------------------------------------------*)
THEOREM Spec => []SlotExclusive

=============================================================================
cfg_text:
CONSTANTS
  Agents = {"Sorter", "Diverter", "Loader"}
  ADMIN  = "ADMIN"
  FREE   = "FREE"

INIT Init
NEXT Next

INVARIANT SlotExclusive

The system consists of a central Scheduler process and several Surgeon processes that each request a specific Operating‑Room (OR) for a time slot. The only shared state is a compare‑and‑swap (CAS) register that holds the identifier of the surgery currently assigned to the next free OR slot, together with a version number. When a Surgeon wants to book an OR, it reads the register, checks whether the desired OR is free (the version has not changed), and then issues a CAS operation to replace the current identifier with its own surgery ID and increment the version. If the CAS succeeds, the Surgeon records locally that it has secured the OR; if it fails, it rereads the register and may retry with a different OR. The Scheduler periodically scans the register and, whenever it finds a version that has not been updated for a timeout, it assumes the last writer (a Surgeon) may have crashed silently and resets the register to “idle” with a fresh version, making the OR available again. All participants treat the register as the single source of truth for which surgery occupies the next OR slot, and any change to the register must go through the atomic CAS operation.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total number of active surgeries scheduled for the same OR slot never exceeds one.

The system has three participants: the Block Controller (BC) that owns a track block, the Train (TR) that requests permission to occupy the block, and the Reconfiguration Manager (RM) that can change the block’s boundaries. Each participant keeps two pieces of state: the current epoch number and the block’s mode (either “clear” or “occupied”). When a train wishes to enter, it sends a request to the BC; the BC replies with a grant that includes the BC’s current epoch, and the train records that epoch before moving into the block. If the RM decides to reconfigure, it increments the epoch, broadcasts the new epoch together with the updated block definition, and the BC adopts the new configuration only after seeing the matching epoch. Because messages can be reordered, every component ignores any message whose epoch does not equal its own current epoch, treating it as stale. This rule ensures that only one train can hold the grant for a block at any given epoch, even when messages arrive out of order.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any moment, a given track block is occupied by at most one train.

The yard is overseen by a **YardManager** who holds a single coarse lock that represents “the whole crane yard is in a safe configuration”.  
When a **CraneController** wants to move a container it first asks the YardManager for the coarse lock; once granted it then acquires a fine‑grained **CraneSlotLock** that protects the specific slot on the ship where the container will be placed.  
A **CapacityMonitor** continuously watches the ship’s remaining weight and volume limits and updates a shared variable **CurrentCapacity**; when the capacity changes, it may lower the allowed number of concurrent CraneSlotLocks, forcing any excess locks to be released before new moves can start.  
The protocol proceeds in three steps: (1) the YardManager grants the coarse lock, (2) the CraneController obtains the fine lock for its target slot and checks that the slot is free and that the capacity permits the load, (3) the CraneController records the allocation in a tiny table **AllocatedSlots** and then releases the fine lock while keeping the coarse lock until the container is physically settled.  
If the CapacityMonitor detects a reduction that would violate the new limit, it temporarily blocks the YardManager from granting new coarse locks until enough slots are freed; already‑granted coarse locks remain valid but no additional fine locks may be taken.  
All participants communicate only through these shared variables, so the whole system can be modeled with the four state variables: YardLock, CraneSlotLock, CurrentCapacity, and AllocatedSlots.  

**SAFETY PROPERTY:** No container is ever placed into the same ship slot more than once.

The system consists of three agents: the Dispenser Controller that physically releases medication, the Inventory Manager that tracks how many doses are stored in each compartment, and the Pharmacist UI that authorizes a dispense request. All agents keep a shared **epoch number**, which is incremented each time the system is re‑configured, and a **capacity value** that records the maximum number of doses any compartment may hold after a runtime change. When the pharmacist decides to increase a compartment’s capacity, the Inventory Manager first proposes the new capacity together with the next epoch number, broadcasts this proposal, and waits for acknowledgments from the Dispenser Controller. Upon receiving acknowledgments, the Inventory Manager commits the new capacity, updates its local epoch, and sends a commit message; the Dispenser Controller accepts the commit only if the epoch matches its current value and then adjusts its internal limits accordingly. A dispense operation is allowed only when the requesting pharmacist’s UI supplies a ticket stamped with the current epoch and the Inventory Manager confirms that the requested compartment still has at least one dose available. If any agent detects a message bearing an older epoch, it discards it and asks the sender to retry with the latest epoch, ensuring that stale configuration information never influences the dispenser. All agents therefore progress only by advancing the epoch together, making capacity changes safe even while dispensing may be happening concurrently.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No medication can be released by a participant that is using an outdated epoch or that has not been authorized by the current pharmacist.

Four vending machines, V₁‑V₄, are linked in a logical ring. Each machine stores two local variables: the number of items currently stocked in its dispense column and a Boolean flag indicating whether it currently holds the exclusive‑access token. When a machine receives the token, it may either serve a pending customer request (decrementing its stock count and incrementing its cash buffer) or, if no request is pending, immediately pass the token to the next machine in the ring. If a machine crashes silently while holding the token, the next machine times out after a short waiting period, assumes the token has been lost, and generates a new token that it marks as “recovered” before forwarding it onward, thus preserving the ring’s ability to grant exclusive access. All other machines ignore any token that does not carry the recovered flag, preventing duplicate tokens from circulating. The token guarantees that at most one machine can modify its inventory or cash buffer at any given time, so concurrent updates never interfere. A crashed machine that later recovers simply resynchronizes by reading the current token holder flag from its neighbor before rejoining the ring. The protocol therefore uses only the three variables (stock, token‑holder flag, and recovered‑token flag) to enforce correct coordination despite a single silent crash.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total number of items being dispensed at any moment never exceeds the total number of items actually present in the combined inventories of all vending machines.

The system consists of two independent car‑wash lines, Line A and Line B, that both draw slots from a single shared pool of conveyor positions. Each line runs a local controller that first requests a coarse “pool lock” to guarantee exclusive access to the pool while it decides which slot to use, and then requests a fine “slot lock” on the particular position it intends to occupy. The shared state variables are (1) poolLocked, indicating whether the coarse lock is held, (2) slotLocked[x] for each slot x, indicating whether that slot is currently reserved, and (3) assignedSlot for each line, recording which slot it has been given. When a line needs to admit a car, it atomically sets poolLocked, scans the pool for a free slot, sets slotLocked for that slot, records the slot in assignedSlot, and finally clears poolLocked so the other line may begin its own allocation. After the car finishes its wash, the line clears its slotLocked entry and resets assignedSlot to “none”. If the coarse lock cannot be obtained because the other line is already allocating, the requesting line simply waits; the fine lock is never attempted without first holding the coarse lock, guaranteeing that two lines never race for the same slot. The protocol therefore coordinates the two instances by serialising the allocation decision while still allowing the actual washing to proceed in parallel on different slots.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No conveyor slot is ever allocated to both lines at the same time.

The fleet consists of a central Scheduler and a set of mobile Robots that move pallets between storage aisles.  
Each Robot stores a local variable “load” indicating whether it is currently carrying a pallet, and the Scheduler keeps a global counter “capacity” that records the maximum number of pallets that may be in the aisle at any time.  
When a Robot wants to pick up a pallet it broadcasts a “request‑pick” message containing its identifier to all other Robots and to the Scheduler.  
All recipients reply with a vote that is “yes” if their own load is empty and the Scheduler’s capacity counter is still positive; the request is approved once a majority of the fleet and the Scheduler have voted yes.  
Upon approval the Robot increments its load, the Scheduler decrements capacity, and the action is executed; if capacity is later increased by an operator, the Scheduler updates the counter and future votes will reflect the new limit.  
A Robot that has completed its delivery sends a “release” message, clears its load, and the Scheduler increments capacity, allowing new picks.  
All Robots constantly maintain the same quorum‑based decision rule, so no two Robots can simultaneously commit a pick that would cause capacity to drop below zero.  

**SAFETY PROPERTY:** Each individual pallet is picked up for transport at most once.

The market consists of a set of **auction processors** (one for each exchange venue) that form a logical ring, a **token** that circulates around this ring, and an **order‑slot pool** shared by two independent opening‑auction instances (the “primary” and the “secondary” auction). Each processor keeps a small state: (1) which auction instance currently holds the token, (2) which order slot, if any, is reserved for its local broker, and (3) whether the shared pool still contains free slots. When a broker wishes to submit an opening order, its processor sends a **slot‑request** to the token holder; the holder checks that the pool has a free slot for the requested auction instance, reserves that slot, and records the reservation in its state before passing the token to the next processor. After the broker’s order is acknowledged, the processor releases the slot back to the pool and the token moves on, carrying the updated pool state. The token always carries the identifier of the auction instance it is currently serving, so the two auctions can interleave token passes without confusing each other’s reservations. If a processor receives the token for an auction instance but the pool is empty, it simply forwards the token unchanged, allowing other processors to continue servicing the other instance. The protocol guarantees that a token can only be held by one processor at a time, and that each reservation is atomically recorded before the token is forwarded.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No order slot is ever allocated to two different brokers in the same auction instance.

The system consists of a Scheduler process and several Surgeon agents that each request an operating‑room (OR) for a surgery.  
The Scheduler holds a single versioned record for each OR, containing the currently assigned surgery identifier and a monotonic version number.  
When a Surgeon wants to book an OR, it reads the OR’s record, proposes a new assignment with the next version number, and sends this proposal to the Scheduler.  
The Scheduler checks whether the version in the proposal still matches the stored version; if it does, the Scheduler updates the record with the new assignment and increments the version, otherwise it rejects the proposal.  
If a Surgeon receives a rejection, it waits a short random back‑off period and then retries the whole read‑propose‑send cycle.  
One Surgeon may crash at any point without sending a final acknowledgment; the Scheduler treats the lack of acknowledgment as a normal timeout and leaves the OR record unchanged.  
Because every successful update requires the version to match, only one Surgeon can succeed in assigning a given OR at a time, even in the presence of retries and a crashed participant.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two surgeries are ever scheduled in the same operating‑room at overlapping times.

The Yard Manager, Crane A, Crane B, and the Shared Pool are the participants in the protocol.  
Each crane keeps a local flag “prepared” that indicates it has reserved a container slot for a move.  
The Yard Manager maintains a single Boolean variable “poolAvailable” that is true only when the shared pool is free for allocation.  
In phase 1, a crane sends a PREPARE request to the manager for the container it wishes to move; the manager records the request only if poolAvailable is true and replies with an ACK, setting its own vote for that transaction.  
In phase 2, after all required ACKs are received, the manager broadcasts a COMMIT; the cranes then clear their prepared flags and physically lift the containers, while the manager sets poolAvailable to false until the transaction completes.  
If any crane cannot prepare or the manager cannot grant a PREPARE because the pool is already claimed, the manager issues an ABORT to all participants and resets its variables, releasing any partial reservation.  
Two independent move transactions may execute concurrently but both consult the same poolAvailable flag, guaranteeing that only one transaction can hold the shared pool at any moment.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two cranes may simultaneously hold the shared pool for moving containers.

The opening auction is run by a central Auction Engine that holds the authoritative order book, while each Broker Agent maintains a local copy of the book to submit buy or sell orders. Both the Engine and all agents keep two pieces of mutable state: the current epoch number, which is incremented whenever a reconfiguration occurs, and the capacity limit that bounds the total volume of orders accepted in the next epoch. When a Broker wishes to change the capacity (for example, to accommodate a sudden influx of orders), it sends a Capacity Proposal to the Engine, which records the proposal together with the epoch number it belongs to. The Engine only applies a proposal after it has collected acknowled‑acks from a majority of agents for the same epoch; at that point it increments the epoch, updates the capacity limit, and broadcasts the new epoch and capacity to all agents. Agents that receive a newer epoch discard any pending order updates that were created under an older epoch, then resend any still‑valid orders using the new epoch number. All order submissions are tagged with the epoch they were generated in, and the Engine processes an order only if its epoch matches the Engine’s current epoch, rejecting or deferring any stale submissions. This coordination ensures that capacity changes can happen at runtime without causing contradictory views of the order book across participants.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No update to the shared order book can be lost or overwritten by an older update submitted in a previous epoch.

The system has three participants: the Collection Center that produces blood units, the Storage Facility that holds them, and the Distribution Hub that ships them to hospitals. A bounded work queue holds transfer tickets that describe a unit moving from the Collection Center to the Storage Facility, and the queue’s size limit is set by a mutable capacity variable reflecting current freezer space. The Collection Center may enqueue a ticket only while the queue is not full; if the queue is full it pauses and waits for backpressure to subside. The Storage Facility dequeues tickets, increments its inventory count, and can change the capacity variable at runtime when freezer shelves are added or removed, thereby automatically restricting further enqueues if the new limit would be exceeded. The Distribution Hub requests a dispatch ticket only after confirming that the inventory count contains the unit, then removes a ticket from a separate dispatch queue that the Storage Facility replenishes after each successful store. When the capacity variable changes, the queue instantly enforces the new limit, blocking further enqueues until the current ticket count fits within the updated bound.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No blood unit is dispatched to a hospital more than once.

The system consists of a set of clearing banks, each running a local settlement node that holds a copy of the current batch ledger, a monotonically increasing batch identifier, and a flag indicating whether the node has voted on the pending batch. When a bank initiates a new inter‑bank transfer, it creates a *TransferRecord* and broadcasts a *ProposeTransfer* message to all nodes; each node records the proposal locally and replies with its vote (yes or no). Once a node receives votes from a configurable quorum of banks, it updates its batch ledger by appending the TransferRecord, increments the batch identifier, and broadcasts a *CommitBatch* message. Nodes that receive a *CommitBatch* verify that the committing node’s batch identifier matches their own expected next identifier; if it does, they apply the same update and set their vote flag to false, otherwise they request the missing commits. Because messages may be reordered, a node may see a *CommitBatch* before it sees some earlier *ProposeTransfer* votes, so it buffers out‑of‑order commits until the corresponding proposal and quorum votes have been recorded. If a quorum later retracts a vote, the node aborts the pending update and removes the buffered TransferRecord, ensuring only agreed‑upon transfers reach the ledger. The quorum mechanism thus guarantees that every committed batch has been approved by enough banks regardless of the order in which messages arrive.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No transfer record that has been committed to one bank’s batch ledger can be lost or overwritten without being reflected in every other bank’s ledger.

The Home Hub, each DoorLock, and a resident’s Mobile App are the three participants in the protocol. The Hub stores a single integer “lock version” and a flag indicating whether a request is currently in progress; each DoorLock stores its own version number and the physical locked/unlocked state; the Mobile App keeps the version number it last read from the Hub. When the user presses “unlock” on the Mobile App, the app sends an UnlockRequest containing the version it knows to the Hub. The Hub first checks whether its stored version equals the one in the request; if they match, the Hub increments the version, sets the in‑progress flag, and forwards an UnlockCommand to the DoorLock; if they do not match, the Hub immediately replies with a Retry message containing the current version. The DoorLock, upon receiving an UnlockCommand, updates its version to the one in the command, changes its physical state to unlocked, clears the Hub’s in‑progress flag, and sends an Acknowledgement back to the Hub. Because messages can arrive out of order, the Mobile App will retry the request whenever it receives a Retry, using the latest version it was given, guaranteeing that only the most recent request can succeed. The protocol thus requires at most three state variables (Hub version, Hub flag, DoorLock version) to be modeled.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The door never becomes unlocked unless the request was issued by the current authorized user whose version number matched the lock’s latest version at the moment the command was executed.

The protocol runs on a set of Bank Nodes that each hold a copy of the pending inter‑bank settlement batch and maintain two local variables: the identifier of the current Leader and the index of the next batch slot to be committed. At any moment a node can initiate a leader election by broadcasting a “Ready” message; the first node whose “Ready” is received by a majority becomes Leader and records its identifier in the Leader variable of all nodes that acknowledge it. The Leader exclusively issues “Allocate(slot)” commands that assign a specific settlement slot to a transaction, increments the next‑slot index, and records the allocation in a shared log that every node appends to in the order received. If a node detects that it has not heard from the Leader for a configurable timeout, it starts a new election, and any nodes that receive a later “Ready” from a higher‑priority candidate will abandon the old Leader and adopt the new one. All messages (Ready, Acknowledge, Allocate, and Heartbeat) are sent over an unreliable network that may reorder them, so each node only acts on a message after checking that its logical timestamp is not older than the last processed timestamp for that type. When a node receives an Allocate for a slot that it has already marked as committed, it discards the duplicate and replies with a “Duplicate” notice, ensuring the batch proceeds without re‑executing the same slot. The protocol therefore guarantees that despite reordering and leader failover, exactly one node ever assigns a given slot at a time.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two distinct Bank Nodes ever allocate the same settlement batch slot to different transactions.

The system consists of a **Spool Manager** that owns the global job queue and a set of **Printer Agents**, each controlling a single printer. The Spool Manager maintains a flag `queueLocked` indicating whether the coarse lock on the whole queue is held, and each Printer Agent maintains a flag `printerLocked` indicating whether its fine‑grained lock is held. When a new print job arrives, a Printer Agent first attempts to acquire the coarse lock by setting `queueLocked`; once it succeeds, it reads the next job from the queue, releases the coarse lock, and then tries to acquire its own `printerLocked` before sending the job to the physical printer. If a Printer Agent crashes while holding either lock, the lock‑owner timeout detector will notice the missing heartbeat and automatically clear the corresponding flag, allowing other agents to proceed. After a printer finishes a job, the agent clears its `printerLocked` flag and reports the completion to the Spool Manager, which updates the job’s status in the queue. All agents repeat this cycle, ensuring that only one agent manipulates the queue at a time and that each printer handles at most one job concurrently, even in the presence of a silent crash.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No update to a job’s record in the queue is ever lost or overwritten by another agent.

The yard contains a set of automated cranes, each identified by a unique crane‑ID, and a shared schedule of loading slots numbered 1 … N. Every crane maintains three pieces of local state: the ID of the current leader (leaderID), a Boolean flag indicating whether it is participating in an election (inElection), and a counter that tracks how many heartbeat intervals have elapsed since it last heard from the leader (missedHeartbeats). Periodically each crane sends a small “heartbeat” message to all others; if a crane’s missedHeartbeats counter reaches a configurable threshold it assumes the leader may have failed and sets inElection to true, broadcasting an “election‑start” message that includes its own ID. All cranes that receive an election‑start compare the sender’s ID with any other election messages they have seen and eventually agree on the highest ID as the new leader, after which they reset missedHeartbeats, clear inElection, and the new leader announces “leader‑announce”. The leader alone is permitted to assign an unallocated loading slot to a container by updating the shared schedule; after the assignment it broadcasts a “slot‑allocated” message so every crane records the slot as taken. If a slow crane later receives a slot‑allocated message it simply records the assignment without attempting to re‑allocate, ensuring that a temporarily delayed participant does not cause conflicts.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two cranes ever allocate the same loading slot for a container.

The protocol involves three roles: the Settlement Processor (SP) that collects individual interbank transfer messages, the Interbank Nodes (IN) that forward their signed debit‑credit entries to the batch, and a privileged Admin who can intervene in emergencies. All participants share a single compare‑and‑swap (CAS) register that holds the current batch identifier together with a version number, which together represent the global state of the batch (open, closed, or overridden). When an IN receives a new transfer, it reads the register, verifies that the batch is still open, adds the transfer’s amount to its local “totalDebits” and “totalCredits” counters, and then attempts a CAS that increments the version and updates the register to reflect the added amounts; the CAS succeeds only if no other node has changed the version in the meantime. The SP periodically scans the register; when it sees the version reach a predetermined limit, it performs a final CAS that changes the batch identifier to “closed”, preventing any further updates. If the Admin detects a fault, she may issue an “override token” that she writes into the register with a special compare value, instantly changing the batch identifier to “admin‑override” and disabling further CAS attempts by INs until the override is cleared. All nodes respect the most recent value read from the register, so only one of the competing updates can succeed at a time, ensuring a consistent view of the batch’s totals. The Admin’s override is a privileged operation that bypasses the normal version check but is recorded in the same register, making the change observable to all participants.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total amount of money recorded in the batch’s debit sum always equals the total amount recorded in the credit sum, so no funds are ever created or destroyed during processing.

The system consists of two or three pharmacy dispenser units that share a common prescription queue; each unit keeps a small record of its current role (leader or follower), the election term it believes is active, and the identifier of the last prescription it has processed. Every unit periodically broadcasts a short heartbeat that includes its term and role; followers listen for the leader’s heartbeat and reset a timeout each time one arrives. If a follower’s timeout expires, it assumes the leader may be down and starts a new election by incrementing its term and asking the other units for a vote. A unit votes for the first election request it receives in a given term, thereby guaranteeing that at most one leader can emerge for that term. When a unit receives a majority of votes, it declares itself the leader, begins processing prescriptions from the queue, and sends a “leader‑announce” message that also carries the identifier of the last prescription it handled. Slow units may miss a heartbeat or a vote request, but they will not start a new election until their own timeout expires, ensuring they do not prematurely trigger failover. The elected leader continues to broadcast heartbeats; if it later stops, the remaining units will repeat the election process, guaranteeing that a new leader is chosen only after the old one is truly unavailable.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No prescription is ever dispensed by a unit that is not the current elected leader or that has processed an older prescription identifier.

The system consists of two independent hospital branches, each running a local inventory manager, and a small quorum of three replicated storage nodes that hold the authoritative count of each blood type. Each manager keeps a local copy of the shared pool’s total units and a version number that is updated only when a quorum commits a change. When a branch wants to record a donation or issue a unit, its manager creates a proposal containing the blood‑type, the amount to add or subtract, and the current version, and it sends this proposal to all quorum nodes. Each quorum node temporarily locks the target record, checks that the requested change does not violate safety limits, and replies with a vote; if a majority (at least two) vote yes, the nodes apply the delta, increment the version, and broadcast the new value back to both managers. The managers accept the broadcast only if the version is exactly one higher than their local version, thereby ensuring that concurrent proposals are serialized by the quorum. Because both branches read updates from the same quorum, they always see the same sequence of committed versions, even when actions originate from both instances at the same time. The protocol therefore requires only the shared total count, the version number, and a boolean flag indicating whether a lock is held, which can be modelled with three state variables.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No update to the shared blood‑type record can be lost; every approved donation or issue is reflected exactly once in the central pool.

The system consists of three participants: a Spooler Manager that receives print jobs, a Printer that consumes the jobs, and a Paper Feeder that supplies the paper required for each job. Each participant keeps a two‑bit status flag – “idle”, “prepared”, “committed” or “aborted” – that records where it is in the two‑phase commit. In the first phase the manager sends a *prepare* request to the printer and the paper feeder; each replies with “ready” if it has enough resources, otherwise it replies “abort”. The manager records the replies; if all are “ready” it broadcasts a *commit* message, otherwise it broadcasts an *abort* message. Upon receiving *commit* a participant moves to the committed state and begins printing, while on *abort* it returns to idle and releases any reserved resources. The paper feeder is the only component that may crash silently after receiving the *prepare* request; if it does not respond, the manager treats the missing reply as a negative vote and aborts the transaction. When a crashed feeder recovers it checks its local flag; if it was in the prepared state it automatically aborts, ensuring no job proceeds without paper.

SAFETY PROPERTY: At most one print job can occupy the printer and the paper feeder simultaneously.

The system consists of several pharmacy dispensing units (Dispensers) that share a single prescription log, each running a local controller that can either read or write the log. Each Dispenser maintains a Boolean flag `hasToken` indicating whether it currently holds the token that authorises exclusive access to the log, and a `pendingRequest` flag that records whether a patient request is waiting to be processed. When a Dispenser receives a prescription request, it sets `pendingRequest` true and waits until `hasToken` becomes true; once it has the token it appends the prescription to the log, clears `pendingRequest`, and passes the token to the next Dispenser in the ring. The token is passed by sending a lightweight token‑message to the next Dispenser only after the current Dispenser has finished its update, guaranteeing that at most one Dispenser can modify the log at any moment. An administrator can invoke an override by broadcasting an `adminOverride` signal; the first Dispenser that receives the signal immediately gains the token (preempting the normal ring order) and enters a privileged mode that allows it to correct or delete log entries, after which it releases the token back to the regular ring. All other Dispensers suspend normal operation while the override is active, and they resume processing pending requests only after the admin releases the token.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The prescription log is never updated concurrently, so no two dispensers can write conflicting entries to the shared record.

The lobby consists of a **matchmaker server** and a set of **player clients** that each want to join a game slot.  
Both the server and each client keep two pieces of state: the current **epoch number** (a monotonically increasing reconfiguration identifier) and the **slot assignment** they believe is active for that epoch.  
When a client wishes to join a game it sends a **join request** tagged with its view of the epoch; the server records the highest epoch it has seen, increments the epoch, and replies with a **slot grant** that includes the new epoch and a unique slot number.  
Clients only accept a slot grant if the epoch in the grant matches the epoch they have recorded; they then update their slot assignment and announce the acceptance to the server.  
If a client crashes silently after receiving a grant, the server will not receive the acceptance and will, after a timeout, start a new epoch and re‑assign that slot to another waiting client, discarding the old epoch’s information.  
All participants ignore messages that carry an epoch lower than their current epoch, ensuring that stale information cannot cause conflicting assignments.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two players are ever assigned the same game slot in the same epoch.

The lobby server creates a match entry that lists the player IDs of the two opponents who have accepted the invitation.  
Each player client holds a local flag “ready” that is initially false and a copy of the match ID.  
When a player presses “Start”, its client sets its ready flag to true and sends a PREPARE message containing the match ID to the server.  
The server records which participants have sent PREPARE; when it has received PREPARE from both players it broadcasts a COMMIT message to each client.  
Upon receiving COMMIT, a client changes its state to “in‑game” and begins loading the game resources.  
If a player crashes after sending PREPARE but before receiving COMMIT, the server will time out the missing PREPARE and abort the match, informing the surviving player with an ABORT message.  
The protocol never proceeds to the in‑game state unless the server has observed PREPARE from both participants for the same match ID.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No player can enter the in‑game state for a match unless the server has previously received a PREPARE message from that same player for that match.

The yard contains a set of container‑handling cranes, each controlled by a local Crane Operator process (C1, C2, C3, …).  All operators share a replicated register that records the *proposed move* of a container (e.g., “lift container A from bay 5 to ship 2”).  When an operator wants to start a move, it writes the proposal to its local register and then asks the other operators for a vote; a move may proceed only after at least three distinct operators have responded “yes”.  Each operator maintains a simple state: the current proposal it sees, the number of affirmative votes received, and a flag that indicates whether an admin override has been issued.  If the privileged Admin process sends an override message, all operators immediately set the override flag and the current proposal is either forced to succeed or cancelled regardless of the vote count, after which the flag is cleared.  Operators continuously broadcast their state changes so that every participant eventually sees the same proposal, vote count, and override flag.  The protocol guarantees that a container is moved only after the quorum condition or an explicit admin override, and that no two cranes will attempt to move the same container at the same time.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two cranes may simultaneously execute a move involving the same container.

The system consists of a Central Load‑Shed Controller and a set of Substation Agents, each of which manages a local pool of controllable loads (the “slots”). Every component stores the current epoch number, the total capacity it may shed in that epoch, and a list of slots it has already assigned to a shed request. When a Substation detects a change in its generation capacity, it sends a Capacity‑Update message to the Controller, which records the new capacity and increments the epoch number for the next reconfiguration round. The Controller then broadcasts a Re‑allocate message that contains the new epoch and a tentative assignment of slots that respects the updated capacities. Each Substation, upon receiving the broadcast, checks that the slots it is being asked to shed are still free in its local list, commits the assignment for the new epoch, and acknowledges the change. All agents only act on assignments that belong to the most recent epoch, so any capacity change is reflected exclusively in the next round of allocations. This epoch‑numbered coordination guarantees that all load‑shed decisions are made consistently despite runtime capacity updates.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No load slot is ever assigned to more than one Substation in the same epoch.

The system consists of a set of student agents that each try to enroll in a particular course, and a single course manager that holds a compare‑and‑swap register representing the number of seats still available. The register stores the current seat count and a version tag that changes only when a successful compare‑and‑swap is performed. When a student wishes to register, it first reads the current seat count and version, decides that it can enroll only if at least one seat is reported, and then issues a compare‑and‑swap that attempts to replace the old pair (count, version) with a new pair where the count is reduced by one and the version is incremented. If the compare‑and‑swap succeeds, the student knows its enrollment is confirmed; if it fails, the student repeats the read‑modify‑write loop using the newly observed values. Because a student may be slow, it might take several attempts before its compare‑and‑swap finally succeeds, but the register never loses updates from other participants. The course manager never aborts the registration process; it only ever decrements the seat count when a compare‑and‑swap succeeds, guaranteeing that the count never goes below zero. All participants eventually observe a stable seat count that reflects exactly the number of confirmed enrollments.

SAFETY PROPERTY: A seat is removed from the course’s available count at most once for each successful enrollment.
spec_text:
------------------------------- MODULE W4C8x7x5x3 -------------------------------
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets

CONSTANTS
    Students, \* a non‑empty finite set of student identifiers
    Seats      \* the initial number of seats (Nat)

VARIABLES
    reg,      \* the compare‑and‑swap register: a record with fields count, ver
    obs,      \* each student’s last observed pair (count,ver)
    Enrolled  \* set of students that have already succeeded

(* ---------------------------- Types ----------------------------------- *)
TypeOK ==
    /\ reg \in [count: Nat, ver: Nat]
    /\ obs \in [Students -> [c: Nat, v: Nat]]
    /\ Enrolled \subseteq Students

(* --------------------------- Init ------------------------------------ *)
Init ==
    /\ reg = [count |-> Seats, ver |-> 0]
    /\ obs = [s \in Students |-> [c |-> Seats, v |-> 0]]
    /\ Enrolled = {}

(* -------------------------- Actions --------------------------------- *)

\* A student reads the current register value.
Read(s) ==
    /\ s \in Students \ Enrolled
    /\ obs' = [obs EXCEPT ![s] = [c |-> reg.count, v |-> reg.ver]]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<reg, Enrolled>>

\* A student attempts a compare‑and‑swap using its last observed values.
CAS(s) ==
    /\ s \in Students \ Enrolled
    /\ obs[s].c >= 1                         \* student believes a seat is available
    /\ IF reg = [count |-> obs[s].c, ver |-> obs[s].v]
          THEN /\ reg' = [count |-> reg.count - 1,
                         ver   |-> reg.ver + 1]
               /\ Enrolled' = Enrolled \cup {s}
               /\ UNCHANGED obs
          ELSE /\ UNCHANGED <<reg, Enrolled, obs>>

(* --------------------------- Next ------------------------------------ *)
Next ==
    \E s \in Students \ Enrolled:
        \/ Read(s)
        \/ CAS(s)

(* --------------------------- Spec ------------------------------------ *)
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<reg, obs, Enrolled>>

(* --------------------------- Invariant ------------------------------ *)
\* Safety: each decrement of the seat count corresponds to exactly one
\* distinct successful enrollment.
SeatsRemovedOnce ==
    Seats - reg.count = Cardinality(Enrolled)

=============================================================================

CONSTANTS
    Students = {s1, s2, s3, s4}
    Seats    = 2

SPECIFICATION Spec
INVARIANT SeatsRemovedOnce
