The system consists of a set of elevator cars (Car1 … CarN) and a central Scheduler that coordinates them.  
Each car stores its current floor (curFloor) and a mutable capacity limit (cap) that Maintenance can change at runtime.  
The Scheduler keeps a global epoch number (epoch) and a table slot[floor] that records which car, if any, holds the exclusive right to serve that floor in the current epoch.  
When a car becomes idle it sends a request for a floor; the Scheduler increments epoch, records the request in slot[floor] with the new epoch, and replies with a grant containing that epoch value.  
The car proceeds only if the grant’s epoch matches its view; if the capacity limit is reduced after the grant, the car aborts the request and releases the slot before the next epoch.  
Maintenance broadcasts any capacity change together with the next epoch increment so that all participants see the same capacity for the upcoming epoch.  
Because assignments are tied to a specific epoch, any slot granted in a previous epoch cannot be re‑assigned, preventing overlap even when capacities change.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: In every epoch, a floor slot is granted to at most one elevator car, so the same floor is never assigned to two cars simultaneously.

The system consists of a set of Spooler Controllers, each maintaining a copy of the current PrintCapacity and the identifier of the next job to be scheduled.  
When a client submits a print job, the receiving controller proposes the job’s identifier to the group and asks all controllers to vote on accepting it.  
Each controller replies with an accept vote if the proposed job would not exceed the known PrintCapacity; otherwise it votes to reject.  
Once a majority of the controllers have accepted, the job identifier is committed and all controllers increment their next‑job counter, guaranteeing a consistent view of the queue.  
A capacity‑change request (for example, adding a new printer) is initiated by any controller, which broadcasts the new capacity value and starts a new vote.  
All controllers vote on the capacity change using their current view; when a quorum agrees, the new capacity replaces the old one on every copy and any pending jobs are re‑evaluated against the updated limit.  
If a controller crashes or falls behind, it must obtain the latest capacity and next‑job identifier from a quorum before it can issue further votes, preventing stale decisions.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No print job is accepted or a capacity change applied unless a quorum of current, non‑faulty controllers votes for it, ensuring that no unauthorized or outdated participant can alter the queue.

The system is composed of a central spooler that holds a single ordered list of pending print jobs and a set of printer agents that fetch jobs from this list. The spooler stores a version number together with the queue; each printer keeps locally a flag indicating whether it believes it currently holds a job. When a printer wants to start work it reads the current version and the first unassigned job, records that job locally, and then attempts to write back the queue with an incremented version number marking the job as assigned. If the version it writes back matches the version it observed, the claim succeeds; otherwise the printer detects that another agent updated the queue and it retries the whole read‑modify‑write cycle. After a printer finishes a job it removes the job from the queue and again updates the version, clearing its local flag. If a printer crashes silently, it stops sending heart‑beats; the spooler notices the missed heartbeat, clears the assignment flag for any job that was marked as in progress by that printer, and the job becomes eligible for other printers to claim. This optimistic‑locking loop with retry guarantees that only one printer ever obtains the right to print a given job at any time.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two printers ever print the same job simultaneously.

The system contains a central coordinator and several district controllers that each monitor a portion of the grid’s demand.  
All participants keep a single shared register that holds the current target amount of load to shed, and each controller also remembers whether it has an outstanding proposal.  
When a controller observes that its local demand exceeds a threshold, it reads the register, adds its own reduction to the value read, and then attempts a compare‑and‑swap operation to replace the old target with the new total.  
If the compare‑and‑swap succeeds, the controller broadcasts the updated target to the other districts; if it fails, the controller rereads the register and retries with the latest value.  
A controller that crashes silently stops responding to messages, and the remaining controllers notice its silence after a timeout and simply ignore any proposal that originated from the missing participant.  
The coordinator periodically checks that at least one controller has successfully updated the register and, if none have, it issues a safe default target to guarantee progress.  
Thus the protocol ensures that every successful update reflects the most recent combined load‑shedding intention of the alive controllers.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The shared target‑shedding register is never overwritten with an older value.

The system consists of a Coordinating Hub that runs a single logical batch and a set of Settlement Engines, one at each participating bank. Each engine stores the current epoch number and a flag indicating whether it has finished processing the batch for that epoch, while the hub stores the epoch number and a map that records which payment slot in the batch is owned by which bank. When an engine is ready, it sends its proposed slot assignments together with the current epoch number to the hub; the hub records the proposals and, once it has a proposal from every engine that has responded for that epoch, it finalizes the slot map, increments the epoch, and broadcasts the new assignment to all engines. An engine that is slow may miss the hub’s broadcast for a given epoch, but it can later request the hub’s latest epoch and slot map and then continue processing without being considered failed. If any bank wants to change its slot usage, it simply includes the new request in the next proposal, causing the hub to advance to a new epoch and reconfigure the batch accordingly. All engines repeatedly perform these steps, ensuring the batch proceeds epoch by epoch even when some participants lag behind.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: In any given epoch, no payment slot is assigned to more than one bank.

The system consists of two library front‑ends, FrontA and FrontB, both of which can serve patrons and share the same pool of reservation tokens for a particular book copy. Each front end keeps a Boolean variable hasToken indicating whether it currently holds the token that grants exclusive right to modify the reservation list. When a patron requests to reserve the book, the front end that holds the token can add the patron’s ID to the reservation queue and then must forward the token to the other front end. If a front end receives a reservation request while it does not hold the token, it buffers the request and waits for the token to arrive. The token ring passes the token in a fixed order FrontA → FrontB → FrontA, and the token carries the identifier of the last processed reservation to ensure both instances see the same ordering. Both fronts also maintain a shared variable lastReserved, the ID of the patron whose reservation was most recently confirmed, which can only be updated by the holder of the token. The two instances never simultaneously hold the token, so at most one reservation is confirmed at any moment.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: Each patron’s reservation for a given book copy is confirmed at most once.

The system consists of a set of **RouterAgents** that move baggage carts between two conveyor zones, and a **CapacityManager** that holds the current maximum number of carts allowed in the downstream zone. Each RouterAgent keeps a local copy of the downstream zone’s **occupancy counter** and a **version stamp** supplied by the CapacityManager. When an agent wants to forward a cart, it reads the current version and occupancy, checks that occupancy + 1 does not exceed the latest capacity, and then writes a tentative new occupancy together with the version it read; this write succeeds only if the version has not changed. If the write fails because another agent updated the version or a capacity change occurred, the agent discards its tentative update, fetches the new version and capacity from the manager, and retries the whole check‑and‑write cycle. The CapacityManager can asynchronously change the zone capacity; when it does so, it increments the version stamp, causing any in‑flight optimistic updates to detect the change and retry. All agents retry until they either succeed in placing the cart or discover that the zone is full under the newest capacity, at which point they hold the cart back at the source.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: At no time does the number of carts in the downstream zone exceed the current capacity announced by the CapacityManager.

The batch consists of a shared settlement ledger record that lists the net amounts to be settled between banks, and each bank runs a participant process called a Settler.  
Each Settler keeps a local copy of the ledger’s version number and a flag indicating whether it has a pending update.  
When a Settler wants to add its net transfer, it reads the current ledger record and its version, computes the new totals, and attempts a compare‑and‑swap on the shared register that stores both the version and the ledger contents.  
The compare‑and‑swap succeeds only if the version it read is still present, thereby atomically publishing the new totals and incrementing the version.  
If the operation fails because another Settler updated the record first, the slow Settler re‑reads the latest version and retries its update, waiting a bounded back‑off before each attempt.  
A Settler that is slow may remain idle for many retries but never aborts, ensuring that every intended net transfer eventually appears in the ledger.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The shared settlement ledger never loses a net transfer update submitted by any Settler.

Each elevator car runs a local controller process called a shuttle node that can act as the coordinator for assigning service requests.  
All shuttle nodes share a small distributed table that records the identifier of the current leader, a flag indicating whether the admin has asserted an override, and a heartbeat counter for each node.  
Periodically each node sends a heartbeat to the others; if a node observes that the leader’s heartbeat has not been updated for two intervals, it initiates a simple election by broadcasting its own identifier and adopting the smallest identifier that replies.  
When the election succeeds, the winning node writes its identifier into the shared leader field and resumes dispatching elevator requests.  
At any time an administrator can press the master console button, which sets the override flag and forces a designated super‑controller node to become leader, regardless of the current election state.  
If the admin override flag is cleared, the next regular heartbeat loss triggers a fresh election, restoring the normal leader‑selection process.  
All nodes respect the current leader by forwarding new floor requests only to that leader, and they drop any request that would create a duplicate assignment for the same elevator car.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any moment there is exactly one designated leader among the shuttle nodes.

The system consists of a set of elevator controllers (one per car), a floor‑request manager that receives passenger button presses, and a capacity manager that can increase or decrease a car’s maximum passenger count while the building is in operation. Each elevator controller keeps a small record of the floor it currently holds a lease for and the lease’s expiration time; the floor‑request manager keeps a single variable that records which elevator, if any, presently owns the lease for each pending floor request. When a passenger presses a button, the floor‑request manager checks the current leases; if no lease exists for that floor it issues a lease request to the elevator controller that has enough remaining capacity to service the request. The chosen elevator controller records the floor as its lease holder and starts a timer; when the timer expires the lease is automatically released so another elevator can acquire the floor. If the capacity manager later lowers an elevator’s capacity below the number of passengers already on board, the elevator controller may voluntarily relinquish any outstanding lease before its timer expires, forcing the floor‑request manager to reassign the floor. All lease grants and revocations are communicated through reliable broadcast messages so that every participant has a consistent view of which lease is active. The protocol therefore coordinates floor service and capacity changes using time‑bounded leases that guarantee exclusive access but can be reclaimed when capacity constraints change.

SAFETY PROPERTY: A floor lease is granted to at most one elevator at any moment and is never granted twice without being released first.

The system consists of a central Load‑Shed Coordinator and two substations, Substation A and Substation B, each of which controls a set of local loads. Each substation keeps a single state variable “vote” that is either *Ready* (it can shed its assigned megawatts) or *NotReady*, and a flag “crashed” that is set to true if it stops responding. In Phase 1 of the two‑phase commit, the coordinator broadcasts a shed request specifying the total megawatts to be reduced and records the votes it receives from the substations. In Phase 2, if both votes are *Ready* the coordinator sends a *Commit* message causing each substation to switch its “shed” state to *Active* and actually disconnect the agreed load; otherwise it sends an *Abort* and all substations keep their loads unchanged. If a substation crashes silently after sending its vote, the coordinator detects the missing reply after a timeout and automatically aborts the operation, leaving any already‑committed loads untouched. The protocol therefore requires only the three variables per participant (vote, shed‑state, crashed) and one global decision variable at the coordinator (commit/abort). 

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total megawatts of load that are shed never exceeds the amount requested by the coordinator, so no additional load is lost beyond the target.

The lobby consists of a fixed set of game servers that form a logical ring, each server holding a single token that grants the right to modify the matchmaking queue. Each server maintains two variables: the identifier of the current token holder and a list of pending player requests that it has accepted from clients. When a server receives a new player request it appends the request to its local list and then forwards the request to the next server in the ring, but it does not change the queue until it holds the token. A server that holds the token scans its own pending list, selects a group of compatible players, creates a match, and updates the global queue; after committing the match it passes the token to the next server. Because network messages may arrive out of order, each server timestamps every forwarded request and discards any request whose timestamp is older than the most recent request it has already processed. The token itself carries the identifier of the last processed timestamp so that a server can detect and ignore stale token passes that arrived after newer ones. If a server receives the token while its local pending list is empty, it simply forwards the token without making any changes.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No match is created by a server that does not currently hold the token or that processes a player request older than the latest request it has already handled.

The system consists of a Lobby Server that holds a single record describing each game lobby’s current player list, its capacity, and a monotonic version number, and a set of Player Clients that may request to join or leave a lobby.  
Each Player first reads the lobby record, remembers the version it saw, and constructs a tentative new player list that respects the currently known capacity.  
The Player then sends an “update” message containing its tentative list together with the version it observed; the Lobby Server accepts the update only if the version still matches its current version, atomically increments the version, and stores the new list.  
If the version check fails because another client has already updated the lobby, the Player discards its tentative list, reads the fresh record, and retries the whole process.  
An Administrator may change a lobby’s capacity at any time; the Admin follows the same read‑modify‑write pattern, updating the capacity field together with the version check, so capacity changes compete with player joins in the same optimistic‑locking scheme.  
Because all updates are guarded by the same version number, any concurrent modifications—whether from Players joining/leaving or from the Admin adjusting capacity—are serialized by retrying until a client’s version matches the server’s, guaranteeing a consistent final lobby state.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No update to a lobby’s player list or capacity can be lost; every successful change is reflected in the lobby record exactly once.

The network consists of a set of vending machines (VMs) and a single lease manager (LM) that controls exclusive access to each product slot.  
Each VM keeps a local record of the slot it currently believes it owns (owner) and the timestamp when that lease expires (expiry).  
When a VM wants to dispense a product from a slot, it sends a lease request to the LM; the LM replies with a lease granting the VM exclusive rights for a fixed period and records the lease in its table.  
The VM may renew the lease before expiry by sending a heartbeat; if the LM does not receive a heartbeat before the expiry time, it automatically revokes the lease, allowing another VM to acquire the slot.  
If a VM crashes silently, its lease simply times out, so the LM can safely reassign the slot without requiring any explicit failure notification.  
A VM that holds a valid lease may dispense the product and then either release the lease early or let it expire, at which point the LM clears the slot entry.  
The LM never grants a lease for a slot to a second VM while a previous lease has not yet expired, ensuring exclusive ownership throughout the protocol.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: At no time does the lease manager assign the same product slot to more than one vending machine concurrently.

The system consists of a **Runway Manager** and multiple **Aircraft Controllers** that each propose a runway assignment for an arriving flight. Both the manager and every controller keep a single record called **CurrentEpoch** that holds the most recent epoch number and the associated **RunwayMap** for that epoch. When a controller wants to change an assignment, it creates a **ReconfigMessage** containing a higher epoch number, the new mapping, and sends it to the manager; the manager updates its record only if the epoch in the message is greater than its CurrentEpoch, then broadcasts an **EpochUpdate** with the same epoch and mapping to all controllers. Controllers, upon receiving an EpochUpdate, replace their local RunwayMap only when the epoch in the update exceeds their CurrentEpoch, thereby discarding any stale information. Because messages may arrive out of order, each participant relies solely on the epoch comparison to decide whether to apply a change, ensuring that older messages cannot overwrite newer ones. The protocol therefore requires only two state variables per participant – the current epoch number and the current runway mapping – plus the logic for sending and processing the epoch‑tagged messages. This mechanism guarantees that all participants eventually agree on the same runway allocation for each epoch, despite reordering of messages. 

SAFETY PROPERTY: No runway assignment record is ever overwritten by a message carrying an older epoch, preventing lost updates to the shared RunwayMap.

The system involves three participants: the dispensing kiosk, the central pharmacy server, and a pharmacist who operates the kiosk; an administrator can intervene through a privileged console.  
The server keeps three pieces of state for each prescription: the identifier of the participant that currently holds the lease, the time at which that lease expires, and a flag that indicates whether an admin override is active.  
When a pharmacist wants to fill a prescription, the kiosk sends a lease request to the server, which grants the lease to that kiosk only if no other lease is active and the override flag is not set, and it records the expiry time a few minutes in the future.  
The kiosk may dispense medication only while its lease is still valid; after the expiry time the server automatically clears the lease holder, preventing further dispensing.  
If an urgent situation arises, an administrator can set the override flag, which immediately suspends the lease check and allows any kiosk to dispense the prescribed medication once the admin confirms the action.  
The override flag is cleared automatically after the medication is dispensed and the server records the event in an audit log.  
Any participant that attempts to dispense while its lease has expired and the override flag is not set is rejected and must retry after obtaining a fresh lease.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No medication is dispensed by a kiosk that does not currently hold a valid lease and is not operating under an active admin override.

The yard runs two autonomous crane controllers, Crane‑A and Crane‑B, that both draw containers from a shared pool of 10 waiting slots. Each controller keeps a local copy of the pool index it believes is free and a version counter that is incremented by the central pool manager whenever any crane successfully reserves a slot. When a crane wants to lift a container, it reads the current version, selects the lowest‑numbered free slot according to its copy, and sends a reservation request containing the slot number and the version it observed. The pool manager checks that the version sent matches its current version and that the slot is still unoccupied; if both hold, it marks the slot as taken, increments the version, and replies with a grant; otherwise it rejects the request. Upon rejection, the crane discards its stale copy, reads the updated version and pool state, and retries the reservation process. The retry loop continues until the crane receives a grant, after which it proceeds to move the container to its target ship. All other crane actions—such as releasing a slot after placing a container—simply update the pool manager’s state and bump the version, enabling the next reservation to succeed.

SAFETY PROPERTY: A container is assigned to a crane for lifting at most once.

The spooler (coordinator) receives a print job and contacts three participants: the pre‑press server, the color printer, that finishes the pages, and the binding robot.  
Each participant keeps a single flag that records whether it has prepared its local copy of the job (PREPARED) and a timestamp of the last job it committed.  
In the first phase the coordinator sends a PREPARE request; a participant that can copy the job sets its flag to PREPARED and replies “YES”, otherwise it replies “NO”.  
The coordinator proceeds to the second phase only if it has received YES from all participants; it then sends a COMMIT message containing the job identifier.  
Upon receiving COMMIT, a participant checks that its PREPARED flag is true and that the timestamp matches the coordinator’s current epoch; if both hold it prints the pages and clears the flag, otherwise it ignores the message.  
If a participant is slow, it may answer the PREPARE request after a timeout, but the coordinator treats the late YES as stale because the job identifier has already advanced, causing the participant to discard it.  
Once all participants have acknowledged completion, the coordinator marks the job as DONE and can start the next job.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No participant that has not freshly prepared the current job identifier may execute a print or finishing action.

The system contains two redundant load‑shed controllers, Controller A and Controller B, that both monitor the same pool of shed tokens representing how many loads may be disconnected without violating grid stability.  
Each controller stores a Boolean flag `isLeader` and an integer `tokensLeft` that together describe whether it believes it is the current leader and how many tokens remain unallocated.  
When a controller’s heartbeat timer expires without hearing a heartbeat from the other, it sets `isLeader` to true, broadcasts a “leader” message, and adopts the `tokensLeft` value from the most recent shared token count.  
The elected leader may issue a “shed request” for a specific load; it decrements `tokensLeft`, records the load’s identifier in a local log, and broadcasts a “token consumed” update to the follower.  
The follower, upon receiving a token update, copies the new `tokensLeft` value and refrains from initiating any shed actions while its `isLeader` flag is false.  
If the leader crashes, its follower detects the missed heartbeats, flips its `isLeader` flag to true, and continues using the last known `tokensLeft` value, ensuring that no token is reclaimed or double‑spent.  
Both controllers periodically recompute `tokensLeft` by reading the shared token pool, which guarantees that at most one controller can consume any given token even though they run independently.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No load is disconnected (shed) more than once during a single load‑shed episode.

The system consists of a central coordinator and a set of local load‑shed controllers (LSCs) that each control a set of curtailable loads. Each LSC keeps a small record of the most recent “slot request” it sent and whether a “slot grant” has been received for the current shedding instance. When a shedding event is detected, the coordinator starts a two‑phase commit for that instance: it first broadcasts a **prepare** message listing the pool of time slots that may be used, and each LSC replies with a **vote** indicating which slot it would like to occupy. After collecting all votes, the coordinator selects a unique slot for each LSC, ensuring that the same slot is not assigned to two LSCs, and then sends a **commit** message that includes the chosen slot for the instance. Upon receiving the commit, an LSC records the slot as “committed” and begins shedding its load at the appointed time. A second, independent shedding instance may start while the first is still in progress, but both instances draw from the same shared pool of slots; the coordinator therefore runs two parallel two‑phase commits, each using the same state variables (requested slot, committed slot) but distinguished by an instance identifier. The protocol guarantees that even with overlapping instances, each slot is granted to at most one LSC in a given instance.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No time slot in the shared pool is allocated to more than one load‑shed controller for the same shedding instance.
spec_text:
---------------------------- MODULE W4C9x2x3x2 ----------------------------
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets, Sequences

CONSTANTS LSCs, Slots, Instances

VARIABLES active, requested, committed

(* --algorithm description
   active[inst] ∈ BOOLEAN                     \* true iff instance inst is in progress
   requested[inst][l] ∈ Slots ∪ {None}        \* slot that LSC l has requested for inst
   committed[inst][l] ∈ Slots ∪ {None}        \* slot finally granted to LSC l for inst
*)

\* ---------- Helper definitions ----------
None == "None"

\* the set of all variable values (used for stuttering)
vars == << active, requested, committed >>

\* No two different LSCs are assigned the same non‑None slot in the given mapping.
NoDup(map) ==
  \A l1, l2 \in LSCs :
    ( map[l1] # None /\ map[l2] # None /\ map[l1] = map[l2] ) => l1 = l2

\* ---------- Initial state ----------
Init ==
  /\ active = [inst \in Instances |-> FALSE]
  /\ requested = [inst \in Instances |-> [l \in LSCs |-> None]]
  /\ committed = [inst \in Instances |-> [l \in LSCs |-> None]]

\* ---------- Actions ----------
Start(inst) ==
  /\ ~active[inst]
  /\ active' = [active EXCEPT ![inst] = TRUE]
  /\ requested' = [requested EXCEPT ![inst] = [l \in LSCs |-> None]]
  /\ committed' = [committed EXCEPT ![inst] = [l \in LSCs |-> None]]
  /\ UNCHANGED << >>

Vote(inst, l, s) ==
  /\ active[inst]
  /\ requested[inst][l] = None
  /\ s \in Slots
  /\ requested' = [requested EXCEPT ![inst][l] = s]
  /\ UNCHANGED << active, committed >>

Commit(inst) ==
  /\ active[inst]
  /\ \A l \in LSCs : requested[inst][l] # None      \* every LSC has voted
  /\ NoDup(requested[inst])                         \* coordinator guarantees distinct slots
  /\ committed' = [committed EXCEPT ![inst] = requested[inst]]
  /\ active' = [active EXCEPT ![inst] = FALSE]
  /\ UNCHANGED requested

\* Stuttering step to avoid deadlock
Stutter ==
  UNCHANGED vars

Next ==
  \/ \E inst \in Instances : Start(inst)
  \/ \E inst \in Instances, l \in LSCs, s \in Slots : Vote(inst, l, s)
  \/ \E inst \in Instances : Commit(inst)
  \/ Stutter

\* ---------- Safety invariant ----------
SafetyInv ==
  \A inst \in Instances : NoDup(committed[inst])

\* ---------- Specification ----------
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

=============================================================================

nl:
The network consists of several vending machines and a token‑ring controller that circulates a single access token among the machines.  
Each machine keeps two Boolean variables: one indicating whether it currently holds the token and another indicating whether it has a pending dispense request for a product from the shared inventory pool.  
When a customer selects an item, the machine sets its pending flag and waits until it receives the token; upon receipt it checks the shared pool for sufficient stock and, if available, dispenses the product and decrements the pool count.  
After the dispense, the machine clears its pending flag, updates the shared pool count, and passes the token to the next machine in the ring.  
Two independent instances of the protocol run on the same physical machines – one for snacks and one for drinks – but both instances draw from the same monetary credit pool that tracks the total amount of cash collected.  
The credit pool is a single integer variable that each instance can increase when a sale succeeds, but only the token holder of the corresponding instance may modify it, preventing concurrent writes.  
If a machine holds the token for the snack instance and also has a pending drink request, it will finish the snack transaction first, then relinquish the token, allowing the drink instance to obtain the token later in the same ring cycle.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: For any customer request, the corresponding product is dispensed at most once.

The system is composed of a Controller, a set of WashSlots placed along the conveyor, and the cars that travel through them.  
The Controller keeps a single coarse lock for the whole line and a numeric capacity that can be raised or lowered while the line is stopped.  
Each WashSlot holds a fine lock that protects entry and exit of one car and a Boolean flag indicating whether the slot is currently occupied.  
When the Controller wants to change the line capacity, it first acquires the coarse lock, updates the capacity variable, and then releases the coarse lock before any car may acquire a fine lock.  
A car that wishes to enter the line checks that the current number of occupied slots is below capacity, then acquires the fine lock of the first free WashSlot, marks it occupied, and releases the lock after moving to the next slot.  
Moving from one slot to the next requires the car to acquire the fine lock of the target slot, verify that the target slot is free, update the occupancy flags, and then release the lock of the previous slot.  
If the Controller needs to shrink capacity, it waits until it can take the coarse lock, then prevents new cars from entering until the number of occupied slots falls to the new limit, after which it releases the coarse lock.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: A car can exit the wash (leave the conveyor line) at most once.

The lobby server keeps a single epoch counter that is increased each time a new match is formed or the player set changes. Every player stores locally the epoch number it most recently heard from the server together with the list of players that belong to that epoch’s lobby. When a player wants to join a match it sends a join request to the server, the server records the request, increments the epoch, and broadcasts the new epoch and updated player list to all participants. A player that receives a broadcast adopts the new epoch and replaces its local lobby list, but if it is slow it may continue to operate with an older epoch until the next broadcast arrives. When the server decides the lobby is full for the current epoch it sends a “start match” message tagged with that epoch; players only start the game if the epoch on the start message matches the epoch they have stored. If a slow player later receives a newer epoch broadcast, it discards any pending start messages from older epochs and synchronizes to the current lobby configuration before proceeding. The server never includes more player identifiers in a lobby than the configured maximum, and all participants agree on the same epoch before any match begins.

SAFETY PROPERTY: At no time does any lobby contain more players than its configured capacity.
spec_text:
---- MODULE W4C5x9x4x3 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets

CONSTANTS MaxCapacity, MaxPlayers

(* The set of all possible player identifiers *)
Players == 1 .. MaxPlayers

VARIABLES epoch, lobby, playerEpoch, playerLobby

(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* Initial state *)
Init ==
    /\ epoch = 0
    /\ lobby = {}
    /\ playerEpoch = [p \in Players |-> 0]
    /\ playerLobby = [p \in Players |-> {}]

(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* Server actions *)

(* A player p requests to join; the server adds p if capacity allows *)
Join(p) ==
    /\ p \in Players
    /\ p \notin lobby
    /\ Cardinality(lobby) < MaxCapacity
    /\ epoch' = epoch + 1
    /\ lobby' = lobby \cup {p}
    /\ UNCHANGED << playerEpoch, playerLobby >>

(* The server broadcasts the current epoch and lobby to all players *)
Broadcast ==
    /\ epoch' = epoch
    /\ lobby' = lobby
    /\ playerEpoch' = [p \in Players |-> epoch]
    /\ playerLobby' = [p \in Players |-> lobby]

(* The server decides the lobby is full and sends a start‑match message *)
StartMatch ==
    /\ epoch' = epoch
    /\ lobby' = lobby
    /\ UNCHANGED << playerEpoch, playerLobby >>

(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* Player actions *)

(* A (possibly slow) player p receives the latest broadcast *)
ReceiveBroadcast(p) ==
    /\ p \in Players
    /\ playerEpoch' = [playerEpoch EXCEPT ![p] = epoch]
    /\ playerLobby' = [playerLobby EXCEPT ![p] = lobby]
    /\ UNCHANGED << epoch, lobby >>

(* Player p receives a start‑match message; it starts only if epochs match *)
ReceiveStart(p) ==
    /\ p \in Players
    /\ playerEpoch[p] = epoch
    /\ UNCHANGED << epoch, lobby, playerEpoch, playerLobby >>

(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* Next-state relation *)

Next ==
    \/ \E p \in Players : Join(p)
    \/ Broadcast
    \/ StartMatch
    \/ \E p \in Players : ReceiveBroadcast(p)
    \/ \E p \in Players : ReceiveStart(p)

(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* Specification *)

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<epoch, lobby, playerEpoch, playerLobby>>

(* ------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* Safety invariant: the lobby never exceeds its configured capacity *)

CapacityInvariant == Cardinality(lobby) <= MaxCapacity

====

\* Model for W4C5x9x4x3
CONSTANTS
    MaxCapacity = 2
    MaxPlayers  = 3
INIT Init
NEXT Next
INVARIANT CapacityInvariant

nl:
The yard contains a set of mobile container‑cranes, each of which can be assigned a *slot* on a single loading bridge. The bridge controller keeps two pieces of state: the identifier of the crane that currently holds the lease on the bridge, and the lease’s expiration timestamp. When a crane finishes a lift it may request a new lease; the controller grants it only if the bridge is free or if the existing lease has expired, then records the new crane’s identifier and a fresh expiration time based on the current workload. Cranes may also voluntarily release the lease before expiry, prompting the controller to clear the lease fields. Because the bridge’s load‑capacity can be increased or decreased by a yard manager at any moment, the controller updates the lease duration whenever the capacity changes, shortening or lengthening the timeout accordingly. All cranes periodically check the lease record; if they see a lease belonging to another crane that is still valid, they wait; if the lease is missing or expired, they attempt to acquire it. The lease‑based mechanism guarantees that at most one crane can command the bridge at any time, even while capacity adjustments modify lease lifetimes.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two cranes may hold the lease for the loading bridge simultaneously.

The system consists of two server instances, Server A and Server B, each capable of acting as the leader for processing book reservations. Each server keeps a small state: a boolean flag called **isLeader**, a counter **term** that increases when a new leader is elected, and a record of the last reserved book identifier **lastReserved**. When a client requests to reserve a book, the leader checks if the book is available in the shared pool, records the reservation by updating **lastReserved**, and acknowledges the client. If a leader crashes or becomes unresponsive, the surviving server increments its **term**, sets its **isLeader** flag to true, and announces the new term to the other server. The announcement forces the other server to clear its **isLeader** flag, ensuring that at any moment only one server believes itself to be the leader. While a server is not the leader it only forwards client requests to the current leader and updates its view of **term** when it receives a newer announcement.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: A reservation for a specific book is recorded and confirmed at most once.

The lobby consists of a set of player processes that each store three local variables: the identifier of the current leader, a monotonically‑increasing election round number, and a flag indicating whether the player last received a heartbeat from the leader. The leader periodically broadcasts a heartbeat containing its identifier and the current round; all other players reset their heartbeat‑timer flag when they receive it. If a player’s timer expires, it assumes the leader may have failed and initiates an election by broadcasting its own identifier together with the next round number to all participants. Each player that receives such an election message replies with its identifier only if it has not already replied for that round, and the initiator selects the smallest identifier among the replies as the new leader. The new leader then sends a “leader‑announce” message that updates every player’s stored leader identifier and round, after which normal heartbeat streaming resumes. A player that is merely slow (e.g., delayed network) still sends its heartbeat when it can, so it will not be excluded from elections unless it fails to reply within the election timeout. All participants repeat this cycle, guaranteeing that a single active leader is always known despite temporary slowness of some members.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: Only the player currently recorded as the leader may issue a start‑game command, and no stale or unauthorized player can do so.

The system consists of a Lobby Server, several Player Clients, and a Capacity Service that can raise or lower the maximum number of players allowed in a lobby.  
Each lobby maintains two mutable variables: a version counter that is incremented on every change, and a list of currently assigned player IDs.  
When a Player Client wants to join, it reads the current version and player list, attempts to append its ID, and sends the updated list together with the version it observed to the Lobby Server.  
The Lobby Server validates the request by checking that the version in the message still matches its own version and that the new size does not exceed the current capacity reported by the Capacity Service.  
If both checks succeed, the server increments the version, stores the new list, and replies with a success acknowledgment; otherwise it rejects the request, forcing the client to retry by rereading the latest state.  
The Capacity Service may independently change the maximum capacity at any time, and the next successful join or retry will see the new limit because the server always consults the service before committing a join.  
A Player Client that receives a rejection must discard its stale version and repeat the read‑modify‑write cycle, ensuring that no client can permanently hold a slot that the server no longer recognizes.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No player can be admitted to a lobby using a version that is stale or beyond the current capacity, preventing unauthorized or outdated joins.

The system consists of a small ring of three processes: the **InventoryNode** that stores the stock levels, the **RequestNode** that nurses use to add or remove units, and the **AdminNode** that can intervene in emergencies. Each node keeps a single Boolean variable `hasToken` indicating whether it currently holds the ring token, and a Boolean variable `adminOverride` that the AdminNode can set to true to claim the token immediately. When a node wants to modify the blood‑type count it first checks `hasToken`; if it is true it performs the update, clears `hasToken`, and passes the token to the next node in the ring. If the AdminNode sets `adminOverride` to true, any node that receives the token must relinquish it, and the AdminNode immediately sets `hasToken` for itself, performs its emergency update, clears `adminOverride`, and then forwards the token to the next node. The token therefore guarantees that only the holder can change the inventory, while the admin override allows the AdminNode to pre‑empt the normal order without breaking the ring structure. All nodes continuously monitor the token flag of their predecessor so that the token is never lost: if a node detects that its predecessor’s `hasToken` is false and it also does not hold the token, it assumes the ring is stalled and restarts the token at the InventoryNode. The protocol therefore requires only the two Boolean state variables per node and a fixed ring topology.

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any moment, no more than one node can have exclusive access to modify a given blood‑type inventory record.

The opening‑auction server holds a single compare‑and‑swap register R that can contain either the value *open* (the auction is not yet fixed), *locked* (price‑determination in progress), or *settled* (the final opening price has been announced).  
Trading participants (bidders) may read R and, if it is *open*, submit a price proposal together with a CAS request that tries to change R from *open* to *locked* while attaching their proposal as a payload.  
If the CAS succeeds, the bidder becomes the “price‑setter” and proceeds to compute the equilibrium price; any other bidder whose CAS later sees R equal to *locked* must wait for the result.  
When the price‑setter finishes, it writes *settled* together with the computed opening price, completing the auction.  
A privileged admin process can at any moment issue an override CAS that atomically changes R from *open* or *locked* directly to *settled* with an admin‑approved price, pre‑empting any in‑flight price‑setter.  
All other processes only observe the register and never rewrite it after it reaches *settled*.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The auction can transition to the *settled* state at most once.

The system has three participants: a **RouterController** that decides which conveyor slot a piece of baggage should take, a set of **ConveyorSegments** each representing a physical slot on the belt, and **SorterWorkers** that physically move the baggage into the chosen slot. Each participant keeps a tiny amount of state: a Boolean *coarseLock* indicating whether the controller is currently deciding a destination, a Boolean *fineLock[slot]* for each slot showing whether that slot is being claimed, and a variable *allocated[slot]* that records which baggage (if any) is currently assigned to the slot. When a SorterWorker receives a new bag, it first requests the RouterController to acquire the *coarseLock*; once granted, the controller selects an empty slot and asks the worker to acquire the corresponding *fineLock[slot]* before writing the bag’s identifier into *allocated[slot]*. After the assignment, the worker releases the *fineLock[slot]* and the controller releases the *coarseLock*, allowing other decisions to proceed. If a SorterWorker crashes silently while holding a fine lock, a watchdog timeout on the controller detects the missing heartbeat, forces the release of that *fineLock[slot]*, and clears *allocated[slot]* so the slot can be reused. All participants respect the lock hierarchy, never acquiring a fine lock without first holding the coarse lock, which keeps the protocol simple enough to be captured with only the three state variables described.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two bags are ever assigned to the same conveyor slot at the same time.
spec_text:
---- MODULE W4C17x8x3x0 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, TLC

CONSTANTS Slots, Bags

(* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
   State variables
   ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
VARIABLES
    coarseLock,          \* Boolean: true when controller holds the coarse lock
    fineLock,            \* Function [Slots -> BOOLEAN]: fine lock per slot
    allocated            \* Function [Slots -> Bags \cup {"NULL"}]: bag assigned or NULL

(* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
   Constants
   ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
NULL == "NULL"

(* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
   Initial state
   ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
Init ==
    /\ coarseLock = FALSE
    /\ fineLock = [s \in Slots |-> FALSE]
    /\ allocated = [s \in Slots |-> NULL]

(* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
   Actions
   ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)

(* A SorterWorker asks the controller for the coarse lock *)
AcquireCoarse ==
    /\ ~coarseLock
    /\ coarseLock' = TRUE
    /\ UNCHANGED << fineLock, allocated >>

(* Controller selects an empty slot for a bag and the worker acquires the
   corresponding fine lock before writing the bag identifier *)
ChooseSlot(bag, slot) ==
    /\ coarseLock = TRUE
    /\ ~fineLock[slot]
    /\ allocated[slot] = NULL
    /\ fineLock' = [fineLock EXCEPT ![slot] = TRUE]
    /\ allocated' = [allocated EXCEPT ![slot] = bag]
    /\ UNCHANGED coarseLock

(* After the bag has been placed, the worker releases the fine lock and
   clears the slot *)
ReleaseFine(slot) ==
    /\ fineLock[slot] = TRUE
    /\ allocated[slot] # NULL
    /\ fineLock' = [fineLock EXCEPT ![slot] = FALSE]
    /\ allocated' = [allocated EXCEPT ![slot] = NULL]
    /\ UNCHANGED coarseLock

(* Controller releases the coarse lock, allowing other decisions *)
ReleaseCoarse ==
    /\ coarseLock = TRUE
    /\ coarseLock' = FALSE
    /\ UNCHANGED << fineLock, allocated >>

(* Watchdog: if a worker crashes while holding a fine lock, the controller
   clears the lock and the allocation *)
WatchdogRelease(slot) ==
    /\ fineLock[slot] = TRUE
    /\ allocated[slot] # NULL
    /\ fineLock' = [fineLock EXCEPT ![slot] = FALSE]
    /\ allocated' = [allocated EXCEPT ![slot] = NULL]
    /\ UNCHANGED coarseLock

(* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
   Next-state relation
   ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
Next ==
    \/ AcquireCoarse
    \/ \E bag \in Bags: \E slot \in Slots: ChooseSlot(bag, slot)
    \/ \E slot \in Slots: ReleaseFine(slot)
    \/ ReleaseCoarse
    \/ \E slot \in Slots: WatchdogRelease(slot)

(* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
   Safety invariant: no two bags are ever assigned to the same conveyor
   slot at the same time.
   ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
NoTwoBagsSameSlot ==
    \A s \in Slots :
        \A b1, b2 \in Bags :
            (allocated[s] = b1 /\ allocated[s] = b2) => b1 = b2

(* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
   Specification
   ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<coarseLock, fineLock, allocated>>

=============================================================================

nl:
The system consists of multiple aircraft that need a runway and a single tower process that owns a compare‑and‑swap register representing the current runway assignment.  
Each aircraft keeps a local variable “mySlot” that is either “none” or the identifier of the runway it believes it has been granted.  
When an aircraft wants to land it sends a REQUEST message containing its identifier to the tower and then reads the register; if the register is empty it attempts a compare‑and‑swap that changes the register from empty to its own identifier.  
The tower, upon receiving a REQUEST, may send a GRANT message with the current register content, but because the network can reorder messages the aircraft may see the GRANT before its own compare‑and‑swap succeeds.  
After a successful compare‑and‑swap the aircraft records the runway identifier in mySlot and proceeds to land; if the compare‑and‑swap fails it discards any earlier GRANT and retries with a new REQUEST.  
When the aircraft finishes using the runway it sends a RELEASE message and performs a compare‑and‑swap that changes the register from its identifier back to empty, guaranteeing that only one aircraft can hold the runway at a time even if RELEASE arrives out of order.  
The tower never writes directly to the register; all changes are mediated by the aircraft’s compare‑and‑swap operations, so the register’s value always reflects the single runway holder.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any moment at most one aircraft holds the runway, i.e., the runway is never assigned to two aircraft simultaneously.

The car‑wash line consists of three stations—Pre‑Soap, Brush, and Rinse—each of which is a participant in a token‑ring that circulates a single token representing the right to load a car into the next empty slot on the conveyor. Every station keeps two variables: `nextSlot`, the index of the first free slot ahead of it, and `hasToken`, a Boolean indicating whether it currently holds the token. When a station has the token it may either assign the car in its buffer to `nextSlot` (advancing the slot number) and then pass the token to the following station, or simply pass the token unchanged if it has no car waiting. The token is passed by sending a small message containing the updated `nextSlot` value to the next station; the receiving station sets its own `hasToken` to true and overwrites its `nextSlot` with the received value if it is larger. If a station crashes silently, it stops forwarding the token, but the preceding station detects the lack of an acknowledgement within a timeout and re‑issues the token addressed to the next operational station, resetting `hasToken` to false for the crashed node. The re‑issued token carries the same `nextSlot` value, ensuring that no slot number is skipped or duplicated while the line recovers. All stations periodically broadcast a heartbeat so that the ring can be re‑configured around a crashed participant without altering the slot counter.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two stations ever assign the same conveyor slot to different cars at the same time.

The scheduler consists of a central Coordinator and two participant services: the Surgeon service that holds the surgeon’s availability and the Room service that holds the operating‑room calendar.  
Each participant keeps a single flag indicating whether it has “prepared” a tentative booking for a requested surgery time slot.  
When a new surgery request arrives, the Coordinator sends a “prepare” message to both participants asking them to reserve the requested slot temporarily.  
Upon receiving a prepare request, a participant checks its own calendar; if the slot is free it sets its flag to prepared and replies with an acknowledgment, otherwise it replies with a reject.  
If the Coordinator receives acknowledgments from both participants, it sends a “commit” message; each participant then writes the confirmed surgery into its permanent schedule and clears the prepared flag.  
If any acknowledgment is missing because a participant crashes silently, the Coordinator times‑out and sends an “abort” message to the other participant, which then discards its prepared flag without modifying the permanent schedule.  
The Coordinator also records the outcome of each two‑phase transaction in a tiny log that can be inspected to recover from a crash.  

**SAFETY PROPERTY:** No surgery booking is ever added to the permanent schedules of the surgeon or the operating‑room without both the surgeon’s availability and the room’s calendar being updated together.
spec_text:
---- MODULE W4C0x2x1x0 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, Sequences, FiniteSets

\* ---------- Constants ----------
CONSTANTS TIME_SLOTS, NoSlot \* NoSlot is a distinguished value not in TIME_SLOTS

\* ---------- Variables ----------
VARIABLES surgeonSched, roomSched,
          surgeonPrep, roomPrep,
          phase, curSlot,
          log

\* ---------- Helper definitions ----------
Idle   == "Idle"
Waiting== "Waiting"

\* ---------- Type invariant (optional, useful for debugging) ----------
TypeOK ==
    /\ surgeonSched \subseteq TIME_SLOTS
    /\ roomSched    \subseteq TIME_SLOTS
    /\ surgeonPrep \in BOOLEAN
    /\ roomPrep    \in BOOLEAN
    /\ phase       \in {Idle, Waiting}
    /\ curSlot     \in TIME_SLOTS \cup {NoSlot}
    /\ log \subseteq TIME_SLOTS \times {"commit","abort"}

\* ---------- Initial state ----------
Init ==
    /\ surgeonSched = {}
    /\ roomSched    = {}
    /\ surgeonPrep = FALSE
    /\ roomPrep    = FALSE
    /\ phase       = Idle
    /\ curSlot     = NoSlot
    /\ log         = {}

\* ---------- Actions ----------
Begin ==
    /\ phase   = Idle
    /\ curSlot = NoSlot
    /\ \E s \in TIME_SLOTS :
          /\ curSlot' = s
          /\ phase'    = Waiting
          /\ surgeonPrep' = FALSE
          /\ roomPrep'    = FALSE
          /\ UNCHANGED <<surgeonSched, roomSched, log>>

SurgeonPrepare ==
    /\ phase = Waiting
    /\ surgeonPrep = FALSE
    /\ curSlot \in TIME_SLOTS
    /\ curSlot \notin surgeonSched       \* slot must be free for the surgeon
    /\ surgeonPrep' = TRUE
    /\ UNCHANGED <<roomPrep, surgeonSched, roomSched, phase, curSlot, log>>

RoomPrepare ==
    /\ phase = Waiting
    /\ roomPrep = FALSE
    /\ curSlot \in TIME_SLOTS
    /\ curSlot \notin roomSched          \* slot must be free for the room
    /\ roomPrep' = TRUE
    /\ UNCHANGED <<surgeonPrep, surgeonSched, roomSched, phase, curSlot, log>>

Commit ==
    /\ phase = Waiting
    /\ surgeonPrep = TRUE
    /\ roomPrep    = TRUE
    /\ curSlot \in TIME_SLOTS
    /\ surgeonSched' = surgeonSched \cup {curSlot}
    /\ roomSched'    = roomSched    \cup {curSlot}
    /\ surgeonPrep' = FALSE
    /\ roomPrep'    = FALSE
    /\ phase'       = Idle
    /\ curSlot'     = NoSlot
    /\ log'         = log \cup {<<curSlot, "commit">>}
    /\ UNCHANGED <<>>

Abort ==
    /\ phase = Waiting
    /\ (surgeonPrep = FALSE \/ roomPrep = FALSE)   \* at least one participant did not ack
    /\ surgeonPrep' = FALSE
    /\ roomPrep'    = FALSE
    /\ phase'       = Idle
    /\ curSlot'     = NoSlot
    /\ log'         = log \cup {<<curSlot, "abort">>}
    /\ UNCHANGED <<surgeonSched, roomSched>>

Next ==
    \/ Begin
    \/ SurgeonPrepare
    \/ RoomPrepare
    \/ Commit
    \/ Abort

\* ---------- Safety property ----------
Safety == surgeonSched = roomSched

\* ---------- Theorem (optional, for model checking) ----------
THEOREM Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<surgeonSched, roomSched, surgeonPrep, roomPrep, phase, curSlot, log>>
PROOF
  OBVIOUS
====

INIT Init
NEXT Next
INVARIANT Safety
CONSTANT TIME_SLOTS = {t1, t2, t3}
CONSTANT NoSlot = "None"

nl:
The swarm consists of a set of surveillance drones, each with a unique ID, and a ground‑control station that can act as a privileged administrator.  
Each drone maintains two local variables: the identifier of the current leader (`leaderID`) and its own status (`active`, `candidate`, or `failed`).  
If a drone stops receiving heartbeat messages from the leader for a configured timeout, it switches its status to `candidate` and broadcasts a *LeaderRequest* that contains its own ID.  
All drones that receive a *LeaderRequest* compare the requesting ID with any other candidate they have heard of; the highest‑ID candidate that is still active wins, and every drone updates its `leaderID` to that winner and returns to `active` status.  
The ground‑control station holds a privileged override flag; when the administrator sets the flag, it sends an *AdminLeader* message naming a specific drone, and all drones immediately adopt that ID as `leaderID`, ignoring any ongoing election.  
During an admin override, drones suppress heartbeat‑timeout processing and candidate messages, but they continue to watch the override flag so they can resume normal operation when it is cleared.  
When the administrator clears the override flag, drones revert to the normal heartbeat‑based election protocol, allowing a new leader to be elected if the previous one is missing.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any moment, at most one drone is designated as the active leader and may control the swarm’s broadcast command channel.

The swarm consists of a fleet of surveillance drones and a ground‑station controller that partitions the wildfire area into numbered sectors. Each drone locally stores two pieces of state: the identifier of the sector it is currently covering (or “none”) and a version counter for the last map snapshot it read from the controller. When a drone wishes to start monitoring a new sector, it fetches the latest snapshot, records the sector id together with the snapshot’s version, and immediately sends a “claim” message to the controller without waiting for a lock grant. The controller accepts the claim only if the sector is still unassigned in the snapshot version the drone reported; it then records the assignment and replies with an acknowledgement that includes the current version. If the drone later discovers that its claim was rejected (because another drone claimed the same sector in the meantime) or if it does not receive an acknowledgement within a timeout, it retries the whole process using the newest snapshot. Should a drone crash silently while holding a sector assignment, the controller detects the loss after a heartbeat timeout and automatically clears the assignment so that another drone can claim the sector.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The number of sectors assigned to drones never exceeds the total number of sectors that are on fire.

The swarm consists of a set of surveillance drones and two mission‑control servers, each server running an independent instance of the coordination algorithm but drawing votes from the same shared pool of drones. Each drone keeps a single record of the most recent action identifier it has voted on and a flag indicating whether it is currently enlisted in Instance A, Instance B, or is idle. When a server proposes a new maneuver—such as “fly to sector 12” or “activate infrared scan”—it broadcasts the proposal together with a fresh identifier to all drones in its instance. A drone that is enlisted in that instance checks whether the identifier is newer than the one it last saw; if so, it records the identifier and sends a “yes” vote back, otherwise it ignores the proposal. The server collects votes and, once it has received acknowledgments from a quorum (more than half of the drones currently enlisted in that instance), it marks the maneuver as approved and instructs the drones to execute it. After execution, the drones reset their vote flag to idle, making them eligible to be recruited by either instance again. The two servers also exchange periodic “pool‑status” messages so that a drone cannot be counted in the quorum of both instances at the same time, preventing double counting while sharing the same physical pool.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No maneuver is carried out based on a quorum that includes a drone that is either not authorized for the active instance or that is using a stale action identifier.

The system consists of a central Load‑Control Server (LCS) and several Regional Controllers (RCs) that each manage a set of substations. The LCS keeps a coarse lock flag indicating whether any load‑shed operation is in progress, while each RC holds a fine‑grained lock for its own substation group and a local record of the current capacity it is allowed to shed. When the grid operator issues a new capacity limit, the LCS first acquires the coarse lock, updates the global limit, and then releases the coarse lock. Afterwards each RC independently acquires its fine lock, reads the updated global limit, computes the amount of load to drop for its region, updates its local capacity record, and finally releases its fine lock. If the operator changes the limit while RCs are still holding fine locks, the new limit is recorded by the LCS but will only be applied by those RCs after they finish their current lock cycle. RCs also periodically broadcast a “capacity‑ready” flag so the LCS knows when all fine locks are free before starting a new coarse‑lock phase. The protocol guarantees that at any moment only one component can modify the shared load‑shed record, and that every modification reflects the most recent capacity value.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No update to the shared load‑shed capacity record can be lost or overwritten without first acquiring the appropriate lock.

The system consists of a central Load‑Shed Controller, a set of Substation Agents that actually disconnect loads, and an Admin Console that can invoke an emergency override. Each participant keeps a tiny local state: the Controller holds a *coarse‑grid lock* indicating whether any load‑shed operation is in progress, each Substation Agent holds a *fine‑lock* that authorizes it to act on its own circuit, and the Admin Console holds an *override flag* that, when set, bypasses both locks. To begin shedding, the Controller first acquires the coarse‑grid lock; while it holds this lock it issues a request to a particular Substation Agent, which then attempts to acquire its fine‑lock. If the fine‑lock is granted, the Substation Agent disconnects the designated load and reports completion back to the Controller, which finally releases the coarse‑grid lock. The Admin Console may at any time set the override flag; when the flag is true the Controller automatically grants all fine‑locks and skips the coarse‑grid lock, allowing an immediate, pre‑emptive shed. After the override period ends, the flag is cleared and normal lock acquisition resumes. All lock acquisitions and releases are atomic messages sent over a reliable broadcast bus, ensuring that no two agents can hold conflicting locks simultaneously.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No load may be disconnected by a Substation Agent that does not currently hold both the global coarse‑grid lock (unless the admin override flag is set) and its own fine‑lock.
spec_text:
---- MODULE W4C9x8x6x5 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, TLC

CONSTANTS Substations, Loads, NoRequest

VARIABLES 
    coarseLock,          \* BOOL: true if the Controller holds the coarse‑grid lock
    fineLocks,          \* [Substations -> BOOLEAN] fine‑lock per substation
    overrideFlag,       \* BOOL: true if Admin override is active
    requestInProcess,   \* Substations \cup {NoRequest}: current substation request
    DisconnectedLoads,  \* SUBSET Loads: loads that have been shed
    AuthorizedDisconnect \* SUBSET Loads: loads that were shed under proper authorization

\* -------------------------- Initialization --------------------------

Init ==
    /\ coarseLock = FALSE
    /\ overrideFlag = FALSE
    /\ requestInProcess = NoRequest
    /\ fineLocks = [s \in Substations |-> FALSE]
    /\ DisconnectedLoads = {}
    /\ AuthorizedDisconnect = {}

\* -------------------------- Actions --------------------------

\* Admin can enable override at any moment
AdminSetOverride ==
    /\ ~overrideFlag
    /\ overrideFlag' = TRUE
    /\ UNCHANGED <<coarseLock, fineLocks, requestInProcess,
                   DisconnectedLoads, AuthorizedDisconnect>>

\* Admin can clear the override flag
AdminClearOverride ==
    /\ overrideFlag
    /\ overrideFlag' = FALSE
    /\ UNCHANGED <<coarseLock, fineLocks, requestInProcess,
                   DisconnectedLoads, AuthorizedDisconnect>>

\* Controller acquires the coarse‑grid lock (only when no override)
ControllerAcquireCoarse ==
    /\ ~overrideFlag
    /\ ~coarseLock
    /\ coarseLock' = TRUE
    /\ UNCHANGED <<overrideFlag, fineLocks, requestInProcess,
                   DisconnectedLoads, AuthorizedDisconnect>>

\* Controller releases the coarse‑grid lock (only when no pending request)
ControllerReleaseCoarse ==
    /\ coarseLock
    /\ requestInProcess = NoRequest
    /\ coarseLock' = FALSE
    /\ UNCHANGED <<overrideFlag, fineLocks, requestInProcess,
                   DisconnectedLoads, AuthorizedDisconnect>>

\* Controller issues a shed request to a particular substation
ControllerRequestShed ==
    \E sub \in Substations :
        /\ ~overrideFlag
        /\ coarseLock
        /\ requestInProcess = NoRequest
        /\ requestInProcess' = sub
        /\ UNCHANGED <<coarseLock, overrideFlag, fineLocks,
                       DisconnectedLoads, AuthorizedDisconnect>>

\* Substation acquires its fine‑lock in response to the request
SubstationAcquireFine ==
    \E sub \in Substations :
        /\ requestInProcess = sub
        /\ ~fineLocks[sub]
        /\ fineLocks' = [fineLocks EXCEPT ![sub] = TRUE]
        /\ UNCHANGED <<coarseLock, overrideFlag, requestInProcess,
                       DisconnectedLoads, AuthorizedDisconnect>>

\* Substation disconnects a load (normal path – requires both locks)
SubstationDisconnectLoad ==
    \E sub \in Substations, load \in Loads :
        /\ requestInProcess = sub
        /\ fineLocks[sub]
        /\ load \notin DisconnectedLoads
        /\ (overrideFlag = TRUE) \/ (coarseLock = TRUE /\ fineLocks[sub] = TRUE)
        /\ DisconnectedLoads' = DisconnectedLoads \cup {load}
        /\ AuthorizedDisconnect' = AuthorizedDisconnect \cup {load}
        /\ UNCHANGED <<coarseLock, fineLocks, overrideFlag, requestInProcess>>

\* Substation reports completion, releasing its fine‑lock and clearing the request
SubstationReportCompletion ==
    \E sub \in Substations :
        /\ requestInProcess = sub
        /\ fineLocks[sub]
        /\ requestInProcess' = NoRequest
        /\ fineLocks' = [fineLocks EXCEPT ![sub] = FALSE]
        /\ UNCHANGED <<coarseLock, overrideFlag,
                       DisconnectedLoads, AuthorizedDisconnect>>

\* Immediate disconnect when override is active (controller automatically grants fine‑locks)
OverrideDisconnect ==
    \E sub \in Substations, load \in Loads :
        /\ overrideFlag
        /\ load \notin DisconnectedLoads
        /\ DisconnectedLoads' = DisconnectedLoads \cup {load}
        /\ AuthorizedDisconnect' = AuthorizedDisconnect \cup {load}
        /\ UNCHANGED <<coarseLock, fineLocks, overrideFlag,
                       requestInProcess>>

\* -------------------------- Next State Relation --------------------------

Next ==
    \/ AdminSetOverride
    \/ AdminClearOverride
    \/ ControllerAcquireCoarse
    \/ ControllerReleaseCoarse
    \/ ControllerRequestShed
    \/ SubstationAcquireFine
    \/ SubstationDisconnectLoad
    \/ SubstationReportCompletion
    \/ OverrideDisconnect

\* -------------------------- Safety Invariant --------------------------

\* A load may appear in DisconnectedLoads only if it was authorized under the
\* required lock conditions (or the override flag).  The set AuthorizedDisconnect
\* records exactly those loads that were shed while the guard was satisfied.
SafetyInvariant ==
    DisconnectedLoads \subseteq AuthorizedDisconnect

\* -------------------------- Specification --------------------------

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<coarseLock, fineLocks, overrideFlag,
                         requestInProcess, DisconnectedLoads,
                         AuthorizedDisconnect>>

====
