CONSTANTS
    Substations = {"S1", "S2"}
    Loads      = {"L1", "L2", "L3"}
    NoRequest  = "None"

INIT Init
NEXT Next
INVARIANT SafetyInvariant

nl:
The system consists of a Central Dispatcher that tracks each track block, a set of Train Controllers that operate individual trains, and the Blocks themselves that hold a lease record.  
Each Block maintains three pieces of state: the identifier of the current lease holder (or none), the expiration timestamp of that lease, and the current capacity limit for how many trains may occupy the block at once.  
When a Train Controller wants to enter a block, it sends a lease‑request to the Dispatcher; the Dispatcher grants the lease only if the block’s capacity limit has not been reached and records the controller’s identifier together with a fresh expiry time.  
The controller must periodically send a lease‑renewal before expiry, which the Dispatcher updates, otherwise the lease is automatically cleared when the expiry time passes.  
If the Dispatcher decides to change a block’s capacity (for example, because a maintenance zone opens), it updates the capacity limit variable while leaving any existing leases untouched until they naturally expire or are renewed under the new limit.  
When a controller finishes traversing a block, it informs the Dispatcher, which immediately clears the lease and makes the slot available for another request.  
Thus all lease grants, renewals, expiries, and capacity adjustments are coordinated through the central lease record, ensuring that no more than the allowed number of trains ever occupy a block simultaneously.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total number of active leases on any block never exceeds that block’s current capacity.

The batch coordinator, called the Settlement Engine, holds a single lease that grants exclusive right to update the current inter‑bank settlement batch. Each participating bank (e.g., Bank A and Bank B) keeps a local copy of three variables: the identity of the lease holder, the lease expiry time, and the batch state (Pending, Processed, or Committed). When a bank needs to apply its transfers it first issues a LeaseRequest; if the current lease has expired, the Settlement Engine assigns the lease to that bank and sets a new expiry deadline. While holding the lease, the bank may broadcast a ProcessMsg to add its transfers to the batch and then change the batch state to Processed. After processing, the bank sends a CommitMsg; the Settlement Engine records the batch as Committed and revokes the lease, preventing any further modifications. If the lease holder does not send a CommitMsg before the expiry deadline, the lease automatically expires, allowing another slow or delayed bank to request a new lease and continue the work without assuming a failure. All parties continuously monitor lease expiry so that a slow participant can recover by re‑requesting the lease rather than being treated as failed.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No settlement entry is committed more than once.

The system consists of a central Load‑Control Center and three regional Substations (A, B, and C) that each monitor local demand. Each node keeps two pieces of state: the most recent load‑shed proposal identifier it has seen and a flag indicating whether it has cast a vote for that proposal. When the Control Center detects that the total grid demand exceeds a safe threshold, it broadcasts a new proposal containing the amount of load to shed and a unique identifier; every Substation that receives the proposal records the identifier, decides locally whether it can contribute the requested reduction, and replies with a “yes’’ or “no’’ vote. The Control Center collects votes and, once it has received affirmative votes from at least two of the three Substations (a quorum), it records the proposal identifier as the agreed load‑shed amount and instructs the voting Substations to apply the reduction. If a Substation crashes silently, its absence is detected after a timeout; the Control Center proceeds with the quorum of the remaining Substations, ignoring the missing node’s vote but never discarding a proposal that has already reached quorum. After applying the reduction, each Substation updates its local record of the agreed load‑shed amount to match the Control Center, completing the coordinated action. The protocol therefore requires only the proposal identifier and the vote‑received flag as state variables at each node.

**SAFETY PROPERTY:** No agreed load‑shed amount is ever overwritten without first being recorded by a quorum of Substations.

The system has two independent front‑end instances, Portal‑A and Portal‑B, each handling registration requests from students. Both portals push request objects onto a single bounded work queue that can hold at most N pending registrations, and they read a shared flag queueFull that indicates whether the queue has reached capacity. When a portal receives a new registration request, it checks queueFull; if the flag is false it enqueues the request and updates the queue length, otherwise it returns a “please try later” response to the student (backpressure). A pool of RegistrationWorker threads, shared by the two portals, repeatedly dequeues the oldest request when the queue is non‑empty, records the student’s enrollment in the central Course‑Enrollment table, and then decrements the queue length, clearing queueFull if the length drops below N. After processing, the worker sends an acknowledgement back to the originating portal so the portal can inform the student of success. Both portals and workers maintain only three pieces of state each: the current queue length, the queueFull flag, and the last processed request identifier. The coordination ensures that no portal can overflow the queue and that workers never process the same request twice, even though the two portals share the same worker pool.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No enrollment record in the Course‑Enrollment table is ever overwritten by a later registration request for the same student and course.

The participants are the Exchange Coordinator, a set of Trading Servers, and the Market Data Feed.  
Each Trading Server keeps two pieces of state: the epoch number it believes is active and the timestamp of its most recent bid.  
The Exchange Coordinator maintains the global epoch counter and the list of servers authorized for that epoch.  
When the opening auction begins, the Coordinator increments the epoch, broadcasts a CONFIG message containing the new epoch and the authorized‑server list, and starts a countdown timer.  
Trading Servers that receive the CONFIG update their local epoch and may then send BID messages tagged with that epoch; the Coordinator only accepts bids whose epoch tag matches the current global epoch.  
Because messages can be reordered, a server may receive a stale CONFIG after it has already sent a bid; the server discards any CONFIG whose epoch is lower than its current epoch and continues operating under the later epoch.  
When the timer expires, the Coordinator gathers all accepted bids for that epoch, publishes the opening price, and sends a CLOSE message containing the epoch number; any later bid bearing that epoch is ignored.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No bid from a server that is not authorized for the current epoch, nor any bid bearing an older epoch, can affect the opening price.

The OpeningAuctionManager receives incoming limit orders and enqueues them into a single BoundedWorkQueue that is shared by two independent OrderProcessor instances, Processor‑A and Processor‑B. Each processor repeatedly dequeues the next order, updates the shared OpeningPrice record, and then posts a completion token back to the queue to signal that it has capacity for more work. The queue tracks a bounded length counter; when the counter reaches its maximum, the manager stops accepting new orders and applies back‑pressure by temporarily rejecting or buffering further client submissions. Processor‑A and Processor‑B each keep a small local flag indicating whether they are currently “busy” or “idle”, which they set before pulling an order and clear after posting the completion token. When the completion token is received, the queue decrements its length counter, allowing the manager to resume accepting orders. The two processors never dequeue the same order because the queue atomically hands out the next available entry to whichever processor successfully claims it. The shared pool of worker slots therefore guarantees that at most the bounded number of orders are in flight, and any attempt to exceed the bound is throttled by the back‑pressure mechanism.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No update to the shared OpeningPrice record performed by one processor can be lost or overwritten without being reflected in the order book.

The system consists of N settlement processors (P1…PN) arranged in a logical ring; each processor holds a local copy of the current settlement batch identifier and a flag indicating whether it currently possesses the token. The token is a unique message that circulates clockwise; only the processor that holds the token may read the batch, add its interbank transfers, and commit the batch to the central ledger. When a processor finishes its work it clears its token‑held flag, updates the batch identifier to the next sequence number, and passes the token to its successor. An administrator can issue an override command at any time; the override message contains a higher‑priority token that pre‑empts the normal token and is forwarded to all processors until one acknowledges it. The processor that receives the override token immediately stops any pending commit, records an “admin override” flag, and forwards the override token to the next node, after which the normal token circulation resumes from the node following the override holder. Each processor also maintains a boolean “batchCommitted” that becomes true only when the processor that holds the token successfully writes the batch to the ledger.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: A given settlement batch is committed to the central ledger at most once.

The system has two active participants: a Patron client that wants to reserve a copy of a book, and the central Reservation Service that records which patron holds the reservation. Both parties share a single compare‑and‑swap (CAS) register that stores a tuple (bookId, version, holder) for each book, where the version number is incremented on every successful reservation. When a patron wishes to reserve a book, it first reads the current tuple, creates a new tuple with the same bookId, an incremented version, and its own patronId as holder, and then attempts a CAS that will succeed only if the register still contains the tuple it originally read. If the CAS fails because another reservation was recorded in the meantime, the patron retries the read‑modify‑write cycle. The Reservation Service can also initiate a reservation (e.g., to move a hold from one patron to another) using the same read‑modify‑write pattern, ensuring that both participants contend for the same atomic update primitive. If a patron process crashes silently after reading the register but before performing the CAS, the register remains unchanged, and any subsequent attempt by another participant will see the unchanged version and proceed safely. The CAS register guarantees that only one of the competing updates will be applied, preventing lost or overwritten reservations even when a participant crashes.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No reservation update to a book’s record is lost; every successful update reflects exactly one patron’s request and preserves the previous version number.

The system consists of a Prescription Server that stores approved prescriptions, a Dispenser that physically releases medication, an Inventory Manager that tracks pill counts, and a Pharmacist Console that initiates reconfigurations. Each component keeps three pieces of state: the current epoch number, the identifier of the prescription it is handling, and a flag indicating whether it has committed to that epoch. When a pharmacist loads a new prescription, the Server increments the epoch, records the prescription identifier, and broadcasts the new epoch together with the prescription to the Dispenser and the Inventory Manager. Upon receiving the broadcast, the Dispenser and the Inventory Manager store the new epoch and prescription identifier, then reply with an acknowledgement that they have committed to the epoch; they may delay this reply but never crash. The Server waits until it has received acknowledgements from both the Dispenser and the Inventory Manager before signalling the Pharmacist Console that the new epoch is active, allowing the Dispenser to start releasing pills. If either the Dispenser or the Inventory Manager is slow, the Server continues to operate in the previous epoch for any pending requests, ensuring that no prescription is processed until all participants have confirmed the new epoch. Once the active epoch is established, the Dispenser reduces the pill count in the Inventory Manager only after both have recorded the same prescription identifier, guaranteeing consistency.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total number of pills recorded by the Inventory Manager never changes except when the Dispenser actually releases a pill to a patient.

The spooler consists of a set of printers (e.g., PrinterA, PrinterB) and a group of three scheduler nodes that form a quorum.  
Each scheduler node stores a local copy of the current job‑slot table, a small map from slot numbers to the printer assigned.  
When a new print job arrives, the requester sends a “reserve slot” request to all scheduler nodes; each node replies with its current view and votes to commit the reservation.  
The requester collects votes from any two of the three nodes (a quorum) and, once a majority agrees, records the chosen slot in its own table and instructs the chosen printer to start the job.  
If a node is slow to reply, the requester simply waits for the quorum rather than aborting, allowing the slow node to catch up later.  
After a job finishes, the printer notifies all scheduler nodes, which each update their slot table to free the slot, again requiring only a quorum of acknowledgements to consider the slot released.  
Nodes periodically exchange their slot tables so that any slow node eventually learns the committed reservations and releases, preserving a consistent view across the system.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two distinct print jobs are ever assigned to the same printer slot at the same time.

The system consists of a set of elevators E1…En that form a logical ring, a floor controller for each floor, and a capacity manager that can adjust the maximum passenger load for each elevator at run time.  
Each elevator maintains two pieces of local state: the number of passengers currently inside and a flag indicating whether it currently holds the token.  
The capacity manager keeps a single shared variable, maxLoad, that can be increased or decreased by the building’s fire‑safety system.  
When an elevator holds the token, it may open its doors, allow passengers to board or alight, move to the next floor, and then pass the token to the next elevator in the ring.  
An elevator is prohibited from opening its doors if its passenger count would exceed maxLoad after boarding, so it must wait for the token to be returned after capacity is lowered.  
The floor controllers simply signal boarding requests to the elevator that currently has the token, and they never issue a request when the token is elsewhere.  
If the capacity manager lowers maxLoad while elevators are in transit, the next token holder must reduce its passenger count by asking riders to exit before opening doors, thereby preserving the invariant that no elevator ever carries more than maxLoad passengers.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: Exactly one token is present in the elevator ring at any moment, so the token is never lost or duplicated.

The swarm consists of a set of surveillance drones and a ground control node that hosts a single compare‑and‑swap (CAS) register representing the current allocation of a surveillance slot (a geographic region for a fixed time interval).  
Each drone keeps two local variables: the identifier of the slot it believes it currently holds (or NONE) and a monotonically increasing request counter that it includes in every allocation request.  
When a drone wishes to monitor a region, it sends a request containing its identifier and request counter to the control node; the control node atomically executes a CAS that replaces the register’s current slot identifier with the new drone’s identifier only if the register still holds the value advertised in the request.  
If the CAS succeeds, the control node replies with an acknowledgment that includes the request counter; the drone then records the slot as owned.  
If the CAS fails, the drone discards the reply, increments its request counter, and retries later.  
Because messages may arrive out of order, a drone accepts an acknowledgment only if its request counter matches the one stored locally, ignoring any stale messages that carry older counters.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two drones can be assigned the same surveillance slot at the same time.

The network consists of a set of vending machines (VM₁ … VMₙ) and a central controller (CC). Each machine keeps a local copy of three variables: the identifier of the current lease‑holder, the lease expiry time, and the number of items it has already stocked; the controller maintains the global capacity limit and a version number for that limit. When a machine wants to add stock it sends a lease‑request to the controller; if no lease is active or the existing lease has expired, CC grants the lease by replying with the machine’s identifier and a fresh expiry time. While holding a lease a machine may increment its local inventory count, but before each increment it checks that the sum of all known inventory counts would stay below the current capacity limit. If the lease expires before the machine finishes, the lease automatically reverts to “none” and the machine must stop stocking. The controller can at any moment broadcast a new capacity limit together with an incremented version number; machines receiving this update replace their stored limit and continue only if their combined inventory stays within the new bound. Any machine that detects that its actions would violate the limit must immediately release the lease and wait for a fresh grant.

SAFETY PROPERTY: At no time does the total number of items stocked across all vending machines exceed the current capacity limit.

The system consists of three Blood‑Depot nodes – Depot‑A, Depot‑B and Depot‑C – each of which stores a local copy of the blood‑bank inventory and can serve hospital requests. Each node keeps a small state: (1) the identifier of the current leader, (2) a monotonically increasing epoch number, and (3) a flag indicating whether it believes the leader is alive. Periodically the leader broadcasts a heartbeat containing its identifier and epoch; followers reset their “leader‑alive” flag when they receive the heartbeat. If a follower’s flag is not reset before a timeout, it initiates a leader election by broadcasting a proposal containing its own identifier and the next epoch number, and the first proposal that is acknowledged by a majority becomes the new leader. When a node receives a proposal with a higher epoch, it updates its stored leader identifier and epoch, acknowledges the proposal, and stops accepting heartbeats from the old leader. Any node that receives a request to allocate a batch of blood checks whether it is the current leader; only the leader may update the global inventory and grant the allocation, then it notifies all followers of the new inventory version. If the leader crashes silently, the timeout mechanism guarantees that another node will assume leadership within one heartbeat interval, ensuring continuous service.

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any time, no two nodes will allocate the same batch of blood to different hospitals.

The system consists of three kinds of participants: each elevator car, a floor‑level scheduler that grants a coarse‑grained “zone” lock, and a shaft‑level lock manager that grants a fine‑grained “shaft” lock. Each elevator maintains three pieces of state: the zone it currently holds (or none), the shaft lock it currently holds (or none), and its current floor. When an elevator wants to travel to a destination floor, it first sends a request to the scheduler for the zone that contains that floor; once the zone lock is granted it immediately requests the corresponding shaft lock from the lock manager. After both locks are held, the elevator moves floor by floor, updating its current floor, and when it reaches the destination it releases the shaft lock followed by the zone lock. Because network messages may arrive out of order, every lock request and release carries a monotonically increasing sequence number and the receiver only processes a message if its sequence number is the next expected one, discarding or postponing out‑of‑order messages. The hierarchical locking guarantees that at most one elevator can occupy any shaft at a time, while the zone lock prevents two elevators from serving overlapping zones simultaneously, keeping the protocol simple enough to be modeled with the three state variables described.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: An elevator can be in a shaft only while holding the corresponding fine‑grained shaft lock, ensuring that no shaft ever contains more than one elevator.

The system consists of a set of broker nodes arranged in a logical ring and a single auctioneer node that holds the order book.  
Each broker maintains two local variables: a flag indicating whether it currently holds the ring token and a counter of orders it has submitted during the current auction window.  
The auctioneer keeps a global variable representing the maximum allowed number of orders (the capacity) and another variable tracking the total number of orders already accepted.  
When a broker receives the token it may, if the total accepted orders is less than the current capacity, submit one new order to the auctioneer, increment its local counter, and cause the auctioneer to increment the global accepted count.  
After submitting (or if it has nothing to submit) the broker passes the token to its clockwise neighbour, guaranteeing exclusive access to the order‑book during its turn.  
The capacity variable can be changed at any time by the regulator, and the auctioneer adopts the new value immediately for the next token‑grant cycle.  
If a broker receives the token while the accepted count already equals the capacity, it must simply forward the token without submitting, ensuring no further orders are accepted until capacity is increased.  
The token ring thus serializes all order submissions while allowing the capacity limit to be adjusted dynamically without violating the bound.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: At no time does the total number of accepted orders exceed the current capacity of the auction.

The lobby consists of a set of players and a single matchmaker service that holds a lease on the right to form a game. Each participant keeps a local record of three variables: the ID of the current lease holder, the time when that lease expires, and the list of players that are waiting to be matched. When a player wants to join, it sends a “join” request to the lease holder; the holder adds the player to its waiting list and periodically sends a “renew” message to all others to extend the lease expiration. If a participant receives a renew message, it updates its local expiration time; if it detects that the expiration time has passed without a renewal, it assumes the holder has crashed and immediately claims the lease by broadcasting a “claim” message with a new expiration timestamp. The new holder then takes over the waiting list, continues to accept join requests, and starts a match once enough players are present, resetting the lease timer each time it sends a renew. Any other participant that later receives a claim with a later expiration will acknowledge the new holder and discard its older lease information, ensuring only one active matchmaker at a time. If the original holder crashes silently, its lease will simply time out and be taken over, so no player is left without a matchmaker.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total number of players in the lobby never changes except by explicit join or leave actions; no player is created or destroyed by the lease protocol.

The YardController oversees a rectangular loading zone that is divided into a few large *zones* (e.g., Zone 1, Zone 2). Each crane – Crane A and Crane B – maintains two local flags: whether it holds the **zone lock** for the zone it is about to work in, and whether it holds the **slot lock** for the specific container slot it will lift. To start a move, a crane first sends a lock‑request for its target zone; when the YardController grants the zone lock, the crane then requests the finer slot lock for the exact container it will pick up. After both locks are held, the crane lifts the container, transports it to the destination slot, puts it down, and finally releases the slot lock followed by the zone lock. If a crane is slow while carrying a container, the YardController does not consider this a failure—it simply refrains from granting any new zone locks that overlap the occupied zone, thereby preventing other cranes from entering the same zone until the slow crane finishes and releases its locks. The protocol therefore requires only three state variables: the current zone‑lock holder, the current slot‑lock holder, and a flag indicating whether a crane is “in‑transit”.  

**SAFETY PROPERTY:** A container can be lifted from its original slot and placed on a new slot at most once.

The elevator bank consists of a **Dispatcher** (the central controller), several **Floor Panels** (one on each serviced floor), and the **Car Controller** for each elevator car. Each participant stores a simple phase variable that can be *idle*, *prepared*, or *committed*, and a vote flag indicating whether it can accept the upcoming move. When a passenger presses a button on a Floor Panel, the Dispatcher initiates a two‑phase commit by sending a **prepare‑move** request to the targeted Car Controller and to all Floor Panels that must display the upcoming floor. Each recipient replies with a *yes* vote if its doors are closed and it is not already handling another request, otherwise it replies *no*; the Car Controller may be slow to respond because it is finishing a previous trip, but it never crashes. The Dispatcher proceeds to the **commit** step only after receiving *yes* from every participant or after a bounded waiting period, then broadcasts a **commit‑move** message that makes the Car Controller start moving and the Floor Panels update their displays. If a slow Car Controller finally sends its *yes* after the commit has been sent, it simply transitions to the committed state and follows the already‑issued command. Once the car arrives, the Car Controller sends a **complete** notification, and all participants return to the idle phase, ready for the next request. 

SAFETY PROPERTY: An elevator car’s doors open for a given floor request at most once.

The system consists of a **Central Scheduler** that holds a coarse lock on the entire blood‑type depot, and several **Clinic Workers** that each request a fine‑grained lock on a specific storage slot (identified by type and unit number). The global state is the flag “depot‑locked” held by the Scheduler and, for each slot, a flag “slot‑locked‑by‑Wk” indicating which worker, if any, currently holds the fine lock. When a clinic needs a unit, a worker first asks the Scheduler for the coarse lock; the Scheduler grants it unless it is already held, causing the worker to wait. Once the coarse lock is obtained, the worker then requests the fine lock for the exact slot it wishes to allocate; the Scheduler checks the slot flag and, if free, records the worker’s identifier and releases the coarse lock so other workers can start their own requests. The worker then updates the slot’s inventory count, records the allocation in its local log, and finally releases the slot’s fine lock. If a worker is slow after acquiring the coarse lock, other workers remain blocked on the coarse lock but cannot corrupt the slot state because the fine lock protects the actual allocation; the slow worker will eventually release both locks, ensuring progress without failures.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two workers can ever allocate the same blood‑type slot at the same time.

Each vending machine in the network runs an agent that can ask for a soda from the shared inventory pool.  
The agents maintain a small local state: a flag that tells whether they are currently holding the token, and a counter that records how many cans they have already dispensed.  
A token circulates in a fixed ring order; when an agent receives the token it may either keep it idle or use it to perform a single update to the shared pool.  
To update the pool, the token‑holding agent checks the pool’s current count, decrements it by one, records the sale in its local counter, and then passes the token to the next machine in the ring.  
Two independent instances of the vending system—say the east‑side and west‑side clusters—share the same physical pool of cans, so the token ring includes machines from both clusters, ensuring that only one cluster can change the pool at any moment.  
If an agent does not need to dispense a soda when it gets the token, it simply forwards the token unchanged, preserving the ring’s progress.  
When a machine finishes a sale it releases the token automatically, allowing the next machine (which may belong to the other instance) to take its turn.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two machines ever update the shared inventory pool at the same time, so a soda can is never removed from the pool without a corresponding recorded sale.

The yard is staffed by a small set of gantry cranes that move containers between the ship’s holds and the storage area. A Capacity Manager maintains the current yard capacity – the number of container slots that can be occupied – and can raise or lower that limit when a new storage block is added or removed. Each crane must first obtain a lease on a specific storage slot before it can place a container there; the lease carries an explicit expiry time after which the slot is automatically considered free again. When a lease is granted, the crane stores locally the slot identifier and the lease deadline, and the Capacity Manager reduces its count of free slots. If the crane completes the placement before the lease expires it returns the lease, causing the manager to increase the free‑slot count; if the lease expires first the manager re‑claims the slot without waiting for a return. When the Capacity Manager changes the total capacity, it adjusts the free‑slot count accordingly but never grants a lease for a slot that does not exist at that moment.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total number of containers present in the yard plus the number of leased slots never exceeds the current yard capacity.

The system consists of a central Load‑Shed Controller and a set of Substation Agents each responsible for a collection of controllable loads.  
Each Substation Agent stores two variables: a version counter that records the last successful load‑shed decision, and a numeric field indicating the current amount of load it has agreed to drop.  
When the Controller decides that a grid segment must be reduced, it broadcasts a “request‑shed” message containing the desired reduction amount and the version it believes the agents are using.  
Each Agent receives the request, compares the included version with its own; if they match, it atomically updates its load‑reduction field, increments its version, and sends an “ack” back to the Controller.  
If the versions differ—because another request was processed in the meantime—the Agent discards the stale request and replies with its current version, prompting the Controller to recompute a new request and retry.  
Because messages may arrive out of order, the version numbers guarantee that an Agent never applies an older request after a newer one, and the Controller only accepts acks that carry the version it sent.  
The protocol therefore proceeds with optimistic locking: agents commit only when their view of the state is current, and the Controller retries until it receives acknowledgments consistent with the latest versions.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total committed load reduction for any grid segment never exceeds the segment’s maximum allowable shed capacity.

A central Scheduler maintains a lease record for each operating‑room, storing the current surgeon’s identifier and the lease’s expiration time. When a surgeon wishes to schedule OR‑3, she sends a *LeaseRequest* to the Scheduler that includes a proposed start time and a unique request number. The Scheduler replies with a *LeaseGrant* that contains the granted start time, an expiration timestamp, and the request number; the surgeon stores this grant as her ownership record. While the lease is valid the surgeon may send *LeaseRenew* messages to extend the expiration, and the Scheduler updates the record only if the renewal’s request number matches the one it last issued. If the lease expires, the Scheduler clears the ownership entry, allowing another *LeaseRequest* to be granted. Because network messages may be reordered, every message carries the request number and the Scheduler only acts on a message whose request number is equal to or greater than the one currently stored, thereby discarding stale or out‑of‑order messages. Surgeons also send *LeaseRelease* when the operation finishes; the Scheduler accepts the release only if the request number matches the current lease, preventing an old release from stealing a newer lease.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No operating‑room can be used by a surgeon whose lease has expired or whose request number is older than the current lease record.

The system consists of two load‑shedder instances, each running a leader‑election component and a shed‑allocation component, that share a common pool of “shedding slots” representing discrete power‑reduction actions. Each instance keeps two state variables: (1) a flag `isLeader` that is true only for the current elected leader, and (2) a table `slotOwner` that records which instance, if any, currently owns each slot. When a blackout risk is detected, the leader broadcasts a `REQUEST(Slot)` message for a free slot; any follower that receives the request replies with `ACK(Slot)` only if its own `slotOwner` entry for that slot is empty. Upon receiving a quorum of acknowledgments (the other instance’s ACK), the leader updates its `slotOwner` to record ownership and activates the corresponding load‑shed command. If the leader crashes, the surviving instance detects the loss of heartbeat messages, sets its `isLeader` flag to true, and re‑runs the election, inheriting the current `slotOwner` table so that already‑allocated slots are not reassigned. The two instances periodically exchange their `slotOwner` tables to guarantee a consistent view of which slots are in use. When a shed slot completes its action, the owning instance clears the entry, making the slot available again for future elections.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No shedding slot can be owned by both load‑shedder instances at the same time.

The system consists of a set of Library Nodes (each managing a collection of copies of a specific title) and a central Lease Manager that grants lease tokens to patrons for reserving a copy. Each Library Node stores two state variables: the current number of available copies (capacity) and the identifier of the patron that holds the active lease, if any. A patron requests a reservation by sending a reservation request to the Lease Manager; the manager checks the current capacity at the target node and, if a copy is free, issues a lease token that is valid for a fixed timeout. The patron must return the lease (by checking out the book or cancelling) before the timeout, otherwise the lease automatically expires and the node marks the copy as free again. When the library decides to add or remove copies of a title, the affected Library Node updates its capacity variable instantly; any lease that is still active remains valid until its expiry, but new requests are evaluated against the updated capacity. If a lease expires while the capacity has been reduced below the number of active leases, the Lease Manager forces the earliest‑expiring lease to be revoked so that the number of held leases never exceeds the current capacity. All messages between patrons, the Lease Manager, and Library Nodes are exchanged asynchronously, but the lease‑expiry mechanism guarantees that no node ever believes a copy is both reserved and free at the same time.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No patron can successfully borrow or retain a reservation for a copy that is not currently owned by a valid, unexpired lease.

The system consists of several Registration Servers, each responsible for a subset of courses, and a single Admin Console that can intervene at any time. Every server keeps two state variables: `leader` (the identifier of the current leader server) and `active` (a Boolean indicating whether it is currently processing registration requests). When a server detects that the current leader has not responded for a timeout period, it initiates a leader‑election round by broadcasting a `vote‑request` to the other servers; the first server to receive a majority of affirmative votes declares itself the new leader and updates its `leader` variable accordingly. The elected leader then accepts enrollment requests from students, updates the course‑capacity counters, and propagates the committed enrollment to all other servers, which set their `active` flag to false while the leader’s `active` flag is true. If the Admin Console issues an override command (e.g., to open a wait‑list or cancel a course), it forces the current leader to relinquish leadership, resets the `leader` variable to a special admin identifier, and temporarily disables all servers from processing further registrations until the override operation completes. After the admin override finishes, the admin clears its identifier, and the servers resume normal leader election to restore a regular leader. All messages are sent over reliable, ordered channels so that each server eventually learns the same leader and the most recent enrollment state.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two servers may register a student for the same seat in a course at the same time.

The system contains two independent runway‑allocation services, NorthAllocator and SouthAllocator, that both send landing‑slot requests to a single shared RunwayPool queue. Each allocator keeps a small counter of how many of its own requests are currently waiting in the pool, while the pool maintains the total number of pending requests and the number of free runway slots. When a new aircraft arrives, an allocator checks the pool’s free‑slot count; if a slot is available it enqueues the request and increments its own counter, otherwise it applies backpressure by signalling the aircraft to hold until space opens. The pool accepts an enqueue only while its pending count is below the configured bound, and it releases a runway slot by dequeuing the oldest request and notifying the originating allocator. Upon receiving the grant, the allocator decrements its counter and marks the runway as occupied for the allocated aircraft. When the aircraft departs, the runway is marked free, the pool’s free‑slot count rises, and any waiting allocators may retry their enqueues.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No runway‑assignment record in the shared pool is overwritten without first being removed from the queue.

The system consists of three participants: a Dispatch Controller that accepts floor‑button presses, a set of Elevator Controllers that execute moves, and an Admin Console that can issue an emergency override. The shared state is a bounded work queue of pending floor requests (with a fixed maximum capacity) and a single Boolean flag `adminOverride` that indicates whether the admin has taken control. When a passenger presses a button, the Dispatch Controller attempts to enqueue the request; if the queue is full it back‑pressures the button panel, causing the request to be delayed until space frees up. Each Elevator Controller repeatedly dequeues the oldest request while `adminOverride` is false, moves to the requested floor, and then marks the request as completed. The Admin Console can set `adminOverride` to true, which instantly clears the queue, inserts a single high‑priority emergency request, and suspends normal dequeueing until the flag is cleared. When the admin clears the flag, normal operation resumes and the queue again accepts new requests up to its bound. All participants respect the queue’s capacity and the override flag, ensuring that no component proceeds with stale or conflicting information.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No floor request that enters the bounded work queue can be lost without either being processed by an elevator or being explicitly removed by an admin override.

The system consists of a fixed ring of settlement nodes, each representing a participating bank that can add settlement instructions to a shared inter‑bank batch. Each node keeps a local copy of three pieces of state: the identifier of the node that currently holds the exclusive token, the current size limit of the batch (the maximum slot number), and the next free slot number that the token‑holder is allowed to claim. When a node receives the token it may either (a) allocate the next free slot to one of its pending instructions, incrementing the next‑slot counter, or (b) forward the token unchanged if it has no work. A special Capacity Manager node can, at any moment, broadcast a capacity‑change message that adjusts the batch size limit up or down; all nodes update their local capacity variable immediately. If the capacity is reduced below the current next‑slot counter, the token‑holder must skip allocation until the counter is brought back within the new limit by rolling back uncommitted slots. After performing its action, the token‑holder passes the token to the next node in the ring, guaranteeing that only one node can allocate a slot at a time even while the capacity variable may be changing concurrently. The protocol terminates when the token makes a full rotation without any allocations and the next‑slot counter has reached the current capacity, indicating that the batch is full or no further work is pending.  

**SAFETY PROPERTY:** No two nodes ever allocate the same batch slot.
spec_text:
--------------------------- MODULE W4C3x1x3x4 ---------------------------

EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets

(* ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* CONSTANTS *)
CONSTANT N          \* number of nodes in the ring (including the manager)
CONSTANT MaxCap     \* upper bound on the batch capacity used by the model

(* ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* DEFINITIONS *)
Node == 1 .. N

NextNode(i) == IF i = N THEN 1 ELSE i + 1

(* ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* VARIABLES *)
VARIABLES token, capacity, nextSlot, alloc

(* ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* INITIAL STATE *)
Init ==
    /\ token = 1
    /\ capacity = MaxCap
    /\ nextSlot = 0
    /\ alloc = [s \in {} |-> 0]         \* empty partial function

(* ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* ACTION: allocate the current free slot *)
Allocate ==
    /\ token \in Node
    /\ nextSlot < capacity
    /\ nextSlot \notin DOMAIN alloc
    /\ alloc' = [alloc EXCEPT ![nextSlot] = token]
    /\ nextSlot' = nextSlot + 1
    /\ token' = NextNode(token)
    /\ UNCHANGED capacity

(* ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* ACTION: pass the token without allocating (e.g., no work or capacity limit) *)
Pass ==
    /\ token \in Node
    /\ token' = NextNode(token)
    /\ UNCHANGED <<nextSlot, capacity, alloc>>

(* ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* ACTION: rollback one uncommitted slot when capacity has been reduced *)
Rollback ==
    /\ token \in Node
    /\ nextSlot > capacity
    /\ LET s == nextSlot - 1 IN s \in DOMAIN alloc
    /\ alloc' = [t \in DOMAIN alloc \ {nextSlot - 1} |-> alloc[t]]
    /\ nextSlot' = nextSlot - 1
    /\ token' = NextNode(token)
    /\ UNCHANGED capacity

(* ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* ACTION: change the batch capacity (broadcast by the manager) *)
CapChange(newCap) ==
    /\ newCap \in 0 .. MaxCap
    /\ capacity' = newCap
    /\ UNCHANGED <<token, nextSlot, alloc>>

CapChangeAction ==
    \E newCap \in 0 .. MaxCap : CapChange(newCap)

(* ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* NEXT STATE RELATION *)
Next ==
    \/ Allocate
    \/ Pass
    \/ Rollback
    \/ CapChangeAction

(* ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* SAFETY INVARIANT: no two nodes ever allocate the same slot *)
NoDupSlotAlloc ==
    \A s1, s2 \in DOMAIN alloc :
        (alloc[s1] = alloc[s2]) => s1 = s2

(* ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* THEOREM (for model checking) *)
THEOREM NoDupSlotAllocIsInvariant == 
    Init => []NoDupSlotAlloc

=============================================================================
cfg_text:
CONSTANTS N = 3
CONSTANTS MaxCap = 5

INIT Init
NEXT Next
INVARIANT NoDupSlotAlloc

The system runs two registration servers, Server A and Server B, each serving a different campus but both drawing seats from a single shared pool for a popular class. Each server maintains a coarse‑lock flag that indicates whether it is currently processing a batch of enrollments, and a fine‑grained seat counter that records how many seats it has allocated in the current batch. When a student’s enrollment request arrives, the server first tries to acquire its coarse lock; if the lock is already held, the request is placed in a waiting queue. Once the coarse lock is secured, the server attempts to acquire a fine lock on a specific seat number; if that seat is already taken in the shared pool, the fine lock is released and another seat is tried. After successfully obtaining the fine lock, the server increments its local seat counter, decrements the global remaining‑seat count, and then releases the fine lock. When the server has finished all pending requests for the batch, it releases its coarse lock, allowing the other server to begin its own batch. Because the two servers never hold coarse locks at the same time and always release a fine lock before taking the next one, the shared pool’s seat count stays consistent across both instances.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The number of enrolled students never exceeds the total number of seats available for the course.
spec_text:
---- MODULE W4C8x8x4x2 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets, Sequences

CONSTANTS Servers, TotalSeats \* Servers = {"A","B"}; TotalSeats = a positive integer

(* ---------- State variables ---------- *)
VARIABLES coarseLock, localCount, available

(* ---------- Helper definitions ---------- *)
Seats == 1..TotalSeats

CoarseFree == \A s1, s2 \in Servers : s1 # s2 => ~(coarseLock[s1] /\ coarseLock[s2])

Allocated == TotalSeats - Cardinality(available)

(* ---------- Initial state ---------- *)
Init ==
    /\ coarseLock = [s \in Servers |-> FALSE]
    /\ localCount = [s \in Servers |-> 0]
    /\ available = Seats

(* ---------- Actions ---------- *)

(* A server acquires its coarse‑lock when no other server holds one *)
AcquireCoarse(s) ==
    /\ s \in Servers
    /\ ~coarseLock[s]
    /\ \A t \in Servers : t # s => ~coarseLock[t]
    /\ coarseLock' = [coarseLock EXCEPT ![s] = TRUE]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<localCount, available>>

(* A server releases its coarse‑lock *)
ReleaseCoarse(s) ==
    /\ s \in Servers
    /\ coarseLock[s]
    /\ coarseLock' = [coarseLock EXCEPT ![s] = FALSE]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<localCount, available>>

(* While holding the coarse lock a server enrolls a student by taking a free seat *)
Enroll(s) ==
    /\ s \in Servers
    /\ coarseLock[s]
    /\ available # {}
    /\ \E seat \in available :
          /\ available' = available \ {seat}
          /\ localCount' = [localCount EXCEPT ![s] = @ + 1]
          /\ UNCHANGED coarseLock

Next ==
    \/ \E s \in Servers : AcquireCoarse(s)
    \/ \E s \in Servers : ReleaseCoarse(s)
    \/ \E s \in Servers : Enroll(s)

(* ---------- Specification ---------- *)
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<coarseLock, localCount, available>>

(* ---------- Safety invariant (the property to check) ---------- *)
SeatSafety == Allocated <= TotalSeats

(* Optional: sanity invariants that help the model checker (not required for the task) *)
CoarseExclusion == CoarseFree

====
cfg_text:
CONSTANTS Servers = {"A","B"}
CONSTANTS TotalSeats = 4
INIT Init
NEXT Next
INVARIANT SeatSafety

The system consists of three nodes—Node A, Node B, and Node C—each running a BloodBankTracker service that can store blood‑unit slots.  
Each node keeps two local variables: `leaderId` (the identifier of the current leader) and `capacity` (the total number of slots it believes the cluster can hold).  
When a node detects that the current leader has failed (no heartbeat for a timeout), it starts a simple bully election by broadcasting its own ID; the highest‑ID node that receives the election messages declares itself leader and updates `leaderId` on all nodes.  
The elected leader receives requests to allocate a slot for a new blood unit and, before granting, checks that the requested slot number is less than or equal to the current `capacity`.  
If the leader learns of a capacity change (e.g., a new fridge is added) from an external sensor, it atomically increments `capacity` and propagates the new value to the followers.  
Followers only accept allocation responses that match the `capacity` value they currently store; if they see a mismatch they reject the response and request a fresh leader update.  
When the leader crashes, the next election uses the most recent `capacity` value stored on the surviving nodes, ensuring that all nodes continue to agree on the maximum number of assignable slots.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two different requests can be granted the same blood‑unit slot number.

The swarm consists of a fixed set of fire‑monitoring drones, each identified by a unique callsign, that are logically arranged in a token‑ring so that exactly one drone at a time may hold the “link token” giving exclusive access to the high‑bandwidth satellite uplink. Each drone stores two local variables: a flag indicating whether it currently holds the token and a counter of how many surveillance images it has already uploaded. The ground controller maintains a single shared variable, the current capacity, which specifies the maximum number of drones that may be simultaneously active in the ring; this value can be increased when a fresh battery pack arrives or decreased when a new high‑risk hotspot is detected. When a drone finishes uploading its images it clears its token flag and forwards the token to the next drone in the ring whose identifier is still permitted by the current capacity; if the capacity has been lowered, the token skips any drones that would cause the active count to exceed the limit. A drone may also request a capacity increase by sending a “scale‑up” message to the controller; the controller updates the capacity variable, and the next token pass will allow more drones to hold the token concurrently. Conversely, a “scale‑down” request causes the controller to lower the capacity, and any drone that discovers it would be the (capacity+1)‑st active holder must voluntarily relinquish its token before passing it on. All state changes depend only on the local token flag, the shared capacity variable, and the straightforward pass‑along step, keeping the whole protocol describable with three state variables.

SAFETY PROPERTY: A fire‑retardant payload can be released over a hotspot at most once.

The exchange runs an opening‑auction manager that holds the global epoch number and a flag indicating whether the current epoch is still accepting bids. Each broker maintains a local copy of the epoch number and a boolean showing whether it has already submitted its bid for that epoch. At the start of an epoch the manager broadcasts the new epoch number to all brokers and sets the accept‑bids flag to true. A broker, upon receiving the epoch, may place a single limit order and then marks its local submitted‑bid flag; it sends the order together with the epoch number back to the manager. The manager records each distinct broker’s order; when it has received orders from all brokers or a short grace period expires, it clears the accept‑bids flag, locks the order‑book, computes the opening price, and finally increments the epoch number for the next round. If a broker is slow, its late order is ignored because the manager has already cleared the flag, but the broker’s local epoch does not cause a failure— it simply waits for the next broadcast. Throughout, only the manager may hold the order‑book lock, and the lock is released before any new epoch begins.

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any time only one epoch may hold the order‑book lock, preventing simultaneous settlement of two opening auctions.

In the opening auction each trader keeps a local copy of the current auction version number and the list of pending orders.  
When a trader wants to add or cancel an order it reads the shared version, creates a new order list with its change, and then attempts to write the new list back only if the shared version is still the one it read.  
If another trader has already updated the version, the write fails, the trader discards its attempt and retries with the fresh version.  
The auction engine never holds a long‑lived lock; it simply validates the version check on every incoming update and, on success, atomically stores the new list and increments the version.  
A privileged admin can issue an override command that bypasses the version check, directly setting a new order list and resetting the version to a special admin value.  
While an admin override is in progress, any trader update that passes the ordinary version test is rejected and must be retried after the override completes.  
Thus the protocol coordinates traders through optimistic version checks and retries, while giving the admin a single, clearly distinguished operation that can supersede normal updates.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No trader can commit an order change that was based on an outdated auction version, and only the privileged admin may perform an override.

The lobby consists of a set of players who request to join a match, a Lobby Server that holds a lease on the match‑making resource, and a privileged Admin who can overwrite any lease. The server keeps three pieces of state: (1) the identifier of the player who currently holds the lease, (2) the timestamp at which that lease expires, and (3) the number of players already assigned to the pending match. When a player wishes to start matchmaking they send a lease‑request; if no lease is active or the current lease has expired, the server records that player as the new lease holder and sets the expiry to “now plus T” seconds. The lease holder must periodically send a lease‑renewal before expiry, which the server extends by another T seconds; failure to renew automatically relinquishes the lease. Any player may voluntarily release the lease, causing the server to clear the holder field and the expiry time. The Admin can issue an override command at any moment, which immediately replaces the current lease holder with the Admin’s chosen player and resets the expiry, regardless of existing lease state. After a lease is granted, the server increments the matched‑player count each time the holder confirms a teammate, rejecting further confirmations once the match capacity limit is reached.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The number of players assigned to a pending match never exceeds the match capacity.
spec_text:
------------------------------ MODULE W4C5x6x4x5 ------------------------------
EXTENDS Naturals, Sequences, FiniteSets, TLC

(* --------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* CONSTANTS *)
CONSTANTS 
    Players,            \* Set of player identifiers
    Admin,              \* Identifier of the privileged admin (unused in logic)
    T,                  \* Lease duration (in time units)
    Capacity,           \* Maximum number of players that can be assigned
    MaxTime             \* Upper bound on the logical clock for model checking

(* --------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* SPECIAL VALUE FOR NO CURRENT LEASE HOLDER *)
NoHolder == "None"

(* --------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* VARIABLES *)
VARIABLES 
    now,                \* Logical clock (0..MaxTime)
    leaseHolder,        \* Current lease holder ∈ Players ∪ {NoHolder}
    leaseExp,           \* Expiration time of the current lease (Nat)
    matchedCount        \* Number of players already assigned to the pending match

(* --------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* TYPE INVARIANT (helpful for debugging, not the safety property) *)
TypeOK ==
    /\ now \in 0..MaxTime
    /\ leaseHolder \in Players \cup {NoHolder}
    /\ leaseExp \in Nat
    /\ matchedCount \in Nat

(* --------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* INITIAL STATE *)
Init ==
    /\ now = 0
    /\ leaseHolder = NoHolder
    /\ leaseExp = 0
    /\ matchedCount = 0

(* --------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* ACTIONS *)

Request(p) ==
    /\ p \in Players
    /\ (leaseHolder = NoHolder \/ leaseExp <= now)
    /\ leaseHolder' = p
    /\ leaseExp' = now + T
    /\ matchedCount' = 0
    /\ UNCHANGED now

Renew(p) ==
    /\ p \in Players
    /\ leaseHolder = p
    /\ leaseExp > now
    /\ leaseExp' = now + T
    /\ UNCHANGED <<leaseHolder, matchedCount, now>>

Release(p) ==
    /\ p \in Players
    /\ leaseHolder = p
    /\ leaseHolder' = NoHolder
    /\ leaseExp' = 0
    /\ UNCHANGED <<matchedCount, now>>

AdminOverride(p) ==
    /\ p \in Players
    /\ leaseHolder' = p
    /\ leaseExp' = now + T
    /\ matchedCount' = 0
    /\ UNCHANGED now

Confirm(p) ==
    /\ p \in Players
    /\ leaseHolder = p
    /\ leaseExp > now
    /\ matchedCount < Capacity
    /\ matchedCount' = matchedCount + 1
    /\ UNCHANGED <<leaseHolder, leaseExp, now>>

Tick ==
    /\ now < MaxTime
    /\ now' = now + 1
    /\ UNCHANGED <<leaseHolder, leaseExp, matchedCount>>

(* --------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* NEXT STATE RELATION *)
Next ==
    \/ \E p \in Players: Request(p)
    \/ \E p \in Players: Renew(p)
    \/ \E p \in Players: Release(p)
    \/ \E p \in Players: Confirm(p)
    \/ \E p \in Players: AdminOverride(p)
    \/ Tick

(* --------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* SAFETY INVARIANT (the property we must check) *)
Safe ==
    matchedCount <= Capacity

(* --------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
(* SPECIFICATION *)
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<now, leaseHolder, leaseExp, matchedCount>>

=============================================================================

The network consists of a VendingMachine controller, an InventoryService that tracks item stock, and a PaymentGateway that authorises funds. Each VendingMachine holds a local version number for the item it is about to dispense, while the InventoryService maintains the authoritative stock count and a matching version, and the PaymentGateway stores a transaction‑status flag. When a customer selects an item, the VendingMachine reads the current version from the InventoryService, attempts to decrement the stock optimistically, and immediately sends a payment request to the PaymentGateway. Both the InventoryService and the PaymentGateway check that the version they received matches the latest one; if it does, they commit their update (stock‑decrement and payment‑approved) and return a success, otherwise they reject and the VendingMachine retries with a fresh version. If either the InventoryService or the PaymentGateway is slow, the VendingMachine waits a bounded timeout and then retries the whole sequence without assuming a failure. The optimistic lock ensures that only one of the concurrent attempts can succeed per version, and the retry loop guarantees eventual progress despite delays. All participants log the version they last successfully processed to detect and discard stale retries.

SAFETY PROPERTY: An item is physically dispensed at most once for each successful payment.

The network consists of three door‑lock controllers installed at the front, back, and garage doors, each of which holds a local variable indicating whether its lock is currently “locked” or “unlocked”. When a resident or guest issues a request to unlock a door, the requesting controller broadcasts a vote‑request to the other two controllers and increments a local counter for each “yes” reply it receives. If the counter reaches two (a quorum of the three controllers) the controller flips its lockState to “unlocked” and notifies the others to do the same. An administrator device can at any time set an admin‑override flag, which causes every controller to ignore any pending vote‑requests and immediately set its lockState to “locked”. The admin override also clears the vote counters so that no quorum can be formed until the flag is cleared. Normal users may also withdraw a request, which simply resets the local counter without changing the lock state.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: At no time can a door be both locked and unlocked simultaneously.
