nl:
The system has several RouterNode processes that sit at conveyor junctions and a central Dispatcher that records which bag ID should be sent to which gate. Each RouterNode keeps a local variable “nextBag” and all nodes share a single AssignmentReg register that holds the current highest processed bag ID and its target gate. When a node is ready to forward a bag, it reads the value of AssignmentReg, computes the next bag ID and the appropriate gate, and then attempts a compare‑and‑swap on AssignmentReg with the old value and the new (ID, gate) pair. If the compare‑and‑swap succeeds, the node updates its local “nextBag” to the new ID and physically moves the bag onto the correct conveyor. If the compare‑and‑swap fails, the node rereads AssignmentReg, discards its stale proposal, and retries after a short wait. Because a node may be slow but never fails, it will eventually observe the most recent value in AssignmentReg and be able to complete its compare‑and‑swap. The compare‑and‑swap therefore guarantees that only one node can claim a particular bag ID at a time, even in the presence of delayed participants.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No bag‑routing assignment stored in the shared AssignmentReg can be overwritten without first being recorded as the latest assignment, ensuring that no update to a bag’s routing information is lost.

The system has three kinds of agents: Track Controllers that issue block‑release requests, Signal Workers that process those requests from a bounded queue, and an Admin Console that can issue a privileged override command.  
The shared state consists of (i) the current queue length (bounded to N entries), (ii) a Boolean flag overrideActive, and (iii) the block‑status record for each track segment.  
A Track Controller adds a release request to the queue only if the queue is not full; otherwise it is blocked until space becomes available, providing backpressure.  
A Signal Worker repeatedly dequeues the oldest request, updates the corresponding block status, acknowledges the controller, and thus reduces the queue length.  
If the Admin Console raises an override, it sets overrideActive, freezes the queue, and the Signal Worker immediately applies the admin‑specified block state, ignoring any pending regular requests.  
The override remains in effect until the admin clears it, at which point the flag is reset and the queue resumes normal processing.  
All participants consult the overrideActive flag before modifying a block status, ensuring that an admin override always supersedes concurrent regular updates.  

**SAFETY PROPERTY:** No block‑status record is lost or overwritten; every request that is processed either updates the record or is preempted by an active admin override, so the final state always reflects the most recent authorized update.

The system consists of three participants: the dispensing unit that holds the medication, the pharmacy server that records the prescription, and the insurance validator that checks coverage. Each participant stores a small state record indicating the current transaction identifier and whether it has “prepared” to dispense the drug. When a patient presents a prescription, the pharmacy server initiates a two‑phase commit by sending a prepare request to the dispenser and the validator, and each replies with a vote to commit or abort. If all votes are commit, the server issues a commit command that causes the dispenser to release the medication and the server to mark the prescription as fulfilled; any abort vote causes all participants to roll back to the idle state. A privileged administrator can issue an override at any time that forces an abort (or, in emergencies, a forced commit) regardless of pending votes, and the override flag is recorded alongside the transaction identifier. The override is respected by all participants, which immediately transition to the overridden outcome and ignore any later messages for that transaction.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No prescription can be dispensed as a result of an action taken by an unauthorized or outdated participant.

The system has three kinds of participants: regular print jobs submitted by users, printer resources (each identified by a printer ID), and an admin operator who can issue overrides.  
The spooler maintains a coarse lock that indicates which printer is currently assigned to a batch of jobs, and a fine‑grained lock for each individual job slot within that batch.  
When a user submits a job, the job first acquires the coarse lock for its target printer; if the lock is free it records the printer ID in the shared variable “currentPrinter”.  
The job then attempts to acquire the fine‑grained lock for an empty slot; once successful it writes its description into the slot variable and releases the fine lock.  
The admin can at any time set the “override” flag; when this flag is true the admin may forcibly release the coarse lock and any fine locks on a printer, clearing all job slots before releasing the flag.  
Normal jobs that see the override flag become blocked until the admin clears the flag, after which they retry the coarse lock acquisition.  
The protocol ensures that only one job can be marked as “printed” for a given printer at a time, and the admin’s override can only clear pending jobs, never resurrect a completed print.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No job is marked as printed more than once.

The system has two kinds of participants: library clients that request a reservation for a specific book copy, and a reservation manager that coordinates the assignment of copies. Each client keeps a local version number for the copy it is interested in, while the manager stores the current version and the reservation status (free or assigned) of every copy. When a client wants a copy, it sends a *reserve‑request* containing the copy identifier and its version; the manager replies with the latest version and either a tentative “grant” token or a “reject” if the copy is already reserved. The client then attempts to commit the reservation by sending a *commit* message with the grant token; the manager checks that the version in the token still matches the stored version and, if so, marks the copy as assigned and increments the version. If the versions differ—because another client’s commit arrived first—the manager rejects the commit, causing the client to retry by reading the latest version and issuing a new request. Because network messages may arrive out of order, the manager always validates the version in each incoming message before mutating state, ensuring that stale grants cannot overwrite newer reservations. 

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any time, no book copy is assigned to more than one client.

The system consists of three kinds of actors: Players, the LobbyManager, and the CapacityController.  
The LobbyManager keeps a bounded queue of pending match requests and a table that records which lobby slots are currently occupied.  
When a Player wants to join a game it sends a Join request to the LobbyManager, which enqueues the request only if the queue is not full; otherwise the player is asked to wait (backpressure).  
The LobbyManager repeatedly dequeues the oldest pending request, looks up the current capacity advertised by the CapacityController, and assigns the player to the first free slot if the number of occupied slots is below capacity.  
If the CapacityController later reduces the lobby capacity, the LobbyManager marks any slots above the new limit as unavailable but does not immediately evict players; instead it stops assigning new players to those slots.  
When a player finishes a game it sends a Leave notification, and the LobbyManager frees the corresponding slot in the table, making room for the next queued request.  
The only shared mutable state that the protocol needs to model consists of the queue length and the count of occupied slots, both of which are updated atomically by the LobbyManager.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two players are ever assigned to the same lobby slot.

The protocol involves a central Settlement Coordinator and a set of participating banks (e.g., Bank A, Bank B, Bank C). Each participant keeps a local copy of the current batch record and a lease descriptor that names the bank that currently owns the right to write to the batch and the time at which that lease expires. When a bank wishes to add its settlement entries, it first checks that no lease is active or that the existing lease has expired; it then writes a new lease with its own identifier and a short timeout, and proceeds to append its entries to its local batch copy. After updating the batch, the bank releases the lease by setting the lease owner to “none” and broadcasts the updated batch to all other participants. If a bank holds a lease but is slow in completing its updates, the lease will automatically expire, allowing any other bank to acquire the lease and continue processing the batch. All banks periodically reconcile their batch copies by adopting the most recent version received from any peer, ensuring eventual consistency even when a slow participant lags behind. The coordinator does not intervene directly; coordination is purely lease‑based, so no participant can overwrite another’s updates while a valid lease is held.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No settlement entry can be overwritten or lost because a bank may modify the batch only while holding a valid, exclusive lease.

There are two banks, Bank A and Bank B, that jointly process a nightly settlement batch stored in a shared ledger record called the SettlementBatch.  
Each bank keeps a local copy of the batch’s version number and a flag indicating whether it believes it holds the lock for updating the batch.  
When a bank wants to add its debit and credit entries, it first reads the current version, writes a tentative new version together with its entries, and records that version in its local flag as the tentative lock.  
After writing, the bank reads back the version from the shared ledger; if the read version matches the version it just wrote, the update is committed, otherwise the bank discards its tentative changes and retries with the new version.  
If a bank crashes after writing but before confirming the version, the other bank will eventually read a version that does not match its own tentative lock and will perform a retry, thereby overwriting any incomplete write.  
The optimistic‑locking protocol therefore coordinates updates without a central coordinator, relying on version comparison to detect conflicts and on retry loops to recover from silent crashes.  
The entire protocol can be captured with three state variables: the shared ledger’s version number, each bank’s local lock flag, and each bank’s pending entry list.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No entry added by either bank to the SettlementBatch can be overwritten or omitted by another bank’s retry, thus the shared batch always contains the union of all successfully committed updates.

The system is made up of a central dispatcher and a small set of elevator controllers, one for each car in the bank.  
Each controller maintains two pieces of state: the car’s current floor and a flag indicating whether it has already voted on the next movement.  
When a passenger presses a floor button, the dispatcher proposes a move for a particular car and asks every controller to vote “yes” if the car’s current floor matches the dispatcher’s view, or “no” if it sees a conflict.  
A quorum is defined as any three of the four controllers; once the dispatcher receives votes from a quorum it broadcasts a commit message that tells the chosen car to start traveling to the requested floor.  
If a controller is slow to reply, its missing vote does not block the action as long as the quorum of faster controllers is reached, and the slow controller later updates its state when it receives the commit.  
When the car arrives, it sends a completion notice to all controllers, which clear their vote flags and remove the request from the pending queue.  
The dispatcher continuously re‑evaluates any remaining requests using the same quorum voting, guaranteeing progress even when some controllers are temporarily delayed.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total number of pending floor‑request tokens in the system is preserved—requests are only transferred between the user queue and a car’s in‑flight list, never created or destroyed by the protocol.

The system consists of a shared PlayerPool, two independent matchmaker instances (Instance A and Instance B), and a LobbyCoordinator that provides hierarchical locks. The shared state is the number of players currently waiting in the pool, a coarse lock flag that indicates whether the pool is reserved, and a fine‑grained match lock owned by the instance that is building a specific game. When an instance wants to start a new match it first requests the coarse lock; if granted it decrements the pool count by the size of the intended match and records that it holds the reservation. While still holding the coarse lock the instance then acquires its own fine lock, selects the exact players for the match, and publishes the match lobby. After publishing, the instance releases the fine lock followed by the coarse lock, allowing the other instance to reserve the remaining players. If the coarse lock is already held by the other instance, the requesting instance waits until the lock is released, guaranteeing that only one reservation of the pool can be active at a time.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two matches can be created using the same player at the same time.

The system consists of a ground controller process and several aircraft processes that request permission to land or take off on a runway.  
The ground controller maintains a coarse lock indicating whether the runway is currently reserved for any operation, and a fine lock that records which specific aircraft, if any, holds the exclusive right to use the runway.  
An aircraft first sends a RESERVE message; the controller replies with a GRANT only if the coarse lock is free, and then sets the coarse lock to “reserved”.  
After receiving the grant, the aircraft sends a CLAIM message containing its identifier; the controller checks that the coarse lock is still reserved, records the identifier in the fine lock, and acknowledges the claim.  
Once the fine lock is set, the aircraft may issue a USE message to start the landing or take‑off maneuver, and after completing the maneuver it sends a RELEASE message to clear both locks.  
Because network messages can be reordered, the controller always processes messages in the order of their logical phase (RESERVE, CLAIM, USE, RELEASE) and ignores a CLAIM that arrives before the corresponding RESERVE has set the coarse lock.  
The protocol therefore guarantees that at most one aircraft’s identifier is stored in the fine lock while the coarse lock indicates the runway is occupied, preventing simultaneous use.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: At any time, at most one aircraft can be occupying the runway.

The system consists of a HomeHub that manages the network, individual DoorLock units on each entry, and user devices such as a homeowner’s MobilePhone and a GuestDevice. Each DoorLock keeps two pieces of state: a **leaseOwner** identifier that records which device currently holds the right to control the lock, and a **leaseExpiry** timestamp that marks when that right ends; the lock also stores a simple **lockState** (locked or unlocked). When a MobilePhone wants to open the front door it sends a **LeaseRequest** to the HomeHub; the hub records the request, chooses the requester as the new leaseOwner, sets leaseExpiry to the current time plus a fixed lease interval, and sends a **LeaseGrant** message back to the DoorLock. The DoorLock will only accept a LeaseGrant if the grant’s expiry time is later than any expiry it has already stored, thereby tolerating reordered messages that might arrive out of sequence. While the lease is valid the MobilePhone may issue an **Unlock** command, which the DoorLock executes only if the sender matches leaseOwner and the current time is before leaseExpiry; the lock then changes lockState to unlocked and starts a short timer after which it automatically re‑locks unless the lease is renewed. A GuestDevice can request a lease as well, but it will only be granted after the current lease expires or is explicitly released, and any stale LeaseGrant that arrives after a release is ignored because its expiry is older than the stored leaseExpiry. The HomeHub can also send a **LeaseRenew** message extending leaseExpiry, and the DoorLock updates its stored expiry only when the new time is strictly greater, ensuring that out‑of‑order renewals cannot shrink the lease.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The door can be permanently unlocked (i.e., set to a non‑revocable open state) at most once.

The system consists of a set of Operating‑Room controllers (OR‑C1 … OR‑Ck) that communicate over an unreliable network and one Scheduler process that can be elected as leader; each controller maintains three local variables: its role (leader or follower), the identifier of the current leader, and the timestamp of the most recent heartbeat it has received.  
The leader periodically broadcasts a HEARTBEAT message that includes its identifier and a monotonically increasing slot number representing the next surgery to start, and every follower updates its stored leader identifier and slot number when it receives the heartbeat.  
If a follower does not receive a heartbeat for two consecutive intervals, it assumes the leader has failed and initiates a leader election by sending an ELECTION message containing its own identifier and its current slot number to all other controllers.  
Upon receiving an ELECTION message, a controller compares the incoming identifier with its own; if the incoming identifier is larger it forwards the message unchanged, otherwise it discards it and, if it has not yet sent its own ELECTION, sends its own message, ensuring that the highest identifier eventually propagates despite reordered delivery.  
When a controller receives an ELECTION message that it originally originated (meaning its identifier is the highest), it declares itself the new leader, switches its role variable to leader, and immediately broadcasts a NEWLEADER message with its identifier and the latest slot number.  
The new leader then resumes the periodic HEARTBEAT cycle and may adjust the schedule by incrementing the slot number to reflect any surgeries that were pending when the failure occurred, guaranteeing that all controllers converge on the same next‑surgery slot.  
All messages carry the slot number so that even if HEARTBEAT and ELECTION messages arrive out of order, a follower adopts the larger slot number, preventing the schedule from regressing.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The number of surgeries scheduled to occupy any operating‑room at a given time never exceeds the room’s capacity of one.

The lobby server keeps a shared version number for the current match list and a map from player IDs to their pending match request. When a player clicks “join”, it reads the version, writes a tentative entry with its ID, and sends the new versioned list to the server as a proposal. The server accepts the proposal only if the version it received still matches the current version; if it does, the server increments the version and records the player in the confirmed match list. If the version has changed because another player’s proposal was committed first, the proposing client retries: it reads the latest version, rebuilds its proposal, and resends it, repeating until it succeeds. A slow participant may take several seconds to respond to the server’s acceptance message, but the server does not treat the delay as a failure; it simply continues to process other proposals and retries the slow client’s proposal once the response arrives. Each retry carries a small back‑off delay to avoid livelock while still guaranteeing eventual progress for all participants. The protocol therefore coordinates optimistic locking with retries while tolerating arbitrarily slow but alive players.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No game room identifier can be assigned to more than one match at the same time.

The system consists of two dispenser instances, DispA and DispB, each serving a separate pharmacy counter but drawing medications from a single shared medication pool. The shared pool is represented by a counter “availableUnits” that records how many doses of a prescribed drug remain. Each dispenser keeps a local flag “requestPending” that indicates whether it is currently trying to allocate a dose. When a pharmacist enters a prescription, the corresponding dispenser sets its flag and reads the current value of “availableUnits”. It then performs a compare‑and‑swap on the shared register: if the read value is greater than zero, it attempts to replace it with the value minus one; the operation succeeds only for the first dispenser that issues it. A successful swap causes the dispenser to dispense the dose and clear its flag, while a failed swap makes the dispenser retry after a short back‑off. Because both dispensers use the same compare‑and‑swap register, at most one of them can decrement the pool for any given prescription, preventing double‑dispensing from the shared stock.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: A dose that has been dispensed from the shared pool can never be dispensed again.
spec_text:
---- MODULE W4C16x7x5x2 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, TLC

CONSTANT InitUnits

VARIABLES availableUnits, pending, readVal, totalDispensed

\* The two dispenser identifiers
Dispenser == {"DispA", "DispB"}

\* Initial state
Init ==
    /\ availableUnits = InitUnits
    /\ pending = [d \in Dispenser |-> FALSE]
    /\ readVal = [d \in Dispenser |-> 0]
    /\ totalDispensed = 0

\* A pharmacist writes a prescription: the dispenser records that it has a pending request
\* and reads the current value of the shared counter.
EnterPrescription(d) ==
    /\ d \in Dispenser
    /\ pending[d] = FALSE
    /\ pending' = [pending EXCEPT ![d] = TRUE]
    /\ readVal' = [readVal EXCEPT ![d] = availableUnits]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<availableUnits, totalDispensed>>

\* Compare‑and‑swap succeeds: the value read is still current and > 0.
CASAttempt(d) ==
    /\ d \in Dispenser
    /\ pending[d] = TRUE
    /\ readVal[d] > 0
    /\ availableUnits = readVal[d]          \* CAS succeeds
    /\ availableUnits' = availableUnits - 1
    /\ pending' = [pending EXCEPT ![d] = FALSE]
    /\ readVal' = [readVal EXCEPT ![d] = 0]
    /\ totalDispensed' = totalDispensed + 1

\* Compare‑and‑swap fails (either value was 0 or another dispenser already changed it).
CASFail(d) ==
    /\ d \in Dispenser
    /\ pending[d] = TRUE
    /\ (readVal[d] = 0 \/ availableUnits # readVal[d])
    /\ pending' = pending
    /\ readVal' = [readVal EXCEPT ![d] = 0]   \* discard stale read, will retry later
    /\ UNCHANGED <<availableUnits, totalDispensed>>

\* The dispenser backs off and clears its flag; it may later start a new request.
Retry(d) ==
    /\ d \in Dispenser
    /\ pending[d] = TRUE
    /\ pending' = [pending EXCEPT ![d] = FALSE]
    /\ readVal' = [readVal EXCEPT ![d] = 0]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<availableUnits, totalDispensed>>

\* The overall next‑state relation
Next ==
    \/ \E d \in Dispenser : EnterPrescription(d)
    \/ \E d \in Dispenser : CASAttempt(d)
    \/ \E d \in Dispenser : CASFail(d)
    \/ \E d \in Dispenser : Retry(d)

\* --------------------  Safety property  --------------------
\* A dose removed from the pool is never removed again.
InvSafety ==
    totalDispensed = InitUnits - availableUnits

\* (Optional type invariant – not used for model checking the safety property)
TypeOK ==
    /\ availableUnits \in Nat
    /\ pending \in [Dispenser -> BOOLEAN]
    /\ readVal \in [Dispenser -> Nat]
    /\ totalDispensed \in Nat

====
cfg_text:
INIT Init
NEXT Next
CONSTANT InitUnits = 3
INVARIANT InvSafety

The system consists of three kinds of participants: a set of storage units that hold numbered blood slots, client processes (such as a hospital’s request service or a mobile collection team) that ask to reserve a slot, and a privileged admin who can intervene. Each storage unit maintains two pieces of state: the current epoch number of the configuration and a map that records which slot, if any, is currently allocated to which client. When a client wishes to reserve a slot it proposes the request together with the epoch it believes is current; the storage unit checks that the epoch matches its own, and if the slot is free it records the allocation and returns an acknowledgment. A reconfiguration event increments the epoch number and resets the allocation map, allowing the system to roll out a new inventory layout without losing consistency. If the admin issues an override command, the admin flag is set, the epoch is forcibly advanced, and the admin may directly assign or free a slot regardless of the normal checks. Normal clients are blocked from making changes while the admin flag is set, ensuring the admin’s actions are applied atomically before regular activity resumes.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No blood slot is ever allocated to more than one client at the same time.

The conveyor line has three active participants: an entry sensor that detects a car arriving at the start, a wash‑station controller that moves the car through the brushes, and an exit gate that releases the car after washing. All three share a single compare‑and‑swap register that stores a “slot token’’ indicating whether the wash slot is free or occupied. When the entry sensor sees a car, it reads the current value of the register and attempts a compare‑and‑swap that changes the token from free to occupied; if the swap succeeds the sensor signals the controller to start moving the car onto the belt. The controller, after finishing the wash cycle, performs another compare‑and‑swap that changes the token from occupied back to free and then notifies the exit gate to open. Because messages (sensor‑to‑controller, controller‑to‑gate) can arrive out of order, each participant always checks the register’s current value before acting, so a stale “start” message will be ignored if the token is already occupied. The compare‑and‑swap operation itself is atomic, guaranteeing that at most one participant can claim the slot at any moment regardless of message reordering. When the exit gate receives a free‑token notification, it only opens if it sees that the token is indeed free, preventing a car from leaving before the wash is complete. Thus the whole line progresses safely even though network delays may shuffle the ordering of the messages.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: A car can be released by the exit gate at most once for each wash cycle.
spec_text:
---- MODULE W4C4x7x5x1 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, Sequences, TLC

(* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
   Constants
   ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
TokenSet == {"Free", "Occupied"}
MsgSet   == {"Start", "Free"}

(* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
   Variables
   ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
VARIABLES token, msgs, opened

(* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
   Type invariant (helpful for debugging, not part of the safety property)
   ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
TypeOK ==
    /\ token \in TokenSet
    /\ msgs \subseteq MsgSet
    /\ opened \in BOOLEAN

(* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
   Initial state
   ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
Init ==
    /\ token = "Free"
    /\ msgs = {}
    /\ opened = FALSE

(* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
   Actions
   ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)

(* Sensor reads the register and successfully swaps Free → Occupied *)
SensorCAS_Success ==
    /\ token = "Free"
    /\ token' = "Occupied"
    /\ opened' = FALSE
    /\ msgs' = msgs \cup {"Start"}

(* Sensor attempts CAS but sees the slot already occupied – nothing happens *)
SensorCAS_Fail ==
    /\ token # "Free"
    /\ UNCHANGED << token, msgs, opened >>

(* Delivery of the start message to the controller; the controller may ignore it *)
DeliverStart ==
    /\ "Start" \in msgs
    /\ msgs' = msgs \ {"Start"}
    /\ UNCHANGED << token, opened >>

(* Controller finishes washing, swaps Occupied → Free and notifies the gate *)
ControllerFinish ==
    /\ token = "Occupied"
    /\ token' = "Free"
    /\ msgs' = msgs \cup {"Free"}
    /\ UNCHANGED opened

(* Delivery of a free‑token notification that the gate ignores (e.g., stale) *)
DeliverFreeNoOp ==
    /\ "Free" \in msgs
    /\ (token # "Free" \/ opened = TRUE)
    /\ msgs' = msgs \ {"Free"}
    /\ UNCHANGED << token, opened >>

(* Gate opens when it sees a free token and has not opened yet in the current cycle *)
GateOpen ==
    /\ "Free" \in msgs
    /\ token = "Free"
    /\ opened = FALSE
    /\ msgs' = msgs \ {"Free"}
    /\ opened' = TRUE
    /\ UNCHANGED token

(* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
   Next-state relation
   ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
Next ==
    \/ SensorCAS_Success
    \/ SensorCAS_Fail
    \/ DeliverStart
    \/ ControllerFinish
    \/ DeliverFreeNoOp
    \/ GateOpen

(* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
   Specification
   ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<token, msgs, opened>>

(* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
   Safety invariant: at most one release (gate opening) per wash cycle
   ---------------------------------------------------------------------- *)
NoDoubleRelease ==
    /\ (token = "Occupied") => (opened = FALSE)
    /\ (opened = TRUE)      => (token = "Free")

====
cfg_text:
SPECIFICATION Spec
INVARIANT NoDoubleRelease

nl:
The batch involves a SettlementCoordinator and two banks, BankA and BankB, each of which can propose a net transfer amount to be settled. All three share a single compare‑and‑swap register that holds a tuple (status, amount); status may be idle, proposed, or committed. When a bank wants to submit its amount, it reads the register; if the status is idle it attempts a compare‑and‑swap to change the tuple to (proposed, its amount). The coordinator periodically scans the register; when it sees status proposed it adds its verification and then performs a second compare‑and‑swap to change the tuple to (committed, totalAmount) where totalAmount is the sum of the two banks’ proposals. After the register shows committed, each bank debits or credits its ledger according to the totalAmount and then resets the register to idle for the next batch. If BankB crashes after writing a proposal but before the coordinator commits, the coordinator will eventually see the status still proposed and will treat the missing bank’s contribution as zero, then commit the batch. The compare‑and‑swap operations guarantee that at most one successful transition from proposed to committed can occur, even if a crash hides a participant’s state.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: For any settlement batch, the committed transfer of the total amount is applied to the banks’ ledgers at most once.

The protocol runs on a set of bank nodes that each can submit interbank settlement messages to a shared batch maintained by a Settlement Coordinator. Each node keeps a local copy of three pieces of state: whether it currently holds the lease for the batch, the time at which that lease expires, and the amount of batch capacity that remains for new settlements. The Coordinator stores the current batch capacity limit, which can be increased or decreased at runtime by a Capacity Manager, and the identifier of the node that holds the lease. When a node wants to add settlements it first requests the lease; if the Coordinator sees no active lease or a lease that has passed its expiry, it grants the lease to the requester together with the current capacity limit. While holding the lease the node may commit settlement entries whose total value does not exceed the remaining capacity, and it updates the remaining capacity accordingly before either renewing the lease or releasing it. If the capacity limit changes while a lease is active, the new limit is applied only after the lease expires, ensuring that all nodes see a consistent capacity while they hold the lease.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total value of settlements recorded in a batch never exceeds the batch capacity that is currently advertised.

The system consists of two runway‑allocation servers, one for domestic flights and one for international flights, that both draw from a single pool of time‑stamped runway slots. Each server keeps a local copy of the shared allocation record, which lists the next free slot and a version counter that identifies the latest update. When a server receives a request for a slot, it reads the current record, chooses the earliest free slot, increments the version counter, and attempts to write the new record back using a compare‑and‑swap operation on the shared register. The compare‑and‑swap succeeds only if the version counter in the register still matches the one the server read; otherwise the server discards its tentative allocation and retries from the updated record. Both servers repeat this loop until their allocation is committed, guaranteeing that at most one server can claim a particular slot at any moment. The shared register therefore serialises the two independent instances without any additional locking mechanism. Because each successful compare‑and‑swap overwrites the previous record atomically, the pool of runway slots remains consistent across both instances.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No runway‑slot allocation record can be overwritten without preserving the most recent assignment, preventing any lost updates to the shared schedule.
spec_text:
---- MODULE W4C1x7x1x2 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, Sequences

CONSTANT MaxSlot \* maximum slot index (bounds the state space)

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Variables
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
VARIABLES shared, lDom, lInt

\* Record containing the next free slot and a version counter
SharedRec == [slot |-> Nat, ver |-> Nat]

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Initial state
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Init ==
    /\ shared = [slot |-> 0, ver |-> 0]
    /\ lDom   = [slot |-> 0, ver |-> 0]
    /\ lInt   = [slot |-> 0, ver |-> 0]

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Helper: compute the next record that a server would try to commit
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
NextRec(rec) ==
    [slot |-> rec.slot + 1,
     ver  |-> rec.ver  + 1]

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Server actions
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Domestic server reads the shared record into its local copy
DomRead ==
    /\ UNCHANGED shared
    /\ lDom' = shared
    /\ lInt' = lInt

\* Domestic server attempts a compare‑and‑swap
DomCAS ==
    /\ IF shared.ver = lDom.ver
          THEN /\ shared' = NextRec(shared)
               /\ lDom'   = lDom   \* keep local copy (it will be refreshed on next read)
          ELSE /\ shared' = shared
               /\ lDom'   = lDom
    /\ lInt' = lInt
    /\ shared.slot < MaxSlot   \* stop allocating after MaxSlot‑1

\* International server reads the shared record
IntRead ==
    /\ UNCHANGED shared
    /\ lInt' = shared
    /\ lDom' = lDom

\* International server attempts a compare‑and‑swap
IntCAS ==
    /\ IF shared.ver = lInt.ver
          THEN /\ shared' = NextRec(shared)
               /\ lInt'   = lInt
          ELSE /\ shared' = shared
               /\ lInt'   = lInt
    /\ lDom' = lDom
    /\ shared.slot < MaxSlot

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Next‑state relation
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Next ==
    \/ DomRead
    \/ DomCAS
    \/ IntRead
    \/ IntCAS

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Safety invariant (the property to be model‑checked)
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* No runway‑slot allocation record can be overwritten without preserving
\* the most recent assignment.  This is captured by requiring that the
\* version counter and the slot index are always equal.  Because each
\* successful compare‑and‑swap increments both by exactly one, equality
\* guarantees that no update can lose the previous assignment.
NoLostUpdate ==
    shared.slot = shared.ver

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Specification
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<shared, lDom, lInt>>

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Theorems (optional, for readability)
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
THEOREM Spec => []NoLostUpdate

====
cfg_text:
INIT Init
NEXT Next
INVARIANT NoLostUpdate
CONSTANTS MaxSlot = 2

The system contains two signalling controllers, C₁ and C₂, each responsible for a distinct track segment but both drawing from the same pool of block‑allocation tokens. Each controller maintains a local flag `want` indicating whether it is trying to claim the next block, and a shared compare‑and‑swap register `Token` that either holds the identifier of the controller currently owning a token or is empty. When a controller needs the next block, it sets its `want` flag true and atomically executes a compare‑and‑swap on `Token`, swapping an empty value for its own identifier only if the register is still empty. If the swap succeeds, the controller treats the token as granted and proceeds to reserve the block; if it fails, it repeatedly retries after a short back‑off while keeping its `want` flag set. When the controller releases the block, it clears its `want` flag and performs a compare‑and‑swap that replaces its identifier in `Token` with the empty value, making the token available to the other instance. Because both controllers use the same register, only one can succeed in the compare‑and‑swap at a time, ensuring that the single token is never duplicated. The protocol therefore requires only two state variables per controller (`want`) and one shared variable (`Token`).  

SAFETY PROPERTY: At no time can both controllers hold a block‑allocation token for the same track segment simultaneously.

nl:
The fleet consists of autonomous robots that need to reserve a storage slot before moving goods, and a lightweight central controller that hosts a single compare‑and‑swap register for each slot. Each robot keeps two pieces of state: the identifier of the slot it is trying to reserve and a flag indicating whether it has successfully claimed that slot. When a robot wants a slot, it reads the slot’s register; if the register currently holds the value “free”, the robot attempts a compare‑and‑swap changing the value from “free” to its own robot identifier. If the compare‑and‑swap succeeds, the robot marks its flag as claimed and proceeds to the slot; if it fails because another robot has already written its identifier, the robot picks a different slot and repeats the process. Because a robot may be arbitrarily slow after a successful claim, the compare‑and‑swap still prevents any other robot from writing the same identifier to that register, allowing other robots to allocate different slots without waiting for the slow robot to finish its movement. The central controller never removes a robot’s identifier from a slot register until the robot explicitly releases the slot after completing its task.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two robots can ever be assigned the same storage slot at the same time.
spec_text:
---- MODULE W4C2x7x3x3 ----
EXTENDS FiniteSets

CONSTANTS Robots, Slots

(*--- Constants for special values ---*)
Free == "free"
Null == "none"

VARIABLES reg, claimed, desiredSlot

(*--- Initialization ---*)
Init ==
  /\ reg = [s \in Slots |-> Free]
  /\ claimed = [r \in Robots |-> FALSE]
  /\ desiredSlot = [r \in Robots |-> Null]

(*--- Robot tries to reserve a free slot ---*)
TryReserve(r) ==
  \E s \in Slots :
    /\ reg[s] = Free
    /\ reg' = [reg EXCEPT ![s] = r]
    /\ claimed' = [claimed EXCEPT ![r] = TRUE]
    /\ desiredSlot' = [desiredSlot EXCEPT ![r] = s]

(*--- Robot releases a slot it has claimed ---*)
Release(r) ==
  /\ claimed[r] = TRUE
  /\ LET s == desiredSlot[r] IN
       /\ reg' = [reg EXCEPT ![s] = Free]
       /\ claimed' = [claimed EXCEPT ![r] = FALSE]
       /\ desiredSlot' = [desiredSlot EXCEPT ![r] = Null]

(*--- Next-state relation ---*)
Next ==
  \E r \in Robots :
       TryReserve(r) \/ Release(r)

(*--- Temporal specification ---*)
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<reg, claimed, desiredSlot>>

(*--- Safety invariant: no two robots claim the same slot at the same time ---*)
NoConflictingClaims ==
  \A r1, r2 \in Robots :
    (r1 # r2) => ~(claimed[r1] /\ claimed[r2] /\ desiredSlot[r1] = desiredSlot[r2])

=============================================================================

nl:
The system consists of a fixed set of tower controllers, each responsible for a single runway and identified as Tower‑1, Tower‑2, … Tower‑N, arranged in a logical token ring. Each tower keeps two Boolean flags: hasToken, indicating whether it currently holds the ring token, and hasRequest, indicating whether an aircraft at that tower is waiting for runway clearance. When an aircraft arrives, the tower sets hasRequest to true and, if it already holds the token, immediately sends a “clear‑runway” command to the aircraft and then clears hasRequest. If the tower does not hold the token, it simply waits; when the token arrives, the tower checks hasRequest, grants clearance if needed, and then passes the token to the next tower in the ring. Token passing is done by sending a small token message to the next tower; the sending tower resets its hasToken flag only after receiving an acknowledgment that the neighbor has stored the token. If a tower crashes silently, the token will not be forwarded; the preceding tower detects the missing acknowledgment after a timeout and re‑issues the token directly to the following live tower, thereby bypassing the crashed participant. All live towers continue to follow the same request‑grant‑pass cycle, ensuring that at most one runway is allocated at any moment.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No aircraft ever receives a clearance from a tower that does not currently hold the token, preventing unauthorized or stale runway usage.

The system consists of three blood‑bank sites—North, Central, and South—connected in a logical ring.  
Each site keeps a local variable “stock” that records the number of units of a particular blood type it currently holds, and a Boolean “hasToken” indicating whether it may modify the stock.  
When a site receives the token, it may either add newly collected units to its stock or ship out units to satisfy a pending request, updating “stock” accordingly, then forwards the token to the next site in the ring.  
To request a transfer, a site sends a “transfer” message to the holder of the token; because messages may arrive out of order, the token holder buffers all incoming requests until it has the token and processes them in the order they were received.  
After processing the buffered requests, the token holder includes an acknowledgment list in the token as it circulates, so that sites can discard stale requests that arrived after a newer one.  
If a site loses the token due to a network glitch, the ring initiates a simple timeout‑based recovery where the next site regenerates the token, guaranteeing that exactly one token exists at any time.  
No site ever updates its stock without holding the token, ensuring that the total number of units across all sites never exceeds the predefined storage capacity.  

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total number of blood units stored across North, Central, and South never exceeds the overall capacity limit of the bank.

The yard contains several gantry cranes, each identified by a unique crane‑id, and a single high‑value container that must be moved from the ship to a storage stack. Each crane stores locally a flag called `busy` indicating whether it currently believes it owns the container, and the yard maintains a single compare‑and‑swap (CAS) register whose value is either “free” or the id of the crane that most recently succeeded in claiming the container. When a crane wants to lift the container it reads the CAS register; if the value is “free” it attempts a CAS operation that changes the register from “free” to its own id, and only if the CAS succeeds does it set its local `busy` flag to true and begin the lift. After the lift is finished the crane writes “free” back to the CAS register and clears its `busy` flag, making the container available again. If a crane reads the register and sees another id, it simply waits and retries later, which tolerates a slow crane because the register is never cleared by a failed or delayed participant. The protocol therefore requires only the CAS register and each crane’s `busy` flag, giving a model with two state variables per crane and one shared variable.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No two cranes can be busy with the same container at the same time.
spec_text:
---- MODULE W4C7x7x0x3 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets, Sequences

\* ---------- Constants ----------
CONSTANT NumCrane               \* number of cranes in the yard
ASSUME NumCrane \in Nat \ {0}

Cranes == 1 .. NumCrane          \* the set of crane identifiers
Free   == 0                     \* special value meaning “container is free”

\* ---------- Variables ----------
VARIABLES cas, busy              \* cas register and per‑crane busy flags

\* ---------- Initial state ----------
Init ==
    /\ cas = Free
    /\ busy = [c \in Cranes |-> FALSE]

\* ---------- Actions ----------
Claim(c) ==
    /\ c \in Cranes
    /\ cas = Free
    /\ ~busy[c]                     \* the crane does not already think it owns the container
    /\ cas' = c
    /\ busy' = [busy EXCEPT ![c] = TRUE]

Release(c) ==
    /\ c \in Cranes
    /\ busy[c]                      \* the crane believes it owns the container
    /\ cas = c
    /\ cas' = Free
    /\ busy' = [busy EXCEPT ![c] = FALSE]

Wait(c) ==
    /\ c \in Cranes
    /\ cas # Free
    /\ ~busy[c]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<cas, busy>>

Next ==
    \/ \E c \in Cranes: Claim(c)
    \/ \E c \in Cranes: Release(c)
    \/ \E c \in Cranes: Wait(c)

\* ---------- Specification ----------
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<cas, busy>>

\* ---------- Safety property ----------
BusySet == {c \in Cranes : busy[c]}

NoTwoBusy == Cardinality(BusySet) <= 1
\* (equivalently: \A c1, c2 \in Cranes : (busy[c1] /\ busy[c2]) => c1 = c2)

====
cfg_text:
CONSTANTS NumCrane = 3
SPECIFICATION Spec
INVARIANT NoTwoBusy

nl:
The system consists of a Lobby Server, a set of Player Clients, and a Matchmaker Coordinator that together maintain three pieces of state: the current epoch number, the list of players currently in the lobby, and the pending match configuration for the next game. When a player joins, the client sends a Join request to the Lobby Server, which increments the epoch, records the new player in the lobby list, and broadcasts the updated epoch and list to all participants. Any participant that receives an epoch‑greater message adopts the new epoch, replaces its local lobby list with the broadcast list, and discards any older pending match configuration. The Matchmaker Coordinator initiates a reconfiguration by proposing a match assignment together with the current epoch; all clients acknowledge the proposal only if they are already at that epoch, otherwise they request the latest state. If a player crashes silently, its absence is detected when the next epoch‑based broadcast fails to include it, causing the server to advance the epoch and remove the missing player from the lobby list. All participants use the epoch number as a version stamp so that stale updates are ignored and the lobby state converges despite the crash. The protocol therefore guarantees that every change to the lobby list or match assignment is applied exactly once and is never overwritten by an out‑of‑date message.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No update to the lobby’s player list or match assignment can be lost or overwritten by a later message that carries an earlier epoch number.
